title: YOZZ: Zero-knowledge webmail
pitch: 🗿 Browser decrypt; server no key. WebMCP only way for 🤖. Server MCP cannot 🙅‍♀️.
about_excerpt: 🗿 Browser decrypt; server no key. WebMCP only way for 🤖. Server MCP cannot 🙅‍♀️. Like 1 Comment Story Updates YOZZ's three-pane inbox with multiple email addresses and a message open Inspiration YOZZ started with a personal problem. For years, I relied on Gmail’s “Send as” feature to send emails from my custom domains. When Google announced it was discontinuing the feature , I went looking for an alternative. After days of searching, I was unable to find anything that satisfied the privacy, aesthetics, and convenience that I was after. That is why I built YOZZ: a zero-knowledge, modern-looking webmail client that is private by design, clean to use, and accessible anywhere in the browser. Zero-knowledge password managers were the main inspiration for YOZZ: secrets are decrypted on the user’s device while the servers only handle data it cannot understand. What if I apply the same idea to webmail? Modern email interfaces and zero-knowledge cryptography were well-established and easy to learn from existing solutions. The real challenge lay in the networking: client-side JavaScript cannot open raw TCP sockets, so a direct connection to mail servers via IMAP/SMTP is impossible. Moving the connection to a backend server would defeat the whole zero-knowledge premise. The entire feasibility of YOZZ came down to whether I could solve that one fundamental constraint. Having previously built a zero-dependency ACME client in TypeScript, I knew low-level cryptographic handshakes were viable in pure JS. The missing link was the transport layer. The breakthrough was a Cloudflare Worker acting as a relay: tunneling WebSocket traffic from the browser into raw TCP connections to the mail servers, while ensuring TLS terminated exclusively between the JS in the browser and the mail servers. The worker sees only encrypted bytes. Once that proof-of-concept held up, I knew the architecture was sound. YOZZ has since become the daily driver for all my custom-domain email. The biggest capability YOZZ lacked was AI assistance. Moving my daily email workflow from Gmail to YOZZ made that clear: I had grown used to Gemini inside Gmail and to ChatGPT’s Gmail connector for more complex tasks spanning my other connected services. I first considered connecting YOZZ to ChatGPT through a conventional connector or server-side MCP. But YOZZ’s service has no readable access to mailbox credentials or mail, and giving it that access would break the product’s zero-knowledge premise. I also tested local models through Transformers.js, but the models I tried were either not reliable enough for work as sensitive as email or too slow and resource-hungry on my hardware. When this challenge introduced me to WebMCP, I realised that a capable external agent could instead work through the user’s active YOZZ client. What it does YOZZ is a zero-knowledge webmail client for supported IMAP and SMTP accounts you already own. Its server-side infrastructure receives no plaintext mailbox credentials or messages. Received mail remains with the existing provider and is cached only on the user’s device. Credentials, drafts and any sent-mail copies stored on the server are encrypted by the web app before reaching D1. YOZZ’s web app and the mail provider are the TLS endpoints. Since browser APIs cannot open the required TCP connections to mail servers, the relay simply forwards the ciphertext between them. It never receives the TLS session keys, mailbox passwords or plaintext messages, so YOZZ’s server-side infrastructure cannot decrypt the traffic it carries. This boundary is deliberately narrow. The existing mail provider retains its access, and an external agent can read mail returned through WebMCP. The user chooses which agent receives that mail; YOZZ’s servers gain no readable access in either case. YOZZ does retain limited operational metadata. “Zero-knowledge” here applies to stored vault contents and traffic crossing the relay. It does not make email end-to-end encrypted or protect against malicious client code delivered to the browser. After the user logs in, YOZZ registers six focused WebMCP tools: get_addresses : list the configured addresses. get_threads : search and read conversations without marking them as read. update_threads : mark conversations read or unread, star them, archive them or move them to Trash. save_draft : create a message, prepare a reply or update an existing draft. delete_draft : discard a draft, recoverable for 30 days. navigate : open a conversation or draft in the interface. Opening an unread conversation marks it read, just like the user’s own click. navigate is the only tool that changes what the user is currently looking at. The other tools work in the background without taking the user away from their current task. Before WebMCP, every multi-message task had to be completed manually inside YOZZ. Now the user and agent can divide the work: the agent can summarise unread mail across every configured address, find messages about a trip or purchase, clean up selected low-value threads and prepare a reply. The resulting draft can be opened inside YOZZ for review, but no WebMCP tool can send mail . Sending is a separate action in YOZZ's visible composer. A browser-capable agent may offer to perform that action, but only after surfacing the draft and requesting the user's confirmation. Why WebMCP belongs here For these workflows, a conventional server-side MCP integration would require moving readable mailbox access from the web app into server-side infrastructure, breaking YOZZ’s zero-knowledge premise. It would need mailbox credentials, an equivalent authorisation token or a server-terminated mail session. Any of those would give YOZZ’s infrastructure readable mailbox access it deliberately does not have. WebMCP instead uses the capabilities already present in the user’s logged-in web app, allowing an agent chosen by the user to work with mail without giving YOZZ’s servers new access. The immediate audience is people who already use custom-domain email or other IMAP and SMTP accounts and want webmail without entrusting another client operator with their credentials. YOZZ supports multiple inbound and send-only addresses, and Google’s upcoming change gives some of these users a concrete reason to seek another client. How I built it YOZZ is a deployed TypeScript application whose server-side infrastructure runs on Cloudflare Workers. Its web app implements TLS 1.3, X.509 certificate validation, IMAP, SMTP and MIME message handling. The API Worker handles three things: User authentication. Storing and updating ciphertext vault records in D1, including records for mailbox credentials, drafts and sent-mail copies. All are encrypted by the web app before reaching the Worker. The WebSocket-to-TCP relay. I initially considered making YOZZ accountless, with users connecting their IMAP and SMTP accounts directly in the web app. That would work on one device, but I wanted to access the same mailbox configuration across multiple devices. I therefore introduced authentication and an encrypted vault. The user’s password or a PRF-capable passkey provides the client-side material needed to unlock the vault. YOZZ’s server stores the wrapped data-encryption key and ciphertext vault records alongside the authentication and operational metadata described above. This provides multi-device access without giving the server the key needed to decrypt mailbox credentials, drafts or settings. The WebMCP tools call the same application services as the user interface. Tool actions immediately appear in the product and follow the same state rules as user actions. I started working on YOZZ on August 16, 2026. The challenge began on August 25, and the first WebMCP implementation was committed on August 26. Before the challenge, YOZZ was already a deployed mail client but had no agent tools. During the challenge, I added the six-tool WebMCP layer, defined the WebMCP no-send and untrusted-content boundaries, added behavioural tests and built the judge infrastructure. The existing TLS, X.509, IMAP, SMTP and MIME implementation is the foundation this extension works through, not challenge-period work. YOZZ lives alongside dozens of other projects in my private monorepo. That private repository contains YOZZ’s original development history and is the source of the dates above. Open-sourcing YOZZ was always part of the plan so others could inspect its implementation and evaluate its zero-knowledge claims. To do so without exposing unrelated private code, I built and published OpenRepo , a tool for cleanly exporting individual projects from a monorepo. I used OpenRepo to publish the standalone YOZZ repository . video_title: YOZZ: zero-knowledge webmail your AI agent can use (WebMCP demo)
video_transcript_excerpt: Hello, I'm Jason. I built a zero-knowledge webmail client called Yoz. Zero-knowledge roughly means the servers can't see your stuff. So, how is Yoz zero-knowledge? When you save sensitive data, your browser encrypts it right there on your machine before sending it off. Yoz's servers only ever store and return scrambled unreadable ciphertext. We don't hold the key and we can't see what's inside. For example, this API response contains my saved mail account, but the actual details are returned as ciphertext. Only the unlocked web app can turn that ciphertext back into something meaningful, in this case, the email address you see here. Mail traffic follows the same principle. The TLS connection runs between the Yoz web app in your browser and the mail server you use. Yoz's relay only transports encrypted traffic. The session keys exist at those two endpoints, so the relay cannot decrypt what passes through it. In short, Yoz's servers are blind. We cannot read your mail. So, how can Yoz connect with AI agents? A traditional server-side MCP is impossible because Yoz's servers are blind, cannot read mail. So, we need something that works purely on the client side that also connects to AI. Wait a second. Isn't this exactly what web MCP's for? Let's see this in action now. Here, I have Yoz open in ChatGPT desktop. Yoz registers six web MCP tools directly with the page. I give ChatGPT a simple request to summarize the inbox. ChatGPT gives me a clear summary of the mailbox. Notice how it also flags the suspicious confirm your mailbox email. Yoz marks tools that return mail as carrying untrusted content. This tells the agent to treat what it reads with caution. By design, every tool except one works in the background. So, you can use Yoz while the agent is working. The one exception is the navigate tool, which is used when the agent needs to show you something for review. Let's ask ChatGPT to reply to Sam about the lunch. It saves the reply as a draft, then uses the navigate tool to open the draft editor in Yoz. Now, I can review the message and press send myself. Together, these tools let your agents read, organize, and draft mail through the unlocked web app without giving Yoz's servers any new access. That is how Yoz brings capable AI to your mailbox without giving up its zero knowledge design.

title: Yolo Learn
pitch: Yolo Learn turns a website's form into a tool an agent can reuse, repairs the saved steps when the page changes, and asks for approval before the final action.
about_excerpt: Yolo Learn turns a website's form into a tool an agent can reuse, repairs the saved steps when the page changes, and asks for approval before the final action. Like Comment Story Updates Hero Heal Four Changes Page Changed Read Once Cache Hit Registered Tools Audit Page YOLO Learn YOLO Learn turns web forms into reusable tools an AI agent can call through WebMCP. It remembers the task, detects changes, and asks a person when a repair needs information the page cannot provide. I built it around a simple question: why should an agent have to work out the same form every time someone needs to use it? Why is this use case a strong fit for WebMCP? WebMCP gives an agent a named tool with defined inputs and an action it can run. YOLO Learn uses this to turn a learned form into a tool while the agent is already using the app. In the demo, the agent reads a clinic booking form. YOLO Learn creates clinic_booking , with inputs based on the form’s fields and available choices. The agent discovers the new tool and calls it without a page reload. WebMCP is the connection between learning the form and actually using it. The saved flow is not just a description for the agent to read; it becomes something the agent can call. How does it create a better user experience? The agent can reuse a saved flow instead of starting over. The person can review the filled-in details before approving submission. When the clinic is redesigned, YOLO Learn compares the saved flow with the current version. The demo contains four changes: a renamed field, a reordered step, different button wording, and a new required insurance field. Three can be repaired automatically. The insurance field needs an answer from the person. YOLO Learn also remembers the structure of public pages. In the recording, recalling the saved W3C survey fetches zero bytes from the source page. This is a cached result, not a freshness check; a refresh is needed to look for changes. An audit view checks accessibility, task completion, and readability. Each finding explains what triggered it, and accessibility checks are distinguished from design preferences. What can people and agents do together that was difficult before? A person can teach a supported flow by demonstrating it, or ask the agent to learn the form. The agent can then use the resulting tool for later runs. They also share the repair process. The app handles changes it can understand from the page, while the person supplies missing information. A new required field becomes a specific question instead of a guessed answer. The approval step keeps the final decision with the person. The agent prepares the action; the person reviews and approves it. How did you implement WebMCP? I built YOLO Learn with React, TypeScript, and Vite, and deployed it on Vercel. The WebMCP integration registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a name, description, input schema, and execution handler. Learned flows become additional tools at runtime, with their inputs derived from the form. Tools such as learn_site , check_flow_health , and heal_flow connect the agent to the learning and repair logic. The flow runner fills the supported form and pauses at the approval gate. Saved flows are stored in the browser, and active run state is kept per tab. Public pages are fetched through server-side endpoints using read-only requests. Remembered-page tools return stored structure by default and fetch again only when explicitly refreshed. The learning and repair logic is rule-based. It does not call a language model internally; the connected AI agent chooses and calls the exposed tools. Why this stack I needed a real website an agent can open, not a plugin. Vite, React, and TypeScript let the page register tools while you are still on it, including a tool that did not exist when the tab loaded. That is what WebMCP is for, so the app had to be a page, not a backend that mints tools somewhere else. Vercel is the host because judges get a public URL, and I can send the Origin-Agent-Cluster header WebMCP requires. Without that header, Chrome refuses registerTool and the whole demo is dead. Fetching other people’s sites has to happen on the server. A browser cannot read another origin. Those functions only GET. They never POST as you, and they refuse private addresses. If a page has no form until JavaScript runs, a headless Chrome pass is there as a fallback — still read-only. There is no model in the product. Drift and heal are ordinary code, so the same redesign heals the same way every time. Saved flows and remembered page structures stay in browser storage. When configured, the backend also stores shared audit summaries. No account. One real use case Someone books the same clinic, or files the same public form, every few weeks. Today an agent re-reads the whole page every visit, then silently fails when the site is redesigned. With this: open the clinic (or paste a public URL). The page learns the task once and registers a WebMCP tool mid-session. Next visit is a lookup — on the W3C survey in the demo, first read was about 46 KB, second read was 0 bytes. When the clinic ships v2, it does not throw the tool away. Four things changed; three it fixes from the page; it asks once for the new insurance field, then runs again. You still approve the submit. That is a person and an agent sharing one live page, with a tool the site author never wrote. Challenges, and what I did ChatGPT could see the tools and still could not call them. Every tools.call crashed on signal.aborted. Our tests followed the spec, so they all passed. ChatGPT’s bridge does not send a signal. I wrap every tool at registration so a missing signal is safe, and I added tests that call tools the way ChatGPT actually does. registerTool threw in production. WebMCP needs the page to be origin-keyed. I ship Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1. The green banner is how you know that worked. Local fetch returned the React app instead of JSON. Vite was falling through /api/fetch-page to index.html, which looks like a parse error. I wired the fetch route in dev the same way as Vercel. A public URL fetch can be turned into an attack on localhost. Every hop is checked. Fourteen SSRF cases are blocked, including cloud metadata. A snapshot from a signed-in tab could keep passwords and hidden tokens. The sanitizer now strips values, hidden fields, and textarea bodies and keeps only the shape of the form. A minted tool only works on the same origin. That is why the demo clinic lives on this site. A pasted URL is remembered read-only; We do not submit on someone else’s checkout. Current limits The clinic is fictional, and no real appointment is booked. The working booking and repair demonstration runs within the app’s own origin. Learning a public URL does not give YOLO Learn permission or access to submit forms on that website. Those tools are read-only. Audit findings are a starting point for review, not a guarantee of accessibility compliance. High-level system design YOLO Learn has three main parts: the browser app, the WebMCP connection used by the agent, and server-side services for reading public pages. title: Heap-4
pitch: Heap 4: Agents recover unfinished workflows, one verified step at a time.
about_excerpt: Heap 4: Agents recover unfinished workflows, one verified step at a time. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Something I dread, as a solo founder, is the potentially overwhelming amount of comments or fixes that need to happen within a short period of time for user retention and enjoyability in an app. I initially wanted something that would scrape the web or bug that user submitted, then fixed them for me. However, this is very security-vulnerable and not good practice. I did see a future product in this though, so I determined the next steps would be to create a minimal yet compliant demo that did some variation of this. That variation landed to be: a user does something, something else goes wrong --> how do we still get it to work? Well, the intention was still there (evidence, what went wrong, why--like an obvious invoice needing to be sent). Heap 4 was inspired by that gap: applications preserve errors, but often lose the user’s intention, partial progress, and safe next steps. *Quick side note on the name: I typically utilize random DSA terms with a number because it sounds cool on miscellaneous projects. AI did not come up with this name (however apparent it may or may not be). The core idea is: Developers define what is legal. The agent discovers what will work. Heap 4 verifies every step. --> define a set of parameters, let the agent do the rest so you don't over-engineer the app with a load of try/catch or if/else statements. What Heap 4 Does Heap 4 is a runtime for unfinished workflows. It captures: The user’s desired outcome What has already succeeded The failed route and runtime evidence Available capabilities Policies and constraints Invariants that must never be violated An agent can then inspect the situation, choose and sequence available actions, observe failures, and replan. The agent does not receive unrestricted access or authority to mutate arbitrary state. Every action is verified by deterministic application code. The Demo The concrete example is invoice delivery. The user wants Acme Corporation to read invoice INV-2841 for $4,850. The invoice is successfully persisted, but the email provider fails with an HTTP 500. Retrying the whole operation could create a duplicate invoice, so Heap 4 preserves the existing invoice and marks the workflow as interrupted. The agent then: Inspects the interruption, customer policy, and available contacts. Attempts Acme’s preferred procurement portal. Observes that the portal is unavailable. Selects Dana Lee, the designated acting AP approver, rather than an archival mailbox. Requests approval for a temporary one-hour, read-only access grant. Creates the scoped grant. Discovers that creating authority alone does not deliver it. Sends a policy-compliant notice without attaching the invoice. Continues monitoring the original email route while Acme remains unblocked. Resumes the existing invoice after a human approves the bounded repair. Revokes the temporary share link. Verifies that the invoice was sent, no duplicate was created, and temporary access has stopped. The application does not contain a single recover_invoice button or a hardcoded “if portal fails, send a link” branch. It exposes smaller primitives whose availability changes with server-authoritative state. How I Built It Heap 4 is built with TypeScript, React, Vite, and native WebMCP. Moreover, help with agents (Codex, GitHub Copilot), although strictly code-only, nothing with idea development. The system is split into three responsibilities: The agent interprets evidence, chooses parameters, sequences primitives, and replans. Heap 4’s runtime preserves intent, exposes state-gated capabilities, and coordinates recovery. The server enforces policy, authorization, state transitions, and invariants. The invoice workflow uses a server-authoritative state machine: active → blocked → mitigated → resumable → completed The alternate route is deliberately staged. Creating a share grant does not satisfy the outcome. A separate send_access_notice capability must verify the recipient, message, attachment choice, and current customer policy before delivery is recorded. The share link is implemented as a real capability: Scoped to one invoice Limited to read_invoice_only Expiring Revocable Stored server-side only as a SHA-256 digest Returned as plaintext only once Tracked with a server-stamped first-access timestamp The repair path is separately bounded. A repair worker reproduces the failure, validates a narrow candidate change, and prepares it for review. Deployment requires explicit human approval. Once deployed, the agent can resume only the unfinished delivery step. The application runs locally through Express and is also deployed as a Cloudflare Worker with D1-backed session state. Native WebMCP registration is used where supported. For browser-agent hosts that can inspect the page but cannot invoke native WebMCP tools, the application provides clearly labeled, parameterized compatibility controls that call the same server-verified transitions. What I Learned I was able to answer a tough question: when does something go form: "a human could engineer this"; "an architecture's best practices should contain fallbacks"; and whatnot. It led me to: a route selector is not enough to demonstrate useful agency. A workflow becomes meaningfully agent-native when the agent must compose multiple independently verified operations whose sequence depends on policy and runtime evidence. Challenges As stated before, I struggled a lot. Not with "what do I want this to be", but rather: "where does agency really belong in a website/workflow?" I had to really separate authority from agency. It was obvious that an agent cannot be responsible for actions, nor should it. However, what use does it bring if it cannot do what's convenient nor has the authority to do so? The second issue I had to tackle was the limitation of the nature of WebMCP: "what can an agent do for me that might be something I don't want to do for myself?" I'm under the impression that an agent with WebMCP strictly does the things you can but with slightly more knowledge and efficiency. Both of the issues were resolved with agency belongs in orchestration; authority belongs in deterministic application code. The agent is allowed to inspect evidence, choose parameters, compose legal primitives, react to failures, and replan. Heap 4 remains responsible for authorization, policy enforcement, state transitions, invariants, and human approval for deployment. The agent can propose and initiate actions, but it cannot directly mutate arbitrary state or make an unsafe action legal. The second question was harder because, for one workflow, a human can often do the same things. A human can select a contact, choose a duration, click a button, and revoke a link. WebMCP does not make the agent magically capable of actions a user could never perform. The value is continuity and coordination. In a normal system, someone would need to notice the failure, understand what already happened, interpret the customer’s policy, choose a valid recovery, monitor the repair, return later, resume only the unfinished step, revoke temporary access, and verify the final state. That is manageable once. It becomes expensive and unreliable across thousands of interrupted workflows. In this project, the agent handles that orchestration while Heap 4 keeps it bounded. It does not receive a single “fix everything” capability. It receives specific tools whose availability changes with the workflow state. It must inspect the situation, attempt the preferred route, react to the outage, request approval for a disclosure change, compose the grant and notice steps, and clean up afterward. <--The earlier defined 'parameters'. A final issue: browser support. The testing browser could report that native WebMCP was unavailable and could not invoke page-defined tools. I intentionally did not install a fake production polyfill. Instead, I added a transparent compatibility path and kept its controls parameterized, so the agent still has to choose the contact, duration, message, attachment handling, and sequence. title: Prompt My Game
pitch: Play a browser game, describe changes to your AI agent, remix and play.
about_excerpt: Play a browser game, describe changes to your AI agent, remix and play. Like Comment Story Updates Real demo: the assistant changes the character to Bobo, then I play the result. Built with KAPLAY; based on KAPLAYGROUND. Ivanna Butterfly Garden: a separately published result at ivanna-butterfly-garden.netlify.app, not a local saved-game sample. Inspiration Making a game is easier to understand when there is already something to play. I wanted a creator to start with a working browser game, describe one change to an AI assistant, and play the new version without first setting up a local development environment. What it does PromptMyGame is my WebMCP-enabled version of KAPLAYGROUND, an existing open-source browser game editor. The live interface still uses the KAPLAYGROUND name. A creator plays the current game, asks for a change in ordinary language, and keeps the editor open while a compatible assistant works. The AI agent can understand the open project, edit it, run it, and return useful checks. The creator remains the creative director and the play tester. The editor also works without an AI assistant. People can play, edit code manually, save projects in their browser, and export portable copies. The open-source foundation KAPLAY is the open-source two-dimensional JavaScript game engine underneath the project. It provides the building blocks for drawing, movement, collision, input, and sound. KAPLAYGROUND is the existing web-based editor for creating, editing, playing, and sharing KAPLAY projects. This entry builds on that editor; I did not create its original engine or editor foundation. KAPLAY grew from Kaboom.js , a JavaScript game engine originally developed by Replit. KAPLAY and KAPLAYGROUND are now maintained by the KAPLAY Team and community contributors. Built-in Crew assets are released under CC0. What I added for the challenge During the challenge period I connected KAPLAYGROUND to WebMCP and added the workflow around it. The editor can identify the exact game an assistant is working on, reject an edit made against an older version, apply related file changes together, and separate different kinds of evidence when it runs a game. What I learned The hard part was defining what a successful result means when a creator, an AI assistant, an editor, and a running game all share the same project. Credits Built with KAPLAY and based on KAPLAYGROUND , by the KAPLAY Team and contributors. KAPLAY grew from Kaboom.js , originally developed by Replit. Built-in Crew assets are CC0. Full license notices remain in the public repository . title: Prism
pitch: Tell Prism what a WebMCP is for, then test whether its tools actually deliver.
about_excerpt: Tell Prism what a WebMCP is for, then test whether its tools actually deliver. Like Comment Story Updates Prism turns a declared WebMCP purpose into an evidence-backed scorecard. Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Prism Inspiration WebMCP evaluation can become a checklist of surface-level signals: did the page register tools, do they have schemas, and can the browser call them? Those checks matter, but they do not answer the product question. A commerce tool set, an editor, and a project workspace need different capabilities and different human-approval boundaries. Prism starts with the job to be done. It evaluates whether a WebMCP implementation covers that journey, whether mutations affect the same state a person sees, and whether consequential decisions remain visible and human-controlled. What it does Prism combines a purpose-aware evaluation dashboard with an open-source, local-first browser companion. A person selects Commerce, Project Operations, Content Editor, or defines a Custom contract. That contract states the intent, expected capabilities, and the action that must remain human-approved. The browser companion then runs on the target page, discovers its live WebMCP tools, executes only selected checks, and records schemas, annotations, timing, and privacy-preserving before-and-after evidence. Prism maps that evidence to four dimensions: purpose coverage; contract quality; observable mutation proof; and runtime hygiene. Every score includes journey-level evidence and a repair that can be tested again. A weak cart mutation, for example, does not merely lose points: Prism explains that the runner could not verify the visible state change and recommends returning a state revision plus a read-back check. Prism is itself a WebMCP app. Its four page-side tools let an agent read the selected contract, switch profiles, run a deterministic evaluation, and read the same score and evidence shown to the person. How we built it The dashboard is React and TypeScript on Vinext, deployed through ChatGPT Sites. Its scoring engine consumes a versioned runner snapshot and keeps the report deterministic and interpretable. The Manifest V3 companion uses the active page's document.modelContext.getTools() and document.modelContext.executeTool() APIs. It runs in the target origin because a hosted iframe or HTTP request cannot truthfully inspect another page's WebMCP tools. It hashes visible before-and-after state, supports an explicit read-back check, and exports only evidence metadata—not page text or tool output. The dashboard registers get_evaluation_context , choose_evaluation_profile , run_sample_evaluation , and get_latest_evaluation with narrow object schemas, annotations, validation, and lifecycle cancellation. The mutation tools update the same React state rendered in the visible interface. Challenges we ran into The hardest design constraint was the browser execution boundary. Cross-origin discovery would have been convenient, but it would also have been misleading. Separating collection from evaluation made the architecture more honest and gave us a useful privacy boundary. Behavioral evidence also needed careful calibration. A DOM digest proves that something visible changed, but not that the semantic change was correct. Prism therefore distinguishes visible-state evidence from stronger tool read-back evidence and does not claim either one proves the target application's human-approval policy. Accomplishments that we're proud of Purpose-specific contracts prevent irrelevant tool count from dominating the score. Every deduction is tied to visible evidence and an actionable repair. The companion is local-first, minimal-permission, and requires a fresh confirmation for mutation checks. Prism's own WebMCP mutations and reads agree with its visible UI. The dashboard, companion, source, tests, and judge guide form one coherent open-source release. What we learned WebMCP quality is not just API design. It is the relationship among intent, page state, agent authority, and the evidence available to a person. The most useful evaluator is therefore not a universal pass/fail scanner; it is a repeatable contract between the product team and the experience they intend to ship. What's next Next, Prism can add reusable contract packs, richer assertions for semantic read-back, shareable evaluation histories, and CI adapters that compare a new snapshot with a reviewed baseline. The same model could support accessibility audits, agent regression testing, and organization-specific approval policies. pitch: Tailwind Canvas is a standalone, browser-based page builder for creating responsive pages with webmcp tools.

Tailwind Canvas is a standalone, browser-based page builder for creating responsive pages with webmcp tools.

 Inspiration 

 I'm a WordPress developer, and I've been building a plugin that brings AI directly into the WordPress editor. 

 The plugin already supports Codex chat inside WordPress and connections to external MCP servers . However, many WordPress users are beginners or non-technical users. Setting up an external MCP server can be confusing, and pairing or configuring an AI coding agent can create even more friction. 

 When I discovered WebMCP , I saw a much simpler approach: instead of asking users to configure integrations manually, they could simply open the editor inside the ChatGPT app and start working with AI immediately. 

 The idea is simple: open the editor, start chatting, and the AI just works. 

 What it does 

 Tailwind Editor with WebMCP is a simplified version of my custom WordPress editor. 

 It provides a visual editor powered by Tailwind CSS and exposes editor capabilities through WebMCP, allowing ChatGPT to interact directly with the page. 

 The AI can understand the available editor actions and use them to modify the website without requiring the user to manually configure an external MCP server. 

 The goal is to make AI-assisted website building accessible even to users who do not know what MCP is. 

 How we built it 

 The demo is based on a simplified version of the custom editor I have been developing for WordPress. 

 The editor uses Tailwind CSS for styling and WebMCP to expose its functionality to AI agents. 

 Instead of building a separate integration layer or requiring users to connect an MCP server, the editor exposes its available actions directly from the web application. 

 ChatGPT can then discover those capabilities and interact with the editor while the user continues working visually. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges with AI-powered editors is not necessarily the AI itself, but the integration experience . 

 Traditional MCP integrations often require users to configure servers, connections, permissions, or pairing steps. That may be acceptable for developers, but it can be difficult for typical WordPress users. 

 Another challenge is designing editor tools that are clear enough for an AI agent to understand while still keeping the editing experience simple for humans. 

 WebMCP helped demonstrate how much of that integration complexity can be moved away from the user. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I'm especially proud that the demo shows how an AI agent can interact with a web-based editor without requiring users to understand the infrastructure behind it. 

 The same type of workflow that would normally require configuring an MCP server can become much closer to: 

 Open the page → ask ChatGPT → see the page change. 

 It also gave me a way to experiment with bringing together three things I've been working with for some time: WordPress-style visual editing, Tailwind CSS, and AI agents. 

 What we learned 

 The biggest lesson was that AI integration is not only about giving the model more capabilities. The way users access those capabilities is equally important. 

 For technical users, setting up MCP manually may not be a major problem. For a large ecosystem like WordPress, however, reducing setup steps could make a significant difference. 

 WebMCP makes the web application itself part of the AI integration layer. This creates an interesting possibility where websites and web applications can describe what an AI is allowed to do without requiring users to configure separate infrastructure. 

 What's next for Tailwind Editor with WEBMCP 

 The current project is a simplified demonstration, but the larger goal is to bring the same WebMCP experience into my full WordPress editor. 

 I want to explore exposing more editing capabilities, such as creating and modifying sections, updating Tailwind classes, changing content, working with images, and managing complete page layouts. 

 Ultimately, I would like WordPress users to be able to open their editor inside an AI-enabled browser or ChatGPT app and simply describe what they want to build. 

 No MCP configuration. 

 No complicated pairing process. 

 Just open the editor and start building with AI .

title: SciStudio-web
pitch: Scientific data workbench with your AI partner.
about_excerpt: Scientific data workbench with your AI partner. Like 1 Comment Story Updates AI help you build and run data analysis workflows A workflow can pause in the middle for your decisions with interactive blocks! Just ask AI to make one! We have great and fun tutorials like a video game! Editing codes for blocks with your AI partner! Our branding Inspiration I built SciStudio because I wasn't satisfied with scientific agents like Rosalind or Claude Science. Scientists find them hard to use because they are AI-chat centered. But scientists want to see the data the whole way through — every intermediate step, all the way to the result. Sometimes interacting with data with a GUI is also important. And I throw away the analysis script every time a session ends, because I have no good way to reuse or automate it. As biological research moves toward multimodality, this shape makes cross-modal data analysis difficult. This made me want to build SciStudio: a standardized workflow system for multimodal data analysis that integrates the capabilities of AI agents. You, and your agent, work together. For AI integration, SciStudio's solution before this hackathon was a desktop application plus a PTY running the codex CLI. But for wet-lab scientists, CLI tools are quite off-putting — I watched them struggle with the various buttons on top, not knowing that it can only be operated with the keyboard, and so on. Another problem is that users (I wish I had...) tend to stick with what they know; therefore, an AI interaction system they're already familiar with would greatly increase the product's appeal. Apps like ChatGPT are the perfect choice. After seeing WebMCP, I realized that our current AI system and prompts could be easily migrated to WebMCP and would naturally gain the ability to integrate the various scientific tools that ChatGPT has. After I ran the protein design tool with my data analysis workflow together within the same session with AI, Bang! That is why I chose to join this hackathon. What it does SciStudio-web is an interactive workflow orchestration system for multimodal scientific data analysis. The unit of data processing here is the block; scientists can get hands-on and use building blocks to create workflows, make plots, and automate their data-analysis work. Combined with a powerful AI agent, they can build workflows, carry out the steps of data analysis, and work through an interactive data-analysis interface, turning it all into assets that individuals and labs can reuse. We hope SciStudio has the chance to become the running partner of AI agents. The scenario I hope to see is one where the user prompts, and ChatGPT, through WebMCP, works together with the user to process data — combining all the other powerful biology tools — and ultimately delivers data visualization, interactive analysis, and a personal/lab asset system. How we built it It's a long story, and I can't believe I could go this far. I'm good at coding in data science, but I actually know nothing about software engineering (I'm a biologist). I started with an idea and asked AI agents to build it directly, then realized it didn't work. I asked why, and the AI told me we needed an architecture. So I wrote the architecture file and let the AI build it, only to realize it still didn't work... This happened for several rounds until I had built a robust software-engineering system for AI coding: architecture, specs, implementation, testing, documentation maintenance, and CI/build QA tools to maintain code quality. Honestly... I learned a lot. Challenges we ran into Failed to deploy, lots of frontend troubles, submission documents (hate it!) Accomplishments that we're proud of The old SciStudio called ChatGPT agents by providing an MCP server and a PTY for CLI apps to run in. During the submission period, I migrated our MCP server system to WebMCP, enabling us to run SciStudio's agentic features directly inside ChatGPT. I also optimized the frontend for a better user experience in ChatGPT. Finally I explored and built some demo projects to show the power of SciStudio. This gives me the benefits of modern scientific agent harnesses and the integration of other agentic tools, plus our reproducible workflow runtime and data-interaction capabilities. SciStudio will surface the hardest question of working with AI: "What did the AI do to my data???" This change is groundbreaking to me, honestly. I struggled with the limited resources I could access as a solo developer. I thought SciStudio was limited because I lacked access to big-data resources and collaborations with other tools and apps. The WebMCP integration changed everything. (I'm also proud that my old SciStudio migrated pretty easily.) What we learned Finding people to use a product is more difficult than building it. What's next for SciStudio-web I don't know, let me get some users first... New & existing work SciStudio is a pre-existing open-source project (desktop app, workflow runtime, MCP server). Everything in this submission repo was built during the WebMCP Challenge submission period: the MCP→WebMCP bridge, the Docker/Cloudflare public deploy, the ChatGPT-facing frontend rework, and the demo case. The full scope is visible in this repo's git history (jiazhenz026/scistudio-web-demo), which starts at the time I joined the hackathon (Sept.3!! Almost missed it!!). title: MOHAE · Explore Korea
pitch: Explore unknown, get random but curated events. Talk and share context with agent. Plan own agents with all participants in travel.
about_excerpt: Explore unknown, get random but curated events. Talk and share context with agent. Plan own agents with all participants in travel. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Three travelers choose independently across Explore, the shared room, and the map. Four WebMCP tools registered on the live MOHAE page in Chrome’s Tool Inspector. The Agent searches MOHAE’s structured Korea place catalog through WebMCP. Inspiration Inspired by exploration vs exploitation in RL. Nowadays people are mostly locked in their everyday routine (exploitation). I wanted people to explore lot more to find possibilities beyond and what they really want to do. I'm the first user of this project mohae. This web gives me events, places, opportunities that I can try. With agent I can put in my context like where I live, current place, what I want right now like cafe or food or events. I can see and get inspiration from given cards and see them in map. Also you can get all random events for exploration. This can also help people who came to korea, and when evolved it will help me traveling other country. You can also put own agent's result in the web and see your result in our template and map. Finally you can share link and plan travel within all the participants in the travel. What it does MOHAE is a mobile-first Korea place discovery product. A traveler can swipe to save or pass places, inspect candidates on a Naver map, and ask a WebMCP Agent to search and render visible candidate scenes. For a shared trip, a host creates an expiring invite link. Travelers join from their own devices, make independent save/pass and map choices, tell their own Agent natural-language needs, and mark their selection complete. The host Agent then reads the accumulated evidence and proposes an approximate ordered plan. Demo flow Open MOHAE and explore Korea place cards by saving or passing. Inspect candidates on the map and save useful places. Create a shared trip and send the expiring invite link. Join from another device, make independent choices, and add a raw trip note through an Agent, such as ‘must-visit food’ or ‘less walking.’ Mark that traveler’s selection complete. Ask the host Agent to read the room context and present an ordered candidate scene. Switch to route mode to see the Agent-supplied order numbered with a guide line. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets an Agent read and change the currently visible shared product state while humans continue choosing in the UI. The browser page is not just a chat attachment: it exposes explicit tools for catalog search, scene rendering, preserving traveler language, and reading room evidence. Agent actions remain visible and inspectable in the same interface the group is using. MOHAE deploys four WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : search_mohae_places : read-only catalog search. present_exploration : renders ordered deck/map scenes and can publish them to the shared room. add_group_trip_note : preserves a joined traveler’s raw natural-language note. get_group_trip_context : reads travelers’ save/pass/map choices, notes, readiness, anchors, and candidates. Provenance and scope Agent-researched external candidates stay provenance-tagged and separate from catalog admission. Route mode displays the Agent-supplied order and a guide line; it does not claim route optimization or travel-time calculation. MOHAE does not provide booking, live queue data, or full realtime presence. How we built it The product uses vanilla JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. WebMCP tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool . Supabase Postgres stores shared-trip data behind protected RPCs and row-level security, with append-only room events. The app is deployed on Vercel and uses the Naver Maps JavaScript SDK. Challenges and lessons The central design challenge was making Agent side effects visible, scoped, and auditable while several people continue using ordinary UI controls. We learned that coordination works better when the product preserves behavioral evidence and each traveler’s original words instead of compressing everyone into a single averaged profile. title: Relay | AI-Adaptive Emergency Training
pitch: WebMCP turns your AI agent into a live drill director, adapting crises to your decisions to train judgment and coordination.
about_excerpt: WebMCP turns your AI agent into a live drill director, adapting crises to your decisions to train judgment and coordination. Like Comment Story Updates Home Simulation exercise begins; user decision During the drill, the Agent automatically generates events Developments in the situation Inspiration Recently, I have often come across reports of natural disasters and everyday accidents, which made me wonder whether AI could help reduce some of the risks associated with these situations. The goal is to give people the opportunity to practice and respond as correctly as possible before they ever face a real emergency. My long-term vision for Relay is to develop it into an accessible emergency simulation and training platform covering many different types of incidents. For this competition, I chose one of the most common scenarios—a building fire drill —to help both building management teams and the general public improve their emergency preparedness. I hope that practicing in advance can ultimately help people make safer decisions during real crises and improve their chances of survival and self-rescue. I chose a building fire because it is a scenario that most people can immediately understand, while also clearly demonstrating how important timely decision-making, clear communication, and coordination can be during an emergency. What Relay Does Relay is an adaptive emergency training prototype . During the exercise, the learner continuously makes decisions, while their own AI Agent participates in and directs the simulation through WebMCP . The system does not follow a fixed, pre-written sequence of questions. The AI Agent observes the learner’s actions, introduces rule-validated complications based on the current situation, plays different roles within the scenario, and records key evidence throughout the exercise for post-simulation review and assessment. How I Built It Relay’s interface was built with React and TypeScript , with Three.js used to create the interactive building environment. WebMCP allows the learner’s AI Agent to directly access a set of structured tools, including: Observing the current state of the exercise Introducing new complications Delivering messages from different scenario roles Recording assessment evidence The simulation combines pre-authored rules with adaptive AI direction . The code controls scenario state transitions and validates whether each tool call is allowed under the current conditions. The AI Agent then decides which eligible intervention is most appropriate for the situation. Role messages can only reference facts that have been authorized within the scenario, and assessments must be grounded in decisions the learner actually made. This architecture keeps the simulation flexible while maintaining a clear and traceable relationship between learner actions, scenario events, and final feedback. Challenges I Ran Into The first major challenge was controlling the scope of the project . At one point, I tried to create a more dramatic hostage-taking scenario , but this type of situation involves a large amount of specialized knowledge and highly complex operational procedures. It was difficult to build something that was both accessible and credible within the available time—and I spent a lot of time exploring that direction. Eventually, I returned to the building fire scenario and focused on creating a first version with a more complete structure and a clearer experience. Another technical challenge was keeping the AI Agent responsive throughout a continuous exercise. Initially, I had the browser wait indefinitely for a pending event request, but this exceeded the browser connection’s time limit. I later designed a renewable event-waiting mechanism . Each time the waiting connection is renewed, the system preserves the relevant event state, so learner actions and events that occur during reconnection are not lost. The visual design also went through many iterations. I experimented with more complex and visually dramatic 3D interfaces, but eventually realized that richer 3D visuals do not automatically make information easier to understand. What I Learned AI has been incredibly helpful throughout the development process. I also learned that the most important part of an emergency simulator goes far beyond dramatic visuals. Learners need to clearly understand: what role they are playing, what information they currently have, and how their decisions affect the overall situation. Meaningful AI integration requires AI to participate directly in the application’s workflow. In Relay, the AI Agent interacts with the application through explicit tools, permissions, and boundaries, while the learner always retains control over the final decisions. What’s Next If I have more time—or enough reason to continue developing the project—I would like to improve: The onboarding experience The interaction design for coordination tasks The presentation of information during exercises, including more detailed scenario feedback I would also like to gradually develop additional scenarios, including: industrial accidents, coastal emergencies, and natural disasters. Before expanding the platform further, I hope to collaborate with qualified emergency-management professionals to review the scenario assumptions, decision logic, and evaluation criteria. At the moment, Relay is still a synthetic training prototype . It is not intended for real-world emergency command and cannot replace formal training provided by professional organizations. If Relay could eventually recreate and simulate real environments and real-world scenarios, I believe that could become one of its most powerful capabilities. Ultimately, the problem I want to solve is simple: to give more people unlimited opportunities to practice difficult decisions before those decisions ever become real. title: Verdiqt
pitch: Verdiqt is an agent-native web app that runs a SaaS idea through a real evidence trial: it gathers live signals, scores the idea across six judges, and returns a Build, Pivot, or Kill verdict.
about_excerpt: Verdiqt is an agent-native web app that runs a SaaS idea through a real evidence trial: it gathers live signals, scores the idea across six judges, and returns a Build, Pivot, or Kill verdict. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI made building software cheap. It did not make building the right software cheap. People now ship a SaaS product in a weekend, and find out at launch that nobody wanted it. Verdiqt moves that painful discovery to before you write the first line of code. You put your idea on trial, and a court decides whether it deserves to live. What it does You file a case: your SaaS idea in a sentence, or a link to a public GitHub repo you already built. Then the courtroom goes to work, and you watch every step happen live: The case file. The court reads your idea and writes it up: who it's for, what problem it solves, what to search for. The investigation. Real research across five real communities : Hacker News, Reddit, GitHub, Stack Overflow, and Product Hunt. Every finding appears on screen with a link to its source, and every source reports honestly: gathered, failed, or empty. If the first search comes back thin, the court automatically widens its search. The deliberation. Six AI judges each take one question: "Is the pain real? Is anyone actively looking for this? Who already exists? Who would pay? Can you reach these people? Can you build it fast enough?" Each judge delivers their score the moment they finish, you literally watch the bench board fill in, one verdict at a time. The ruling. A presiding judge reads the entire case file and rules: BUILD, PIVOT, or KILL —> with a score out of 100, the reasoning behind every number, and exactly one recommended next step (a real, cheap test you can run this week). A full trial takes about a minute. And if you refine your idea and try again, the court remembers: the evidence you marked as important and the previous ruling follow your case, so every iteration builds on the last. How we built it Zero cash out of pocket. The whole product runs on free tiers and hackathon credits: one small server runs the website and the research pipeline, the AI judges run on free model APIs, and when one provider's daily quota runs dry, the court automatically switches to a backup provider mid-trial and keeps ruling. Constraints became design: the court paces itself under rate limits, shows its deliberation while it works, and never wastes a token. The model argues; the code rules. Anti-hallucination isn't a prompt, it's enforced in code. Judges may only cite evidence the court actually gathered: invented citations are stripped automatically, and a high score that loses its citations gets capped. When public evidence is thin, the judge is allowed to use domain judgment but the ruling must say so, out loud, in the rationale. Uncertainty is never dressed up as certainty. Privacy without accounts. No sign-up. Your browser gets an unguessable key; only its fingerprint is stored. Your cases are yours, anyone else asking for them gets an identical "not found.", don't worry. Challenges we ran into Running a multi-stage AI pipeline on free tiers meant treating every token and every request as scarce... the wait-and-retry pacing, the provider failover, and the one-at-a-time trial queue all exist because of it. And WebMCP is new enough that the tool contract itself was a design problem: we learned that the workflow belongs inside the tool descriptions, so agents teach themselves the journey. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete, evidence-cited validation trial in about a minute. A deliberation you can actually watch. A surface that serves two audiences at once... humans get a courtroom, agents get a toolbox, and each can see the other working. What we learned Never think you have enough time to build something. What's next for Verdiqt GitHub sign-in to put your whole repo graveyard on trial at once, re-trials over time to watch a verdict change as markets move, and Reddit's expanded API access for even deeper community evidence. title: 0x1 Expedition Vault
pitch: A WebMCP learning roguelike where humans and browser agents share one branching expedition state.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP learning roguelike where humans and browser agents share one branching expedition state. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most learning apps expose a human UI and leave agents to scrape the DOM. We wanted the opposite: a learning world where the human and browser agent share one explicit game state and can genuinely take turns. What it does 0x1 Expedition Vault turns a topic, YouTube lecture, public article/PDF, pasted notes, or uploaded text into a branching learning roguelike. Learners study sources, answer quizzes, build causal chains, defend models in adversarial dialogue, choose risk/recovery branches, accumulate strikes, fail runs, recover, and defeat a final systems boss. The branching map is not cosmetic: unresolved splits expose multiple selectable paths. A route is marked taken only after the learner or agent commits to it; same-row alternatives become skipped for that run, matching the source expedition semantics. Why WebMCP The page registers four tools directly on document.modelContext : ingest_learning_material explore_module submit_solution inspect_progress The key point is that these tools do not maintain an agent-only copy of the course. Human clicks and agent tool calls mutate the same expedition graph, active room, checkpoint, belief trajectory, strikes, branch choices, mastery, and failure state. An agent can forge a course, inspect progress, choose a branch, submit a solution, fail the same run, or advance the same map the learner sees. Better together A human can watch a source video and clear a checkpoint; the agent can then inspect the resulting state and continue from the newly available branch. Or the agent can ingest a new topic and generate an expedition that appears immediately in the learner UI. WebMCP removes the brittle layer of DOM guessing and makes the collaboration explicit, structured, and inspectable. Cognition, not keyword recall Generated expeditions separate source study from hidden cognition checks. Later rooms test causal transfer, source-vs-inference separation, falsification, adversarial prediction, and integrative defense. Hidden checks conceal their rubric and discount terms already present in the prompt. Human and WebMCP text answers use the same semantic evaluator; verbose nonsense cannot clear a checkpoint. How we built it The app uses SvelteKit/Svelte 5, Vite, native document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , a deterministic source-grounded curriculum generator, serverless-native PDF extraction, opportunistic YouTube transcript extraction with source-honest metadata fallback, and persistent browser-local expedition state. The map runtime ports the original expedition engine's seeded node/edge geometry and explicit path-choice semantics. Reliability The deployed build was tested end-to-end on Vercel: source ingestion, branching path selection in both directions, three-strike run failure, restart, staged Back-EMF causal chain, Lenz adversarial dialogue, five-variable boss system model, WebMCP failure parity, and visible progression all pass. title: Desksembly
pitch: An agent-ready desk, assembled in front of you.
about_excerpt: An agent-ready desk, assembled in front of you. Like Comment Story Updates Problem Buying a complete desk setup is a multi-product decision disguised as unrelated product pages. Shoppers must compare categories, resolve exact variants, track budget and availability, remember their choices, and reproduce the final decision in a cart. A generic browser agent can imitate clicks, but it has no reliable contract for non-DOM state inside a visual workspace and can overwrite a choice made while it was planning. Solution Desksembly gives the shopper and their browser agent one shared, directly manipulable miniature desk world. The experience starts with a human-locked orange lamp and a natural-language request for a cozy US work-from-home setup under $350. The browser agent reads the current scene, composes Shopify-native discovery with Desksembly's site-owned WebMCP tools, validates exact product IDs, and stages the proposal through visible parcels. The shopper can inspect, drag, move, lock, unlock, or remove products through either the 3D canvas or its equivalent accessible list. When the shopper changes the constraints to a 90 cm desk, a $300 budget, and US availability, a stale agent call is rejected. After refreshing, the agent preserves the locked keyboard and all unaffected IDs, returns only the conflicting plant, and stages one replacement. Before any cart consequence, Desksembly produces an exact, versioned review. Approval is digest-bound, expiring, and single-use. Partial cart outcomes remain partial and block checkout. Why WebMCP Desksembly demonstrates an open interaction model where the human owns taste, spatial corrections, locks, and approval; the agent owns repetitive discovery, validation, and precise execution; the website owns state correctness and consequential-action boundaries; and commerce facts never come from model output. The defining WebMCP moment is a browser agent operating a non-DOM 3D world, surviving a concurrent human edit through optimistic versioning, and composing site-owned capabilities without scraping buttons or embedding a store-specific chatbot. Human + Agent Collaboration The shopper can manually reshape the desk and lock products they want to keep. The agent works from the same versioned scene, stages visible proposals, and must refresh after a human edit instead of silently overwriting it. The final cart action happens only after an exact human review and one-time approval. Implementation Desksembly exposes five focused site-owned WebMCP tools alongside Shopify-native tools: deskbuilder.get_scene deskbuilder.preview_plan deskbuilder.stage_plan deskbuilder.move_product deskbuilder.get_review Tool inputs use strict Zod schemas, and every scene mutation carries an expected version. Next.js and Shopify Hydrogen provide SSR, typed Storefront queries, ShopifyScripts, native WebMCP, Standard Actions, and request routing. Zustand supplies fresh synchronous state reads. React Three Fiber and Three.js render the world; GSAP owns cancellable transactions; Motion renders the activity ribbon. Key Features Five focused deskbuilder.* tools alongside Shopify-native tools Retryable STALE_SCENE failures and exact scene versioning Cancellable parcel arrival, opening, reveal, and placement Accessible product list plus keyboard and manual controls Visible human-owned product locks Constraint shock that preserves exact unaffected IDs Reduced-motion replay with the same five-item result SHA-256 proposal/review digests and one-time approval Partial deterministic cart truth and disabled-checkout disclosure Manual and deterministic fallback when WebMCP is unavailable AI and Codex The deployed application hosts no model API. It relies on a compatible browser agent to interpret free-form requests and compose Shopify's native tools with Desksembly's WebMCP tools. AI output is never trusted as price, availability, cart, or checkout truth. OpenAI Codex supported WebMCP and Shopify research, product planning, architecture review, implementation, debugging, automated testing, browser verification, deployment, evidence capture, repository publication, and submission preparation. Testing Open the live app in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Confirm the Shopify tool family plus exactly five deskbuilder.* tools. Run the deterministic replay, lock the QuietType keyboard, apply the 90 cm / $300 / US constraint shock, and prepare the exact review. The final deterministic cart flow demonstrates accepted-only receipts, single-use approval, preservation of an unrelated line, and explicitly unavailable Shopify Checkout. Verified matrix: 30 Vitest tests, 10 integration tests, 5 Playwright journeys, and 10 prompt-family evals. A clean public clone passed npm ci , typecheck, and production build. No credentials are required. title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation.
