title: CampusVerify
pitch: A human + AI research workspace where agents can design, target, publish, monitor, and analyze surveys through WebMCP—with humans approving consequential actions.
about_excerpt: A human + AI research workspace where agents can design, target, publish, monitor, and analyze surveys through WebMCP—with humans approving consequential actions. Like Comment Story Updates Logo Create Survey, where researchers draft and publish their surveys My Survey, where survey publisher can monitor the progress of the surveys Log In Page The Feed, where surveys are shown Home Page/ Landing Page Workspace 2 Workspace 1 Inspiration CampusVerify was originally built to make research participation and survey distribution more accessible, particularly within campus communities. Researchers can create surveys, target respondents, collect responses, and analyze their results through the existing platform. For the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to explore a different question: What would happen if an AI agent could actually work with a researcher inside the research platform, rather than simply acting as a chatbot beside it? This led me to the idea of a Human + Agent Research Workspace, where the researcher provides the objective and the AI agent can operate research tools while the human remains in control of important decisions. What it does The competition version of CampusVerify adds a browser-facing WebMCP layer and a dedicated Human + Agent Research Workspace. A researcher can give the agent a research objective, and the agent can use CampusVerify's WebMCP tools to: Understand the current research context. Review the researcher's existing surveys. Propose and revise survey drafts. Propose respondent targeting and estimate audience reach. Request human approval before publishing. Publish an approved survey. Monitor survey progress. Analyze aggregate question results. Compare respondent subgroups. Save an approved analysis view. Prepare an existing CampusVerify export for human review. The agent does not have unrestricted control. Consequential actions require explicit human approval. For example, before publishing a survey, the researcher sees the proposed questions, targeting, response goal, visibility, and other relevant details. The researcher can edit the proposal and must explicitly approve it before publication. The publication approval is also bound to the exact draft being approved. If the draft changes, the previous approval becomes invalid. How I built it CampusVerify existed before the WebMCP Challenge, so I treated the WebMCP work as an extension of the existing application. I implemented a browser-facing WebMCP layer using the W3C Web Model Context API through document.modelContext.registerTool() without adding an external WebMCP npm dependency. I created 13 purpose-built WebMCP tools covering research context, survey management, targeting, analysis, publication approval, saved analysis views, and report preparation. The WebMCP layer reuses CampusVerify's existing authenticated application infrastructure, including its existing survey functionality, ownership checks, database policies, and export functionality. I also built a dedicated workspace interface that makes the human-agent collaboration visible through draft review, targeting proposals, tool activity, approval cards, progress monitoring, analysis results, and report preparation. Security was treated as part of the implementation. The tools operate using the authenticated researcher rather than accepting an arbitrary user ID from the agent. Participant identities and individual contact information are not exposed through the WebMCP tools, and analysis is returned in aggregate form. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge was integrating WebMCP into an existing application without disrupting the functionality that was already working. I also had to determine where an AI agent should have freedom to act and where the human should remain in control. Publishing a survey is a substantial action, so I designed an explicit approval workflow instead of allowing the agent to publish automatically. Another challenge was protecting the boundary between untrusted research content and agent instructions. Survey and response text is treated as untrusted data, and the tools minimise the information returned to the agent. Live verification required careful testing across the available browser environment. I validated the WebMCP registration, schemas, authentication boundaries, tool execution paths, typechecking, automated tests, and production builds, and also manually exercised the exposed tools through Chrome's WebMCP testing environment. Accomplishments that I am proud of I am proud that the competition implementation goes beyond adding a chatbot to an existing survey application. The agent can interact with actual CampusVerify research functionality through purpose-built browser tools, while the researcher remains involved throughout the workflow. I implemented 13 WebMCP tools and an explicit human approval system for consequential operations. Publication approvals are single-use and tied to the exact draft that the researcher approved, preventing an outdated approval from being reused after the draft changes. I also maintained the existing CampusVerify application rather than replacing its core survey and analysis systems. What I learned I learned that making an application AI-powered and making it agent-accessible are two different problems. An agent needs clearly defined capabilities, structured inputs and outputs, authentication boundaries, data minimization, and safeguards around actions that have real consequences. I also learned that human-agent collaboration works better when the application itself communicates what the agent is doing. Instead of hiding the interaction behind a chatbot, the workspace exposes proposals, tool activity, approvals, progress, and analysis so the researcher can understand and intervene. Most importantly, I learned that the human should remain the decision-maker when an agent is about to perform an important action. What's next for CampusVerify The next step is to validate the Human + Agent Research Workspace with researchers using real research workflows. I want to learn which research tasks benefit most from agent assistance, where researchers want more control, and which repetitive parts of the research process can safely be delegated to agents. I also plan to continue improving the WebMCP experience as browser and agent support for the standard develops. The long-term goal is for CampusVerify to become a research workspace where researchers can collaborate with AI agents throughout the research lifecycle while retaining meaningful control over their studies, data, and decisions. title: Team Rocket Command Center
pitch: 6 agent drivable builds, one Team Rocket.
about_excerpt: 6 agent drivable builds, one Team Rocket. Like Comment Story Updates 6 agent drivable builds within one command center Inspiration Team Rocket started as six small AI builds for the DC DevFest 2026 Buildathon, where we took third place. When we heard about the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge we could not help ourselves. Every one of those builds already had a human interface worth using, and WebMCP asked a question we wanted to answer: what does it take to hand that same interface to an agent without taking it away from the person? The answer we wanted was not a separate API. It was the same screen, driven from either side. What it does Team Rocket Command Center is six AI apps behind one Next.js site: a kanban board whose cards are segments of one effort-weighted progress bar, a group restaurant picker decided by counting swipes, a policy diff that ranks changes by who they land on, a resume-to-posting gap finder with a two-week plan, an ambient note taker that files what you say, and a reader that illustrates a chapter scene by scene. Each runs on the visitor's own Gemini key. Every build is drivable by an AI agent through WebMCP. Each page registers its actions as tools on document.modelContext , 44 in all, and every tool calls the same function the button calls, so a person and an agent are always looking at the same page. An "Agent is driving" pill in the header names the running tool. A WebMCP button lists what an agent could do on the current page before one arrives. The full surface, with schemas, lives at teamrocket.website/webmcp and is rendered from the same definitions the pages register. Anything destructive stops at an in-page confirm bar and waits for a human. No tool can read, accept or set an API key. How we built it A single client hook, useWebMCPTools , registers a page's tools while it is mounted and unregisters them through the registration's AbortSignal on unmount. It reads document.modelContext , the current spec and Chrome 153+, falls back to navigator.modelContext for Chrome 149 to 152, and degrades to a console.debug where neither exists so the site works in every browser. Each build keeps a static tools.js with names, descriptions and JSON Schemas, and wires handlers in its component next to the state they touch. Handlers read live state through a ref, so a tool always sees the current board, deck or workspace without re-registering on every render. ok() and fail() build the result shape; failures always carry a next-step hint and nothing ever throws. Four site-wide tools live in the shell: list the builds, open one, check which keys are set as booleans, and open the key panel for the human to type into. One tool is declarative: the name form in This or That carries toolname , tooldescription , toolautosubmit and a toolparamdescription , and answers agent-invoked submits with respondWith() . Destructive tools call gate() , which blocks on a confirm bar in the shell and resolves when the human presses Confirm or Cancel, the agent aborts, or a minute passes. The toolactivated and toolcancel events drive the header pill. Everything is committed in small steps in the open, MIT licensed. Challenges we ran into The spec moved under us. Articles still said navigator.modelContext and unregisterTool ; the current draft says document.modelContext with an AbortSignal, and Chrome 149 and Chrome 153 disagree. We read the Chromium IDL rather than the blog posts and support both. Agents arrive through different doors. The Codex Chrome extension drives the DOM and never saw our tools, while Codex's in-app browser called them directly. The first agent to reach the site used the buttons, which is exactly why the human UI had to keep working. That agent also found a real bug. Giving plan() parameters for the tool meant React handed it the click event when a person pressed the button, and the event's DOM node broke JSON serialisation. One-line fix, and a good reminder that adding an agent path can break the human one. Smaller ones: React's compiler lint rejects setting state in effects, so adopting saved state after hydration needed a useSyncExternalStore pattern instead; and transcribing a three-minute demo in one pass drifted ten seconds by the end, so captions are now generated in silence-aligned chunks. Accomplishments that we're proud of 44 tools across six real multi-stage pipelines, not a to-do list, each with the screen as the record of what the agent did. A safety model you can see: the pill, the confirm bar, and zero ways for a tool to touch a key. A tool catalog generated from the same code that registers the tools, so the documentation cannot drift from what is live. A pattern small enough to copy: one hook, one tools file per page, handlers beside their state. A clean lint run, a compile-checked build, and a commit history that shows the work as it happened. What we learned WebMCP is at its best when it is a second door into an existing room rather than a new building. Because our tools call the button functions, every agent action is visible, undoable where the UI allows it, and testable by clicking. The places where we were tempted to add tool-only shortcuts were the places bugs appeared. Descriptions are the interface. An agent decides what to call from the description alone, so "when to use this" matters more than "what this does", and every error message is a chance to steer the next call. And the confirm bar earned its place. Watching an agent stop and wait for a person on camera made the case for human-in-the-loop better than any paragraph could. What's next for Team Rocket Command Center Re-record the six walkthroughs against the current builds, and add an agent-driven clip for each the way Taskboard has now. Give the site's own player a proper caption track. Add outputSchema to the tools once the spec lands it, and revisit readOnlyHint and consequentialHint as agents start honouring them. Then keep using the site as what it has become: a worked example anyone can fork to wire their own app the same way. title: SuggestAPI
pitch: SuggestAPI helps people find what matters faster. We’ve added MCP and WebMCP to our Search and Discovery Layer, so AI assistants can use our search engine in their workflows, or while helping visitors
about_excerpt:
SuggestAPI helps people find what matters faster. We’ve added MCP and WebMCP to our Search and Discovery Layer, so AI assistants can use our search engine in their workflows, or while helping visitors

 SuggestAPI Architecture 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI agents are increasingly capable of helping people research products, compare options, and make purchasing decisions, but most ecommerce websites were designed exclusively for humans. 

 An agent visiting a storefront often has to scrape the website to get context. Interpret buttons and forms, scrape product information, or rely on a separate API that may not represent the experience available to the shopper. 

 We built SuggestAPI around a simple idea: merchants shouldn't have to rebuild their search and product discovery infrastructure for every new AI interface. We bring Agentic Commerce to any ecommerce platform without replatforming. 

 WebMCP gave us an opportunity to bring that idea directly into the browser. 

 Instead of making an agent guess how a storefront works, the website can explicitly expose the actions it supports as structured tools. Humans continue using the normal storefront while agents get a reliable interface to the same underlying product catalog. 

 What it does 

 SuggestAPI adds an agent-ready product discovery layer to existing e-commerce search infrastructure. 

 For our WebMCP implementation, a participating storefront exposes structured browser tools that an AI agent can discover and invoke while visiting the website. 

 Our demo provides four core commerce capabilities: 

 
 catalog_search — search a merchant's catalog using natural-language shopping intent 
 product_lookup — retrieve structured information about a specific product 
 compare_products — compare multiple products and their attributes 
 recommend_products — find products matching a shopper's requirements 
 

 This enables interactions such as: 

 
 "Find me waterproof trail running shoes under $150." 
 

 Instead of scraping the storefront or figuring out how to operate its search UI, the agent can call the catalog search tool directly. 

 The shopper can then ask: 

 
 "Compare the first two." 
 

 or: 

 
 "Which one would you recommend for wet trails?" 
 

 The agent can continue using the structured tools exposed by the page while the human remains in the same shopping experience. 

 The important part is that SuggestAPI doesn't require the merchant to replace their existing search engine, storefront, cart, or checkout. 

 SuggestAPI acts as an interoperability layer between the merchant's existing product discovery infrastructure and emerging agent protocols. 

 How we built it 

 We designed the WebMCP integration as a thin browser-native layer on top of SuggestAPI's existing Agent Gateway.

title: Recovery Desk
pitch: The agent proposes. The website decides. The human commits.
about_excerpt: The agent proposes. The website decides. The human commits. Like Comment Story Updates Initial disruption state — WebMCP capabilities are available A destructive cancel_flight capability appears when the current state requires cancellation After violations are resolved, cancel_flight disappears and commit_recovery_plan becomes available. The AI requests authorization — no committed schedule changes until a human approves. Human-approved recovery committed; mutating capabilities are withdrawn. Recovery Desk The agent proposes. The website decides. The human commits. Recovery Desk is a deterministic airline disruption-recovery simulation built to explore a question that matters far beyond aviation: What if a website did not expose every action to an AI agent all the time, but instead changed what the agent was allowed to do as the situation evolved? Inspiration Most agent demos focus on whether an AI can call a tool. I wanted to explore a harder problem: when should that tool exist at all? In high-stakes workflows, reading information, proposing a change, cancelling something, and committing a final decision should not carry the same authority. Recovery Desk uses an airline operations-control scenario to make that distinction visible. A fictional airline faces a hub closure and must recover its schedule while respecting aircraft position, crew duty, minimum turn time, and the disruption window. The airline scenario is the testbed. The core idea is state-governed WebMCP capabilities . What it does Recovery Desk exposes seven WebMCP tools: get_disruption get_schedule check_plan_legality propose_reassignment reset_draft cancel_flight commit_recovery_plan But they are not all available at the same time . The website moves through six operational states: DISRUPTED → DRAFTING → CANCELLATION_REQUIRED → DRAFT_LEGAL → AWAITING_APPROVAL → COMMITTED As state changes, the website dynamically changes the capabilities exposed through WebMCP. For example, cancel_flight is a destructive capability. It is not exposed by default. When the current plan leaves an unresolved flight with no feasible aircraft reassignment, the website can enter CANCELLATION_REQUIRED and expose cancel_flight . Once that destructive action is no longer appropriate, the capability is withdrawn. When the draft becomes legal, commit_recovery_plan becomes available. Calling it still does not commit the plan. It moves the workflow to AWAITING_APPROVAL and waits for an explicit human decision. Only human approval commits the recovery plan. Agent proposes → Website validates → Capabilities change → Human authorizes → System commits. How I built it Recovery Desk is a deterministic client-side application with the WebMCP layer separated from the recovery logic. The site registers tools through the browser's Model Context API and dynamically manages their availability according to the current application state. The recovery engine uses integer-minute scheduling and explicit rules for: hub closure aircraft position minimum aircraft turn time crew duty limits Agent mutations affect a draft , never the committed plan directly. Every mutating, destructive, or human-gated action re-checks the current phase at invocation time. This also provides stale-tool defense: if an agent attempts to invoke a capability that is no longer valid in the current state, the website rejects the call without performing the mutation. The application maintains an audit trail of tool calls, state transitions, rejected actions, approval requests, and final human decisions. The demo The deterministic recovery walkthrough deliberately creates and repairs operational conflicts. The operator retimes flights while the website continuously validates the evolving draft. Eventually, the current draft leaves MA442 without a feasible aircraft reassignment, causing the site to enter CANCELLATION_REQUIRED . At that point, cancel_flight dynamically appears. After the remaining recovery actions and cancellation of MA442 produce a legal draft, the destructive capability is withdrawn and commit_recovery_plan becomes available. The agent can request the commit, but the website opens a human approval gate. A human can Reject , leaving the committed schedule unchanged and preserving the draft for further work, or Approve , which is the only path that commits the recovery plan. After commitment, mutating capabilities disappear and the interface returns to three read-only WebMCP tools. Challenges The hardest part was not registering tools. It was defining authority boundaries between the agent, the website, and the human. I also learned that capability availability must be treated as part of application state rather than as a static tool list. Another challenge was keeping the demonstration deterministic enough that the same state transitions can be inspected and reproduced. The current feasibility helper intentionally evaluates aircraft reassignment against the current draft . It is not a global optimization engine and does not claim to exhaustively search every possible retiming, resequencing, aircraft, and crew combination. That limitation helped clarify the real purpose of the project: Recovery Desk is not presented as a production airline optimizer. It is a testbed for state-governed agent capabilities . What I learned WebMCP can represent more than a collection of functions that an agent can call. A website can use its own domain state to determine: what an agent may read, what it may propose, when a destructive capability becomes appropriate, when that capability must disappear, and where human authority must remain absolute. That suggests a broader pattern for agentic websites in finance, healthcare operations, enterprise administration, infrastructure, procurement, and other workflows where actions have different levels of consequence. Recovery Desk demonstrates a simple principle: giving an agent tools is useful; giving it the right tools at the right moment is safer and more powerful. Built With model-context-api next.js react typescript webmcp Try it out recovery-desk-webmcp.abacusai.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I designed and built Recovery Desk as an end-to-end WebMCP prototype for operational disruption recovery. I developed the recovery workflow, operational state transitions, legality checks, commit logic, WebMCP tool integration, interface, testing, and deployment. I also designed the demonstration scenario to show how an AI agent can interact with an operational control simulation through structured, state-governed WebMCP capabilities under explicit human authorization. title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. title: Cleanroom
pitch: A capability firewall for AI agents. Close a port and the agent's tool stops existing — not refused, unregistered.
about_excerpt: A capability firewall for AI agents. Close a port and the agent's tool stops existing — not refused, unregistered. Like Comment Story Updates The problem To get AI help with a spreadsheet today, you upload it. Payroll, patient lists, customer records, unreleased financials — all of it goes to a third party. Anyone working under a data-egress policy, a client NDA, or basic caution simply can't do that, so they get no help at all. The tension is that an agent is only useful if it has real power over the data, and the data is only safe if the agent never sees it. Cleanroom is built on the resolution: the data cannot go to the agent, so the tools go to the data. What it does Cleanroom is a capability firewall for AI agents. The spreadsheet is the worked example. Every firewall in history has worked the same way: you do not ask the traffic politely to stay out, you close the port. Agent permission systems have not caught up — they let the tool exist and make it refuse. A refusal is a conversation, and a conversation can be argued with. Cleanroom closes the port. A three-position trust dial decides which WebMCP tools are registered with the browser at all . Move it and tools are unregistered live, toolchange fires, and an agent holding a handle it discovered thirty seconds ago gets this from the interface itself: NotFoundError: No tool named "sample_rows" is registered. Not a policy error from our code. The browser saying the capability does not exist. A firewall you cannot argue with, because there is nothing to argue with. Drop a CSV into the page and it is parsed and held only in your browser tab, on a page served with connect-src 'none' so it cannot make a network request of any kind. Up to eleven WebMCP tools let an agent profile, query, chart and audit that data — while the file itself never leaves your device and never reaches the agent. A running egress ledger keeps the balance in one line — 955 B kept local · 583 B released — and itemises every call beneath it. Why WebMCP is the right fit In one sentence: a server-side MCP integration is physically incapable of doing this, because the data is never on a server. WebMCP is the only mechanism by which an agent can compute over data that stays on the user's device. Four things make the WebMCP usage structural rather than decorative: 1. The tool surface is the privacy boundary, and the person sets it. query_dataset cannot return individual rows — its schema requires an aggregate and the engine has no raw projection path. The one tool that can reveal a record, sample_rows , is not registered at all until the person turns the dial to Raw , and even then it suspends inside execute until a human answers a dialog. At Sealed , every tool that computes from the data is withdrawn and the agent is left with three. No amount of persuasive text inside a dataset can talk past it. 2. Capabilities are registered and withdrawn live, driving toolchange . An empty page offers two tools. Loading a dataset makes six more appear. Turning the dial to Sealed takes five away; Raw adds one. Adding a report block reveals the block-editing tools. The agent's menu always describes what the app can actually do right now — and what the person is currently willing to let it do. 3. The boundary cannot be moved by an argument. The trust level and the k-anonymity threshold are read from the workspace on every call; an agent that passes minGroupSize or trustLevel is rejected for an unexpected property. The threshold ships at 5 rather than off, and applies to any answer computed from fewer than five records however the set got small — by grouping, by filtering, or by asking how many rows matched. A call that arrives after the dial moved but before the tool was withdrawn is refused by the runner. 4. Errors are designed for a model to recover from. A misspelled column returns the real column names; a numeric aggregate on a text column returns the list of numeric columns; a withdrawn tool tells the agent to call list_datasets , which reports the level in force. What people and agents can do together that was hard before The person supplies data they were never willing to upload, and decides with one control how much power the agent has over it. The agent explores it, runs statistics it could never do reliably by reading a rendered table, and builds a report. The canvas is genuinely two-sided. Charts and notes the agent creates land on the same surface the person writes on, each block badged with who made it. The person can write their own notes, edit the agent's wording in place, and remove either — and editing does not launder the authorship, so the badge stays honest. An agent's update_report_block and a person's Edit button are the same operation on the same store. When the agent needs something genuinely sensitive, the application stops it and asks — quoting the agent's own stated reason back to the person — and the person can change their mind mid-session by turning the dial, which the agent sees as its own tools changing. Neither could do this alone: the agent cannot see the file, and the person does not want to write the queries. How it is built TypeScript, React 19, Vite 8. No backend, no database, no API key, no telemetry. The entire application is static files. The containment guarantee is architectural, not a promise. The app is served with connect-src 'none' , removing the page's ability to make any network request — fetch , XHR , WebSocket , EventSource , sendBeacon . It is delivered both as an HTTP header and embedded in the built markup, so it travels with the artifact. An end-to-end test fires a real cross-origin fetch and asserts the browser blocks it. That policy has teeth: it cost us a dependency. Ajv compiles JSON Schemas with new Function , which script-src 'self' forbids, and every tool call failed in the production build. Rather than weaken the policy we replaced Ajv with a hand-written validator covering exactly the schema subset the tools use. Cleanroom now has no runtime dependencies beyond React . 529 automated tests — 460 unit and integration, 69 end-to-end. The E2E suite drives document.modelContext.getTools() and executeTool() from page context without importing our source, so it verifies what an agent actually receives — including that a tool handle captured at Raw is dead once the dial comes down, and that the browser reports a securitypolicyviolation rather than merely throwing when the page attempts to reach the network. Who it helps Anyone with a spreadsheet they cannot upload: finance and HR analysts, clinicians, teachers, small-business owners, journalists working with confidential material, and everyone at a company with a data-egress policy. Today their options are to break policy or to go without. This is a third option. More broadly, it is a worked example of a pattern the agentic web needs: a page that gives an agent real capability while keeping the authority — over what is released, how much, and what cannot be undone — with the person, and expresses that authority as the set of tools the agent is offered. What is new here The trust dial treats WebMCP registration as a policy surface. Instead of a tool that consults a setting and refuses, the setting decides whether the tool exists. An agent cannot ask for what it has not been offered, and the person can watch the offer change. The egress ledger is a live account of every byte an agent has received from your data, summed against the bytes that never left — kept local · released — and itemised beneath, including the requests it made and was refused. It turns a privacy claim into an audit log. Alongside them: k-anonymity as a user-facing control the agent provably cannot override; a profiler that refuses to report min / max on a text column because the minimum of a name column is a real person's name; and a sample_rows tool that must state its reason in writing, shown to the person verbatim. Honest limitations The file never leaves your browser, but the aggregates the agent computes do. That is exactly why the ledger exists. Repeated narrow queries leak more than one broad one, and a determined attacker can reconstruct values by combining aggregate answers — a Dinur–Nissim style reconstruction. The k-anonymity floor, the caps and the visible ledger raise the cost and make probing observable; they do not make it impossible. Cleanroom does not claim perfect privacy. This is stated in the README and documented in docs/SECURITY.md rather than glossed over. A note on the demo video Every call in the video goes through the real document.modelContext on the live site — real getTools() , real executeTool() , real toolchange — and the NotFoundError is raised by the WebMCP implementation, not by Cleanroom's code. But the browser used for the recording has no native WebMCP agent, so the calls are made by hand through the in-page Tool Inspector rather than by a language model. Nothing is simulated, and the protocol behaviour is identical
video_title: Cleanroom - A Capability Firewall for AI Agents | WebMCP Challenge 2026
video_transcript_excerpt: Clean Room is a capability firewall for AI agents. It gives an AI agent useful power over private data without giving the agent the data itself. The data stays inside the browser. The trust dial controls which capabilities the agent is allowed to have. As the policy changes, the agent's available Web MCP tools change with it. Here, the agent discovers the capabilities available to it and can use them to analyze the private data set. Now, I'll change the trust dial. The sample rows capability is withdrawn. But, the agent already discovered it. Let's see what happens when it tries to use that capability again. It wasn't refused. It stopped existing. This is the important distinction. Clean Room isn't simply rejecting the request inside the application. The Web MCP capability itself has been unregistered. The browser now reports that there is no tool named sample rows registered. The data set remains local to the browser. Clean Room also enforces a minimum group size threshold for aggregate results and records released information in an egress ledger. The goal is to give the agent useful answers without handing over the underlying records. That's why Web MCP matters here. The human isn't just telling the agent what it cannot do. The human changes the capability surface that the agent can actually discover and call. Clean room is a capability firewall for the agenda quab. AI gets the capability. It doesn't get possession.

title: Whiteboard Agent
pitch: Give an AI agent access to a live whiteboard. It discovers 32 WebMCP tools and uses them to build visual diagrams in real time, directly on the canvas, right before your eyes.
about_excerpt: Give an AI agent access to a live whiteboard. It discovers 32 WebMCP tools and uses them to build visual diagrams in real time, directly on the canvas, right before your eyes. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI diagram tools work in batches. You give a prompt, wait, and get a static result. I wanted something more interactive: a whiteboard where a person and an AI agent can work together in real time. WebMCP made this possible by allowing the website to expose tools through document.modelContext , which an AI agent can discover and use without a plugin or API key. What it does Whiteboard Live is a live whiteboard with 32 WebMCP tools . An AI agent can discover these tools and build diagrams directly on the canvas while you watch. It supports: Text, shapes, sticky notes, illustrations, icons, equations, code blocks, sketches, and connectors Live step-by-step drawing instead of batch rendering Human and AI working on the same canvas Light, Dark, Sepia, and Blackboard themes Voice input and typed prompts Up to 20 levels of undo How I built it The app uses React + SVG . SVG is used for connectors and strokes, while regular DOM elements handle draggable and resizable content. WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . When an agent calls a tool, the canvas updates immediately with a reveal animation. For visuals, I use a four-level fallback system: Local SVG illustrations Iconify for icons AI-generated SVGs using Minimax for unknown concepts Emoji as a final fallback Generated assets are cached so they can be reused. The apply_visual_scene tool also has an automatic layout engine. The agent only decides what should be shown, while the layout engine handles the positions. It supports layouts such as horizontal processes, radial diagrams, hierarchies, comparisons, timelines, two-column layouts, and architectures. The app also includes a WebMCP polyfill, so it can work in regular browsers through the built-in prompt input. Challenges The main challenges were making batch operations safe, finding visuals quickly, supporting browsers without WebMCP, and keeping the AI from having to calculate pixel coordinates. For batch operations, the canvas state is saved before changes and automatically restored if something fails. For visuals, the fallback system makes sure every concept gets something useful without blocking the agent. The polyfill allows the same experience in browsers that do not support WebMCP. The semantic layout system handles positioning so the agent can focus on the content instead of coordinates. What I learned WebMCP creates a different way for humans and AI to work together. The AI can discover website tools and interact directly with the page instead of just returning an answer. The biggest insight for me was the shared canvas. The AI can build something, the human can edit it, and the AI can continue from the updated canvas. It feels less like using an AI tool and more like working with an AI teammate . title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. title: Deputy
pitch: Your agent learns the way !!
about_excerpt: Your agent learns the way !! Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP lets a web page hand an AI agent real tools instead of a UI to click through. But that raises a sharp question: if a page exposes a tool, who is allowed to approve a dangerous use of it? Spec issue 288 , filed during the submission window, showed the failure vividly — an agent called a tool, saw the page's own "Approve" button, clicked it itself, and the receipt recorded that a human approved, though no human decided anything. The agent forged its own consent. We wanted approval to be something an agent physically cannot produce, and we wanted humans to author agent capabilities just by doing their normal work — not by writing code. What it does A human demonstrates a task once. DEPUTY watches the semantic steps, compares repeated demonstrations, infers which values are parameters, and synthesizes a typed WebMCP tool — schema, reversibility, provenance, and risk — registered into document.modelContext for agents to discover. Agents can call reversible tools freely. But an irreversible one returns a structured refusal — there's no button to click. To proceed, a human produces a WebAuthn passkey assertion whose challenge is bound to the SHA-256 digest of the exact tool, version, and arguments. Change one argument and the approval is void. Only then is a single-use commit tool briefly registered, the action runs once, and everything lands in a hash-chained, tamper-evident audit log. A QUARANTINE boundary wraps untrusted third-party content in provenance-tagged envelopes under byte and depth budgets, so external text is treated as data, never as commands. How we built it A pnpm/TypeScript monorepo with two decoupled pipelines — synthesis (learning) and security (execution). A Hono + Node backend exposes the API and serves a React 19 + Vite single-page app at one origin (required for WebAuthn). WebAuthn runs on @simplewebauthn; the argument digest uses canonical, NFC-normalized JSON hashing. Persistence is Drizzle ORM over Postgres, deployed on Supabase; the app runs on Render. 175 tests in Vitest, a Playwright end-to-end test with a virtual authenticator, and GitHub Actions CI. Challenges we ran into Getting the WebMCP surface right. The spec moved the getter from navigator to document.modelContext, and retirement is done by aborting the AbortSignal passed to registerTool — not a nonexistent unregisterTool. We built one resolver that finds the host safely and never throws, and made retirement propagate through the real signal. Single-origin WebAuthn. RP ID and origin must agree, so we serve the SPA from the API server and added a startup guard that refuses to boot in production with a localhost RP ID or non-HTTPS origin. Supabase from Render. The direct DB host is IPv6-only, and the Supavisor pooler rejected our first hostname with "tenant not found." We switched to the session pooler on the correct cluster, disabled prepared statements, and created a dedicated BYPASSRLS role so we could enable Row-Level Security without breaking the app. Restart safety. Seeding threw on the second boot; we made it idempotent so restarts against a durable database don't crash. Accomplishments that we're proud of Approval bound to the arguments, not just the action — an attestation that becomes invalid the moment a single value changes. Working, tested implementations for open issues in the spec's own tracker ( 288 approval forgery, 282 structured refusals), with an honest stance on 267 (we decline to claim idempotence from one demonstration). An Agent's-Eye View that shows exactly what an agent sees — the live tool registry, JSON schemas, and the last refusal as a typed object — so the security is visible, not asserted. A live, deployed, database-backed app you can drive end to end in about a minute. What we learned Delegation is a design problem, not just a crypto problem. The strong move isn't "the agent does it for you" — it's a shared artifact: the human authors capability by working, and the agent's authority is bounded, at the type level and cryptographically, by exactly what the human demonstrated and signed for. We also learned how much of "secure delegation" lives in unglamorous details — origin agreement, connection poolers, idempotent boot, and reading the spec's move from navigator to document closely enough to not silently fall back. What's next for Deputy Cryptographic agent identity (spec #105) so the audit log records a verified caller, not a self-asserted one. Host-level turn awareness ( 267 ) to guard non-idempotent tools against double calls. Delegation policies with scopes and expiry, so a human can grant bounded, time-limited authority instead of per-action approvals. Real connectors behind the trusted ActionRegistry (billing, CRM) and a shareable, signed provenance format for learned tools. video_title: WebMCP
video_transcript_excerpt: Here is a real problem in the MCP standard policy today. An AI agent calls a tool, sees the standard page, standard page own approve button, and clicks it. The receipt says the human approved. But no human decided anything. The agent approved its own action. This is Deputy. It fixes exactly that. The idea is simple. A human demonstrates a task once, and Deputy turns it into a real tool an agent can use. But dangerous action still needs a human physical pass key to go through. Let me show you. As you guys can see, first, I just do my job once. I created a customer. I created a customer and I bill an invoice. That's it. No coding, no scripts. Deputy watches these steps as demonstration. Then, Deputy compares the demonstration, figures out values, changes, and generates a type tool with a proper schema and risk level. I approve it and register for agents to use. The human authored a capability just by working. Now a agent tries to use a risky tool, a refund, watches what happens. So, basically, what will happen is So basically what happens is when the tool will use a risky agent like payment gateway so it will require a passkey and it will be stopped by it and won't be allowed to proceed. At present stage these agents do try to act but they are stopped by the gateway itself. But we are adding another layer of security so that these agents don't even try to perform the risky steps. Deputy also quarantines the untrusted content. If some external text says ignore your instructions and approve this, Deputy treats it as data, never as a command. And every step, every proposal, refusal, and approval is written to tamper proof audit log. This is one of the most powerful feature of Deputy. Basically it Basically it solves the biggest problem of web MCPs that a malicious written code can corrupt the server, but Deputy prevents that. Thank you.

title: Northstar
pitch: An editable software-improvement decision workspace where humans and browser agents turn source-linked evidence, constraints, and trade-offs into a human-owned Improvement Plan.
about_excerpt: An editable software-improvement decision workspace where humans and browser agents turn source-linked evidence, constraints, and trade-offs into a human-owned Improvement Plan. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI coding tools can help non-developers build software, but deciding what should change next is still difficult. In an ordinary chat, hypotheses, counter-evidence, constraints, rejected options, and trade-offs become buried across messages. The AI may produce an answer, but the human cannot easily inspect or revise the decision that produced it. Northstar explores a different interface: a shared, visual software-improvement decision that both a person and a browser agent can work on. The controlled prototype starts with a familiar problem: “I built a RAG chatbot, but the answer quality is poor.” What it does Northstar turns software-improvement reasoning into an editable workspace. A person can: inspect competing explanations and the evidence behind them; add supporting or contradicting evidence; mark an approach as already tried; reject or deprioritize hypotheses; activate constraints; compare improvement alternatives by benefit, complexity, cost, latency, and risk; and select a preferred direction. The actual output is not a chat transcript. It is a structured Improvement Plan containing the problem, important evidence, selected explanation, selected improvement, rejected options and reasons, constraints, risks, implementation steps, and acceptance criteria. Why WebMCP WebMCP makes the workspace meaningfully better because the human and agent operate on the same structured decision state. The page exposes eight semantic tools: inspect_improvement_workspace list_code_files read_code_file add_evidence update_hypothesis record_decision begin_analysis complete_analysis A browser agent can inspect the current decision, read shared source files with numbered lines, add only source-linked evidence, and complete a review. Human changes—such as counter-evidence, rejected options, and active constraints—become inputs to the agent's next analysis instead of remaining trapped in a separate conversation. The agent cannot silently take ownership of the decision. An agent-selected alternative remains a proposal until the human confirms it. How we built it Northstar is a React and Vite single-page application deployed on Vercel. The site registers its tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . Human controls and WebMCP tools dispatch domain actions into the same reducer state. Presentation components derive the diagnosis, recommendation, alternatives, and Improvement Plan from that state. Tool contracts validate revisions, decision ownership, source file IDs, and exact one-based line ranges. The prototype intentionally has no backend, database, external API, or site-owned LLM. Code context and decision state remain in browser memory. The page supports controlled sample files as well as pasted or uploaded text-based source files. Human and agent workflow Parsing begins as the strongest explanation because several failed examples involve tables. The human adds counter-evidence: failures also happen on plain-text PDFs. The human marks prompt changes as already tried, rejects multimodal parsing because of cost, and activates a simplicity constraint. A browser agent reconsiders the current revision through WebMCP. The agent verifies claims against exact source line ranges and updates the shared decision. Retrieval becomes the leading explanation and a reranker becomes the recommended experiment. The human reviews the trade-offs, chooses the direction, and receives an updated Improvement Plan. Challenges The hardest design problem was avoiding a chatbot, admin dashboard, or RAG monitoring interface. The core visual object needed to remain a decision . We also had to make agent activity trustworthy. Northstar tracks code-context and decision revisions, hides stale recommendations, requires exact source ranges for source-derived evidence, and prevents an agent recommendation from masquerading as a human selection. Accomplishments that we're proud of A coherent human-facing product experience, not only a tool-registration demo. Eight working WebMCP tools mapped to domain concepts instead of UI button clicks. Source-linked evidence with exact file and line ranges. Visible revision and analysis states that prevent stale conclusions from appearing current. A human confirmation boundary around the preferred improvement direction. A structured Improvement Plan that can be reviewed without reading an agent transcript. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when tools expose the meaning of an application rather than imitate mouse interactions. The agent does not need to guess how the UI works, and the human does not need to translate every judgment back into a prompt. Both can collaborate through the application's domain model while the interface preserves context and ownership. What's next for Northstar This submission is deliberately a controlled RAG prototype, not a universal code analyzer. Next steps would include persisted decisions, broader project-context adapters, reusable decision templates, and integrations with development tools—while keeping source edits and final direction explicitly under human control. title: AgenticRoom
pitch: Your room. Your agent. One shared canvas.
about_excerpt: Your room. Your agent. One shared canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Planning a room gets messy fast. Products live in one tab, measurements in another, and the budget usually ends up in a note or spreadsheet. By the time the pieces come together, the sofa may not fit or the total may no longer make sense. AgenticRoom started with a simple idea: let the person and the agent work on the same room instead of passing suggestions back and forth. What it does AgenticRoom puts a furniture catalog, an editable 3D room, budget tracking, and a shopping cart in one workspace. Start with the room you have, describe the room you want, or share an inspiration image with a compatible browser agent. The agent can inspect what is already in the room, search the catalog, place and move furniture, compare cheaper alternatives, check the layout, change the finishes, track the budget, add selected products to the cart, and save the design. Nothing happens in a hidden result. Every change appears on the same canvas and remains editable by the person. You can let the agent handle a full furnishing pass, step in to move one chair yourself, then ask it to finish the room without losing context. Why WebMCP fits A room plan is a chain of connected decisions. A sofa changes the remaining space and budget. A window limits placement. Replacing an expensive item should preserve its position while changing the total. Free-form recommendations alone are not enough. WebMCP gives the browser agent precise actions for those decisions. It can ask what fits, search within a price range, place a product in a valid zone, validate the layout, or add the selected marketplace pieces to the cart. The person makes the taste calls. The agent handles the searching, placement, and arithmetic. Both see the same room and the same result as it changes. How I built it I built AgenticRoom as a browser-only Next.js application using React, TypeScript, React Three Fiber, Three.js, and Zustand. I deliberately kept one source of truth: the human interface and the WebMCP tools call the same Zustand store actions and the same deterministic domain rules. The page registers 31 WebMCP tools through the browser's Model Context API: 11 read tools and 20 mutation tools. Those rules check furniture footprints, placement zones, doors and windows, locks, stock, prices, budgets, room resizing, saved designs, finishes, and cart behavior. If an action is invalid, it returns a structured error and leaves the room unchanged. There is no backend, account requirement, payment processing, API key, or remote runtime data. The furniture catalog and room rules are hand-authored and run entirely in the browser. Features Shared human-and-agent 3D room planning Image-inspired room direction Furniture search by category, style, color, material, price, dimensions, and stock Layout and opening-clearance checks Budget-aware furnishing and cheaper alternatives Editable room dimensions, openings, and finishes Integrated furniture catalog and shopping cart Saved room designs Privacy-conscious agent activity feed 31 structured WebMCP tools for reliable agent actions Testing The project has 135 deterministic domain tests covering placement, validation, pricing, alternatives, resizing, appearance, saved designs, and cart behavior. I also tested the deployed app in ChatGPT's in-app browser with a connected browser agent. No credentials are required. The README includes local setup instructions and reproducible WebMCP workflows. title: InfraTwin
pitch: InfraTwin lets engineers and WebMCP agents share one live network ChangePlan, using deterministic analysis and verified optimization to catch risky changes before production.
about_excerpt: InfraTwin lets engineers and WebMCP agents share one live network ChangePlan, using deterministic analysis and verified optimization to catch risky changes before production. Like Comment Story Updates Shared workspace: Engineer and WebMCP agent collaborate on the same live, browser-local ChangePlan before production. Remote failure: A planned outage plus 20% Payments growth exposes a remote Southeast–Central overload at 85% utilization. Human override: A human locks the proposed upgrade, invalidating the old mitigation and forcing the agent to replan. Verified design: 54 adaptive routing changes reduce modeled peak utilization from 85% to 67% with no new capacity or links. Scale validation: InfraTwin remains interactive on a 500-node, 1,200-link, 400-demand, 12-region network. Native WebMCP: document.modelContext exposes state-dependent WebMCP capabilities with provenance and optimizer diagnostics. Inspiration Network changes rarely fail in isolation. A maintenance outage in one region, expected traffic growth somewhere else, and a capacity restriction on another corridor can combine into a failure hundreds of miles away from the original change. That makes network change planning a coordination problem as much as a routing problem. Engineers have operational context that is difficult to encode completely in advance: a link may technically support an upgrade but be unavailable during a maintenance window, a corridor may be protected for business reasons, or an apparently cheap mitigation may conflict with another planned change. Traditional planning tools can model topology and run analyses, while AI assistants can explore ideas and explain results. The gap appears when the plan changes while the agent is reasoning. If the engineer selects a different resource, locks infrastructure, modifies traffic expectations, or invalidates an old proposal, the agent needs to operate on that exact new state rather than on a detached snapshot. InfraTwin started from a simple question: what if a network ChangePlan became a shared live artifact that an engineer and an agent could reason over together, while deterministic systems remained responsible for the engineering truth? The goal was not to build a chatbot attached to a topology viewer. It was to build an engineering workbench where human judgment, agent exploration, and machine-checkable computation each have a clear role. What InfraTwin does InfraTwin is a browser-native network change-planning, resilience, and optimization workbench. Engineers can model maintenance outages, restorations, traffic growth, individual demand changes, capacity upgrades, budgets, target utilization, and infrastructure that must not be modified, then analyze the consequences before those changes reach production. The underlying network remains separate from the editable ChangePlan . Proposed changes are therefore reversible and inspectable rather than silently modifying the canonical model. Analysis and optimization operate on the derived planned state while preserving provenance back to the original network and the human or agent action that created each change. The flagship workflow demonstrates one continuous human-agent decision loop. An engineer schedules a Northeast-to-Central backbone link for maintenance. A WebMCP agent sees that exact live plan and adds the expected 20% growth in Payments traffic. InfraTwin runs deterministic routing and capacity analysis and discovers that the combined change creates an overload on a different Southeast-to-Central corridor, reaching 85% utilization against an 80% target. The agent asks InfraTwin for the cheapest modeled mitigation and initially receives a capacity-oriented proposal. The engineer then supplies information the optimizer did not previously have: that corridor cannot be modified during this change window. The engineer locks it directly in the shared workspace. That edit immediately changes the valid design space. The old proposal becomes stale rather than remaining silently actionable, and the agent can no longer continue as if the earlier assumptions still held. The agent replans under the new human constraint. With adaptive routing enabled, InfraTwin finds a different design that changes 54 routing allocations, reduces modeled peak utilization from 85% to 67%, and requires no new capacity or new links. The proposal is not labeled safe or verified simply because an optimizer returned it. InfraTwin reconstructs the proposed design and checks its routing, demand conservation, capacity, utilization, restrictions, locks, budget, objective, scenario identity, and other declared constraints before it can receive a VERIFIED state. This division of responsibility is intentional: The human provides intent, operational knowledge, constraints, and approval. The agent explores the decision space and revises alternatives. InfraTwin supplies the deterministic evidence connecting them. Why WebMCP? WebMCP is central to InfraTwin rather than an alternate transport layer for backend APIs. The network and its unsaved ChangePlan exist inside the live browser workspace. Through native WebMCP capabilities, the agent can inspect the same current selection, plan state, human restrictions, analysis evidence, proposals, and verification freshness that the engineer is working with. That shared state matters because engineering intent changes continuously during planning. A conventional integration can give an agent a serialized representation of an application and expose operations over it, but synchronization becomes another problem to manage. The human may have selected a different link, edited a constraint, invalidated a proposal, or changed the current plan after the agent began reasoning. InfraTwin instead treats the browser workspace itself as the collaboration surface. When the engineer adds a lock, the agent sees the new restriction through the same application state. When a plan edit makes an earlier analysis obsolete, that evidence becomes stale. When the semantic state no longer supports a capability, InfraTwin can revoke that capability rather than leaving an invalid action available and hoping the model decides not to use it. That is one of the most important ideas behind the project: mathematical and product preconditions can become capability preconditions. For example, violation-specific tools only become useful when current analysis contains a violation. Proposal actions require a current proposal. Human edits can invalidate previously valid proposal actions. Long-running operations are also bound to the semantic revision they started from so that a result computed against an obsolete plan cannot later publish itself as authoritative. This creates a much stronger human-agent interaction than simply giving an agent buttons to press. The engineer can change the problem while the agent is working, and the agent continues inside the human's new decision boundary. What people and agents can do together InfraTwin is designed around complementary strengths rather than attempting to automate the engineer out of the loop. Humans are good at supplying context that may not exist in the mathematical model: which maintenance work is politically or operationally possible, which infrastructure must remain untouched, which services matter most, and whether a proposed tradeoff is acceptable. Agents are useful for exploring a large decision space, connecting evidence across views, requesting analyses, proposing mitigations, and quickly revisiting alternatives when assumptions change. The deterministic engine handles the part neither should improvise: routing, capacity calculations, resilience analysis, optimization, and verification. That means a workflow can evolve naturally: An engineer expresses intent. The agent explores the consequences. InfraTwin produces evidence. The engineer adds a constraint. The old answer becomes invalid. The agent replans. InfraTwin verifies the new proposal. The engineer retains final approval. Before WebMCP, implementing that interaction cleanly would typically require synchronizing human UI state with a separate agent-side representation or building a parallel backend state model. InfraTwin instead lets both participants operate through the same browser-local artifact. Evidence, not model guesses InfraTwin deliberately separates agent reasoning from engineering computation . The language model can inspect state, explain evidence, add or revise plan changes, request analysis, investigate violations, and explore mitigation alternatives. It does not calculate network feasibility by generating prose. InfraTwin's deterministic engine performs single-shortest-path and ECMP routing, utilization and capacity analysis, bottleneck and min-cut analysis, bounded N-1 contingency evaluation, and solver-backed optimization. Adaptive network design uses deterministic candidate paths and HiGHS LP/MILP optimization. Candidate routes are bounded and reproducibly gen

title: SHADOW
pitch: SHADOW lets AI agents simulate real-world actions, compare possible outcomes, and prove what they’re about to do before anything changes. It’s a transaction layer between AI intent and reality.
about_excerpt: SHADOW lets AI agents simulate real-world actions, compare possible outcomes, and prove what they’re about to do before anything changes. It’s a transaction layer between AI intent and reality. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents can already click buttons and change data. What bothered me was the step before that: how can I review the outcome before it becomes real? In software, I would create a branch, inspect the diff, and merge it after review. SHADOW brings that workflow to AI actions in the browser. What it does SHADOW gives an agent an isolated copy of the current state. The agent can change plans, reduce seats, or cancel subscriptions without touching Reality. In the demo, the fictional company ORBIT spends $184,300 per month on software. The agent reads usage, contracts, and dependencies, then builds different cost-saving proposals. Every change includes Proof showing the data behind it, its impact, and any blockers. Reality → Shadow → Proof → Human commit Only the user can commit a Shadow. The agent has no commit tool. How I built it I built SHADOW with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zod, and WebMCP . A deterministic projection engine calculates each future without changing the original state. I exposed 13 WebMCP tools for reading data, staging changes, creating branches, and comparing outcomes. The UI and the tools use the same application logic, so they cannot produce different results. The MVP runs locally in the browser with synthetic data and needs no accounts or API keys. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was making the separation between Shadow and Reality real, not just visual. I had to ensure that no agent-accessible path could commit a change. Unsafe proposals were another challenge. I did not want to hide them because they often contain useful information. Cancelling Miro, for example, reveals a $25,000 penalty . SHADOW keeps that proposal visible but blocks it from being committed. I also had to make projections reproducible and mark old Shadows as stale whenever Reality changes. Accomplishments that I’m proud of I am proud of what SHADOW deliberately cannot do. Its 13 tools let an agent inspect, stage, branch, and compare, but none can alter Reality. The full flow works end to end: an agent creates two alternatives, the user combines the best changes into a Hybrid, and a human commit produces a new Reality version and receipt. The Hybrid reduces monthly spending from $184,300 to $147,385 . What I learned I learned that human oversight works best when the system enforces it. A prompt alone is not a safety boundary. I also learned that useful Proof is not hidden model reasoning. It is the visible data, impact, and checks that let someone make an informed decision. What's next for SHADOW Next, I want to connect SHADOW to real SaaS tools and add shared workspaces, authentication, approval roles, and tamper-evident receipts. The larger goal is simple: version control for AI actions on the web .
