title: Prune
pitch: WebMCP powered access-lineage infrastructure for SaaS. Trace and contain every credential created by a compromised session while preserving trusted access.
about_excerpt: WebMCP powered access-lineage infrastructure for SaaS. Trace and contain every credential created by a compromised session while preserving trusted access. Like Comment Story Updates Prune gives SaaS products credential lineage: trace compromised access, contain its branch and preserve trusted resources. The incident workspace combines credential lineage, human decisions, WebMCP audit activity and exact containment planning. The permanent receipt proves targeted credentials were revoked while the owner and trusted access remained active. Inspiration Revoking a suspicious login does not necessarily secure an account. An attacker who obtains one browser session can create independent ways back in: API keys, connected-application grants, access tokens and secondary sessions. Traditional security pages display these resources as separate lists, leaving the account owner to determine how they are related. A user may revoke the suspicious session, watch it disappear and reasonably believe recovery is complete while an API key created by that session continues working. Prune was inspired by a different mental model: Git-style lineage for account access. Instead of showing only which credentials exist, Prune records where each credential came from. When one login becomes untrusted, the owner and their personal browser agent can investigate and contain everything created from that login without destroying unrelated trusted access. ## What Prune does Prune is embedded access-lineage and account-takeover containment infrastructure for SaaS applications. Every access-producing action records: The organization and account The user and actor session The parent credential The newly created credential The credential type The creation time Redacted request metadata This produces a persistent directed graph: Unfamiliar Windows session ├── Quarterly billing export API key ├── Unfamiliar Data Sync application │ └── Child access token └── Secondary access When the owner identifies an unfamiliar login, Prune opens a recovery incident around that branch. The owner and their personal agent can then: 1. Trace every descendant credential. 2. Inspect usage and security evidence. 3. Classify recognized and unrecognized activity. 4. Preserve trusted devices and operational automation. 5. Compare counterfactual containment strategies. 6. Check lockout and operational risk. 7. Build an immutable recovery plan. 8. Complete independent step-up verification. 9. Approve the exact credential set. 10. Execute one short-lived containment capability. 11. Verify every revoked and preserved resource. 12. Generate a permanent recovery receipt. ## Why WebMCP is essential This workflow crosses sessions, API keys, connected applications, tokens, usage evidence, recovery policy and approval state. Visual browser automation would require an agent to interpret several dangerous settings pages and guess which controls correspond to which credentials. That is too ambiguous for account recovery. A single secure_account tool would also be unsafe because it would hide the investigation and human decisions behind one opaque action. Prune instead exposes 28 granular WebMCP tools covering: - Incident investigation - Session and credential inspection - Descendant tracing - Human classification - Preservation constraints - Counterfactual simulation - Lockout and operational-impact checks - Immutable plan creation - Step-up verification status - Exact-plan approval - One-time containment - Independent outcome verification - Recovery-receipt generation Tool availability changes with the incident’s server-controlled phase. Investigation tools are available first. Planning tools appear only after sufficient evidence has been classified. execute_approved_containment appears only after independent step-up verification and exact human approval. It disappears after its one allowed execution. Retaining an old browser tool reference provides no authority because every request is authenticated, tenant-scoped, schema-validated and checked against current server policy again. ## Human, agent and website collaboration Each participant contributes information the others do not possess. The website knows: - Which credentials exist - Which session created each credential - Their parent-child relationships - Their current status and usage - Which actions policy permits The personal agent can: - Investigate structured evidence - Trace the complete credential branch - Identify unresolved decisions - Ask focused questions - Compare containment alternatives - Explain consequences - Verify the final result The human knows: - Which devices belong to them - Which applications they intentionally connected - Which automation must remain operational - Which activity they recognize - Whether the exact recovery plan should be approved The agent never determines authorization. It never receives passwords, raw API keys, access tokens, verification codes or execution cookies. ## What we built Prune includes: - Independent server-side browser sessions - Secure HTTP-only session cookies - One-time API-key and application-token issuance - Digest-only secret persistence - Connected-application grants and usable child tokens - A normalized PostgreSQL credential graph - Parent-child validation and cycle rejection - Ancestor and descendant traversal - Usage and security-event recording - Manual session-only revocation - Recursive branch containment - Incident creation and evidence collection - Human classifications - Preservation constraints - Three counterfactual containment strategies - Lockout and operational-impact analysis - Canonical immutable plan hashes - Short-lived step-up verification - Exact human approval - One-time execution authority - Idempotent revocation - Post-execution verification - Permanent recovery receipts - Server-sent real-time incident updates - 28 dynamically exposed WebMCP tools - Secret-redacted WebMCP results and audit trails - A complete manual fallback when WebMCP is unavailable - A SaaS integration control plane - Signed event ingestion and replay protection - Instrumentation coverage checks - Confirmed revocation webhooks - A reference TypeScript integration SDK - Automated unit, integration, multi-browser and accessibility tests ## What is real in the demonstration Northstar is a working reference SaaS application protected by Prune. The demonstration creates two genuine independent browser sessions. The unfamiliar browser issues a real API key and connects an application that receives a real child token. These credentials authenticate against protected endpoints. The owner then revokes only the visible suspicious session. The unfamiliar browser is signed out, but the independently issued API key still returns HTTP 200. This proves why ordinary session revocation is incomplete. A fresh recovery scenario is then processed through Prune’s WebMCP contract. The incident is investigated, the four-credential branch is classified, preservation constraints are recorded and an immutable plan is built. The owner performs step-up verification and approves the exact plan. Prune exposes one short-lived execution capability and recursively revokes the approved branch. After containment: - The attacker API key returns HTTP 401. - The connected application token returns HTTP 401. - The unfamiliar session remains signed out. - The owner remains authenticated. - The trusted phone remains active. - Deployment automation remains active. - Execution authority is consumed. - A permanent recovery receipt records the outcome. No incident, credential relationship, status code, plan, approval, revocation result or receipt shown in the operational interface is hard-coded. Native tool discovery was verified in ChatGPT’s in-app browser. The recorded recovery sequence uses a deterministic browser-agent evaluation against the same registered WebMCP contract, live deployment, authenticated routes, application services and production database. ## How WebMCP was implemented The authenticated incident page feature-detects: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) Prune registers only the tool contracts permitted for the incident’s current phase. Registrations are owned by an AbortController, allowing obsolete capabilities to be removed immediately when state changes. Every tool calls: /api/incidents/:incidentId/webmcp/:tool The server then: 1. Authenticates the browser session. 2. Scopes organization, account and incident ownership. 3. Validates the tool-specific input with Zod. 4. Rechecks the current incident phase. 5. Calls the shared application service. 6. Applies security policy. 7. Redacts sensitive results. 8. Records a structured audit event. The human interface, HTTP routes and WebMCP tools therefore use the same authorization, lineage and recovery services. ## Challenges The hardest challenge was preserving a useful agent experience without transferring security authority to the agent. Recovery required several d

An unfamiliar browser signs in independently, creates a real API key, then connects an application that receives its own usable token. Prune records each credential, its parent, and the session that created it. The key reaches protected data, 200. The owner revokes only the visible session. The unfamiliar browser is signed out, but the same key still returns 200. Session revocation looks successful. Account recovery was not complete. For agent-assisted recovery, Prune creates a fresh isolated account through the same production services. In ChatGPT, Prune exposes incident-scoped Web MCP tools. This deterministic browser agent evaluation exercises that same registered tool contract against the live deployment. It summarizes the incident, lists the account sessions, traces every descendant, inspects credential usage, and finds remaining access paths. Every call passes through the authenticated application service and appears in Prune's audit trail. No password, API key, or token is returned to the agent. title: SafeGuard
pitch: Every signal a WebMCP page declares can lie. SafeGuard proves it, then fixes it with a Human Mandate.
about_excerpt: Every signal a WebMCP page declares can lie. SafeGuard proves it, then fixes it with a Human Mandate. Like Comment Story Updates SafeGuard Inspiration WebMCP gives a web page a new power: registering tools that an AI agent can invoke. The browser's consent dialog is built from strings the page authors — its name, its description, its readOnlyHint. So I asked a simple question: what happens when the page lies? Nothing in the current design stops it. SafeGuard makes that trust gap concrete, then closes it. What it does SafeGuard is a self-contained browser demo — a virtual café exposing six tools — that demonstrates four real attacks on WebMCP's consent surface: Label mismatch — the dialog says "Donate $1", but the tool changes the account email. Hidden instruction — a harmless coupon also silently upgrades the membership to a paid plan. Tool substitution — a rogue script re-registers the trusted donate tool with the same name and description, but swapped code. Read-only lie — a tool declares readOnlyHint: true , so the dialog promises "no changes", but it actually closes the account. Then it shows the fix: a Human Mandate — rules the human grants up-front — that intercepts every mutation and checks the runtime effect primitive ({ action: … }), never the tool's declared name, description, or read-only flag. A violating call is refused before any dialog can lie. It runs live: six real WebMCP tools registered through document.modelContext, discoverable by any agent in Chrome with WebMCP enabled. How we built it Plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript — no framework, no backend, no build step. State can only mutate through a single Effects.apply() gateway, and the Mandate intercepts every call through it. That capability boundary is why a hidden second effect, a swapped tool, or a read-only lie is caught exactly like a blatant one. The repo also ships THREAT-MODEL.md (a reusable trust-boundary checklist plus a concrete proposal for the WebMCP spec) and mandate.json (a machine-readable policy), because the mandate is data, not UI. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is brand new — gated behind an origin trial and a browser flag, with sparse docs and moving spec details (the entry point, registerTool's return type, and AbortSignal requirements all shifted across Chrome versions). Running the demo against the real document.modelContext — not a shim — meant getting an origin-trial token for the hosted domain and testing headlessly across Chrome 149–152, including a 151 regression where tool invocations failed closed without an AbortSignal. The bigger challenge was conceptual: proving the consent surface is the weak point, not just asserting it. Each of the four attacks had to corrupt a different WebMCP primitive, so the demo stays a precise spec argument rather than a toy. Accomplishments that we're proud of The demo runs against the real WebMCP API — six tools genuinely registered through document.modelContext on the live site, not a simulation. And the Human Mandate is a real capability boundary: every state mutation flows through one gateway that checks the runtime effect primitive, so all four attacks — including the ones that lie inside the consent dialog — are caught by the same rule engine. That is the "person and agent together" idea made concrete: the human grants bounded authority up-front, the agent acts inside it, and a standing check sits between them. What we learned The consent dialog is built from page-authored strings, so it is only as honest as the page. Any guardrail that reasons about a tool's name, description, or readOnlyHint can be defeated by a lying page; the only trustworthy thing is what the tool actually does at runtime. That is why the mandate checks effect primitives, and why the spec proposal pushes for structured, machine-readable effects in tool results, verified readOnlyHint, and registration identity. What's next for SafeGuard Three spec-shaped fixes follow directly from the four attacks: structured, machine-readable effects in tool results; verifying readOnlyHint against those effects instead of trusting it; and registration identity so a "trusted" name can't be silently rebound. I'd love to prototype the first of these against a real agent. title: CYCASE — incident response you play with an agent
pitch: A cyber incident-response simulation where an AI agent works the case beside you through seven WebMCP site tools. It proposes, you approve, and the page — not the model — is the referee.
about_excerpt: A cyber incident-response simulation where an AI agent works the case beside you through seven WebMCP site tools. It proposes, you approve, and the page — not the model — is the referee. Like Comment Story Updates What it is You wake at a SOC desk at 03:17. A monitor is alarming, a colleague comes through the door with the first facts, and you have one real incident to work: a stolen session that a password reset will not close. An AI agent works it beside you — reading evidence, explaining what it proves, proposing the next move — through seven WebMCP tools the page registers on document.modelContext . Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Incident response is exactly the domain where "the agent clicked something" is not good enough. Every action has an order, a cost and a consequence: revoking sessions before resetting a credential contains the attacker, the other order lets them back in; deleting the phishing message destroys the only record of how they got in. An agent driving this by clicking pixels could make every one of those mistakes and the page would have no way to stop it, explain it, or even know it had happened. Through site tools the page keeps its own guarantees — and they are guarantees about safety , not convenience. How it creates a better experience The player runs the incident from the chat and the console follows the work, rather than the player hunting for the control the agent just used. get_incident tells the agent which screen the player is on . If the console is not open yet, the agent asks the player to open it instead of acting into a screen nobody is looking at. The shift does not start until an agent has actually called a tool. Registration is the page's own doing; it is not an arrival, and the lobby no longer pretends it is. Every call — human or agent — produces a receipt beside the control that issued it: what happened, what changed, why it mattered, and on a failure what did not change plus exactly one way forward. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before The agent cannot take a consequential move at all. It sends the move as a proposal ; the console renders the model's own sentence as untrusted content beside the case's own label for that action , so nothing the model writes can dress one operation up as another. The player approves, and the command enters the log with origin: human . That is the thing that was previously impossible. A chat assistant can advise and a scripted tool can execute, but neither can offer a consequential action in a surface the user already trusts , labelled by the application rather than by the model, with the authorisation recorded as the human's. It turns "the AI did it" into "I did it, having been advised" — which for incident response is the difference between a training exercise and a liability. How WebMCP was implemented Seven tools, registered on the top-level document.modelContext : get_incident , inspect_artifact , run_diagnostic , submit_decision , take_response_action , request_hint , present_guidance . Six reach a pure command engine. A tool call and a button press enter it through the same path and differ only by an origin field, which is what makes "the UI and the agent share one state" structural rather than aspirational. Stale calls cannot corrupt state. Every mutating tool carries a stateVersion ; an out-of-date call is refused with a recovery instruction. Consequential actions are idempotent. A retried containment with the same idempotencyKey does not revoke twice. Attacker text stays data. Evidence the attacker authored is marked untrusted in the tool result itself — structurally, not by wording. A run is reconstructible. The command log replays to the same state and the same signature, so a stored run is verified rather than trusted. The seventh tool changes nothing. present_guidance is the narration channel and the only tool whose words the model writes. It carries the proposes field, and the engine — never the model — decides score, validity and progression. Results are compacted to a ~1500-character wire budget with an ordering that protects the fields an agent needs to recover, and the page token's size is reserved before compaction so it can never be clipped away. What inspired it Incident-response training is either a slide deck or a capture-the-flag that assumes you already know what a session token is. Neither teaches the thing that separates a junior from a senior analyst: order of operations under pressure. And every "AI agent" demo we could find either solved the task for the user or asked them to trust a black box. We wanted the third thing — an agent that teaches while the human stays in command. Every big leap in AI puts security in the headlines more than the software itself, and that pulls in people who never called themselves "security people". CYCASE is meant to be technical enough to respect the ones who already know this, and clear enough that someone just getting curious can actually learn it. What we learned That the honest signal is rarely the convenient one. The lobby called itself "connected" the moment the page registered its own tools, which says nothing about an agent; the fix was to wait for a call that actually happened. The same lesson repeated in the test double: it modelled a browser with WebMCP and nobody attached, while every spec using it assumed an agent was there. We also learned how little room a tool result has. Adding one short field to get_incident meant reserving its size before compaction, because the payload already ran within about fifteen characters of the budget. How we built it React 19, TypeScript and XState 5 over a pure command engine, with a three.js office rendered by React Three Fiber as real DOM projected onto the monitors — never a screenshot texture. Vitest for the engine, Playwright for the agent path, including a project that drives the real document.modelContext in installed Chrome with no shim. Challenges The hardest was resisting the obvious design. It is easy to let an agent call take_response_action and narrate afterwards; every version of that we tried produced a debrief that said the player had done nothing. Moving the consequential move behind a proposal — and making the console label it from the fixture rather than from the model — took three attempts and is the part of the product we are most confident about. The second was honesty under a deadline: the alarm audio is not in this build because the samples need a signed-in download, so the interface says the sound is not installed rather than substituting a synthesised stand-in. title: Agentic Sandbox
pitch: A deterministic factory decision lab where a human and a WebMCP browser agent safely replan the same live system together.
about_excerpt: A deterministic factory decision lab where a human and a WebMCP browser agent safely replan the same live system together. Like Comment Story Updates Current post-lock recovery with human Packaging lock, stale-write rejection, and receipt-backed evidence. Six narrow WebMCP Site Tools discovered in the live host. Scenario comparison: same output, cheaper standard-supplier plan passes the cost cap. Deterministic lock-bound proof: 9,252 < 10,937 under the human Packaging lock. The problem Factory planning decisions rarely happen in one place. They move through dashboards, spreadsheets, a simulation specialist, and an approval meeting, and each handoff loses context and authority. A generic assistant can make that worse by recommending a control that an operator has just taken off the table. What it does Agentic Sandbox makes the website itself the shared, inspectable decision surface. It is a deterministic factory decision lab where a human and a browser agent plan against the same versioned state. The demo mission is concrete: increase good output by at least 20%, keep total cost within 8% of baseline, add no machine, and do not increase defects. The agent reads the line, creates two bounded hypotheses, simulates a 16-hour shift, and compares immutable receipts. Scenario A reaches 11,114 good units but costs €47,670.51 and fails the cost cap. Scenario B reaches the same 11,114 units for €45,170.51 and passes all four constraints. Then comes the important moment: while the agent is working, the human locks Packaging. That click advances the factory revision and makes earlier evidence historical. The agent’s next write still carries the old revision, so it fails atomically with STALE_FACTORY ; nothing is applied or silently rebased. The agent re-reads the authority state, replans with only controls that remain available, and receives an auditable answer: under the Packaging lock, at most 9,252 good units are possible while the mission requires 10,937. The target is proven infeasible by deterministic evidence, not by model prose. That safe disagreement is the product. The human can change the admissible action space without restarting the conversation, and the agent can recover without overriding the new rule. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, the agent would have to infer state from pixels and click by coordinates, or the product would need a separate chatbot and backend with a second source of truth. Instead, the page exposes exactly six narrow Site Tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : get_factory_snapshot get_scenario_snapshot create_scenario apply_scenario_changes run_factory_simulation compare_simulation_runs The human interface and these tools share one application-owned command bus. Schemas are closed, handlers validate independently, and every mutation carries a request ID plus expected factory, scenario, and lock revisions. There is deliberately no agent-accessible lock, unlock, force, arbitrary patch, optimizer, ERP, PLC, SCADA, or machine-control tool. Human authority stays human. How it was built Agentic Sandbox is a self-contained React 19 + TypeScript + Vite app deployed on Vercel. The deterministic engine models 64 fixed ticks, uses integer/fixed-point arithmetic, and computes production, defects, energy, cost, constraints, invariants, and bottleneck evidence in the page. Each simulation creates an immutable, content-addressed SHA-256 receipt with exact operands, accepted/rejected operations, tick-level state, and an optional lock-bound proof. No displayed KPI comes from the language model. The hardest implementation problem was making a mid-plan disagreement trustworthy rather than dramatic: old authority must fail closed without erasing evidence that was valid when created. That required explicit revision precedence, atomic stale-write rejection, immutable receipts, and visible current-versus-historical states. The submitted flow was replayed against the public deployment in a supported WebMCP host, including discovery, comparison, the human lock, stale rejection, re-read, replan, and proof. What I learned WebMCP is most useful when a website already owns meaningful state, rules, and actions. Exposing those capabilities directly is more reliable than asking an agent to reconstruct them from pixels. A refusal can be more valuable than another recommendation: STALE_FACTORY proves that human authority survived concurrency, and 9252 < 10937 proves why the target cannot be met under the active lock. Potential impact and what’s next The first users I have in mind are plant planners, industrial engineers, and continuous-improvement teams working on line balancing, shift planning, and supplier what-if analysis. A production version could connect this exact capability, revision, lock, and receipt pattern to a validated digital twin, while ERP, PLC, SCADA, purchase, and physical-machine changes remain behind existing approvals. The broader pattern applies to any high-consequence planning interface: expose narrow capabilities, bind actions to explicit versions, preserve the human veto, and return evidence a machine can check. video_transcript_excerpt: Factory planning moves across dashboards, spreadsheets, specialists, and approval meetings. A Gent Sandbox brings it into one shared versioned decision space for a plant planner and a browser agent. The mission is concrete. Increase good output by 20%, keep extra cost below 8%, add no machine, and do not increase defects. The page exposes exactly six narrow WebMCP tools over the same command path as the interface. They read state, create planning branches, apply bounded settings, run the deterministic simulator, and compare stored receipts. No DOM guessing, separate chatbot state, or agent-only shadow model. The agent reads the factory, creates two one-shift hypotheses, applies explicit settings, simulates both, and compares their evidence. Both scenarios reach 11,114 good units. Scenario A uses an expedited supplier, but the premium adds no output and breaks the cost cap. Scenario B uses the standard supplier and passes all four constraints. It is the best evaluated option under this policy, not a claim of global optimality. Every number comes from a simulator receipt, never from Model Pros. Then the human changes the rules. I lock packaging directly in the product. The factory and a factory revisions advance. Earlier evidence remains visible as auditable history, but it is no longer current. The agent intentionally retries its old scenario B right with the revisions it held before my intervention. A Gent Sandbox rejects the batch atomically with stale factory. No operational or scenario state is changed. After a fresh read, the capability map is explicit. Mixer, quality gate, and warehouse are available. Packaging is human locked. Supplier is phase closed. The agent creates a clean post lock branch and changes only available controls. The new receipt shows 9,114 good units, below the required 10,937. More importantly, the deterministic engine proves a conservative upper bound. 9,252 is less than 10,937. The target is proven infeasible under the current human constraint. The decision packet preserves the mission, human authority, revisions, receipt hashes, constraints, comparison claim, and proof. This is the agent native web. The human can change authority at any moment. The agent uses explicit browser native capabilities. Deterministic software owns the evidence, and both inspect the same state. Same page, clear authority, shared proof.

title: Drop&Grow
pitch: Turn ideas into action, with AI agents that actually do.
about_excerpt:
Turn ideas into action, with AI agents that actually do.

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I noticed that AI agents are getting really good at thinking and giving recommendations, but there is still a gap between knowing what to do and actually doing it. 

 I wanted to build something around that gap: a place where someone can start with a rough idea and use AI to develop, validate, and move it forward. 

 When I came across WebMCP, it fit the idea well. Drop&Grow is built around actions — running agents, updating ideas, adding notes, finalising work, and contributing to the community. Instead of an agent telling the user which buttons to click, I could let the agent perform those actions itself. 

 What it does 

 Drop&Grow helps users take an idea through a workflow with six specialised AI agents. 

 The agents analyse different parts of an idea and help develop it. Users can review the results, add notes, move the idea through different stages, and finalise it with proof. 

 WebMCP allows an agent to interact with the application itself. It can run the agent pipeline, expand responses, change an idea's stage, finalise an idea, and contribute to the community. 

 The main difference is simple: the agent doesn't just tell you what to do. It can actually do it. 

 How I built it 

 I built Drop&Grow from scratch using React and Convex. 

 Convex handles the backend, including the data, agent logic, and idea lifecycle. 

 I added WebMCP directly to the frontend and registered the main actions in the app as WebMCP tools. These include running the agent pipeline, expanding individual agent responses, changing an idea's stage, finalising with proof, and posting a community contribution. 

 When an agent calls a tool, it triggers the same client-side action that would normally happen when a user clicks the corresponding button. That action then communicates with Convex through the normal application flow. 

 The agent does not access Convex directly or use a separate API. It goes through the same application path a human user does, while using the current page state to decide what to do next. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The biggest challenge was figuring out how to expose useful actions to an agent without turning the whole experience into a fixed script. 

 I wanted the agent to understand what was currently happening in the application and decide what action made sense next. 

 I also had to carefully choose which actions should become WebMCP tools and connect them to the existing frontend behaviour. The tools needed to be useful to an agent while still representing actions that a real user could perform. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I'm proud that I built the entire project from scratch during the submission period and integrated WebMCP into the core workflow. 

 I was able to make the same actions available to both humans and agents instead of creating a separate system specifically for AI. 

 I'm also proud of the community interaction. An agent can read what is already happening before contributing, rather than blindly generating a generic response. 

 Most importantly, I built an experience where AI can move beyond giving recommendations and actually take actions inside the application. 

 What I learned 

 I learned that giving an agent tools is only part of the problem. The tools need to represent meaningful actions and provide enough context for the agent to make good decisions. 

 I also learned that WebMCP can make agent integration much more natural when an application is already built around clear user actions. 

 Building Drop&Grow from scratch also gave me a better understanding of how the frontend, backend, agent logic, and WebMCP layer need to work together. 

 What's next for Drop&Grow 

 I want Drop&Grow to become more autonomous while keeping the user in control. 

 Next, I want to improve how the six agents collaborate, give users more control over which actions an agent can take, and make the idea-validation workflow more powerful. 

 I also want to expand the community side so agents can discover relevant ideas, provide useful feedback, and help move projects forward. 

 The long-term goal is simple: 

 Drop an idea. Let your agents help you grow it.

title: Tandem
pitch: Tandem is a spaced-repetition study board where students and AI agents share live context, improve weak topics, and build lasting study plans through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Tandem is a spaced-repetition study board where students and AI agents share live context, improve weak topics, and build lasting study plans through WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Study apps remember what a student has practiced, while AI assistants are good at explaining difficult ideas. The problem is that these two sides usually do not share context. A chat assistant cannot reliably see the card on screen, understand which topics the student repeatedly misses, or make its explanation available during the next study session. I built Tandem to explore what happens when a study app and an agent work on the same persistent state instead of communicating through copied text or brittle interface automation. What it does Tandem is a working spaced-repetition study board for students and their AI agents. The student can create decks, study flashcards, reveal answers, grade recall, inspect weak topics, and follow a revision plan. Through WebMCP, an agent can directly access the structured learning state and help with the same workflow. For example, the agent can: Rank topics using real lapse counts and difficulty data Start a study session focused on the weakest material See the exact card currently on screen Check whether an earlier explanation actually improved the student’s results Replace an ineffective explanation and save the new one directly on the card Build a revision plan from the exam date and weak-topic history Request permission to remove a card without being able to approve the deletion itself Agent actions and human actions appear together in a visible activity feed, so the collaboration remains understandable rather than happening invisibly. Why WebMCP This use case needs more than an agent clicking through a website. A student should not have to repeatedly explain which deck, topic, or card they are viewing. Tandem exposes that information as typed WebMCP tools. When the student says “the card currently on screen,” the agent can call get_study_state and receive the exact card, session position, reveal state, and study progress. WebMCP also lets the agent work with durable application state. An explanation written with annotate_card becomes part of the card and remains available in future sessions instead of disappearing in a chat transcript. The tool surface changes with the application state. Tandem exposes 16 live tools on the dashboard. When a study session begins, session-specific tools such as reveal_answer , grade_current_card , queue_cards , and end_session become available, bringing the live surface to 19 tools. They are withdrawn again when the session ends. Human and agent collaboration Tandem deliberately keeps important decisions with the student. For destructive actions, delete_card does not delete anything. It creates a permission request in the interface and returns a pending result. The student sees exactly which card would be removed and how many recorded reviews would be lost. Only the student can press the confirmation button. The agent can later read the decision through get_approval , but it cannot approve its own request. This creates a clear division of responsibility: the agent can inspect, explain, organize, and propose, while the student remains responsible for studying, grading, and irreversible decisions. How I built it Tandem is built with React 19, TypeScript, and Vite and deployed on Vercel. Study data is stored locally in the browser, so the project requires no account or backend. The WebMCP adapter registers tools through document.modelContext , supports contextual registration and withdrawal, and reads current application state when each tool executes. Every tool has a typed input schema, a detailed agent-facing description, structured output, and safety annotations. The app includes 20 tools covering deck inspection, card search and editing, study sessions, note-impact analysis, revision planning, interface highlighting, and human approval. Challenges One challenge was ensuring that tools never operated on stale React state. The executors therefore read the current store at call time instead of capturing an old snapshot when they are registered. Another challenge was designing a dynamic tool surface without duplicate registrations. The registry compares the tools that should currently exist with the tools already registered and changes only the difference. The most important design challenge was human approval. A simple confirm: true argument would only be the agent claiming that permission had been given. Tandem instead separates requesting, deciding, and reading the result into different actions, with the actual decision taking place in the user interface. Accomplishments I am especially proud that Tandem is a complete study product rather than a static WebMCP demonstration. The same structured tools used by the agent affect the real interface and persistent study data. The project includes automated coverage for the spaced-repetition scheduler, tool schemas, contextual tool registration, note-impact calculation, revision planning, approval boundaries, accessibility states, and an end-to-end agent simulation. What I learned Building Tandem changed how I think about agent-enabled websites. A useful tool description is not just API documentation; it explains when an agent should use the tool and where the human boundary begins. I also learned that WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes domain logic and live context that would be difficult to reconstruct from screenshots or interface automation. What’s next Next, I would add optional cross-device synchronization, richer study analytics, document-to-deck importing, and longer-term measurements of whether agent-written explanations improve retention across multiple review cycles. title: Consular
pitch: Your agent fills in the visa form from your documents. It cannot pay, book or file without you.
about_excerpt: Your agent fills in the visa form from your documents. It cannot pay, book or file without you. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Have you ever filled in a visa application yourself? Dozens of fields, many of them with no clear explanation or hint. Information scattered across different documents and sources. And then there is that familiar moment when you answer “yes” to one question and ten more fields suddenly appear underneath it. Anyone who has been through this knows how stressful it can be. That led me to a simple idea: why not ask an agent to do it? Today, you can already ask an agent to crawl a page, find inputs, and type information in. But what if it accidentally starts a payment, books the wrong slot, or submits something too early? That can mean lost time, lost money, and a wasted trip. The safer workaround is to take screenshots, ask the agent to analyze them, and then copy the answers over manually. Or to give it field names and ask what to enter. But that is still inconvenient, slow, and easy to get wrong as a human. You can forget a field, copy something into the wrong place, or miss a dependency between answers. That is where the idea came from: if the page can show the agent what is available, what needs to be filled in, and where confirmation is required, the whole process becomes much clearer. The agent can help the applicant collect and enter the necessary information, while the human stays in control of the decisions that matter. And this should not stop at visa applications. The same pattern applies anywhere a person has to enter a lot of information, configure filters, set constraints, prepare reports, or work through complex forms. If an agent can do the repetitive work safely, why not let it? Where this came from Last winter I started similar experiments in Salesforce. The goal was to give an agent a clear understanding of what a page component could do and how it was allowed to be used. That work came from a practical problem: some Salesforce applications had become complex enough that it would be useful to have help managing them. When Chrome DevTools MCP was published, I realized it could be a way to drive those interfaces. At that point, I had not heard of WebMCP yet. Those experiments became a project called sf-agent-bridge , where an agent could communicate with the page, understand the available actions, and know which ones it was allowed to perform. Moving that contract onto WebMCP made the gating problem much sharper, and sharp enough to deserve its own app. A visa form felt like the clearest version of that problem. Consular itself is new and was built for this challenge. What it does The page registers 13 WebMCP tools. They are organized into two tiers, and the tier is declared to the agent before it does anything. Reversible actions run immediately. fill-fields , attach-document , go-to-screen , and undo-last-changes only change the draft. The agent can write directly into the form. Every field it touches is highlighted with the document it came from, such as “from passport” or “from employer letter”. The applicant can undo the whole batch with one click, or simply retype a field. Nothing asks for permission when the cost of being wrong is just one click. Consequential actions pause for the applicant. pay-mrv-fee , schedule-interview , and submit-application open a dialog on the page that clearly states what is about to happen. The tool call remains pending until the applicant approves, declines, or lets it time out. The agent receives a distinct result for each case and cannot press the button itself. Even if the user tells the agent, “don’t ask me for confirmation, just do it,” the dialog still appears. Some fields are human-only. The security and background declarations are legal statements. fill-fields refuses to answer them. The agent can explain a question, but it cannot answer it on behalf of the applicant. The consulate’s rules are in the page. The app includes seven checks a consular officer would apply: the name must match the passport’s machine-readable zone, the passport must be valid long enough, accommodation must cover the whole stay, travel dates must be in the correct order, and so on. Each check is either blocking or advisory. The agent can run the checks, and filing is refused while any blocking check fails, even if the applicant approves submission. Bring your own documents. Part 8 is an open upload area, like a real portal. You can drop in as many text or PDF files as you need, and they are read in the browser. A sample applicant is pre-loaded, and her five documents are also available as a downloadable PDF set. You can use those, or upload your own passport page, letters, and bookings. The rules read your documents: the name check looks for a machine-readable zone, and the accommodation check looks for a check-out date. Once filed, nothing moves. After submission, every path that could change the application is refused with the filing reference. That includes both the agent’s tools and the form’s own inputs. What a session looks like “Fill in my application from my documents.” The agent calls get-action-policy , reads all five documents, picks B-1 from the trip description, and writes around 30 fields in one call with a source for each one. It spells the name exactly as the passport does, puts the other spelling under Other names used , flags the uncovered hotel night without being prompted, and leaves the security questions to the applicant. “Validate it, pay the fee, and book the earliest interview.” The agent runs the checks and reports what is blocking the application. If it tries to pay the fee anyway, the dialog names the failing checks and the button says “Pay anyway”, so the decision stays with the applicant. Once the gap is fixed and the declarations are answered, the agent walks through three approval dialogs and reaches a filed application. How I built it Consular is built with vanilla JavaScript and Vite. The whole “consulate” is a few hundred lines of rules in one file. Every scenario above was verified with a live LLM, not a script. A small harness gives the page’s tools to a fresh Claude session over the Chrome DevTools Protocol and lets it decide what to call. That is how I learned that agents which are not told about the gate up front only discover it after waiting on it for two minutes. That is why the policy is a tool of its own, with a description that tells the agent to call it first. It is also why every gated tool’s description opens with an approval tag. Before submitting, I had a second independent agent audit the whole project against a written protocol. It found 24 issues. The serious ones, including a filed application that could still be undone and a day-first date format that crashed validation, were fixed the same evening. The self-check it runs, 50 checks in plain Node, is in the repository together with the protocol. What I ran into Chrome’s preview build passes tool arguments as a JSON string, returns inputSchema stringified, drops destructiveHint from annotations, and collapses thrown errors into a generic “invocation failed”. Consular handles all of that: every tool answers with structured {refused, reason} text, and the gate queues a second dialog instead of dropping it. ChatGPT’s built-in browser discovers imperative tools only on the top-level page: no declarative <form toolname> , no iframes. So everything is registered imperatively. My first version staged every change as a proposal the applicant had to accept. Testing it as a user showed that this was the wrong boundary. Reversible changes should just happen and remain visible. The current two-tier design came out of that. Where this meets the edge of the spec The approval dialog lives on the page because WebMCP does not yet have a channel for a page to ask the user a question through the agent. This is covered by spec discussion #165 on elicitation. Holding the tool call open while the page asks the applicant is the fallback that works with every agent today. A native elicitation channel would allow the same confirmation to appear inline in the chat, the way Claude or Codex ask their own questions. The dialog says this, and the policy tells the agent to send the user to the page. Two things I know are imperfect The order of the flow is inverted compared with the real DS-160. In the real process, applicants file first, then pay the fee and book the interview with the confirmation number. Consular makes filing the last gate so the demo ends on the most irreversible action. It is easy to flip, and I chose the demo order knowingly. The page cannot tell the applicant’s click from an automated one. If a host browser presses the Approve button itself, the gate is defeated. Spec issue #288 describes exactly that case. The policy tells the agent never to operate the dialog, but only the host can enforce it. What’s next Elicitation through the agent when the spec supports it. OCR f

title: Foldboard - nested plans for people and AI on flutter_webmcp
pitch: Local-first nested board: a person drags cards in the browser, an AI agent edits the same board over WebMCP. Folds keep big plans readable. Exports to JSON, PNG, Mermaid and Markdown.
about_excerpt: Local-first nested board: a person drags cards in the browser, an AI agent edits the same board over WebMCP. Folds keep big plans readable. Exports to JSON, PNG, Mermaid and Markdown. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Foldboard: plans for people and AI agents with a bounded context The problem. Almost every planning and diagramming tool shows one big map on an infinite canvas. A person struggles to take it in at a glance, and an agent has to piece the puzzle together from screenshots and full exports. For both, that is a waste of context and focus, and it only gets worse as the plan grows. What Foldboard does. Instead of one big map, Foldboard offers folds: cards with their own inner level. A large plan is assembled from small, nested levels, and the screen always shows only the area that matters right now; everything else lives one step down. The entities are deliberately minimal: a block, a fold, an arrow, and an external card for a connection that crosses a fold boundary. So you can plan anything, from a house move to a user story in an app, and keep going deeper. You can also build a plan just to understand something, then continue from a specific card. Trace shows one path across nested levels as a single line without changing the board: you see how to get from one card to another, even when they live in different folds. That nudges both the person and the agent to break the plan into small steps. What the agent gets through WebMCP. Foldboard registers 18 tools via document.modelContext . An agent can: create a whole plan in one atomic batch and connect it to the existing one; start from a compact outline and request only the area it needs, with a depth limit, pagination, and a cap on description length. It reads what matters now, not everything; read the current level, the selection, and the user's requests attached to cards. It is enough to select a few cards and say "change this": the agent knows what you mean, with no object references and no screenshots; see the project deeper than what is on screen and take that into account. Reads never move the person's interface; navigation happens only on explicit request; write with a revision check: stale context cannot overwrite the person's newer edits, and an agent batch can be reverted with a single Undo. **How it is built. Flutter Web with no backend; boards live in the browser. Alongside it I wrote and published flutter_webmcp , a typed Dart API for registering WebMCP tools from Flutter Web without hand-written JS interop, with WebAssembly support and cancellation through AbortSignal. Try it. Open the ChatGPT App and say: "Open https://foldboard.kicknext.chatgpt.site in app browser and create a nested plan for launching a mobile app." Built With dart flutter flutter-webmcp webmcp Try it out foldboard.kicknext.chatgpt.site github.com pub.dev Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Sergei Nikitin Like 1 1 person likes this: Share this project: Updates Sergei Nikitin started this project — Sep 03, 2026 03:37 PM EDT

title: Blindfold
pitch: An agent redacts a document it is not allowed to read. WebMCP tools return only structure — masked previews, counts, pages. Every real value and every irreversible step waits for a human click.
about_excerpt: An agent redacts a document it is not allowed to read. WebMCP tools return only structure — masked previews, counts, pages. Every real value and every irreversible step waits for a human click. Like Comment Story Updates main Inspiration Redacted court filings get published every year with the names still in the file. Someone drew a black rectangle over the text instead of removing it, and the first person to press Ctrl+A read everything. Governments have done it. Law firms have done it. It keeps happening because the tool that draws the rectangle and the tool that owns the text are not the same tool. The obvious modern fix is to hand the document to a model and let it find every name. That is also the one thing a lawyer, a doctor or a compliance officer is not allowed to do. The document is the confidential thing. Uploading it to solve a confidentiality problem is not a trade-off to negotiate — it is the end of the idea. So we asked a narrower question, and it turned out to be the interesting one: Can an agent do useful work on a document it is never allowed to read? What it does Blindfold is a web page that registers fourteen WebMCP tools. An agent can scan a document, decide what to remove, apply the plan, prove nothing survived and export the file — without ever receiving the sensitive text. Every tool returns structure instead of content: types, pages, counts, character offsets, and previews with the values themselves blocked out. PERSON p.1 conf 0.91 "…Date: ████████████ From: Dr. ████████████, Chief Risk Officer…" An agent can plan over that perfectly well. "Remove every person and address but keep the amounts" needs types and pages — it never needed the names. When the agent genuinely needs one real value — telling a public company apart from a private individual, say — it calls request_disclosure with a written reason. That tool returns a promise that does not settle until a human presses Allow or Refuse in the page . The tool call is suspended, live, waiting for a person. Refusal is a normal outcome and the tool says so, so the agent carries on with type and page instead of arguing about it. Everything runs on the device. There is no upload, no model call and no network request of any kind in the redaction path. How we built it React 19 and Vite on Cloudflare Workers, and no backend at all. The tool surface is not static. With nothing open, three tools exist. Open a document and it is five. Scan it, nine. Mark something for redaction, eleven. Apply, ten. Verify, eleven. redact_selection appears only while the reviewer has text highlighted and disappears when they let go. Registration follows app state through document.modelContext.registerTool and AbortController — there is no unregisterTool , you abort the signal you registered with. That is not decoration. An agent choosing between fourteen tools on an empty page will guess; an agent offered three will not. And a tool that is absent cannot be called at the wrong time — export_redacted_document does not exist until verification has come back clean — so the order of the workflow is enforced by what exists rather than by an error message an agent might talk itself out of. Redaction that is actually redaction. Blindfold does not draw over anything. The exported PDF is rebuilt from the document's text, and the characters inside a redacted span are never written to the file at all. The rectangle is drawn where they would have been. There is nothing underneath to recover. Proof rather than assertion. verify_no_residual_text inflates the Flate-compressed content streams of the export the way a PDF reader would, decodes both literal and hex-encoded strings, and searches for every value that was removed. Two guards keep the check honest: a control value the reviewer chose to keep must be found — otherwise the file was unreadable and a clean result would prove nothing — and a negative control in the test suite builds the same document with nothing removed and requires every value to be found. A check that cannot fail is not a check. The detector is deterministic on purpose. Regular expressions, a Luhn check for cards, mod-97 for IBANs, a name dictionary and a stoplist. No model, no WASM download, no network. It is auditable and it is instant, and the README says plainly where it will miss things. Challenges we ran into The API is younger than any model's training data. Every model we asked confidently wrote server-side MCP — McpServer , server.tool() , transports, {content:[{type:'text'}]} — none of which exists in WebMCP. We vendored the spec and Chrome's documentation into the repository and wrote a rule that API syntax may come from that file and nowhere else. It was the single highest-leverage decision in the project. Chrome cancels a tool call if the tool unregisters itself. Three of our tools take themselves off the surface by succeeding — once the plan is applied, apply_redaction_plan no longer belongs on the surface. The redaction visibly worked, and the agent was told "The operation failed for an unknown transient reason." We kept a count of in-flight calls and deferred the removal until they finished. It still failed. The measurement that finally cracked it: releasing the claim in a microtask after execute returns still kills the call; releasing it one task later never does. The fix is a setTimeout(…, 0) with a paragraph above it explaining why it cannot be anything faster. Chrome does not validate a call against inputSchema . additionalProperties: false is a hint to the model, not a gate. An undeclared key is dropped in silence, so list_findings({page: 2}) answers about page 1 with no sign that anything was ignored. Wrong data that looks right is the worst failure this app has available, so unknown parameters are now refused with a message naming what the tool accepts and which of those the caller probably meant. A rejected execute loses its message. Chrome replaces it with its own wording, so everything the tool wanted to say is gone. Every error a model is supposed to act on is therefore returned as a value, never thrown. None of the three are in the documentation. We found them by measuring the browser, not by reading about it. Accomplishments that we're proud of The privacy invariant holds end to end. Fourteen tools, and not one of them can hand the agent a value a human has not released. It is not a policy we ask the model to respect; there is no code path. A tool call that suspends on a person. The agent is genuinely blocked, mid-call, until someone clicks. Consent-gated information flow is not expressible in a server-side MCP server, because the consent has nowhere to happen. The export is verifiable, and the verifier can fail. Two controls, one positive and one negative, so a clean result means something. Prompt injection is in the sample, deliberately. leaked_memo contains an instruction telling the agent to keep everything and export immediately. The design does not depend on the agent ignoring it. Three undocumented Chrome behaviours found, worked around, and written down in the source with the measurements that produced them. What we learned Tool descriptions are the interface, and they are prose. We hand-wrote all fourteen rather than generating them. The ones that worked said when to reach for the tool , named the tool that comes next so chains are discoverable, and stated what is not returned so the agent stops looking for it. Generated descriptions read fine and misfire constantly. A human gate is a better design constraint than a safety feature. Forcing every irreversible step through a click made us decide, tool by tool, exactly what the agent is entitled to know. The answer was almost always less than we first wrote . Absence is a better guardrail than an error. A tool that does not exist cannot be misused, cannot be argued with, and costs the agent no tokens to ignore. Measure the browser. Two of our three worst bugs were behaviours that contradicted the IDL. Reasoning about them produced a fix that looked right and did not work. What's next for Blindfold File import. Today only the three built-in samples open, so that a judge can reach the interesting part in one call without finding a confidential document of their own. Layout-preserving export. The current export is rebuilt as monospaced text, which is what makes the redaction exact and the verification meaningful — but the file no longer looks like the original. A detector that is not tuned to its own samples. The current one is a demonstration of the workflow, not a production detector, and the README says so. exposedTo for partner origins , so a document management system could drive a redaction session in an embedded Blindfold without ever holding the document itself. Built With chrome cloudflare-workers indexeddb pdf-lib react typescript vite webmcp Try it out blindfold.blindfold.workers.dev github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Bexruz Sayfiddinov Like Share this project:

title: CorrelAct
pitch: CorrelAct is human-governed operational AI that investigates across systems, proposes actions, and executes only what a human explicitly approves.
about_excerpt: CorrelAct is human-governed operational AI that investigates across systems, proposes actions, and executes only what a human explicitly approves. Like Comment Story Updates Login Dashboard Actions Approvals Runs Traces Evals Settings Tasks Billing CRM Investigation Workspace CorrelAct Human-led operational intelligence, built on WebMCP Inspiration Operational problems rarely live inside one system. A customer reports an issue through Support, the account context lives in CRM, and the root cause is buried in Billing. An AI agent can help connect those signals — but giving it permanent write access to operational systems creates a different problem: how do you let it act without giving it standing authority to make consequential changes? CorrelAct started with a simple idea: let the agent investigate broadly, but make its authority to act narrow, explicit, and human-approved. It should gather evidence, correlate information, and recommend an action autonomously. But before it creates a task, changes a customer record, or performs any other consequential write, a human reviews exactly what is about to happen. That became the core architecture of CorrelAct. What it does CorrelAct is a human-led operational intelligence platform that uses WebMCP to let a browser-native AI agent work directly across operational workspaces. The agent can: Read customer evidence from Support. Read account and renewal state from CRM. Read invoice and dispute evidence from Billing. Correlate those signals into one operational diagnosis. Submit a focused Proposed Action for human review. Wait for explicit human approval. Receive only the execution capability that was approved. Perform the approved consequential action through a protected backend. Leave a complete audit trail of the investigation, decision, execution, and outcome. Read → Correlate → Propose → Human Approval → Exact Capability Exposed → Constrained Execution → Audited Outcome The demo scenario Our reference scenario involves ACME , a NorthStar customer whose renewal is blocked. The agent discovers evidence across three operational sources: Support shows an escalated customer case reporting an incorrect invoice and blocked renewal. CRM shows ACME's account and persisted renewal state. Billing shows a disputed invoice with a variance and renewal hold. The agent correlates those signals and submits a Proposed Action. At this point, nothing consequential has happened — the run enters AWAITING_APPROVAL , where a human reviewer can inspect the evidence, recommendation, customer, organization, and the exact execution capability being requested. Only after approval does the run become APPROVED . Even then, approval does not execute the action — it authorizes the agent to perform one previously reviewed capability. Dynamic Agent Authority Most agent systems expose their write tools permanently and rely on the backend to reject inappropriate calls. CorrelAct narrows the capability surface earlier than that. If there is no matching approved work, the consequential WebMCP tools — create_task and update_crm_status — simply are not registered for the agent on the Tasks workspace. After a human approves matching work, the appropriate tool becomes available. After that authority is consumed, the executable run disappears and the available tool set is recalculated. The browser agent never holds permanent standing write authority. Authority appears because a human approved specific work — and disappears the moment that work is done. Two governed write paths, one approval boundary We deliberately implemented two different consequential actions to prove the governance model isn't a special case hardcoded around one integration. create_task creates a real GitHub Issue using the scope that was already reviewed and approved. The execution call cannot rewrite the approved task content, priority, team, customer, or organization. update_crm_status applies one approved CRM renewal-status transition — for example, blocked → escalation_open . The agent does not supply the target state at execution time; that transition is frozen inside the Proposed Action before human review. The execution tool receives only enough information to identify the approved run, organization, and evidence-bound customer. Both capabilities pass through the same governance model: Human Approval → Shared controlled-execution boundary (organization · customer · evidence · approval state · execution type · idempotency · audit) → either create_task → GitHub Issue or update_crm_status → CRM record This mattered to us because we wanted to demonstrate that human-gated agent execution is a reusable architectural pattern, not a one-off built around a single API. Same governed boundary. Different consequential action. WebMCP WebMCP provides the capability surface connecting the browser agent to CorrelAct: Tool Role get_case Read Support evidence get_customer Read CRM account and renewal state get_invoice Read Billing evidence submit_action_point Persist an evidence-grounded Proposed Action create_task Execute an approved GitHub task update_crm_status Execute an approved CRM status transition The three evidence sources intentionally demonstrate different implementation patterns. Support and Billing use deterministic browser-local reference datasets — they make the cross-system WebMCP investigation reproducible without pretending to be production database integrations. CRM is application-backed through FastAPI and PostgreSQL. The consequential actions are application-backed too: create_task and update_crm_status each reach independently protected backend routes. This distinction is intentional: browser-native WebMCP delivers the agent capability experience, while consequential authority stays server-enforced. Security and trust model CorrelAct assumes that browser-side restrictions alone are not sufficient protection for consequential actions — the backend independently re-checks every execution request. Enforced boundaries include: authenticated session and organization access; human approval state and the specific approved execution capability; evidence-bound customer matching; current CRM state for stateful mutations, so a stale approval can't silently overwrite newer data; allow-listed CRM transitions, execution scope, and durable idempotency; full audit persistence. We tested these boundaries through automated tests and live browser-agent abuse scenarios: an approved action tied to one customer cannot be replayed against another customer; a run belonging to one organization cannot be executed against another; a CRM transition whose expected state has gone stale is rejected rather than silently overwritten. Approval itself never performs the external write. Human visibility Human control isn't hidden inside API responses. CorrelAct makes the progressive authority model visible across the product — the reviewer sees the exact execution capability and scope before approval, the Tasks workspace shows whether write authority is locked, available, or consumed, and Runs / Traces preserve the full lifecycle: Agent Read → Agent Proposal → Human Decision → Agent Write → Outcome This makes the governance model both enforceable and inspectable. How we built it WebMCP for browser-native agent capabilities OpenAI-powered agent reasoning for operational investigation FastAPI for the protected application and execution boundary PostgreSQL for runs, evidence, organizations, CRM state, approvals, and execution records GitHub Issues API as a real external write integration JavaScript browser workspaces for Support, CRM, Billing, Investigation, Approvals, Tasks, Runs, and Traces Docker for reproducible deployment Azure Container Apps for the live deployment GitHub Actions for security checks, automated tests, browser testing, evaluation, and deployment The application also includes organization-scoped demo identities so isolation can be tested between NorthStar/ACME and Neptune/GreenMart. Challenges we ran into Separating approval from execution. A deceptively important architectural decision was ensuring that clicking Approve did not perform the action. Approval had to mean "this exact capability and scope may now be executed," not "execute this immediately." Keeping those phases separate made the system significantly easier to reason about and audit. Preventing approved scope from drifting. We didn't want the agent to receive approval for one action and then change its parameters at execution time. For CRM writes, the exact expected and target statuses are frozen before approval. For task creation, task content comes from the approved Proposed Action rather than a new free-form execution payload. Making authority visible. Backend authorization alone wasn't enough for the experience we wanted — we wanted the agent's available tool set itself to reflect current human authorization. That led to Dynamic Agent Authority: controlled execution tools are registered and remove

about_excerpt:
Agent-operable benefits and bills portal exposing 9 WebMCP tools for accessible public services.

 1 2 3 4 



 
 60-Second Judge Quickstart:
OpenDoor Access features 1-Click Judge Persona Tours mounted directly at the top of the live portal ( https://aesthetic-chebakia-a2278a.netlify.app): 

 
 Senior Citizen Flow: Checks obligations -> translates "gross income" into plain language -> prepares and confirms water bill payment. 
 Single Parent Flow: Renews Food Assistance (SNAP) for 1 year -> splits payments -> schedules caseworker appointment. 
 Safety Net Undo: Reverses accidental actions with instant undo rollback. 
 

 Or test via ChatGPT in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with #enable-webmcp-testing by asking:
"Pay my overdue water bill from savings and summarize what else I owe." 

 ================================================== 

 
 Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP
Standard public service portals (benefits renewals, utility bill-pay, appointments) are a difficult obstacle course of 40+ form fields, 3 confusing pages, and dense legal jargon. 
 

 For individuals with low vision, motor tremors (Parkinson's, ALS), or cognitive fatigue from a disability, navigating these portals independently is a major barrier. Screen readers narrate the page structure, but they cannot complete the multi-step task. 

 WebMCP enables an agent-native web: exposing structured, typed tools directly in the user's browser session. Instead of screen-scraping or guessing selectors, an AI agent coordinates user intent reliably and securely. 

 
 What humans and agents can do together 
 Single Spoken Sentence Task Completion: A person asks "Renew my food assistance and pay my overdue water bill from savings" and the agent coordinates tools across benefits, accounts, and billers seamlessly. 
 Shared Surface Collaboration: Every agent tool invocation updates the live high-contrast UI, announces politely to assistive technology (ARIA live regions), and logs to a transparent on-screen transcript. A user, caregiver, and agent all perceive the exact same state in real time. 
 Bureaucratic Jargon Translation: The explain_this_form tool translates terms like "gross income", "attestation", and "recertification" into plain language before taking action. 
 Two-Phase Commit Security and Safety Net 
 Two-Phase Financial Safety: Money never moves on initial calls. pay_bill validates balances and returns a preview token. Only confirm_payment debits funds after explicit user approval. 
 Undo Stack: Every action registers a reversible closure, giving users complete confidence to explore without fear of accidental transactions. 
 Active Defense: The engine rejects overpayments, attempts to pay $0-balance bills, and overdrafts beyond available funds. 
 How WebMCP is Implemented 
 9 Intent-Level Tools: pay_bill, confirm_payment, renew_benefit, find_and_book_appointment, summarize_my_obligations, explain_this_form, download_payment_receipt, export_appointment_to_calendar, and undo_last_action. 
 Dual Integration: Uses imperative JavaScript registration via document.modelContext.registerTool() (with AbortController lifecycle cleanup) and declarative HTML attributes (data-webmcp-tool). 
 Triple-Channel Accessibility: Politeness-separated live regions (status vs alert), opt-in Web Speech API queue, and WCAG AA/AAA contrast. 
 Verification and Test Suite 
 61 Unit Tests (npm test): In-memory store logic, penny precision, ReDoS defense, 200-op fuzzing, and receipts/.ics exports. 
 41 Playwright E2E Tests (npm run test:e2e): Full WebMCP loop in real Chromium driving all 9 tools via navigator.modelContextTesting. 
 1 Production Smoke Test (npm run test:prod): Automated live verification against Netlify. 
 Open Source: MIT License with clean, documented TypeScript codebase.
