title: Hustl
pitch: Hustl connects your training, recovery, nutrition, and progress in one adaptive coaching system—where you collaborate with AI while keeping every change under your control.
about_excerpt: Hustl connects your training, recovery, nutrition, and progress in one adaptive coaching system—where you collaborate with AI while keeping every change under your control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I’ve been skinny for most of my life. I tried apps like Strong to track my workouts and MacroFactor to manage my nutrition. Both were useful, but each understood only one part of what I was trying to achieve. I still relied on ChatGPT or Claude for advice. That meant repeatedly explaining my training history, diet, recovery, and goals, then manually carrying their suggestions back into each app. I built Hustl because I wanted those pieces to work together. The same problem exists whether someone wants to gain muscle, improve performance, or lose weight without sacrificing strength: good coaching needs the full picture. What it does Hustl connects training, recovery, nutrition, progress, and AI coaching in one app. It also brings in health and activity data from outside Hustl through Apple Health and Health Connect on Android, including data shared by compatible apps such as Google Fit. This gives the coach a broader view of the athlete’s workouts, sleep, heart rate, recovery, and daily activity. An AI assistant can understand what the athlete has trained, how their exercises are progressing, whether they have recovered, what they have eaten, and what their current goals are. It can then help with practical tasks such as: reviewing workout and exercise history; interpreting readiness, sleep, HRV, and resting heart rate; comparing food intake with calorie and macro targets; logging or correcting meals; proposing nutrition targets; building and revising workout templates; adapting a workout when recovery is poor; and showing proposed changes inside the Coach inbox. Hustl supports both MCP and WebMCP. MCP lets compatible assistants work with Hustl directly. WebMCP gives an assistant tools related to the Hustl screen currently open in the browser. The important part is the collaboration. The assistant studies the evidence and explains its recommendation. Hustl turns that recommendation into a concrete proposal. The athlete reviews, refines, accepts, or rejects it. How I built it Hustl is a Flutter application backed by a TypeScript and Next.js API, Supabase and PostgreSQL, native Apple Health and Android Health Connect integrations, and an MCP server. For WebMCP, I built a coordinator that registers tools according to the visible route. Train exposes training and progression tools. Recover exposes readiness data. Nutrition exposes the food diary and nutrition proposals. Coach exposes trends and pending changes. Templates and active workouts expose their own focused capabilities. When the user changes screens, the old tool handles become stale. This prevents an assistant from retaining a capability simply because the user visited that page earlier. Actions use strict schemas and explicit outcomes. Coaching changes normally become pending proposals rather than being applied silently. They appear in Hustl’s regular Coach interface, where the athlete can inspect the rationale and proposed values. For the challenge, I also created a public evaluator using Hustl’s real Flutter interface and WebMCP coordinator. Private services were replaced with deterministic, in-memory data. It contains no production credentials, personal health records, analytics, or backend connection. Its runtime also blocks unexpected network and browser-credential access. Challenges I ran into The first challenge was resisting the temptation to build a small, isolated demo. Hustl is meant to support the whole coaching loop, so the WebMCP experience needed to work across the real training, recovery, nutrition, Coach, template, and workout screens. Navigation was harder than it appeared. The visible screen, browser URL, and registered tool catalogue all needed to agree. I found cases where a detail screen opened without correctly taking ownership of its route. I also had to ensure that tools disappeared and old handles failed safely after navigation, reloads, and account transitions. Proposal state required similar care. A successful request might be pending, applied, duplicated, dismissed, reverted, or rejected by validation. Those outcomes needed to remain distinct in both the tool response and the interface. Finally, I needed to make the source inspectable without publishing Hustl’s private backend or user data. The public evaluator therefore uses synthetic fixtures, explicit no-op integrations, source manifests, and checks for private paths, credentials, and unexpected network origins. Accomplishments that I’m proud of The public evaluator exposes 20 route-scoped WebMCP tools across training, recovery, nutrition, coaching, templates, and active workouts. Those tools support a complete coaching story. An athlete can describe a goal, let the assistant study twelve weeks of training and exercise progression, account for a poor recovery day, compare nutrition with current targets, and receive concrete changes for review. I am especially proud that the safety model is visible in the product: tools follow the screen the athlete is using; stale handles fail closed; proposal status is explicit; duplicate requests do not create duplicate changes; workout and nutrition-target proposals require human review; and the public evaluator cannot access production systems or personal data. This is not a separate interface made for the challenge. It is a safe, deterministic version of Hustl’s real Flutter experience and coaching architecture. What I learned More autonomy does not automatically make an AI coach more useful. Better context and a clear review process matter more. I also learned that the interface can act as a meaningful permission boundary. Route-scoped tools make the assistant’s access easier to understand because its capabilities follow what the athlete can currently see and do. Most importantly, AI collaboration works better when the result becomes part of the product’s normal workflow. A recommendation should not disappear inside a chat transcript. It should become something the athlete can inspect, refine, follow, and revisit. What’s next for Hustl The next step is to make the collaboration continuous rather than limited to a single planning session. I want Hustl to support richer long-term recovery analysis, clearer progression explanations, and weekly coaching check-ins that compare the plan with what actually happened. I also want the same experience to work consistently across web, desktop, and mobile assistants through MCP and WebMCP. The principle will remain the same: Hustl provides the evidence, AI helps interpret and propose, and the athlete controls what changes. Built With apple connect context dart firebase flutter health healthkit javascript model next.js postgresql protocol supabase typescript vercel watch webmcp Try it out hustl-webmcp-challenge.vercel.app github.com hustl-two.vercel.app testflight.apple.com appdistribution.firebase.dev Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I designed and built Hustl, from its Flutter app and coaching experience to its backend, MCP, and WebMCP integrations. My goal is to make training, recovery, and nutrition data easier to understand and act on. title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ . title: Formulate
pitch: Your AI agent fills forms, explains jargon, and asks before it submits , powered by 12 WebMCP tools and a natural language data vault.
about_excerpt: Your AI agent fills forms, explains jargon, and asks before it submits , powered by 12 WebMCP tools and a natural language data vault. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration 67% of people abandon government forms at the first confusing field. We've all been there — staring at a 40-field form that asks for your CIN number, your GSTIN, your TDS rate, and nobody explains what any of it means. In India alone, 900 million voters interact with the Election Commission's Form 6. Millions fill out business registrations, insurance enrollments, and rental applications every year. Most people either pay someone to fill these forms or give up entirely. We asked: what if an AI agent could fill the form for you — explain every confusing field — and you just approve at the end? What it does Formulate is a WebMCP-powered form assistant with three parts: 1. Natural Language Data Vault You describe yourself in plain text: "My name is Mohammed, I work at TechVentures in Bengaluru, my PAN is ABCPM1234K." The vault extracts your data using pattern recognition — PAN format, Aadhaar format, phone numbers, PIN codes, email, employer, job title, city, state. No form to set up a form-filler. 2. Smart Form Engine Five real-world forms with 172 total fields: Rental Application (39 fields), Health Insurance Enrollment (27 fields), Small Business Registration (25 fields), Airtel Business Enterprise Registration (40 fields), and India's Election Commission Voter ID Form 6 (41 fields). Every confusing field has an inline plain-language explanation. 3. 12 WebMCP Tools Registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() — the agent calls structured tools instead of scraping the page: get_form_fields — reads the entire form structure fill_field — fills a text/number/date/phone field select_option — selects from a dropdown check_checkbox — toggles a checkbox explain_field — returns a plain-language explanation validate_form — checks for empty required fields get_form_progress — returns filled/total counts review_form — summarizes all values before submission clear_field — removes a value autofill_from_vault — checks what can be auto-filled apply_vault_suggestions — fills all matching fields from vault submit_form — requires human approval before proceeding How we built it Next.js 16 with App Router and TypeScript Tailwind CSS v4 with shadcn-style design tokens (2 colors: foreground and muted) WebMCP — supports both document.modelContext and navigator.modelContext for Chrome compatibility Pattern recognition vault — regex-based extraction for PAN, Aadhaar, GSTIN, CIN, Udyam, phone, email, PIN codes, plus keyword extraction for name, employer, job title, address Playwright — 30 end-to-end tests covering tool registration, field filling, validation, approval flow, and activity panel Vercel for deployment The execute function returns { content: [{ type: "text", text: "..." }] } per the Chrome WebMCP spec. Input parsing handles both JSON strings and parsed objects so it works regardless of how the host agent calls the tools. Challenges we faced The biggest challenge was WebMCP spec compliance. The API migrated from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext in July 2026, and different hosts (Chrome vs ChatGPT) may use either surface. We had to support both. We also discovered that executeTool sends arguments as a JSON string in some hosts but a parsed object in others — so we added defensive input parsing. The natural language vault was tricky because names, cities, and job titles don't have fixed formats. We combined regex patterns for structured data (PAN, Aadhaar, GSTIN) with keyword-based extraction for unstructured data (name, employer, address), with confidence scoring to show users what was extracted and how sure we are. What we learned WebMCP changes the relationship between websites and AI agents from "scrape and guess" to "structured collaboration." A form that registers 12 tools gives the agent complete understanding of what's possible, what's required, and what needs human approval. That's fundamentally different from an agent trying to parse HTML and click buttons. What's next Let users add custom forms by pasting any form URL Support for PDF form filling (upload a PDF, agent fills it) Multi-language field explanations for non-English speakers Integration with DigiLocker for verified document data in India Built With css next.js playwright react tailwind typescript vercel webmcp Try it out github.com formulate-ten.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Mohammed ek Like Share this project: Updates Mohammed ek started this project — Sep 02, 2026 11:57 AM EDT

title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: CashLatch
pitch: Manage your money with ChatGPT- while CashLatch protects your limits and keeps you in control.
about_excerpt: Manage your money with ChatGPT- while CashLatch protects your limits and keeps you in control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Managing money often means checking balances, remembering bills, tracking savings goals and doing the same calculations repeatedly. ChatGPT can help compare options, but a normal conversation does not automatically know what is currently saved in a financial tool. It may also continue using an old recommendation after the balance or bills have changed. I built CashLatch to connect these two parts. ChatGPT helps the user understand their options, while CashLatch keeps the current information, checks the user’s limits and requires approval before recording a recommendation. What CashLatch does CashLatch is a browser-based money workspace where users can: Track their current balance, expected income and expenses. Add monthly bills with amounts and due dates. Create savings goals and monitor their progress. Choose the minimum balance they want to keep. Limit how much one recommendation can put toward goals. See how their balance may change over 30, 60 and 90 days. Use different currencies and separate money workspaces. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT can read the money workspace currently open in CashLatch. It can calculate what the goals need, estimate future balances, compare different funding options and prepare a recommendation on the webpage. The user can review the exact amount, where it will go and how much money may remain. ChatGPT cannot approve the recommendation for them. After the user approves it, ChatGPT can apply only that exact recommendation, and only once. If the balance, bills, goals or limits change, CashLatch cancels the old approval. ChatGPT must read the updated information and prepare a new recommendation. CashLatch is a planning workspace. Applying a recommendation updates its local records; it does not transfer real bank funds. How I built it CashLatch is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript modules. The interface is responsive and includes money workspaces, currency selection, monthly bills, savings goals, transactions, balance estimates, safety limits and recent activity. The app uses the WebMCP imperative API through document.modelContext.registerTool . It provides tools that let ChatGPT: Read the open money workspace. Add or update savings goals. Add or update monthly bills. Record income and expenses. Estimate future balances. Calculate how much each goal needs. Check different ways to fund goals. Prepare a recommendation for review. Propose safety-limit changes without applying them. A recommendation cannot be applied immediately. When the user approves an exact recommendation on the webpage, CashLatch temporarily creates a one-time apply tool for it. Before applying, CashLatch checks the latest balance, bills and safety limits again. The approval expires after five minutes, disappears after one use and is cancelled by any financial change. A SHA-256 fingerprint helps CashLatch detect whether the information used for approval has changed. Money-workspace data is stored in the browser using localStorage . CashLatch does not require an external financial database or an OpenAI API key. Challenges I faced The biggest challenge was making WebMCP useful instead of simply adding chat controls to a webpage. The important difference is not that ChatGPT can calculate a recommendation. It is that ChatGPT can work with the information currently open in CashLatch, while the website independently checks the result and keeps the user in control. Another challenge was designing the approval flow. The first version used technical terms such as staging, allocation, authorization and stale state. These were difficult for normal users to understand. I replaced them with clearer terms such as recommendation, money added to goals, approve, apply once and needs an update. I also worked through browser permissions, dynamic tool registration, local persistence, responsive navigation, form contrast, graph readability and clear monthly-bill presentation. What I learned I learned that WebMCP is most useful when the website remains responsible for its own data and rules. ChatGPT is good at understanding a request and comparing options. CashLatch is responsible for checking the numbers, showing the exact result and requiring user approval. I also learned that approval should depend on current information. If the user’s money changes after approval, continuing with the old recommendation may no longer be appropriate. Finally, I learned that a technically correct workflow is not enough. The interface and tool responses must use language that non-technical users can understand. What I am proud of CashLatch demonstrates a complete WebMCP workflow: ChatGPT reads the open money workspace. It compares multiple ways to fund a goal. CashLatch checks the recommendation against monthly bills and safety limits. The user reviews and approves the exact recommendation. A financial change cancels that approval. ChatGPT prepares a new recommendation using the latest information. The newly approved recommendation can be applied once. The balance, goal progress, confirmation and recent activity are updated. This gives ChatGPT useful access without giving it unlimited control. What’s next The next steps are broader browser testing, improved accessibility and clearer first-time guidance. Future versions could also support optional encrypted cross-device sync and connections to external financial services. These would require proper authentication, consent and additional security controls. title: Agent WebMCP
pitch: Turn server operations into a browser-native agent surface: inspect health, control services, run durable jobs, and service agents through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Turn server operations into a browser-native agent surface: inspect health, control services, run durable jobs, and service agents through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Agent WebMCP Inspiration Most server operations tools were designed for one human clicking through dashboards, opening terminals, copying logs, and translating what they see into the next command. AI agents can help reason about those systems, but they usually sit outside the actual operational interface. That means the human still has to bridge the gap between what the dashboard knows and what the agent can safely do. Agent WebMCP explores a different model: the operations console itself becomes an agent-capable surface. Instead of building a second automation API just for AI, the application exposes the same typed operations used by the human UI through WebMCP. Humans can inspect and control their server visually, while an agent can discover those same capabilities directly from the page and execute them with structured inputs. What it does Agent WebMCP is a Java-based operational control plane for managing services, inspecting system health, and running durable jobs on a remote machine. The browser console provides a human-friendly view of the machine. WebMCP turns that same page into a structured tool surface for agents. Key workflows include: Inspecting system status and runtime metrics. Discovering managed services and viewing their current state. Inspecting individual services, recent output, and operational details. Starting, stopping, restarting, and reloading services through bounded operations. Adding and removing services from the managed inventory. Scheduling durable service jobs for actions that should run later or recur. Running optional agent-assisted jobs through an installed Codex CLI when a job needs reasoning instead of a fixed service action. Inspecting job state, execution results, and logs. The important part is that these are not separate demo-only AI tools. They are projections of one canonical operation catalog shared by the UI, HTTP API, CLI, WebMCP, and a bounded MCP endpoint. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Operations software already contains the exact context an agent needs: available actions, service state, health data, logs, job history, and the constraints around what may be changed. Without WebMCP, an agent interacting with an operations dashboard usually has to infer intent from rendered UI, scrape text, or rely on a separately maintained automation API. Those approaches are brittle and can drift away from the product that humans actually use. With WebMCP, Agent WebMCP publishes explicit tools directly from the page using document.modelContext.registerTool(...). The browser becomes both the human interface and the agent capability surface. That creates a much cleaner collaboration loop: A human opens the operations console and sees the current machine state. The agent discovers the operations that this exact page supports. The human can ask for an outcome instead of manually translating it into a sequence of service actions. The agent executes bounded, typed operations through the same backend used by the UI. The resulting state remains visible and understandable to the human in the console. This is the part that was difficult before: the human interface and the agent interface can finally describe the same system instead of pretending they are unrelated products. How I built it Agent WebMCP is implemented as a Java application with a lightweight browser frontend and a canonical operation runtime. Canonical operation catalog The backend owns a typed catalog of operational capabilities. Each operation defines its identifier, description, access characteristics, input schema, and execution behavior. Those operations are projected onto multiple surfaces rather than being reimplemented for each one: Human web console HTTP/JSON API CLI Browser-native WebMCP Bounded MCP endpoint This keeps behavior consistent. A service restart means the same thing whether it was initiated by a button, an HTTP call, or an agent using WebMCP. Browser-native WebMCP The production browser integration loads the canonical operation catalog and registers operations through document.modelContext.registerTool(...). Each registered tool receives: A stable operation name A human-readable description A generated JSON input schema Read-only annotations where appropriate An execute callback that forwards to the canonical operation endpoint The WebMCP execution AbortSignal, propagated into network requests for cancellation The browser therefore exposes real application capabilities, not a hard-coded list maintained separately from the backend. Services and durable jobs Service control is intentionally bounded. Agent WebMCP does not expose a generic shell, arbitrary command execution, or unrestricted filesystem mutation. Service operations work through a managed inventory and provider layer. Durable jobs allow operational work to survive beyond one interactive request and make scheduled or recurring actions first-class parts of the product. A service job can be completely deterministic, such as scheduling a restart or cleanup. It can also optionally include a prompt for an installed Codex CLI when the job genuinely benefits from agent reasoning. That separation matters: not every automation problem needs AI, and the product should not pretend otherwise. Human and agent UX The UI is designed as an operational cockpit rather than a chat wrapper. Humans can browse machine health, services, jobs, activity, and execution details normally. WebMCP adds agent capability without replacing that interface. The result is a shared operational surface where people remain able to understand and control the system while agents handle multi-step execution when useful. Safety model Agent WebMCP deliberately avoids exposing a generic remote shell as an AI tool. The operation catalog is bounded and typed. Service lifecycle actions operate on managed services, job execution is structured, recursive job execution is rejected, and the separate MCP projection exposes only an intentionally limited subset of capabilities. The project can also run in a NO_AUTH mode for localhost or user-controlled private-tunnel setups, but that mode is intentionally treated as private-machine functionality rather than something that should be exposed casually to the public internet. Challenges I ran into Avoiding two sources of truth. It would have been easy to create one set of backend operations and another set of WebMCP tools. Instead, WebMCP is generated from the canonical operation catalog so the two cannot quietly drift apart. Keeping powerful operations bounded. Remote operations software naturally wants to become a shell with nicer buttons. I deliberately constrained the surface around typed service and job operations instead. Supporting both deterministic automation and agents. A restart at 3:00 AM does not need an LLM. A diagnostic or remediation task might. The job model keeps those use cases separate while allowing them to share one scheduler and execution history. Making the agent surface feel native to the product. The goal was not to bolt a chat panel onto an admin dashboard. The page itself publishes its capabilities through WebMCP while remaining a useful standalone operations console. Validating the same behavior across surfaces. The project uses runtime, browser, and operation-level tests to make sure WebMCP executes the same canonical operations as the rest of the application. Accomplishments I'm proud of Built a real browser-native WebMCP implementation using document.modelContext.registerTool(...). Projected WebMCP tools from a canonical typed Java operation catalog instead of maintaining an AI-specific duplicate API. Built a coherent human operations console around the same capabilities. Implemented bounded service lifecycle control without exposing generic shell execution. Added durable jobs for scheduled and recurring operational work. Added optional Codex-assisted jobs without forcing AI into deterministic service tasks. Kept a separate MCP endpoint intentionally narrower than the browser WebMCP surface. Added end-to-end browser coverage proving that discovered WebMCP tools execute through the canonical backend. What I learned WebMCP is most compelling when a web application already owns meaningful actions and context, not when tools are invented solely for an agent demo. The browser can become a clean capability boundary between a person, an application, and an agent. A single canonical operation model dramatically reduces drift between human and agent interfaces. Explicit schemas and bounded operations are much safer and easier to reason about than arbitrary remote execution. AI is more useful in operations when it is optional and composable, not when every scheduled task is forced through a model. title: BeforeApply
pitch: An agent inspects web work and prepares reversible changes for a human to review, approve, and apply—with a clear before-and-after trail.
about_excerpt:
An agent inspects web work and prepares reversible changes for a human to review, approve, and apply—with a clear before-and-after trail.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Web agents often have to operate web applications by reading the screen, finding controls, clicking through menus, and guessing whether an action succeeded. That approach can be slow and fragile. On the other hand, fully automatic changes can make it difficult for a person to understand or review what happened. 

 We wanted to explore a better human-agent workflow: the agent should be able to inspect web work and prepare useful changes, while the human keeps the final decision visible and authoritative. 

 What it does 

 BeforeApply is a human-agent change-review workspace. 

 The demo uses a seeded marketing page and guides the user through a complete workflow: 

 
 Inspect the current page. 
 Find priority issues. 
 Explain an issue. 
 Prepare a proposed change. 
 Review the before-and-after result. 
 Stage the proposal for approval. 
 Approve or reject it as a human. 
 Apply the change only after approval. 
 Generate a concise change report. 
 

 For example, the workspace can identify that the hero button label “Learn more” is too vague, prepare the alternative “See how it works,” and show both values before anything is applied. 

 How we used WebMCP 

 When WebMCP is available, the page registers 12 structured tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . 

 The tools cover workspace inspection, issue discovery, explanations, proposed changes, previews, approval, application, reporting, and resetting the demo. 

 The tools use strict input schemas and explicit descriptions of their side effects. Preparing a change is separate from applying it. The apply operation is blocked unless the proposal has reached the human-approved state. 

 The app also includes a manual fallback. It uses the same state handlers and approval gate so the complete workflow can still be tested in a browser that does not yet expose WebMCP. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is not only about making buttons easier for an agent to click. The tool descriptions, input schemas, state transitions, and safety boundaries are equally important. 

 A useful agent-native web experience should expose meaningful operations, return clear structured results, and preserve the human’s ability to inspect and approve consequential changes. 

 How we built it 

 The project is a self-contained static web application built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It uses deterministic in-memory data so judges can reproduce the same workflow without creating an account, configuring an external API, or providing private credentials. 

 The live demo is hosted on Cloudflare Pages. 

 Challenges we faced 

 WebMCP is an emerging browser capability, so browser support is still evolving. We handled this by detecting support at runtime, showing the current tool status, and keeping a transparent manual fallback available. 

 We also designed the state machine so that the agent cannot bypass the human approval boundary by calling the apply operation directly.

pitch: A dictionary of AI jargon that grows from evidence, not opinion. Bring an article; the agent reads it and reports how each term was actually used.
about_excerpt: A dictionary of AI jargon that grows from evidence, not opinion. Bring an article; the agent reads it and reports how each term was actually used. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Read any article about AI and you hit ten words nobody defined. Some of them the author explains. Some they assume you already know. Some are there to sell you something. You cannot tell which is which — and looking each one up gives you a textbook definition that has nothing to do with how the word was just used at you. You ask your AI. It tells you. Then it's gone, and the next person who reads the same article asks the same question. Existing AI glossaries are written top-down: an editor decides what a word means and the entry sits there. But these words are not settled. "MCP" means one thing in Anthropic's spec and something else in a vendor's brochure. A dictionary that picks a winner is lying about the state of the language. **nomos** (νόμος) is Plato's word for meaning that is agreed, not given. That is the side this dictionary sits on. What it does ai-nomos is an AI-term dictionary with no input box. You don't type — you send your AI. Hand your agent a link and it reads the article itself, in your browser, using the WebMCP tools this page registers. It finds the words you named, brings back ones you didn't, and rules that some of yours aren't AI terms at all. Then you decide whether any of it goes into the dictionary. The dictionary never rules on what a term means. It collects how the term is actually used — one record per term per document, each carrying the sentence it came from and a link back. When eleven articles define MCP eleven different ways, you see all eleven, split by the language the source was written in. Current corpus: 133 plain-language entries, 1,325 sightings from 343 documents, 302 distinct terms — 1,217 Chinese, 101 English, 7 Japanese. There is one write path and no editorial back door. The agent proposes, a person confirms, and only then is anything stored. No entry can be edited into existence by hand. How we built it **Five tools**, dual-registered on `document.modelContext` (ChatGPT desktop, Chrome 152+) and `navigator.modelContext` (older spec drafts): - `feedDocument({url, requested_terms?})` — read-only. Returns the extraction rules verbatim, a thin lexicon index, and the JSON Schema for a finding. The page never fetches the article; the agent does. - `reportDocument` — read-only, called after the agent opens the article and before it extracts anything: title, byline, date, length, one-sentence gist. Nothing is stored. It exists because one tool call that takes a minute leaves the screen blank for a minute — splitting the task into stages is what makes progress real rather than a fake spinner. The title doubles as proof the agent actually reached the page. - `submitFindings` — hands the findings to the page and answers `pending_review`. It does not write. - `lookupTerm`, `trending` — read-only, the public read side. A second agent on any other site can ask this dictionary what a term currently looks like in the wild. It gets quotes and sources, never a ruling. **One data contract** (`context/contract.md`, English, versioned) is the single source of truth for page ↔ agent and page ↔ server. Changes go through a `contract:` commit, never through conversation. **Three server-side locks** every finding must pass — the sentence must contain the term, the definition quote must be a verbatim substring of the context, and a borderline term with no quote is dropped as noise. A Python reference implementation and a JS implementation are diffed against the same fixtures before every deploy, so the page and the server cannot drift apart. Static HTML/CSS/JS, no framework, no build step. Vercel serverless for the write path, Upstash Redis for sightings. Interface in Chinese, English and Japanese. Challenges we ran into **The spec has no page-side confirmation, so the page had to stop being the thing that writes.** Our probe found no working confirmation API: `requestUserInteraction` was removed from the WebMCP spec in PR #205 (June 2026, "not fully specified, no implementations"), and ChatGPT's shim returns "requestUserInteraction is not supported by the Codex WebMCP shim". Rather than pretend to gate, we moved the write out of the tool call entirely: `submitFindings` returns `pending_review` and holds the findings on the page; the person confirms and *the page* posts to `/api/findings`. No tool call can write on its own. **Order of work has to live where the agent reads first.** We put the sequence (feedDocument → reportDocument → submitFindings) in the rules blob and the agent skipped `reportDocument` in a live run. Moving it to the opening line of each tool description *and* into a `next_step` field in the response body fixed it. **An ungrounded model will happily invent a definition.** So the contract forbids it: `definition_quote` must be a verbatim substring of the surrounding context, and the server rejects the finding if it is not. The agent judges; the quote proves it. **The server has to have the last word.** The page runs the same locks the server does, so the agent gets instant feedback. But `PII_DETECTED` is server-only, and the server's verdict is what the page displays — a finding can pass on the page and still be rejected, with the reason code shown. Accomplishments that we're proud of **Tool descriptions are the product.** `reportDocument` exists purely so the human sees evidence of progress while the agent reads. That is a UX decision expressed entirely as a tool description — there is no UI for it, and no other way to build it. **The agent is not a courier.** `submitFindings` explicitly instructs the agent to disagree with the user: find each requested term and rule on it (a requested term that is not an AI term still gets a finding, with `domain: not` — that is the agent's verdict and the user sees it), and add terms the user missed. In our test runs the agent added roughly as many terms as the user asked for. **It still works without an agent.** WebMCP is not everywhere yet. With no `modelContext` present, the page degrades to local matching: paste text, see which of the 133 known terms are in it. The site is not a dead page for the 99% of visitors without a flagged browser. **Multilingual by construction.** `lang` is derived per source document, not per term — an English term quoted in a Japanese article is a Japanese sighting. A term page shows each language side separately, because a word is not used the same way in two language communities. What we learned **A person and an agent can do something here that neither can do alone.** The person brings judgment about *which article matters* and *which words bothered them*. They cannot read 343 articles to see how a word is drifting. The agent reads the article closely and applies the same rules every time. It has no idea which article is worth reading, and left alone it will confidently define a term from memory instead of from the page. The dictionary holds the accumulation neither of them can — so that when you bring article #344, the page can put its definition of "RAG" next to the other ways other authors used it. **Anti-spam is a limit, not a security feature.** An anonymous browser-held id and a salted document hash deduplicate honest use. Neither stops a determined actor, and we do not claim they do. **What we verified, and what we did not.** Verified 2026-08-27: `registerTool` works, tools execute, the agent channel is live in ChatGPT desktop (Work mode, GPT-5.6 Terra). Chrome 152 exposes `document.modelContext` natively. Not available anywhere we tested: page-side write confirmation. We report it as a spec gap and designed around its absence rather than around a feature that does not exist. What's next for ai-nomos **Scale.** Reads are already shaped for growth — looking up a term is `ZRANGE by_term:{key}`, both touching one index rather than the corpus. What breaks first is honest and known: the home page loads every sighting into the browser to compute its stats (661 KB at 1,325 sightings; ~49 MB at 100,000), the sightings API caps at 200 rows unless asked for a wider window, and there is no pagination anywhere. The fix is counters incremented on write instead of a full scan on read. It is not built yet because at this size a full scan is simpler and cannot go stale. **More languages.** The corpus is 92% Chinese today because that is where the feeding started. The architecture is already per-document-language; it needs readers, not code. **The read side as a public good.** `lookupTerm` and `trending` are already open to any agent on any site. The interesting version of this dictionary is not people visiting it — it is other agents asking it what a word currently means in the wild, and getting evidence instead of a ruling. title: Ikuyo: Plan Your Next Adventure!
pitch: Full-fledged collaborative travel-planning application for humans and agents.
about_excerpt: Full-fledged collaborative travel-planning application for humans and agents. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Ikuyo trip home Ikuyo trip timetable ChatGPT and Ikuyo Ikuyo task list Ikuyo expense list [Disclosure: the following is written with help AI correcting grammar and sentence structure; the idea and draft is originally human-written] Inspiration Travel planning is a living conversation of ideas, changes, and constraints. A useful itinerary must preserve all of that context. I want to empower people with agents, not replace them in the planning process. What it does Ikuyo is a collaborative itinerary workspace for travellers and their agents. Through WebMCP, agents can read a trip and create or update activities, accommodations, day plans, tasks, expenses, and comments. The result is not a one-off itinerary, but a shared plan that remains editable, visible, and understandable to the people travelling. The problem Planning a trip with an agent is a back-and-forth process of tuning and refining, not one-shot prompting. People need to feel in control of their plans while staying flexible when they change. Chat apps do not feel flexible enough, while spreadsheets are too rigid. What collaboration looks like The user asks the agent to draft a realistic travel plan around the fixed bookings, with a few itinerary suggestions. The agent creates it using Ikuyo's WebMCP tools. The user then studies and revises the plan, asking the agent for more suggestions. The agent sees the latest changes through WebMCP and uses them to give further suggestions. This goes back and forth until both parties are happy with the final itinerary. Why Ikuyo does not have an in-app agent In today's landscape, LLMs evolve very quickly, and everyone's preferred agent changes often. Committing to a specific agent provider requires significant ongoing maintenance for Ikuyo. It also conflicts with my goal of keeping users in control. Instead of providing an agent for users, I expect them to bring their own agent to help with travel planning. Why WebMCP is essential Because I expect users to bring their own agents, they would otherwise need to copy and paste information between Ikuyo and an agent's chat interface. This is inefficient. Another option is for the agent to control Ikuyo through browser automation. That is not ideal either: Ikuyo is built for people, so an agent must read and guess at HTML elements before performing actions. This makes each operation slow and unreliable. WebMCP solves this by exposing Ikuyo's product actions as tools with typed input and output schemas. The agent can discover the current trip, create and update itinerary objects, and read comments and costs from the live source of truth. Tool availability follows the user's role: viewers can read, editors can plan, and owners manage sharing. Destructive operations remain deliberate, human-confirmed UI actions. How we built it This project started in 2024, when I had the idea of making a Google Calendar-like web application for travel planning. The application uses React and Radix Themes for the frontend, MapTiler for maps, and PHP/Laravel/MySQL for the backend. It originally used InstantDB, but I migrated away from it in late August after its shutdown announcement. The calendar grid uses CSS Grid, and all frontend time and date calculations use Temporal. During this hackathon, I extended the application to support WebMCP, with the help of LLM agents (GPT-5.6). I imported Modern Web Guidance's WebMCP skill and used it while building. Afterward, I tested a range of prompts to fine-tune the tool descriptions so future agents can fill them in correctly. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was treating WebMCP as more than another function for calling backend APIs. I had to consider it from the user's point of view and align the UI capabilities with the WebMCP tools, so they could call the existing backend APIs more efficiently. I also adjusted some backend API fields to make them more intuitive for agents to use. The application initially focused on people, so I naturally built it around adding or editing one object at a time. However, when agents performed operations one by one, they were still slow to reach the desired outcome even when the plan was already synthesised in the context. I then added batch versions of the WebMCP tools so agents could create and edit itinerary activities more efficiently. Accomplishments that we're proud of I'm proud that this travel-planning application now integrates deeply with agentic capabilities. People can bring their preferred agents to interact with the site while remaining in control of their own travel plans. What we learned I learned that building for agents is different from building for people. People receive hints through the visual UI, while agents can access only the tool descriptions. I therefore need to fine-tune the capabilities so agents can operate correctly and efficiently. I also learned that agents work faster than people, so they need ways to batch-create and batch-edit activities. What's next for Ikuyo I have used Ikuyo to plan my own travels, and other people have shared that they completed trips using it. However, it still lacks some human-to-human collaboration capabilities, such as expense splitting and combining. It also needs better support for travel plans that span multiple regions and time zones. Those are the areas I plan to tackle next. title: MoveToGermany.lol
pitch: Moving to Germany? Skip the 30 tabs. One application. Two operators. One shared state.
about_excerpt: Moving to Germany? Skip the 30 tabs. One application. Two operators. One shared state. Like Comment Story Updates Move To Germany One shared workspace where you and your agent build your new life in Germany. Inspiration Moving to another country means rebuilding almost your entire everyday life from scratch. Bank account. Health insurance. Doctors. Groceries. Transportation. Paperwork. Jobs. Local services. Appointments. The information is out there, but it is scattered across dozens of websites, search results, forms, tabs, and directories. I know this problem personally. I've been traveling since 2019 as a German, just not to Germany. ;-) We're a digital nomad family of five, and every time we arrive somewhere new, we have to rebuild parts of our everyday life again. Finding the information isn't even the hardest part. The hard part is turning hundreds of search results, websites, providers, and options into your plan. That's what made me curious about WebMCP. What if an agent didn't have to look at a website and guess how to use it? Which button should it click? What does this field mean? What state is the application currently in? Instead, what if the application could expose its capabilities directly to the agent, while the human continued using the normal website? That's the experiment behind MoveToGermany.lol. What it does MoveToGermany.lol explores a different future: instead of doing all of this alone, you and your agent work together inside the same web application. The agent does the repetitive work. The human makes the decisions. Humans + agents together The core idea behind MoveToGermany.lol is simple: the agent doesn't replace the website, and it doesn't replace the human. A user can say: I'm moving to Berlin, postal code 10115. I'm a software developer, I have a dog and I only speak English. Set me up with the essentials. The agent can turn that request into actions inside MoveToGermany: create an arrival profile, discover relevant services, and start building a personalized relocation plan. But the results don't disappear into a chat. They become part of the actual application state. I can inspect the recommendations myself, change the shortlist, remove something, pick another provider, or leave a note: "English-speaking only." Then I can hand control back to the agent. It reads the state I just changed manually and continues from there. For example, it can see that I rejected a provider, understand my note, find a better alternative, and continue building the plan. That's the part of WebMCP I find most interesting: Human intent → Agent action → Shared application state → Human decision → Agent continues What can the agent actually do? MoveToGermany exposes WebMCP tools across different parts of the relocation journey. Underneath that workflow is a discovery layer of more than 1.16 million real places across 81 categories in Germany. The agent can: build a personalized arrival profile and starter plan discover nearby services manage and reason over the user's shortlist read notes and decisions made directly in the UI compare providers and find jobs help with paperwork and draft outreach find bookable services and propose appointments The goal wasn't to build one impressive AI command. I wanted to see what happens when the whole web application becomes a workspace that a human and an agent can operate together. Why WebMCP? An agent could theoretically operate MoveToGermany by looking at the page and trying to click through the UI. But the application already knows what it can do. Why make the agent guess? Without structured tools, the interaction looks something like: Agent → inspect page → guess UI → click → inspect again → hope With WebMCP, we get closer to: Human intent → Agent → WebMCP tool → Application This isn't a chatbot added on top of the website. The WebMCP tools operate on the same application state the human sees and edits, so the human can take over, make a decision, and the agent can continue from there. WebMCP turns the website itself into the shared workspace. How I built it Tech stack Next.js React TypeScript Tailwind CSS Supabase / PostgreSQL Vercel WebMCP The WebMCP tools are registered directly in the application using document.modelContext.registerTool() : document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "...", description: "...", inputSchema: { // structured input }, execute: async (input) => { // interact with the application } }); That's the whole mechanism: one underlying application state, read and written by both the regular UI and the agent. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge wasn't exposing individual functions as tools. It was deciding where the agent should act autonomously and where the human should remain in control. Searching through hundreds of providers is a great job for an agent. Filtering and comparing them is, too. But choosing the final provider, approving outreach, or confirming an appointment should remain a human decision. Another challenge was shared state. If the agent builds a plan and the human changes it manually, the agent shouldn't continue working from an outdated version of reality. That pushed me to treat every state change as something either side could make, and to design the tools to read the current state instead of assuming their own version of it. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud that I could reuse a service dataset I had built previously as the discovery layer for a completely new WebMCP application. I'm also proud that this shows agents can make a small, unglamorous problem, one that a lot of people run into, genuinely easier. An agent working through MoveToGermany can meaningfully reduce the amount of searching, tab-switching, and manual comparison involved in settling into a new country. What I learned My biggest takeaway from building MoveToGermany.lol is that making websites usable by agents isn't only about automation. It's about collaboration. Agents are good at searching, filtering, comparing, and repetitive work. Humans provide context, preferences, judgment, and final approval. The interesting part happens when control can move naturally between the two: work gets done, reviewed, changed, and picked back up again. That feels less like automating a website and more like designing a new kind of interface. What's next MoveToGermany.lol is about relocation, but the experiment is bigger than relocation. I want to explore what happens when more websites stop treating agents as visitors that need to imitate humans, and start exposing meaningful capabilities directly, while keeping the human in the loop. One application. Two operators. One shared state. Built With next.js postgresql react supabase tailwind typescript webmcp Try it out github.com movetogermany.lol Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I built this solo, front-end, back-end, and the WebMCP integration. It was my first time working with WebMCP, so most of the effort went into figuring out where the tools should live in the app and how to keep the UI and the agent working on the same state without stepping on each other. I reused a service dataset I’d built for an earlier project as the discovery layer, which saved me from sourcing 1.16M places from scratch. I definitely learned a lot about designing for two operators instead of one. shufflethis Wuebbe husband. father. slowmad. title: HARMONYIA
pitch: Agente que combina las capacidades de webmcp para poder trabajar con asesores en un entorno armonico
about_excerpt:
Agente que combina las capacidades de webmcp para poder trabajar con asesores en un entorno armonico
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 Story

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Me inspire porque me intereso bastante y queria presentar este caso en un CRM para immboliarias haci que quise probar herramientas que combinen el webmcp y acoplarlo a la baja adpcion del CRM para usuarios nuevos. 

 What it does 

 HARMONIYA es un agente de conversacion que para este caso de uso es gestion de leads, manejar leads es un problema estar analizando uno a uno demora con el modelo podriamos usar los filtros que expone para que un modelo de voz le hable directamente y puede ejecutar operacion de manera unida entre la ia y un asesor aparte de facilitar las tareas del asesor esto ayudaria a eliminar la baja adopcion de los usuarios en usar un crm. 

 How we built it 

 La aplicación fue construida utilizando Astro como base, integrando React para los componentes interactivos y WebMCP para exponer las capacidades del CRM mediante herramientas que pueden ser utilizadas por agentes. 

 Implementamos Harmony como un asistente de voz capaz de convertir la voz del usuario en texto, interpretar su intención mediante un modelo de lenguaje y utilizar las herramientas disponibles para consultar o modificar información del CRM. Finalmente, la respuesta generada es convertida nuevamente a voz mediante Text-to-Speech. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Uno de los principales retos fue diseñar correctamente el flujo de interacción por voz: recibir el audio, transcribirlo, interpretar la intención, decidir qué herramienta utilizar, ejecutar la acción, generar una respuesta y finalmente convertirla nuevamente en audio. 

 Otro desafío importante fue la implementación de WebMCP y la definición de herramientas reutilizables que pudieran ser utilizadas tanto por Harmony como por otros agentes compatibles con el estándar. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Uno de los mayores logros fue conseguir construir y conectar todo el flujo funcional en un tiempo limitado: desde la interacción por voz hasta la ejecución de acciones reales dentro del CRM. 

 Más allá de la implementación técnica, también estoy orgulloso de haber mantenido la constancia y el compromiso con el proyecto, dedicando tiempo y esfuerzo para convertir la idea inicial en una aplicación funcional. 

 What we learned 

 Aprendimos qué es WebMCP y cómo utilizarlo para exponer las capacidades de una aplicación mediante herramientas estandarizadas. 

 Esto nos permitió entender cómo podemos diseñar nuestros agentes de forma más interoperable, evitando crear integraciones diferentes para cada agente. En el futuro, nuevos agentes pueden utilizar las mismas herramientas que ya expone la aplicación, manteniendo una única capa de capacidades y reduciendo la necesidad de crear múltiples implementaciones o bifurcaciones.

title: coSynth
pitch: A synthesizer you control by talking to AI. Describe a sound. The AI turns the knobs, plays it, shows every change, and guides you through the controls so you can tweak it and learn as you go.
about_excerpt: A synthesizer you control by talking to AI. Describe a sound. The AI turns the knobs, plays it, shows every change, and guides you through the controls so you can tweak it and learn as you go. Like Comment Story Updates Full Wavetable Synthesizer GIF Active AI state and tool visible in the UI coSynth – AI Web Synthesizer Sound design is hard to get into. A real synth has hundreds of knobs. coSynth lets you describe and get a sound. The AI turns the knobs, plays the result, listens to what it made, and shows all the changes in the UI. You keep it, undo it, tweak it, or ask the AI to show you how it got there. You can also ask AI to teach a complext topic and AI will guide you through step by step. Live: https://coSynth.vercel.app Code: https://github.com/brunnolou/coSynth (MIT) Why WebMCP fits A synth is a terrible thing to operate through text or screenshots. Too many parameters (in this case 224), knobs to drag, LFO curves to draw, etc. An agent can misclick, can miss an exact value, and can't hear the audio. The UI is too complex for someone to easily find things when they are not used to it. That makes a synthesizer one of the best interfaces for WebMCP. For the AI agent: It communicates to the synth directly. Every parameter has a name, a unit, and a range that can be edited directly in bulk. When the agent plays a note, it gets back attack time, decay, spectral centroid, and harmonics, then compares that with a reference clip. So it can "hear" with a tool call. For humans Instead of starting from scratch, you get very close to what you want. Then you can see the exact changes and tweak manually. If you don't know a concept or want to find something, AI can show you the exact location or teach you step by step. You can leverage AI's world knowledge to create any synth sound! What used to need trained ears you now can achieve by sending a reference sound and asking AI to replicate. How I Made the AI<>Human UX Better Each knob the AI touched gets a small animated marker. A status line shows which tool is running. You can reject a whole AI iteration and keep your own edits. Undo covers AI changes and yours. Old branches stay reachable in history. The AI can highlight controls step by step and explain them. Every AI performance is saved, so "play that again with my new adjustment" is one click. AI can save as a preset, and you can download it. How I implemented WebMCP Vanilla TypeScript and Vite. DSP in an AudioWorklet, UI in Canvas, WebGL2 and DOM. WebMCP sits on top of the same engine the UI uses, and the synth works without it. Tools register with document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) . There are 24, each with a JSON Schema input and a readOnlyHint : Reading : get_synth_state , get_parameter_schema , get_ui_targets , list_presets , get_history Editing : update_parameters , set_modulation , set_fx_order , apply_patch , save_preset , load_preset , delete_preset , export_preset Sound : play_notes , render_audio , capture_audio , analyze_audio , analyze_reference_audio , compare_audio , suggest_patch , stop_performance Together : show_ui_guide , navigate_history , replay_history All 24 register at page load. play_notes needs the human to click Start first, because browsers won't play audio without a gesture. render_audio uses an OfflineAudioContext, so the agent can design and measure before anyone clicks anything. The page also documents itself. A clipped agent brief in the DOM, a JSON descriptor, ai-tools meta tags, llms.txt and robots.txt . An agent given only the URL can read the page and know what to do. How I tested the agent experience I want to ensure AI could call the tools easily. So I built a loop. A harness exposes only what a real WebMCP client sees, and logs every call. A fresh agent gets a fixed prompt and is never allowed to read the repo. Each round runs on Claude and Codex. When * both trip in the same place( , the tool is wrong . Fix the top blocker, run again. In self-improving loop. Four evals, each asking one question. Can the agent find out what to send ( docs/agent-ux-eval.md ). Can it steer toward a sound it cannot hear ( docs/agent-match-eval.md ). Given a "how do I" question, does it teach rather than edit ( docs/agent-teaching-eval.md ). Given only a URL, does it find the tools at all? Prompts, agent reports and raw logs are all in the repo. Learning all 224 parameters went from 45 calls to 1 . Failed calls went to zero on both models. The matching loop went from 87 calls to 36 . How to test Open https://cosynth.vercel.app in the ChatGPT in-app browser, or in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . ChatGPT Desktop was the most reliable client for me. Click "CLICK TO START AUDIO" once. Try: "Make a bright plucked bass and play a short riff." "Show me where the amp envelope is and how to shorten the release." "Save that." Watch the markers, click the status dot for before and after values, and use Keep or Reject. No login. Presets and reference audio stay in the browser. What was already there, what is new I started from Soundgineer by noisyloop ( https://github.com/noisyloop/soundgineer , MIT). Its DSP engine and original UI date from July 6 to 11, 2026, and that version is still up at https://soundgineer.vercel.app . Everything WebMCP-related is from the submission period, August 26 to September 3, 2026, about 200 dated commits: the WebMCP layer and all 24 tools, offline rendering and audio analysis, change markers and Keep/Reject, shared undo history and replays, guided walkthroughs, the interface redesign, the four evals with their harness, and the in-page agent brief. title: AIR — Agent-Native Architectural Design Workspace
pitch: Architects speak in design intent. WebMCP lets AI understand, sketch, and act inside the same live architectural workspace.
about_excerpt: Architects speak in design intent. WebMCP lets AI understand, sketch, and act inside the same live architectural workspace. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Architectural AI tools are becoming very good at generating images, but the workflow is still surprisingly fragmented. An architect has design intent, preferences, project history, references, sketches, and ongoing conversations with an AI assistant. Yet when that architect opens an image-generation application, most of that context disappears. The agent is forced to operate a visual interface like a human — clicking buttons, navigating galleries, and guessing what is on screen. We wanted to explore a different model: What if the AI already understood the architect, and the architectural web application exposed its real design capabilities directly to that agent? That is the idea behind AIR with WebMCP. What it does AIR is an architectural AI design workspace for exploring, developing, and refining design ideas. With WebMCP, AIR becomes a workspace shared by both the architect and the AI agent. The agent can: read the current AIR canvas and design state structurally load an existing architectural design without navigating the Gallery UI explore multiple architectural directions using AIR's native Explore and Batch workflow mark an exact architectural region with AREA sketch a proposal directly onto AIR's canvas with Draw read an architect's modifications to that sketch back as structured design context execute an agreed design change through AIR's native generation workflow access higher-level workspace capabilities such as project context, moodboards, and video The important difference is that the agent does not imitate AIR's interface. The agent uses AIR's capabilities. Human + agent collaboration The goal is not full automation. Architectural design moves repeatedly between exploration and judgment. A typical AIR + WebMCP workflow can look like this: ChatGPT brings its ongoing understanding of the architect into the current AIR design. AIR explores several design possibilities. The architect chooses a direction. The agent identifies an exact architectural area worth developing. The agent sketches an idea on the shared canvas. The architect modifies that sketch directly. The agent reads the architect's change back as design context. Only after agreement does AIR execute the design. This creates a design conversation on the actual artifact instead of a sequence of disconnected prompts. Before WebMCP, an agent would need to infer screen state and reproduce human browser interactions. With WebMCP, the website exposes structured, high-level architectural actions directly. Why WebMCP AIR is a strong fit for WebMCP because architectural applications contain far more meaning than their visible controls expose. A button labelled "AREA" is not the important concept. The important concept is: "This is the exact architectural surface we are discussing." A Draw tool is not simply a drawing widget. It can become: a shared visual language between an architect and an agent. WebMCP lets AIR expose these meanings directly through structured capabilities rather than browser-coordinate automation. That makes agent interactions faster, more reliable, and — most importantly — more useful as part of an actual design process. How we built it AIR exposes high-level capabilities through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The WebMCP layer is intentionally thin. It does not recreate the product or automate the UI. Instead, WebMCP adapters connect directly to AIR's existing application state and native workflows. Examples include: air_get_canvas_context air_apply_canvas_markup air_execute_design_request air_execute_sketch_request air_finish_image workspace, moodboard, context, and video capabilities Canvas markup uses normalized image coordinates so AREA and Draw remain independent of screen size and browser layout. Shared markup also carries structured lineage. This allows AIR to distinguish an agent-authored sketch from a sketch that the architect subsequently modified, turning the visible canvas into two-way design context. The same principle applies throughout the integration: If AIR already has a native capability, WebMCP exposes that capability instead of teaching the agent how to click its UI. What was built during the WebMCP Challenge AIR 4.0 existed before the challenge. The work submitted here is the WebMCP extension developed after the challenge began on August 25, 2026. During the challenge period we added the agent-native capability layer, including structured canvas context, high-level design execution, direct asset intake, shared Draw and AREA markup, human-edit readback, workspace/context capabilities, and the human-agent collaborative workflow demonstrated in the video. The public repository contains a runnable open-source Challenge Edition focused specifically on this new WebMCP interaction model, while the live AIR application demonstrates the integration inside the full architectural product. Accomplishments The part we are most excited about is not that an agent can control another application. It is that the agent and architect can now communicate through the same design artifact. The architect can say less. The agent can understand more. And AIR becomes the place where that understanding becomes visible and actionable. FAIR understands design. AIR acts on it. What's next The next step is to connect this interaction model with deeper architectural research and reasoning. An agent should eventually be able to move naturally between precedent research, material and construction knowledge, project constraints, design exploration, visual markup, and final architectural decisions — while the architect remains in control of the moments that require judgment. We see WebMCP as an important foundation for that future: a web where professional applications are designed not only for people or agents, but for both working together.
