title: SIGNAL
pitch: An incident war room where the agent's tools appear and disappear with the incident's phase. It can't roll back production, the tool doesn't exist until a human escalates.
about_excerpt: An incident war room where the agent's tools appear and disappear with the incident's phase. It can't roll back production, the tool doesn't exist until a human escalates. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every engineering team I know wants an agent in the incident channel, and every one of them has the same objection: not the button. Reading dashboards, correlating a latency spike against a deploy log, drafting the status page, that's work a machine should do at 3am. Rolling back production is not. The industry's current answer is a line in a system prompt: do not roll back without approval . That's a request, not a control. It's the security model of a sticky note on a server rack. WebMCP suggested a different answer. If tools are registered from the page, and the page knows what state the incident is in, then permission stops being something you ask the model to respect and becomes something the tool surface simply doesn't offer. What it does (→ why this is a strong fit for WebMCP) SIGNAL is an incident response console that a human operator and their agent drive together. The active incident moves through four phases, and the agent's tool surface is recomputed on every transition. In TRIAGE the agent has nine read-only tools: metrics, logs, deploys, topology, plus record_hypothesis to write its reasoning onto a timeline the operator can see. rollback_deploy is not in its list. Tell it to roll back and it doesn't refuse; it reports that it has no such capability, and calls request_escalation . That paints a confirmation surface showing exactly which six capabilities would be granted and what the agent intends to do with them. A named human approves. toolchange fires. Six tools light up. Now it can act, each action still gated behind a confirmation showing the blast radius. When the metrics recover, the agent calls declare_mitigated , which withdraws its own write access , and the surface contracts again to verification tools, then to postmortem tools. This is a strong fit for WebMCP specifically because the permission boundary and the user interface are the same object. The operator isn't reading a description of what the agent can do; they're looking at the browser's own tool registry, rendered. getTools() is the source of truth for both the agent's abilities and the human's understanding of them. No server-side agent framework can offer that, because the human isn't there to see it. How it creates a better user experience Before: an operator with six dashboards open, correlating timestamps by eye under time pressure, while an agent in another window offers suggestions it has no way to verify and no way to execute. With SIGNAL: the operator watches the agent investigate in a shared timeline, sees its hypothesis with the evidence attached, and makes one decision, do I trust this enough to unlock write access instead of twenty small ones. The agent handles correlation; the human handles judgement. Each is doing what it is good at, and the seam between them is a visible, auditable interface rather than a prompt. The status page update is the sharpest example. The agent drafts; the operator gets that draft in a live text field and rewrites it; the tool resolves with their version, and the return value tells the agent it was edited and what actually shipped. That's not approval, it's co-authorship, and the agent's next update matches the operator's register because it can see what they changed. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Three things, all specific to tools running in the page rather than on a server. A tool can hand you a decision and wait. request_escalation 's execute() renders a surface listing the exact capabilities to be granted and does not resolve until a human acts. A remote MCP server can return text asking a question. It cannot show you the blast radius, block, and continue with your answer, because it is not in the room. A tool can come back edited. publish_status_update and draft_postmortem both return the human's revision, not a boolean. The agent learns from the diff. The human can see the agent's power, live. The capability panel is fed by document.modelContext.getTools() on toolchange . When the phase changes, tools visibly light up or strike through. Nobody has been able to watch an agent's permissions change before, the registry was always somewhere else. And the inverse: capability scoping by construction. Prompt-based restrictions fail under adversarial input; an unregistered tool has no attack surface. search_logs carries untrustedContentHint for the same reason , log lines are attacker-influenceable and should be treated as data. How we implemented WebMCP Imperative API throughout, 21 tools via document.modelContext.registerTool . The core primitive is a useTool(def, enabled) hook that ties registration to React lifecycle through an AbortController . Phase is derived state in a Zustand store; each tool's enabled flag is a predicate over it. When the phase changes, React unmounts the effect, the controller aborts, and the capability genuinely leaves the registry. This is not a mock, the Tool Inspector extension shows the list shrinking. toolchange plus getTools() drive the capability panel. AbortSignal is threaded from execute(input, { signal }) into every elicitation promise, so cancellation from either side tears down the dialog rather than stranding it. annotations.readOnlyHint marks the ten observational tools; untrustedContentHint marks log search. Telemetry is a deterministic seeded simulation where metrics are a pure function of (service, region, time, mitigations applied), so rolling back the bad deploy actually recovers the curves. There's no second dataset. No backend, no network calls, nothing that can be down when a judge opens it. Challenges Getting the agent to reason about its own permissions rather than bumping into silence. Early on, told to roll back during triage, it would either hallucinate a tool or go quiet. The fix wasn't prompting, it was making get_incident_overview return the agent's current capability set and name request_escalation as the way to ask for more. Tools that describe the system's shape are as important as tools that act on it. The second was tool selection between scale_service and rollback_deploy . Both plausibly address a saturated connection pool. It resolved by putting the reasoning in the description tha, t scaling relieves symptoms but won't fix a bad code path, rather than adding a rule. Accomplishments The moment the agent says "I don't have that capability in this phase, may I escalate?" and it's true, not a scripted refusal. What we learned Tool descriptions are the real interface. The behaviour we wanted came from sentences, not code. And the return value is a prompt: a tool that returns "OK" wastes the most valuable channel it has. What's next Real integrations behind the same phase gate, PagerDuty, Datadog, GitHub. The pattern generalises past incidents to any console with a destructive action: billing, admin panels, clinical systems. The interesting version is a policy engine that derives the tool surface from an org's existing RBAC, so the agent's capabilities are automatically a subset of the operator's. title: PrismLaunch - Launch Video Creator
pitch: Your AI agent creates your product's promo video. You direct it on a shared timeline, review each stage, and decide what ships.
about_excerpt: Your AI agent creates your product's promo video. You direct it on a shared timeline, review each stage, and decide what ships. Like Comment Story Updates Dark-mode editor: an editable 45-second promo on a shared timeline, with layered visuals and frame-accurate playback. Style frames: review reusable brand, typography, UI and sound elements before the agent builds the animatic. Saved activity: review the agent’s tool calls, captured frames, revisions and human approvals alongside the current film. Modular project files: separate JSON for creative stages, elements, tracks and activity keeps each part easy to inspect. Light-mode storyboards: play each shot’s composition and movement before approving the film’s visual direction. Inspiration I build products, but I don't know how to make a good promo video. Learning motion graphics is a whole other job, and it becomes another thing standing between finishing a product and showing it to people. I wanted my AI agent to help with that. It already understood the product I was building. The missing piece was an editor it could actually use. Asking an agent to control a video timeline through screenshots, dragging, and clicking was a fragile way to work. WebMCP gave me a practical way to expose the editing operations directly. That became PrismLaunch: a promo video editor built for a person and their agent to use together. What it does You give your agent the product, the audience, and the message. It develops the film in PrismLaunch while you review the work in the studio. The process moves through a brief, concepts, script, visual storyboard, style frames, animatic, polish, and final build. Storyboards show the composition and timed movement of each shot. Style frames show the reusable elements and sample compositions the agent plans to use. You can approve each stage or send it back with a note. The agent revises the same project, and a saved activity log records submissions, decisions, and edits. Review panels stay focused on the work; manual editing tools live in the editor. The shared timeline combines text, images, video, audio, shapes, device frames, motion, and editable HTML components. Reusable elements let the agent define a piece once and update its placements throughout the film. The finished composition can be encoded as an MP4 in the browser. I used PrismLaunch to make the promo video for PrismLaunch itself. Watch the promo video made with PrismLaunch . Why WebMCP fits Video editing involves precise operations: placing a clip at a frame, changing its duration, moving it to another layer, adjusting typography, or updating a reusable element. Those operations are much easier to express as structured tools than as a sequence of mouse movements. PrismLaunch exposes tools for project context, creative stages, layers, elements, clips, preview, frame capture, and render requests. The agent can inspect the current project and make a specific edit. The person sees the result in the same editor and gives feedback there. This makes it possible to work with an agent on an editable film throughout the process. Human review is part of that workflow: stage approval and render approval are controls in the studio, not tools exposed for the agent to call. PrismLaunch does not contain its own model. You bring the agent you already use. How I built it I came up with the idea from my own painful experience and used Claude Code to build the core functionality. I then used Codex to test the WebMCP workflow in the browser and fix issues that my Claude Code setup could not directly exercise. The studio uses Next.js, React, and TypeScript. WebMCP tools register via document.modelContext.registerTool , with a compatibility path for browsers that expose the older API location. Zod validates tool inputs, and human edits and agent edits go through the same state and timeline operations. Remotion renders the composition for preview and export, with WebCodecs encoding the MP4 in the browser. Projects can live in a linked local folder or in browser storage, with separate JSON files for each creative stage, element, and track, plus a saved activity log. The app is hosted on Vercel, and its source is available under the MIT license. Challenges and what I learned The hardest part was teaching an AI how to make a good promo when I am still learning video editing myself. I analysed successful promo videos, turned what I learned into a filmmaking guide, and built reusable elements that an agent could combine in its own films. Pacing, hierarchy, and knowing what to leave out mattered as much as having editing tools. Making PrismLaunch's own promo became a practical test of the product. Early storyboards looked too much like scripts, so I built visual boards with positioned subjects and timed movement. The first animatic also exposed a gap in the method: copying storyboard roughs onto a timeline did not produce a finished sequence. I strengthened the filmmaking guide and added a check that refuses animatic submissions while storyboard roughs remain visible. That workflow uncovered product bugs too. I fixed review notes that failed validation, activity that disappeared after reopening, and style-frame reviews that exposed editing tools. I split browser-stored projects into separate files for creative stages, elements, tracks, and activity. I also improved media preparation and playhead synchronisation to address interruptions during playback. Real WebMCP testing exposed issues that the local fallback did not. Multiple components initially registered the same tools, causing partial registration failures. Later, ChatGPT's built-in browser disabled discovery because the growing tool catalogue exceeded its supported limits. I introduced shared registration and five compact toolsets—workflow, graphics, media, elements, and edit—with prism.use_toolset to switch between them. Long sessions can still require reconnecting when a host retains earlier catalogues. Publishing a skill was not enough to ensure an agent received it. Creative WebMCP edits now require that both the operating guide and the filmmaking guide be delivered via prism.read_guide . The agent still has to apply that guidance well. I learned that an agent-friendly editor needs precise tools, inspectable state, visible feedback, and a clear point where the person decides whether the work is ready. What I am proud of PrismLaunch made its own promo video. That took the idea beyond a tool-registration demo and into the task I originally needed help with. I also tested the WebMCP experience in Chrome and ChatGPT's built-in browser. Working through those differences helped turn the editor into something I could actually use with an agent. Current limitations This is an early editor with a small motion library. External agents need a browser and client with native WebMCP support; the fallback registry is only usable within the page. Tool discovery can vary between hosts, and long sessions may require reconnecting if the host retains earlier tool catalogues. Local folder access depends on browser support and a person granting permission. Browser storage is an alternative, but an agent must edit those projects through the page's tools rather than ordinary filesystem tools. MP4 export depends on browser codec support and the resources available on the user's device. What's next I want to build a much richer motion graphics library that agents can draw from when making promo videos: more reusable elements, more visual treatments, and more ways to clearly communicate a product. Built With claude-code codex next.js react remotion tailwind-css typescript vercel webcodecs webmcp zod zustand Try it out tryprismlaunch.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I conceived PrismLaunch, directed the product and video workflow, built the core with Claude Code, and tested and refined the WebMCP experience with Codex. I developed the filmmaking guide and reusable elements, reviewed each creative stage, and used the app to make its own promo. title: PodHood — WebMCP for Podcasts & YouTube
pitch: Turn any podcast or YouTube library into a surface your agent can drive: 8 WebMCP tools that search, filter, read timestamped transcripts, and cue the player on the page you're both looking at.
about_excerpt: Turn any podcast or YouTube library into a surface your agent can drive: 8 WebMCP tools that search, filter, read timestamped transcripts, and cue the player on the page you're both looking at. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into* Live demo → https://aiengineer.podhood.com * — a real production library of 1,065 talks. Open it in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or in Chrome with WebMCP enabled, and just start asking. Inspiration Podcasts and conference talks hold an enormous share of what a field actually knows, and almost none of it is reachable. Search gives you an episode, not a moment. A transcript is a 20,000-word wall. "Where did she explain the eval harness?" is a question no podcast page can answer today. Agents don't fix this — they inherit it. An agent that lands on a podcast page can do one of two unpleasant things: swallow the entire transcript and burn its context on filler, or drive the UI by guessing at pixels. Either way it works around the page instead of with it. WebMCP changes where the agent is standing. It is already here, in the browser, next to the person, looking at the same screen. That turns out to change what a tool is even allowed to be. What it does PodHood turns any podcast or YouTube channel into a structured library — summaries, chapters, key moments, speaker-diarized and word-aligned transcripts, recognized people, companies and products — and then registers that structure as eight WebMCP tools via document.modelContext , across two surfaces. On the library page search_episodes — search the catalog by meaning or keyword; returns episodes with timestamped citation links filter_episodes — apply topic / person / company / product / collection / year filters; the visible list and the URL change list_episodes — read back exactly what the visitor is looking at right now, with IDs open_episode — navigate the visitor to an episode page On an episode page read_episode — summary, speakers, and the chapter + key-moment outline with timestamps search_transcript — find exact text and highlight it in the transcript panel read_transcript — speaker-labeled, timestamped transcript windows, by chapter or time range play_moment — seek the player to a moment and start playback play_moment is the whole thesis in one call. The agent is not handing you a link to go read later. It moves the playhead in the player in front of you, and you hear the thing. That is only possible because the agent shares the view with a human — which is exactly the shape WebMCP has and no other agent interface does. What a human and an agent do together here On https://aiengineer.podhood.com — 1,065 talks from the AI Engineer conference series, 86 collections, 1,033 speakers, 880 companies — the loop looks like this: "What's actually being said about evals at these conferences?" → the agent runs search_episodes , then filter_episodes on the Evaluation & Observability topic. Your screen changes. You are now looking at 83 talks, and so is it. "Only 2026, and only speakers from model labs." → filter_episodes narrows again. You watch it happen, and you can undo it by clicking, because they are the same filters you would have clicked. "Open the second one and find where he explains the harness." → open_episode , then search_transcript . The line lights up in the transcript panel. "Play it." → play_moment . The player seeks and starts. You ask a follow-up while it plays; the agent has read_transcript scoped to that chapter and answers with a citation that points at your domain, at the right second. No copy-paste, no tab-switching, no "here's a link, go find it yourself." The agent does the navigating; the human does the listening and the deciding. Why WebMCP is the right primitive for this We already run a hosted MCP server for podcast catalogs, so we can compare the two honestly. An external MCP connector is a good way for an agent somewhere else to query a catalog. It cannot touch the page a person is looking at. It has no playhead, no transcript panel, no filter rail. WebMCP inverts that assumption, and the tools change shape as a result. filter_episodes is not a query — it is a UI mutation the person watches happen. search_transcript is not a string match — it is a highlight. This is the only agent interface where "tell me" and "show me" are the same call. Three properties we deliberately locked in: Read and view-state only. No writes, no accounts, no purchases. An agent can only change what the visitor could already change themselves — filters, highlight, playhead — all visible on screen and reversible with a click. There is no state an agent can reach that a human cannot see it reach. Show-branded, not platform-branded. The tools present as belonging to the creator's show, on the creator's domain — not to PodHood. Domain-native citations. Every link an agent produces resolves to the creator's own domain with a timestamp. Agent traffic lands on the creator, which is the only version of this that is sustainable for the people making the content. Why this needs more than a transcript Every tool here is downstream of structure that has to exist before the tool can be honest: search_episodes needs a semantic index over the catalog, not ctrl+F. filter_episodes needs entities disambiguated — "Claude" the model versus a person named Claude, three different speakers named Chen. play_moment needs word-level audio alignment . A timestamp four seconds off makes the entire feature feel broken. read_episode needs chapters and key moments that were actually extracted, not guessed at read time. This is the part of WebMCP we think is under-appreciated: good tools are a consequence of good data modeling. You can bolt document.modelContext onto anything. You can only make it useful on top of a page that already knows what it contains. How we built it The tool layer registers on document.modelContext when each surface mounts, with JSON-schema'd inputs and compact, agent-shaped return payloads — never raw DOM, never a whole transcript. Tools are bound to the same client state store the UI reads from , so an agent's filter_episodes and a human's click on the filter rail go down one code path. There is no drift between what the agent believes is on screen and what is on screen — and list_episodes exists precisely so the agent can re-ground itself against the real view at any point. read_transcript is windowed by chapter or time range, because handing a model ninety minutes of speech is how you get a confident wrong answer. Tool names and descriptions were tuned hard. A model will reach for search_episodes when it wants search_transcript unless the boundary is stated explicitly in the description. Next.js (App Router) + TypeScript, deployed on Vercel. Our origins are registered for the Chrome WebMCP origin trial, so document.modelContext is available with no flags — including on creators' custom domains. Zero creator configuration. The tools ship automatically with every published PodHood library. Nothing to enable, nothing to write. Agents without WebMCP support see a completely normal page; nothing degrades. Challenges we ran into Sizing outputs. The first read_transcript returned everything and the agent drowned. Chapter-scoped windows plus a "next window" affordance fixed it. One state, two drivers. Making agent-driven and human-driven state genuinely the same object took a refactor. Anything less produced ghost states, where the agent was filtering a list the human was not seeing. Restraint. The tempting move is to expose thirty tools. Eight sharply-described verbs outperformed a larger surface every time we tested. Testing against a moving target. WebMCP is an origin trial. ChatGPT desktop plus Chrome flags plus a live registered origin is not a fast dev loop. What we learned The best WebMCP tools are not an API bolted onto a page — they are the page's own verbs, named. Everything that worked here was already something the site could do: filter, highlight, seek. WebMCP just let an agent do it on the human's behalf, in front of them. The tools that tried to be more than the page could do were exactly the ones models misused. What's next Cross-library tools, so an agent can work across a creator's entire network of shows at once. A compare_moments tool for putting two speakers' claims side by side with both timestamps. Publishing the WebMCP tool layer as a standalone open-source package, so any media site can adopt the same eight verbs. Prior work vs. work done during the submission period PodHood is an existing product. The ingestion pipeline, the Brief data model (chapters, key moments, diarization, entity recognition, word-aligned transcripts), the search index and the player all predate this hackathon. Everything in the WebMCP layer is new work built during the submission period (August 25 – September 3, 2026): all eight tool definitions and their schemas, the document.modelContext registration for both surf

title: Sundae Metrics
pitch: A sales dashboard that hands agents 6 WebMCP tools instead of a picture of a chart. Same question, same page: 4m 38s without the tools, 36 seconds with them.
about_excerpt: A sales dashboard that hands agents 6 WebMCP tools instead of a picture of a chart. Same question, same page: 4m 38s without the tools, 36 seconds with them. Like Comment Story Updates An agent just changed the dashboard: the amber WRITE entry in the Agent activity rail, with an Undo on it. Inspiration Ice cream chains are the smallest business that genuinely needs analytics: four shops, six flavors, wildly seasonal, and no data analyst. The products already sold to them - HioPOS, Sipos, GETPOS, Vendty - all ship the same dashboard, and every question that dashboard cannot answer ends the same way: an Excel export. An assistant looking at that screen is in a worse position than the owner. Ask it "how much did North's sales change between February and March?" and, without WebMCP, it has to drive the whole interface: find the store selector in the DOM, synthesize a click, wait for a re-render with no signal that it finished, set the month range through a native picker, read the values back and do the arithmetic itself. It gets there - and I measured that rather than assuming it, which is what the section below is about. What it cannot do is get there cheaply. An interface built for eyes makes an agent pay in clicks, re-renders and round trips for something the page already knows exactly. What it does Sundae Metrics is a sales dashboard for Glace , a fictional chain of 4 artisanal ice cream shops: 12 months x 4 locations x 6 flavors. It is a normal dashboard - KPI cards, a 12-month bar chart, a flavor breakdown, a compare-periods view. The product is the layer underneath. The page registers 6 tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() : Tool What it does readOnlyHint list_stores Lists the locations on this dashboard true get_sales Exact units and revenue for one location in one month true compare_periods Percentage change between two months true get_top_flavors Flavor ranking - best sellers or slow movers true get_summary Revenue across every location over a date range true set_dashboard_view Changes what the user is looking at false The February-to-March question becomes one call: await compare_periods({ store: "north", monthA: "2026-02", monthB: "2026-03" }); // {"revenueChangePct":-17.1,"unitsChangePct":-15.4} And the dataset carries a case the chart actively hides. In January 2026 the North location's pistachio sales collapse from 2,099 units to 554 - down 74%, from the 3rd best seller to the 6th - a supply shortage. But January is also North's highest-revenue month of the year: the other five flavors each rise about 24% and absorb the gap, so the tallest bar on the chart is the one hiding the problem . Nothing on screen shows it. get_top_flavors({store: "north", month: "2026-01", limit: 3, order: "bottom"}) shows it immediately. set_dashboard_view runs the other way. Ask for the South location and the screen changes in front of you: the agent acts on the same interface the human is looking at, not on a copy of the data somewhere else. The measurement The demo video is not a mock-up. Both halves were filmed in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser - same model, same question, same page, changing only ?webmcp=off : Without the tools With the tools Time 4 min 38 s 36 s Work navigated the UI month by month, then asked permission to download the page's data file 5 tool calls Answer pistachio 2,099 -> 554 (-74%) same, "fell from third-best seller to last" Both are right, and that is the honest claim. Without the tools the agent still gets there - the chart prints its values as text, so it reads them. What it cannot do is get there cheaply. It also tried to escape the screen entirely: three minutes in, it asked to download the dashboard's JavaScript data file rather than keep reading the interface. That request was denied on camera, because bypassing the rendered page is precisely what a real app with a backend would not allow. How I built it Vite + React + TypeScript, client-side only, no backend. Plain CSS with custom properties, no Tailwind. The chart is twelve div s with percentage heights, no charting library. Two dev dependencies beyond the template: vitest and webmcp-types . src/lib/queries.ts is the only place in the codebase that computes anything. The dashboard and the tools consume the same pure functions, so a number on the chart and a number returned by a tool cannot drift apart. 39,871 is what get_sales returns, what is printed on the March bar, and what the KPI card shows - one function, three consumers. 56 tests cover that layer, the state and the tool definitions. State is a module-level store exposed through useSyncExternalStore - mutable from outside React, which is exactly what set_dashboard_view needs. The dataset is generated by a seed script with no randomness at all : running it twice produces a byte-identical JSON, and the test file is the only place in the repo where the expected figures are written by hand. If the seed drifts, the tests fail. Accomplishments I'm proud of order: "bottom" is not decoration. The KPI those POS products actually sell to ice cream shops is "best sellers and slow movers", because owners use the second half to decide what to drop from the menu. It costs one parameter, not a seventh tool. No tool carries untrustedContentHint , and that is a decision, not an omission. Every value comes from a committed seed file, so no tool output can carry third-party text an agent might read as instructions. The hint exists for tools that return content someone else wrote; claiming it here would be noise. The Agent activity rail is the security answer, not chrome. How much a site should have to reveal about what an agent did on it is still open in the standard - prompt injection ( webmcp#11 ) and hints for consequential actions ( webmcp#176 ) are both unresolved. This dashboard's response is to make every call visible as it happens: tool name, input, output, elapsed time, output size against Chrome's 1,500-character ceiling, and an Undo on the one call that changed something. Indigo means the agent read; amber means the agent wrote. Nothing an agent does here is invisible. Challenges I ran into Chrome drops a malformed tool without raising anything. Exceed the name limit (30 chars), the tool description limit (500), a parameter description (150) or the output ceiling (1,500) and the tool is simply not registered - no error, no warning. annotations placed as a second argument instead of inside the tool object is ignored the same silent way. The fix was to compare getTools() against the six expected names after registering and log the difference, and to route every execute through one helper that truncates output to 1,500 characters. The question you ask changes whether the agent finds the anomaly. Asked "look at the flavor breakdown and tell me if anything looks off", the tool-driven agent fetched January only and concluded the anomaly was passion fruit - the cheapest flavor per unit. It failed that way twice in a row. With one month of flavor data, 554 units is not remarkable; the agent without tools got it right precisely because navigating the UI forced it through December as well. Asking for the comparison explicitly fixes it without naming pistachio. That is a WebMCP design lesson, not a demo detail: a tool that answers one month invites a one-month answer. The wording that shipped, identical in both halves of the video: "For the North store, what happened to sales in January 2026? Compare the flavor breakdown against December and tell me if anything looks off." Agents are not deterministic. Across five runs of the same question the figures never moved - 15,826 units, $50,800, pistachio 554 against 2,099 - but the conclusion was worded differently every time. The narration was written to whatever the agent actually said, rather than re-asking until a nicer sentence came out. What I learned That the interesting half of WebMCP is not exposing data - it is deciding what a tool is allowed to be . Six tools with one write among them, each one answering a question an owner would actually ask, beats twenty tools that mirror the internal data model. And the write tool is where the standard gets genuinely new: it is the first time an agent and a person can be looking at the same screen, and the agent can change it. What's next for Sundae Metrics Hourly granularity, channel mix (counter / dine-in / delivery), and a real backend behind the query layer - the tool contracts would not change, which is the point. The interesting open question is the trust model: the activity rail is one answer, but the standard has not settled on one yet. title: Ceiling
pitch: A WebMCP action gate that gives agents narrow tools, requires one-use user activation for changes, and produces a verifiable session receipt chain.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP action gate that gives agents narrow tools, requires one-use user activation for changes, and produces a verifiable session receipt chain. Like Comment Story Updates Universal adapter conformance across content, access, and spending policies. Seven-case Defense Matrix: authority, replay, concurrency, and receipt attacks. Hard policy denial: unsafe changes are refused before authority is considered. Unarmed effect control: an admitted proposal still cannot apply itself. Ceiling: a bounded WebMCP change gate with visible authority and evidence. Ceiling Why I built it Agents are getting better at working inside websites. That is useful, but it creates a basic problem: how do I let an agent help without handing it every action available in my signed-in session? Ceiling is my attempt to answer that question with something people can actually try. It is a small release-policy workbench where an agent can read the current state, prepare a change, and explain why it wants that change. The page decides whether the request fits its rules, and a person remains in control of the final action. I did not want the safety story to be a warning banner or a promise in a README. I wanted the boundary to be visible in the interface and testable from the agent side. What it does The demo follows four simple steps: The agent proposes one change. Ceiling checks the value and shows the difference. A person can authorize that specific change for a few seconds. The page applies or rejects it once and records what happened. Unsafe requests stop before the approval step. In the demo, an attempt to turn off signed artifacts is denied immediately. A safer request to change the rollback window from 30 to 45 minutes is allowed into review, but the agent still cannot apply it on its own. Approval is deliberately narrow. It is tied to the current policy, the proposed value, and the requested operation. It expires quickly and cannot be reused. Rollback follows the same rule instead of acting as an unprotected escape hatch. Every decision adds a linked receipt. The page can verify the chain again and export the session evidence as JSON. A built-in Defense Matrix also tries seven ways to break the boundary, including replay, expiry, parallel application, and receipt tampering. Why WebMCP fits Without a structured interface, an agent either has to guess from pixels or a site has to expose a broad action API. WebMCP gives the page a better option: it can publish a small, discoverable set of tools with clear inputs. Ceiling registers 11 tools directly through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Four are read-only. Seven cover the review workflow. An agent can inspect the available tools, read the policy, propose a change, test the safety boundary, and verify the receipts without being given deployment, credential, payment, messaging, or cross-origin powers. The result is a better experience for both sides. The agent does not have to guess what it is allowed to do, and the user does not have to trust a vague confirmation dialog. How I built it Ceiling is dependency-free HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The WebMCP tools use closed input schemas, and the interface reports whether registration succeeded, partly succeeded, or is unavailable. The release-policy demo sits on a reusable scalar-change core. I also tested that core against publishing, access-control, and spending-policy examples to make sure the pattern was not tied to one screen. The focused suite currently includes 78 tests, a 23-case policy evaluation, and 50 cross-domain adapter checks. I used OpenAI Codex during implementation, testing, adversarial review, and release packaging. A separate non-author review initially rejected the release because of three packaging and claim-boundary problems. I corrected those problems before preparing this submission. What was difficult The hardest part was defining what a click actually proves. Browser automation can produce trusted input, so Ceiling does not call a click proof of identity or proof that no automation was involved. It treats the gesture as short-lived permission for one visible operation and no more. I also found a concurrency bug in an earlier receipt implementation. Parallel writes could reuse the same sequence information. I kept that behavior as a regression fixture, serialized the active write path, and added full-chain verification. Chrome on my test machine did not expose WebMCP during the recorded fallback pass. The page says that plainly and keeps the fallback controls separate. The working WebMCP demonstration was verified in the ChatGPT/Codex in-app browser. What I learned The most useful lesson was that refusal is part of the product. A trustworthy agent interface should make denied actions, missing capabilities, and failed preconditions as clear as successful ones. I also learned that evidence is only useful when it is easy to inspect and hard to accidentally overstate. The final project deliberately claims less than the larger system I hope to build. What's next Ceiling is session-local by design. The next steps would be reviewed host adapters, optional signed or externally anchored receipts, and carefully scoped persistence. Each would need its own authority boundary rather than silently expanding the one demonstrated here. title: SwitchBack
pitch: Switchback makes planning for your hike fun again. Collaborate with the agent and save time on research for the next adventure! It provides verified routes to best fit your idea of a great day.
about_excerpt: Switchback makes planning for your hike fun again. Collaborate with the agent and save time on research for the next adventure! It provides verified routes to best fit your idea of a great day. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I am usually short on time for planning my next hike or trail run. I always leave it until the very end. It is hard to Google "ChatGPT" and get routes from AllTrails or Wikiloc. They are unverified, and more than once I have been on closed hikes or dangerous segments. Also, I think we need to be able to co-create with agents. Planning a hike is not really a question with a single text answer. It is a shared, spatial decision: where to start, whether a route genuinely closes as a loop, how far it is, what the ascent looks like, and what the current planning context is. I built Switchback around a simple idea: ask for a loop, then see the ground truth. Rather than having an agent recommend a walk somewhere in a random place, a person and an agent work on the same Collserola–Vallvidrera map and can inspect the same route, evidence, and limitations. What it does Switchback is a WebMCP-native trail planner for short, car- or public transport-accessible walks around Collserola in Barcelona, Spain. It is the closest national park to the town. A person can ask for a family loop, a specific distance, or an evening option in natural language. The agent discovers the WebMCP tools, selects from graph-verified circuit options, validates a route before changing the map, and renders the result directly in the shared interface. The result stays inspectable: A closed circuit is drawn on the map. The route card shows measured distance and sampled ascent. Forecast, daylight, and official Park notices appear as clearly labeled planning context. Every agent action is visible in a shared worklog and trail ledger. The agent can prepare a briefing or GPX trace, but the person remains in control: they review/copy the briefing and manually click Download GPX . How I built it Switchback is a static TypeScript app hosted on Netlify. It registers fourteen page-bound WebMCP tools through the browser’s model context, with strict JSON schemas and the same planner functions used by the manual UI. Routing happens locally in the browser over a 66-tile directed Collserola TrailPack assembled from OpenStreetMap data and the Park’s published public-use network. The planner only offers routes that the available graph can close without a long retraced leg. I have used the official PDF and the park's website. I added route-aware forecast/daylight context via Open-Meteo and official Park-alert context through a same-origin adapter. Original Catalan notices remain visible; English is clearly labeled as machine translation. I used the AWS Translate service and Amazon Location services for the translations and maps. Challenges I ran into The hardest problem was avoiding an impressive-looking but untrustworthy route suggestion. A distance target alone does not prove that a loop closes, and a forecast does not prove that a hike is safe. That led to a few important product constraints: Routes are graph-validated before they render. Short, Medium, and Long are distance profiles, not difficulty labels. Difficulty is only described conservatively when the available ascent and terrain data support it. Forecasts and Park notices are planning signals, never a safety clearance. The agent cannot auto-download GPX files, send messages, or access external accounts. What I learned WebMCP is most compelling when the agent is not treated as a chat layer bolted onto an app Sometimes, it was hard for ChatGPT to use the tools because the agent's skill was not working correctly. I even fixed my local installation of ChatGPT with Codex. title: Loadshed
pitch: A page's own cut list for agents.
about_excerpt: A page's own cut list for agents. Like Comment Story Updates Measured result: a 320 ms frame hitch cuts Crowd from 480 to 48 while Live trace and Mixer stay protected. Before pressure: the agent-set 100 ms promise and second protected element agree with the visible receipts. Guardrail: Loadshed refuses to pin the last measured-relief step while the responsiveness promise is active. Pressure alone is not enough: at 100% Crowd load, Loadshed waits for a real frame-hitch signal. After the hitch: Crowd drops to 48, protected controls keep working, and the receipt records why. Same runtime, different page: Sale protects Hold my size while cutting aisle shimmer from 480 to 48. When a page gets slow, who decides what survives? A live show desk, a checkout on a mid-range phone, a control room dashboard: each one already has a private answer. Somebody hand-tuned what degrades first. An agent looking at the DOM cannot see that answer, so it either guesses or does nothing. Every latency-sensitive page already has this cut list. Loadshed makes it explicit, agent-readable, and auditable. Loadshed lets the page publish the answer. The page declares a click-latency ceiling, the element that must stay useful, and an ordered ladder of work it is willing to drop. It registers six WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , so an agent can inspect the promise, negotiate the ceiling, protect a second element, apply or reverse one bounded cut, and read a receipt for everything that happened. On the deployed Desk, a person drags crowd load to maximum and clicks once. The page measures a long frame of about 320 ms, drops the crowd layer from 480 items to 48, and leaves the live trace and mixer untouched. The agent set that contract, and the receipt names the frame signal, the caller, and the click that proved it. Turn the promise off and everything comes back. The honest part: the runtime rejects agent-injected clicks as evidence, refuses cuts on protected or pinned work, and fails closed when the browser has no frame-hitch signal. The Sale page proves the same runtime protects a different task, Hold my size, without knowing the Desk's DOM. No build, no backend, MIT licensed, 50 Node tests. title: Agent Process
pitch: Agent Process lets teams turn repeatable browser tasks into reusable workflows that run directly in Chrome. It exposes them as WebMCP tools so assistants like ChatGPT can trigger them on the page.
about_excerpt: Agent Process lets teams turn repeatable browser tasks into reusable workflows that run directly in Chrome. It exposes them as WebMCP tools so assistants like ChatGPT can trigger them on the page. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Running List of processes - Tools History of execution No-code Recording using Inline Manual Builder No-code Recording using Inline Manual Builder Inspiration AI assistants are getting better at using websites, but they still often have to figure out the interface from scratch every time. We wanted to make it easy for anyone to teach their AI assistant a repeatable process on top of any website, regardless of whether that website has MCP or WebMCP implemented. Even when a website already exposes MCP functions, users are still limited to the tools and workflows the developer decided to provide. We wanted users to be able to create their own personalized workflows around the way they actually work. Instead of asking an agent to understand the whole UI and decide what to click every time, a user can record a process once and reuse it. This can be useful for repetitive internal workflows, sharing processes between colleagues, making execution more predictable, reducing token usage, and making tasks faster and easier to debug with an execution log. We also wanted the creation side to be completely no-code. We reused the Inline Manual Builder so a user can simply record what they are doing in the browser and turn that workflow into an Agent Process. What it does Agent Process is a browser extension that lets users turn repeatable workflows on almost any website into WebMCP tools that AI assistants can use. A process can be created in two ways: by importing a JSON definition with the individual steps, or by recording the workflow using the Inline Manual Builder. The user can also define inputs that the AI assistant should provide when the process is executed. For example, you can create processes such as: Create a lead Add a customer Create a ToDo Publish an article Update a record in a CRM The Agent Process extension then exposes these processes as WebMCP tools directly in the browser. When an AI assistant calls one of these tools, Agent Process executes the predefined browser interactions instead of requiring the AI to inspect the interface and figure out every step again. Processes can include parameters, for example values that should be entered into forms, so the same process can be reused with different data every time it runs. This effectively lets users create their own personalized WebMCP tools on top of existing websites. The website itself does not need to implement WebMCP, expose an API, or be modified in any way. How we built it We built Agent Process as a browser extension that combines WebMCP with our existing Inline Manual process-recording technology. The Inline Manual Builder acts as the no-code recorder and editor. It captures the individual steps of a workflow, the elements being interacted with, and the parameters that can be provided when the process is executed. These processes are exported as JSON and imported into the Agent Process extension. The extension registers them as WebMCP tools, executes the predefined browser interactions when a tool is called, and records the result in an execution history log. We used Codex extensively to build the browser extension, with supervision, testing, and product decisions from our team. Our previous experience building browser-based product guidance with Inline Manual helped us move quickly, especially around reliable element targeting, working with dynamic web applications, handling overlays and different browser behaviors, and executing interactions on third-party websites. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was discovering that the ChatGPT browser extension does not currently automatically discover or use WebMCP tools in the way we initially expected. To make the integration work reliably, we currently need to add custom instructions telling ChatGPT to look for and use the available WebMCP tools. That made testing the complete experience slightly different from our original assumption, but it also gave us a much better understanding of how WebMCP discovery currently works in practice and where some of the limitations are for browser-based AI assistants. Our use of MCP is also slightly different from the typical implementation. We are not adding tools to an application we own; we are adding them on top of any existing website. While exploring the architecture, we even built our own MCP server before realizing that a traditional MCP server was not the right fit for what we wanted to achieve. WebMCP running directly in the browser turned out to be the key piece. Without browser-level WebMCP support, exposing personalized tools on top of arbitrary websites in this way would be much more difficult. On the Agent Process side, development went relatively smoothly thanks to our previous experience building Inline Manual and working with browser applications. Browser automation itself still comes with the usual challenges: every website behaves differently, with dynamic interfaces, overlays, delayed elements, and different frontend frameworks. Those are challenges we already know well from Inline Manual, though, and are separate from the WebMCP API itself. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that we managed to make WebMCP useful on top of websites that were never designed for it. A user can take an existing website, record a process without writing code, turn that process into a reusable WebMCP tool, and let an AI assistant execute it with parameters. We are also proud that the process remains fully under the user’s control. Instead of being limited to whatever MCP tools an application developer decides to expose, users can create workflows that match the way they actually work. Another accomplishment is that we were able to reuse our existing Inline Manual recording technology in a completely new way. Something originally built for creating product guidance can now also be used to teach AI assistants how to perform tasks. The early feedback has been especially encouraging. People immediately understand the idea of recording a process once and then letting an AI assistant reuse it, which makes us think there is something genuinely useful here beyond the hackathon. What we learned We learned a lot about how WebMCP works in practice, how tools are exposed inside the browser, and how AI assistants currently discover and use them. We also learned that our use case sits somewhere between traditional MCP and browser automation. We are not exposing backend capabilities from an application we own. Instead, we are giving the user a way to define their own tools on top of an existing interface. One of the most important things we learned is that AI does not always need to figure out how to complete a task from scratch. If the user already knows the exact process, it can be more efficient to record that process once and let the AI decide when to use it and what parameters to provide. In our testing, this approach can make execution faster, transparent and more predictable, reduce the amount of page analysis the AI needs to do, and potentially save tokens. It also gives us better control over what actually happens in the browser and provides a clear execution log when something succeeds or fails. That changed how we think about browser agents. Full autonomy is useful when the path is unknown, but for repetitive and well-understood tasks, a reusable process can often be the better tool. What's next for Agent Process The current version supports a limited set of browser interactions, so one of our next priorities is expanding the types of actions that can be recorded and executed reliably across different websites. We also want to make the recording experience much smoother. The goal is that a non-technical user can simply open the Inline Manual Builder, perform a task once, and end up with a reusable Agent Process without needing to understand selectors, JSON, or WebMCP. Sharing is another big part of what we want to build next. Today, processes are exported and imported manually. We would like to create a backend where teams can maintain a shared library of processes and make them automatically available to colleagues and their AI assistants. From there, we can see Agent Process becoming a form of team process memory: a shared collection of repeatable workflows that captures how a team actually works, not just what individual applications expose. We would also like to explore a public process library or marketplace, where people can publish and reuse processes for common applications instead of recording everything themselves. Another direction is composable processes. A larger workflow could be built from several smaller Agent Processes, allowing users to combine existing actions into more complex workflows. title: Three in the Loop
pitch: A WebMCP research workbench where agents do the legwork and humans decide what counts as evidence.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP research workbench where agents do the legwork and humans decide what counts as evidence. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 3-in-the-loop-human-agent-research-workbench how-it-works human-approve-reject-retry-sourcing-method human-approved-artifact-ready flow-chart Inspiration Three in the Loop began with a practical question: what should research look like when a human, an agent, and a website work together in the same live workspace? We began with the WebMCP specification, Chrome developer and agent/tool security guidance, OpenAI developer demonstrations, community/practitioner demonstrations, and repeated internal dogfooding. Together, those sources made the website-declared tool model concrete. Our product question was what should remain under human control. Research was the test case we kept returning to. It rewards speed in gathering and punishes speed in judging. So we built the smallest workbench that could test the boundary between useful research delegation and human evidence judgment. Repeated dogfooding refined that boundary until it matched the workflow. What it does Three in the Loop is for researchers, analysts, and technical teams doing fast-moving evidence-based research where recency, authority, and provenance matter. It is a research workspace shared by a person and a WebMCP-enabled agent in the same live browser workspace: Human defines → Agent researches → Human curates → Agent synthesizes → Human approves You set the research question, audience, and evidence limit. The agent reads the workspace, searches OpenAlex, inspects sources, and proposes evidence. Then it stops. You accept or reject each proposal in the Workbench and control evidence membership. The agent drafts an Evidence Brief whose findings may cite only human-accepted evidence. You edit and review the brief, mark it reviewed, approve it, and download the approved Markdown. The Research Cycle shows whose turn it is at every stage. A WebMCP activity readout records real tool calls as they land, so agent work is visible without exposing private reasoning. The application embeds no model and makes no OpenAI API calls; intelligence comes from a compatible external agent using the site’s bounded tool surface. Why WebMCP The interesting question was never whether an agent can search. It was which operations the site should expose as structured tools and which decisions should remain in the human workflow. WebMCP lets the site declare that boundary on its structured tool surface. Three in the Loop exposes exactly five tools: get_research_workspace search_sources get_source_details propose_evidence draft_evidence_brief Accepting evidence and approving the brief are deliberately absent from the WebMCP tool surface. They are buttons, not tools. For the operations the site does expose, the agent can use structured calls instead of scraping the interface or imitating human clicks. Both actors work against the same bounded browser workspace. It is the same page, with the turn changing hands. Challenges The hard problem was not building tools. It was deciding where useful delegation should stop. We began with read-only tools and added exactly two state-changing operations when the workflow needed them: propose_evidence can stage a proposal, and draft_evidence_brief can place or replace a review-required draft. Evidence acceptance or rejection, evidence membership, brief editing and review, and final approval remain outside the WebMCP tool surface. That boundary looks obvious in hindsight. It took repeated use to find it. Two smaller problems followed. The site cannot know that a person has spoken to an agent or that the agent is thinking, so it only reports AGENT WORK IN PROGRESS after a real WebMCP call lands in the current stage. And persistent rehearsal state kept reviving old missions, so the workspace now uses session-scoped browser storage: same-tab refreshes survive, while a new browser session starts clean. What we learned We began by treating the tool as the main unit of WebMCP design: name it well, type it well, keep it narrow. That is necessary. It is not what made the product work. What made it work was the handoff. The agent works until evidence selection returns control to the human. The human changes the evidence set. The agent continues from that decision, not from scratch, and drafts from the accepted evidence. The human reviews and signs off. Each time we clarified one of those transitions, the product became simpler and more useful. Looking at tools in isolation never explained the workflow as clearly as the handoffs did. Next time, we would design the journey between the person, the agent, and the page first; the tool set should follow from that journey. The final product does not try to show how much the agent can do alone. It shows how clear the responsibility is at every step. What's next The application is frozen for submission. What follows is evaluation before expansion. Planned assurance work includes deterministic checks of workflow invariants, WebMCP registration and cancellation lifecycle testing, response and serialized-output measurement, model-facing indirect prompt-injection evaluations, browser-agent evaluations of human-authority boundaries, and adversarial retesting after approved hardening. Product directions remain open too: richer evidence comparison without a fake credibility score, additional structured research providers, reusable research sessions, and collaboration. Expansion follows evidence from the evaluations while preserving the principle that made the product useful: The agent gathers. You decide what counts. title: Stagehand
pitch: A WebMCP-native frame-animation studio where agents storyboard scenes, author held cels, generate lip sync and local voices, program SFX, and export deterministic WebM.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-native frame-animation studio where agents storyboard scenes, author held cels, generate lip sync and local voices, program SFX, and export deterministic WebM. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Creative agents should direct animation through stable, semantic controls instead of guessing where to click. Stagehand began as a rigging experiment, but rigid puppets produced fragile seams and inconsistent results under a deadline. I pivoted to a simpler idea that matches traditional limited animation: distinct drawings held on exact frames. What it does Stagehand is a browser-based 2D frame-by-frame animation studio with 27 native WebMCP tools. A person or agent can inspect a project, write a multi-scene storyboard, manage assets, author and duplicate held cels, set an exact playhead, regenerate estimated lip-sync mouth cues, design procedural sound effects, generate voice through a restricted local bridge, validate the project, inspect any rendered frame, export PNG, and render an audio-bearing WebM. The release includes three original multi-scene demos: Ship the Brick , One More Deploy , and Land Money . Each has character dialogue generated locally with distinct voice designs plus deterministic procedural sound effects. The submission narration uses a consented local OmniVoice clone of my own voice; the reusable reference and voice prompt never enter the public repository. How I built it The app uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Canvas 2D, Web Audio, and MediaRecorder. A shared held-cel evaluator selects the latest authored drawing at or before an integer frame with no interpolation. Preview, storyboard thumbnails, frame inspection, PNG export, and WebM rendering all use that same evaluator. The WebMCP surface is registered with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Every mutation accepts an optional expected revision and idempotency key. Invalid targets return structured failures without incrementing state. Read tools omit binary asset payloads, and export tools return bounded metadata. The local voice bridge binds to loopback, restricts browser origins, caps input size, detects an OmniVoice-compatible endpoint, and preserves an offline preview fallback. WebM export mixes decoded dialogue and optional music with deterministic procedural SFX. Challenges The biggest challenge was recognizing that the technically ambitious rigging path was the wrong product constraint. Switching to held cels improved visual stability and made scene direction, lip sync, and rendering much easier to reason about. Other difficult parts were keeping UI and agent mutations on one revisioned state model, mixing browser audio into WebM, timing local speech against scenes, and testing native WebMCP registration rather than only testing JavaScript in isolation. Accomplishments Exactly 27 public WebMCP tools with concurrency and idempotency guards Three multi-scene animations with dialogue, lip sync, and procedural sound One deterministic evaluator shared across preview, inspection, PNG, and WebM Responsive desktop and 390 px layouts Public MIT-licensed repository with no credentials or private voice material Hosted browser and native WebMCP smoke tests against the production URL What I learned The right agent interface is less about exposing every low-level capability and more about choosing stable creative primitives. Held drawings, scenes, captions, cues, and exact frames give both humans and agents a vocabulary they can verify. I also learned to treat generated media as provenance-bearing project data and to keep personal voice material local by design. What's next I want to add denser cel packs, more backgrounds and prop variants, automatic phoneme alignment, editable exposure sheets, reusable style bibles, and richer nonlinear scene assembly while preserving the same deterministic tool contract. Since my partner is not an engineer, she prefers to use ChatGPT's in-built browser with WebMCP to implement the changes / drive the results with minimal manual work. title: Presence
pitch: The trust layer for live human-agent software.
about_excerpt: The trust layer for live human-agent software. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent requests a seat Human and agent share live state The boundary is real Work stays provisional You decide what becomes real Every session leaves a receipt Give agents a seat. Not the keys. Browser agents can now understand and act inside live software. But there is a problem: once an agent enters a shared workspace, what is it actually allowed to touch? Presence is a trust layer for live human agent collaboration. Instead of giving an agent the same authority as the human, Presence gives it an explicit seat with bounded capabilities. Humans and agents can work in the same live state without silently sharing control. The idea Presence reduces agent collaboration to four primitives: Seat Where an agent may be present. Scope What the agent may do. Revision The state the agent observed before acting. Receipt What actually happened during the session. Together they create a simple rule: Presence does not trust an agent to respect a boundary. The application enforces the boundary. The demo The demo uses one responsive project with three live surfaces: Desktop is the reference. Tablet is the agent's seat. Mobile belongs to the human. A browser agent discovers Presence through WebMCP and asks to join as a responsive collaborator. The human can inspect the requested capabilities before admitting it. Once admitted, the agent can inspect the project and propose work for Tablet while the human continues editing Mobile. Then comes the important part. The agent attempts to modify Mobile. Presence rejects the operation because Mobile is outside its granted scope. The same agent can successfully propose a Tablet change because Tablet belongs to its seat. Its work remains provisional: even the agent itself cannot publish it. Only a human acceptance can make the proposal canonical. Presence also tracks the revision an agent observed. If the human changes the project while the agent is acting on older state, the stale operation is rejected before it can mutate canonical state . The human's newer work remains untouched. Every significant action is recorded in a structured audit trail. Accepted proposals produce a verification receipt containing the agent identity, granted scope, revisions, operations, protected surfaces, and before/after state fingerprints. Finally, the human can revoke the seat. The agent loses its authority while accepted work remains part of the project. Why WebMCP WebMCP makes the website itself an agent interface. Presence exposes semantic operations for discovering the workspace, inspecting available roles and constraints, requesting admission, inspecting project state, proposing scoped changes, reviewing state, and releasing a role. The agent does not need DOM coordinates or a scripted sequence of clicks. It can reason about the application's actual concepts while Presence remains responsible for authorization and state integrity. How I built it Presence is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, and WebMCP. The UI and WebMCP tools operate on the same domain model. Mutations pass through the Presence domain layer, where admission, scope, ownership, and revision rules are enforced before canonical state can change. Agent proposals are provisional by default. Agents cannot publish their own work. Humans retain final authority. Presence also records structured audit events, computes deterministic state fingerprints, and generates verification receipts after accepted proposals so the collaboration can be inspected and verified after the fact. Challenges The hardest part was not exposing tools to an agent. It was deciding what should happen after an agent discovers those tools. A useful agent needs enough authority to accomplish real work, but giving it unrestricted access destroys the distinction between assistance and control. That led to the central design principle behind Presence: Authority should be explicit, scoped, temporary, and visible. Another challenge was concurrency. If an agent begins working from one revision while a human continues editing, the system cannot simply trust that the agent's eventual change is still safe. Presence revalidates the expected revision at mutation time and blocks stale operations before they reach canonical state. Presence explores what software could look like when agents are not merely chatbots beside an application, but participants inside it with boundaries the application can actually enforce. What's next The responsive workspace is one demonstration of the model, not the limit of it. Presence already applies the same collaboration model to a second application, demonstrating that the security model is not tied to responsive design. The same Seat, Scope, Revision, and Receipt primitives could govern agents working inside operations software, content systems, developer environments, and other collaborative applications. The larger idea is simple: As agents enter live software, applications need a way to decide not only what agents can understand, but where they may act. I focused on exploring how humans and agents can safely collaborate in the same live software without giving agents unrestricted control. title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about.
