title: ReTrade
pitch: Rethink the strategy before you trade.
about_excerpt: Rethink the strategy before you trade. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The hackathon itself was my first source of inspiration. I wanted to build something with WebMCP and explore what an AI-first product could look like. By AI-first, I mean a product where the main way to interact is through an AI agent such as ChatGPT. The interface still matters, but instead of clicking through every step manually, the user can describe what they want and let the agent work with the application. I started thinking about tasks that are difficult for an ordinary person to complete through a conventional interface. That led me to trading. I remembered using TradingView and trying to test different strategies. I wanted to answer some basic questions. Is this actually a good strategy? Could it make a profit? What are its weaknesses? Does the strategy work, or does it only look successful because of the particular data used in the test? I did not know the answers, and finding them was not simple. So I decided to build a product that could help investigate these questions. ReTrade was built in about five days. The project became much more promising than I expected, and I genuinely enjoyed working on it. What it does ReTrade helps people describe, organize, and test trading strategies before trying them with real capital. A user can choose supported stocks or ETFs and define a strategy using technical indicators. They can work through the interface manually, but the main workflow uses an AI agent through WebMCP. The user can describe a strategy in natural language or by voice. The agent turns that description into structured rules and prepares the strategy inside ReTrade. The user can then review and confirm those rules before running the test. ReTrade returns information about how the strategy behaved. It shows whether the result was profitable, fragile, too dependent on a small number of trades, or simply unsuccessful. The user can inspect individual trades, failed tests, market periods, costs, and alternative versions of the strategy. The goal is to give the user more than a final profit number. ReTrade helps them understand why the result happened and whether there is enough evidence to trust it. How I built it I built ReTrade primarily with Codex, mainly using GPT-5.6. I researched interfaces from trading platforms and other financial products to collect ideas for the layout and user experience. Then I worked iteratively. I implemented a version, tested it, used the product, found the parts that felt confusing, and changed them. A large part of the process was live coding with Codex. I described the behavior I wanted, reviewed the implementation, ran tests, and checked the application in both local and production environments. I kept repeating that process until the product felt useful rather than looking like a short hackathon prototype. Challenges I ran into The first major challenge was the UI and UX. ReTrade is an AI-first product, but it still needs a strong interface. A person must be able to inspect what went wrong, understand the evidence, and test a strategy manually without WebMCP. Designing both workflows was difficult. The agent and the user had to work with the same strategy, evidence, and application state. The interface also needed to explain complex results without overwhelming the user. WebMCP was another challenge. It is still a new technology, so there are fewer examples and established patterns than there are for traditional APIs. I had to study the documentation and give Codex precise instructions. Without enough context, tool registration and browser interactions were easy to implement incorrectly. Debugging the complete workflow was also new to me. A problem could come from the interface, WebMCP registration, the API, application state, authentication, or the database. I had to test the real interaction instead of assuming that working code meant a working product. Accomplishments that I am proud of I am especially proud of the interface. I like how ReTrade looks and how it presents a complicated investigation without turning it into a page full of raw statistics. I am also proud of the WebMCP interactions. A user can describe a strategy to an AI agent, ask it to test the strategy, and then inspect the result inside the same application. The agent can open specific evidence, examine failed periods, and create controlled variations of the strategy. The person can make a selection in the interface, and the agent can understand what they selected. The final result feels like a real interaction between a person, an AI agent, and a product. It does not feel like a chat window attached to an unrelated website. What I learned The main thing I learned was how WebMCP works and what it can add to a product. WebMCP gives an AI model a structured way to understand a website and perform actions inside it. The model does not have to guess what is happening from screenshots or depend on fragile browser automation. I now see many ways I could use WebMCP in future products. It can make complicated software easier to use because the user can describe the desired result instead of learning every part of the interface first. I also learned more about working with Codex and AI agents. Before this project, I mostly used Codex for individual coding tasks. During the hackathon, I used it to implement features, test browser behavior, review the UI, debug production problems, and run scenarios in isolated environments. I plan to keep experimenting with this way of building software. What is next for ReTrade I do not have a final business plan yet, but I would like to continue improving the product after the hackathon. One possible direction is to turn ReTrade into a focused paid tool for strategy testing. Large trading platforms provide many features, and their subscriptions can be expensive for someone who mainly wants to test and understand a strategy. ReTrade could offer a simpler alternative focused on that specific job. A user could describe a strategy, test it, inspect its weaknesses, and compare possible improvements without paying for a much larger trading platform. Before introducing pricing, I would need to improve the product, test it with real users, expand the supported strategies and data sources, and make sure the results remain clear and trustworthy. title: Portego
pitch: Setting up a smart home is still slow and fragmented. Portego lets you and an AI agent design the floor plan together, then bind it to real devices through a local gateway.
about_excerpt: Setting up a smart home is still slow and fragmented. Portego lets you and an AI agent design the floor plan together, then bind it to real devices through a local gateway. Like Comment Story Updates Portego WebMCP Canvas Portego Gateway Config Gateway Setup Inspiration Smart-home setup is still fragmented. Every brand has its own app, and those apps rarely treat the home as rooms, doors, and devices. I built Portego to try a different sequence: describe the home in conversation, refine it on a shared canvas, then connect that plan to real hardware. What it does Portego is a digital twin of the home. People and agents share one model of floors, rooms, and devices. A Linux gateway on the local network binds that model to real hardware, so the house you designed is the house you can switch. You can create floors, rooms, doors, windows, and devices by hand, or ask an agent to create them through WebMCP. Both write the same home document. You can drag a room after the agent makes it, and the agent can read the new layout and continue. The canvas works without an account. Login and hardware connectivity are private beta. The gateway opens an outbound WebSocket to Portego. It shows a pairing code, finds supported devices on the LAN, and lets you bind them to devices in the model. The connection is outbound, so the house does not need an exposed port or a public IP. Why WebMCP The home is structured data. Asking an agent to read pixels or click around a canvas would be fragile. Portego registers operations such as home.add_room , home.add_device , home.get_document , and home.apply_changes . Those tools use the same model and validation as the editor. A compatible agent is operating Portego, not a separate chat bolted onto it. How people and agents work together You describe a house; the agent produces a first layout. You move rooms, rename devices, add openings, or undo. The agent reads the revised document and continues from there. Once a physical device is discovered and bound, device.set_state goes through the gateway to the real device. How I built it The frontend is Next.js on Vercel. Konva draws the home. A validated HomeDocument is what actually gets saved. The page registers twenty WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Tool calls and UI actions share the same operations, validation, history, and persistence path. A FastAPI service on Render handles authentication, stored homes, gateway pairing, device bindings, and command relay. The Linux gateway connects out to the backend over an authenticated WebSocket and runs protocol adapters for local devices. Shelly is the first working adapter. Matter discovery is in the repo; Matter commissioning is not enabled yet. There is also an optional Cloudflare Worker and Durable Object relay, so long-lived gateway connections do not have to live on the API process. Challenges The hard part was keeping agent edits, canvas interactions, undo history, and persisted data on one model. Geometry needed real validation. An agent-generated layout is only useful if rooms, openings, and devices stay valid and still editable by hand. Local hardware added another constraint: remote control without opening inbound ports into someone's home. Guest designs also have to survive login without being duplicated or dropped. What I learned Structured operations are much more reliable than asking an agent to drive a visual UI. The useful loop was a strong first draft from the agent, then both of us revising the same home. I also think this only scales if devices ship agent-native. If every product keeps a private app, agents go back to guessing at UIs. Building that access has to become ordinary product work, or there needs to be a shared protocol so each brand is not inventing its own. What's next Public signup, OAuth for the remote Portego MCP server, a packaged Raspberry Pi gateway, more protocol adapters, and Matter commissioning. Longer term I want the agent-native part to be reusable: either make it cheap to ship a device that already exposes structured operations, or settle a protocol others can implement. Portego is one attempt at that for the home (WebMCP on the model, adapters on the gateway). Try it at tryportego.com . title: tandem
pitch: Your ears are the eval.
about_excerpt: Your ears are the eval. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for tandem Inspiration People can describe sound as muddy, harsh, thin, tiring, or unclear without knowing how to translate that feeling into equalizer settings. An agent can reason about language and structure an experiment, but it cannot hear through the user’s ears. tandem turns that limitation into the collaboration model: the agent stages controlled tests, and the human supplies the evidence only listening can provide. What it does The user loads tandem’s built-in demo loop or a local audio file that never leaves the device. A browser agent reads the calibration skill and session state, then stages two bounded EQ profiles. tandem randomizes them to A and B, routes one synchronized audio source through both processing chains, hides the settings, and asks a simple listening question. The human switches between A and B, votes, adds tags or a note, and reveals the mapping only after the judgment is recorded. After at least two trials, the agent can propose a final profile using the actual feedback. The human compares that proposal with the original audio, then approves, rejects, requests another test, saves locally, or exports the session. The timeline labels agent staging, human preferences, agent proposals, and human approval. How we built it tandem uses React, TypeScript, Vinext/Vite, Zustand, Zod, and the Web Audio API. One looping AudioBufferSourceNode feeds independent A, B, and Original paths so playback stays synchronized. Each processed path has five BiquadFilterNode bands, conservative output headroom, and a short output-gain crossfade. Four imperative tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool : two read-only tools teach and inspect, while two mutation tools stage blind trials and final proposals. Tool handlers read Zustand through getState() , validate strict schemas, require current revisions and idempotency keys, and update the same visible state as the human interface. There is intentionally no API, key, backend, account, analytics, or separate MCP server. Challenges The most important design challenge was preserving responsibility rather than maximizing automation. A WebMCP tool that votes would make the demo faster but erase the product’s core truth: the agent cannot hear the result. The state machine, tool names, schemas, provenance, and tests all enforce that boundary. Audio comparison also required avoiding false preferences caused by playback drift or obvious loudness changes. tandem uses one shared source, synchronized paths, gain headroom, bounded profiles, and a short crossfade while retaining playback position. Accomplishments Page-owned WebMCP tools over the same durable state shown in the UI Blind randomized A/B tests with post-vote reveal Human-only listening, voting, approval, save, and export Stale-revision protection and request-id idempotency Manual mode that remains functional without WebMCP Local-only audio processing and clearly documented privacy boundaries Unit and end-to-end tests for the agent/human responsibility boundary What we learned Human-agent collaboration is strongest when each participant has a capability the other genuinely lacks. The useful contract is not “the agent does everything.” It is “the agent makes a disciplined experiment possible, and the human contributes irreducible evidence.” What’s next Potential future work includes more listening-question templates, user-authored band presets, offline spectral guidance that never leaves the browser, and richer export visualization. These remain secondary to keeping the experiment bounded, interpretable, and human-controlled. title: Edgewright
pitch: A redirect console a human and an agent drive together, over WebMCP. Test, audit and fix routing across 11 hosts, then prove a migration never breaks a link.
about_excerpt: A redirect console a human and an agent drive together, over WebMCP. Test, audit and fix routing across 11 hosts, then prove a migration never breaks a link. Like Comment Story Updates Edgewright turns your redirect and rewrite rules into a live console a human and an AI agent work together, over WebMCP. Test any URL, catch the rule that shadows another, translate a config to another host, then prove nothing breaks, all in the browser. The problem: redirect rules are ordered and first-match-wins. A broad rule above a specific one makes the specific one dead code, so a link works locally then 404s in production. Edgewright makes that visible and fixable, by a person or by an agent on the same page. How the tools are used: the console registers fifteen tools with document.modelContext.registerTool. In the demo the agent runs test_url to find the 404, audit_rules to name the shadowed rule, reorder_rule to fix the order, then test_url again. Read-only tools carry readOnlyHint so the agent runs them without a prompt. The tools that change rules omit it, so the agent asks first. The UI and the tools mutate one shared store, so a human clicking a button and an agent calling a tool run the exact same code. The product is three apps on one engine: the Console, Preflight (a pre-deploy gate), and Studio (migrate a config between hosts and prove every URL still resolves). Live: https://edgewright.vercel.app Source: https://github.com/zkasuran/edgewright Video: https://youtu.be/8Hry7ozQTe8 Built for the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge. The engine, @edgewright/core, covers eleven hosting platforms grounded in their own docs, with 148 passing tests, no build and no dependencies. For platforms whose routing is code, like Fastly and CloudFront, the engine resolves the trivial static patterns and labels the rest as not-simulated rather than guessing. Everything shown in the demo is the deployed product on the live URL or a real source file. The narration is synthesised speech. The design, the code, the review and the verification are the author's. title: TestPilot
pitch: Agent-native QA mission control that turns release risk into traceable evidence.
about_excerpt: Agent-native QA mission control that turns release risk into traceable evidence. Like Comment Story Updates 01-initial-dashboard-at-risk 02-webmcp-14-tools 03-req-003-coverage-gap 04-ai-created-tc-004 05-exe-004-negative-inventory 06-def-001-traceability 07-final-not-ready Inspiration A green test dashboard does not always mean a release is safe. Important requirements can remain untested, execution evidence can be scattered across different tools, and defects can lose their connection to the tests and requirements that exposed them. QA leaders and release managers often spend more time assembling this context than making the release decision itself. I built TestPilot to demonstrate a better model: one shared release workspace where a human can review the evidence visually while an AI agent can discover and invoke the same QA capabilities as structured WebMCP actions. What it does TestPilot is an agent-native QA Mission Control application for requirements, test cases, executions, defects, traceability, and release readiness. The demonstration starts with fictional e-commerce release 2.4. All existing tests pass and there are no critical defects, but the release is still AT RISK because REQ-003 - the critical requirement preventing concurrent customers from purchasing the final inventory item - has no test coverage. The user asks: “Check whether version 2.4 is safe to release.” The agent then: Inspects the release and its requirements. Detects the missing REQ-003 coverage. Creates TC-004 for two simultaneous purchases of the final item. Runs the new test. Observes both purchases succeeding and inventory reaching -1 . Diagnoses a non-atomic concurrent inventory update. Creates a critical defect with structured evidence. Links the defect to TC-004 and REQ-003. Reassesses release 2.4 as NOT READY . Every action immediately appears in the human-facing dashboard, producing a complete evidence chain from requirement to test, execution, defect, and release decision. How I built it TestPilot uses React, Next.js, strict TypeScript, and Vinext for the application interface and server endpoints. It is hosted publicly on OpenAI Sites, with Cloudflare Workers and Cloudflare D1 providing persistent, isolated demo state. Drizzle ORM manages the data model, Zod validates inputs, and Vitest verifies the important release logic. The page registers 14 semantic tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . These include get_coverage_gaps , create_test_case , run_test , inspect_failure , create_defect , link_defect_to_test , and get_release_readiness . These are business-level QA actions, not low-level instructions such as clicking buttons. The UI and WebMCP tools use the same domain services, APIs, and persistent state, so there is no separate agent-only version of the data. Each browser receives an isolated anonymous workspace. This allows judges to run and reset the deterministic demonstration without creating an account or interfering with another evaluation. Challenges I ran into The main challenge was keeping the human interface and agent workflow synchronized around one authoritative state. An agent-created test or defect needed to appear in the dashboard without duplicating business logic or maintaining a second data model. Another challenge was making the demonstration deterministic. A real concurrency failure can be timing-dependent, which is unsuitable for a short judging session. I designed TC-004 to reproduce the negative-inventory result reliably while keeping the evidence realistic and structured. I also needed to expose meaningful semantic tools with clear descriptions, typed inputs, validation, predictable JSON responses, and useful errors. Finally, the public application had to support anonymous access while keeping every visitor’s mutable demonstration data isolated. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am proud that TestPilot demonstrates an end-to-end agent workflow rather than adding a chatbot beside an existing dashboard. The agent can discover missing coverage, create and execute a test, diagnose a failure, create a critical defect, link the evidence, and produce a release recommendation using structured WebMCP actions. At the same time, the human sees every state transition and can inspect or reset the workflow. The final result is a clear trace: REQ-003 → TC-004 → failed execution → DEF-001 → NOT READY The entire TestPilot project - including its concept, interface, application code, WebMCP integration, automated tests, documentation, and deployment - was created during the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge hackathon period. What I learned I learned that agent-native applications should expose intent rather than presentation details. A tool such as create_defect remains meaningful even if the website’s layout changes, while DOM-based automation can break when a button label, loading state, or responsive layout changes. I also learned that trustworthy agent workflows require shared state, input validation, deterministic evidence, explicit error responses, and visible human oversight. A release verdict is much more valuable when the user can trace exactly how the agent reached it. What's next for TestPilot The current e-commerce system and test runner are intentionally simulated to provide a reliable competition demonstration. A production version could connect the same domain and WebMCP boundaries to real CI/CD pipelines, automated test runners, requirements platforms, defect trackers, source-control checks, and deployment approval systems. Future versions could also add organization authentication, role-based access, configurable release policies, audit retention, notifications, historical risk trends, and human approval gates. title: Morphus - the 3D world editor your agent can operate
pitch: A WebGPU 3D world editor that hands its real authoring tools to your browser agent. Sculpt terrain, grow forests and build scenes by asking...the scene graph is the API, not the pixels.
about_excerpt: A WebGPU 3D world editor that hands its real authoring tools to your browser agent. Sculpt terrain, grow forests and build scenes by asking...the scene graph is the API, not the pixels. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most attempts to let an AI agent drive a creative tool try to make the model see the screen: screenshots, pixel coordinates, guessing where a button is and hoping the click lands. For a 3D editor that's close to hopeless, because the interesting state isn't on screen at all. It's a scene graph, a modifier stack, a spline running through a forest field. Meanwhile our editor already had a complete, precise description of everything it could do. Tool declarations written for its own built-in Copilot, each with a JSON Schema. That surface existed, and it was locked inside one chat panel. WebMCP is the piece that was missing. It lets a page hand its real command surface to whatever agent the user is already talking to. So the question stopped being "how does a model learn to use our UI" and became "why is our UI the interface at all?" What it does Morphus is a WebGPU 3D world editor that runs entirely in the browser. It sculpts terrain, grows forests, blocks out levels, casts combat VFX, and lays out procedural cities. With WebMCP it registers all 154 of its tools with the browser, so an agent can build a world in the page the person is looking at . No server, no API key, no separate MCP process. Ask it for a landscape and it calls create_mesh_terrain , then terrain_sculpt_stroke along a path of world-space points, then create_forest_field and grow_forest_field to plant a stand of trees along a spline. Ask it for a city and it runs a whole pipeline. generate_street_grid lays avenues and cross streets with real junctions, kerb returns and lane markings. generate_city_massing divides the blocks between them into lots that front the street and extrudes them into volumes. generate_city_buildings replaces the tallest of those with actual architecture: limestone banks, setback towers, corner headquarters with colonnades and cornices. Throughout, it reads back with get_terrain_state , get_street_network and list_nodes , so it acts on what's really in the scene rather than on what it assumed. The scene graph is the API. A heavy GPU application becomes operable by a model that never has to render a frame. How we built it The core decision was to build a bridge, not a second implementation : await document.modelContext.registerTool( { name: "terrain_sculpt_stroke", description: "Sculpts the terrain along a path of world-space points...", inputSchema: { /* JSON Schema, shared with the in-app Copilot */ }, annotations: { readOnlyHint: false, untrustedContentHint: true }, execute: async (input, { signal }) => { /* ... */ } }, { signal: controller.signal } ); WebMCP asks for exactly the shape the Copilot declarations already had, so src/lib/webmcp/tools.ts reuses both the declarations and the same executor. A browser agent and the in-app Copilot run identical code paths and cannot drift apart. The payoff showed up when we built the city. Nine new tools became agent-drivable the moment they existed, with no bridge changes, no registration code, and no separate schema to maintain. The surface went from 145 to 154 by writing the features. Everything else followed the platform's guidance rather than working around it: Annotations derived, not hand-listed. readOnlyHint comes from the tool's name prefix, because a hand-kept list of read tools beside 154 declarations goes stale the first time someone adds a get_ . One tool lies about itself: capture_mesh_modeling_base captures topology as the base of a live modelling stack , so it writes. It's named as an explicit exception. A tool wrongly marked read-only is worse than one left unmarked, because it invites an agent to call a mutation speculatively. Lifetimes via AbortSignal . There is no unregisterTool . Aborting the registration controller is how tools go away, so they disappear cleanly with the editor. A second signal on execute cancels a call mid-flight, which matters when a sculpt covers a 4 km terrain. A visible record. Tools run in the page, so the only trace of a call is the one the page chooses to show. The menu bar carries an AGENT readout: tools registered, and the name of the last call. Challenges we ran into We shipped a curated 20, then reversed it. The original argument was sound. A tool list is a prompt, and every entry spends the agent's attention. But it cuts the other way at this scale. The editor's real capability is the whole surface, and an agent that cannot inset a face or lay a street is operating a demo of the editor rather than the editor. Curation became the agent's job, and ours became making that job possible: order the list so read and world-building tools lead, and annotate every entry honestly. Character budgets are a design problem, not a formatting one. Chrome recommends 500 characters per description. Truncating the overruns turned out to be exactly wrong, because the tail of a good description is the part that says when not to reach for the tool. We rewrote those by hand, aliased four over-long names, and wrote a budget check that fails the build. The same logic applied to results. A silently truncated result reads as a complete answer, which is how an agent ends up confidently acting on half a scene graph. A forest was planted thirty metres underground, and reported success. The viewport draws two different terrains depending on renderer backend, and they are not the same surface. The forest sampled one; the viewport drew the other. Measured, they differ by 26 to 30 metres, so every stand was buried and every tool call returned "success": true . There is now exactly one function that answers "how high is the ground here", and everything placed on the ground goes through it, so forests, streets and buildings can only ever be wrong together. Roads that bridge their own kerbs. Sampling terrain once at a street's centreline and reusing that height across its full width buries the uphill kerb and floats the downhill one by half the width times the gradient. On a 16m avenue that was 2.3 metres of float. Sampling per edge took the worst deviation across 228 vertices from 2.303m to 0.000m. We later replaced the hand-rolled ribbon entirely with three-roads , an OpenDRIVE-style model that owns lanes, kerb returns and paint properly. A building grammar that can't build a city. We vendored procedural-bank , a shape grammar producing early-twentieth-century commercial architecture, and measured before trusting it: 142,552 triangles from 478 kit modules per building, in about 300ms. Turning every knob down, with no ornament, no colonnade and no crown, reached 117,660. A saving of 17%, because the cost is in the modules and not the decoration. Building all 456 volumes of a modest grid would be roughly 62 million triangles and two minutes of blocking work. So it generates a few dozen landmarks standing among massing boxes, which is what a downtown looks like anyway. Resizing a canvas is not resizing a renderer. On WebGPU the render targets and depth texture are allocated when the renderer is built, so a canvas that grows afterwards leaves them behind and every frame fails validation against a black viewport. The sting is in the fix. The poll that waits for a real size cannot use requestAnimationFrame , because a page that isn't being composited doesn't run animation frames at all. The one mechanism that looks right is guaranteed to be asleep exactly when it's needed. Testing an API most browsers don't have. WebMCP needs Chrome's origin trial or chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . So we built a stub. ?webmcp=stub installs a minimal modelContext plus a console harness, exercising the same registration path and the same tool code with no model in it. window.__webmcp.list().length; // 154 window.__webmcp.describe("generate_street_grid"); // the schema an agent sees await window.__webmcp.call("generate_street_grid", { columns: 4, rows: 3 }); It settles the deterministic half of the question, "did this tool run and return what it promised", that Chrome's own guidance says to answer before writing evals. Accomplishments that we're proud of No parallel implementation. The agent's tools and the app's tools are the same tools. Nine city tools shipped with zero bridge changes. Budgets enforced by a check that fails the build , rather than by good intentions. The human stays the one who understands the document. Geometry appearing in a 3D scene is ambiguous. Did the person do that, or the model? The activity readout answers it on every call. It degrades cleanly. In a browser without WebMCP the editor behaves exactly as before: no crash, no chip, no console noise. Bugs closed by measurement, not by eye. Planted heights matching terrain to 0.000m, road vertices conforming to 0.000m, triangle budgets sampled across seven configurations. On a project where the camera can sta

title: Sable
pitch: A watercolor studio shared by a human and an agent. Oh and sable is a fine-point brush prized by watercolor and oil painters!
about_excerpt: A watercolor studio shared by a human and an agent. Oh and sable is a fine-point brush prized by watercolor and oil painters! Like Comment Story Updates Fox Painting by GPT Terra (Test) Landscape Painting by GPT Terra (Test) Jellyfish Painting by Opus 5 (Test) Flower Painting by Opus 5 (Test) Sable UI Duet Mode on Sable ( Agent and Human drawing a specific canvas) WebMCP Tools in Use Stroke Selection WebMCP Tools Replay Mode Sable One sheet, two painters. A watercolour studio where you and an AI agent both hold the brush. Where it came from Every time I make a picture with a model, I get the same feeling: I am standing outside the thing I made. One petal is wrong, and my only move is to rewrite the prompt and roll the dice on the whole image again. What comes back is a bitmap. Every decision that produced it is already gone. Although the results are amazing, I WANT SOMETHING FUN Then I read the WebMCP spec and realised it is the same complaint, but in a different setting. An agent poking at a website by guessing which pixel is a button is stuck in exactly that position: it can only act on the whole thing from the outside. Hand it real handles. So Sable keeps the decisions. Every mark is an object with a pigment, a water level, a brush, a layer and a path, whether a person dragged it with a mouse or an agent wrote it as an SVG path ( just a nerdy way to say brush stroke) through a tool call. Either of you can pick up any mark, including the other's, and change it. The agent isn't generating anything, but rather drawing with you, which I think it's a cool new path compared to generative AI. Why watercolour? Because it's the hardest possible case for that argument. You don't control watercolour by specifying an outcome. You choose how much water is on the brush and then live with wherever it goes. If a structured, revisable document beats prompting anywhere, it had better beat it here. It also gives the agent numbers that mean something. water: 0.9 isn't a style token. It decides how far pigment creeps into the paper and whether the edge blooms. So that also makes the agent decisive about what settings to use, and where. Let me be honest about the pictures They are not good. A fox that could just as easily be a marmot, or a new squirrel evolution. Poppies a child would beat. A landscape that holds together mostly because watercolour forgives everything (and to look at it like modern art) . I am not going to pretend otherwise, and you should look at them knowing that. and PLEASE go easy on it. But look at what they are . Nobody prompted them. There is no diffusion model anywhere in this project, and no image model of any kind. Every mark in every one of those pictures was placed by an agent choosing a path, a pigment, a water level and a brush, then looking at what the water actually did with them and deciding what to do next. Each painting is a list of about twenty decisions, and you can open any one of them and change it. That is a genuinely different mechanism from generating an image, and right now it is much worse at it. It is also version one of something I have not seen anyone try properly: generative AI that draws rather than generates. The picture is a document the model and I are both editing. Prompted image generation started out worse than this and got where it is because enough people agreed it was worth pushing on. I think this is worth pushing on for a different reason: I want a picture I can reach into and argue with, and a bitmap has never once let me do that, and I have fun drawing with my artistic friend. So treat these as the first plates from an experiment. What it does Twenty-three tools on document.modelContext , and no prompt box anywhere. Three of them I'm quietly proud of. The paint answers back : every paint call returns what the water decided rather than what you asked for, so the agent hears that its wash finished 109 units outside the path it gave, went soft on the top left, and fused with something still wet. The sheet dries on a clock , so painting into an open passage now fuses the marks and waiting means it won't. And it can squint : a blur and a posterize down to four flat tones, which is the cheapest thing in the codebase and by a mile the most useful, because the faults that sink a painting are invisible in a normal look at it. AND it feels like a true artist moving back and squinting at your art to see where it's at. A duet is one picture split into named parts. No turns. Either painter grabs whatever's free, and grabbing it is a click for you and duet_take_part for the agent, both writing to the same board. The parts make you need each other: the agent's foliage has to hang off branches you actually drew, and they never end up where the score assumed. Any painting also folds into a link, and I mean the painting, not a picture of one. Every mark travels with its seed, so it re-renders identically and whoever opens it can change anything in it. That's why the share URL is incredibly long (sorry). How it's built The renderer is Canvas 2D written from scratch. No image models, no libraries, no pre-baked brush textures. The brush footprint gets subdivided and each new midpoint pushed sideways in proportion to its edge, over and over, so the boundary gains detail at every scale. Everything composites with multiply , because paint over paint filters the light twice. You can always deepen a passage and never lighten one, and that constraint is most of what makes the medium feel like the medium. The important architectural decision is boring: the WebMCP handlers have no private door into the document. They call the same commands the mouse does. One undo stack, every stroke records its author, and an agent literally cannot reach a state the UI couldn't have produced. The toolbox is also alive. Select a mark and two new tools come into existence, and one of them names the mark you just picked in its own description, so "make this one wetter" needs no lookup. undo only exists when there's something to undo. Everything I got wrong first The duet used to take turns. Twelve passes, strictly alternating, nobody allowed to touch the paper out of order. It proved two painters can share a picture the way a metronome proves you can play music. Half the time you spent in it, you were being told to wait. I deleted the queue, its supposed to be a messy canvas you both work on, and ruining each other's work kind of get's you to bond with it. The page called the agent's marks mine. An agent whose browser couldn't bridge WebMCP did the sensible thing and used the mouse, and every mark it made got logged as mine, with the cursor beside it cheerfully reading "You". On a page whose entire subject is two authors sharing a document, that's about the worst thing it could get wrong. There's no reliable way to tell an agent's mouse from a person's, and guessing from how the pointer moves would occasionally inform a real human that they're a robot. So the page offers a handle instead of inferring an answer: a real, named button sitting in the accessibility tree that says the brush is the agent's now. One tool call weighed 44,000 characters , nearly all of it base64. Fine if the client understands image blocks. Catastrophic if it just stringifies them into the model's context. Every image is bounded now and re-encodes smaller until it fits. Same sheet, 13,000 characters, no harder to judge. And the two painters were getting different materials on one sheet. My marks looked like paint. The agent's looked like television static. Neither number was wrong: granulation fills whatever shape it's clipped to, so a small mark shows a fragment of the texture and reads as paper tooth, while a big flooded wash gets the whole tile several times over and reads as noise. Scale was doing the damage, and only one of us ever paints at the scale where it shows. Texture now falls off as a mark grows: $$\tau(r) \;=\; \frac{1}{1 + \dfrac{\max(0,\; r - 110)}{420}}$$ which is a claim about how eyes work rather than about pigment, and it belongs in the renderer for the same reason the drying rim does. What I'd tell anyone building one of these A tool that returns { ok: true } leaves the agent painting blind. Give it a picture back and it can look, judge and correct. Although I really wanted to try to have it draw without any support, giving it a reference image would help a lot, and while testing with the agents, I asked them what they struggled with and what is one tool it wanted to make this drawing better, and that is what they all asked for which was quite interesting. Tool descriptions are the API. I spent more time on the prose inside inputSchema than on most of the functions behind it. And build for the bridge failing, because it will. The fallback isn't a worse version of your product. It's the accessibility tree, and it can carry a three-line recipe for calling every one of your tools through evaluated JavaScript. An agent that just read your DO

title: Proof Courier
pitch: The agent carries proof, not your private records. WebMCP blocks overreach, unlocks one consent-bound export, and leaves final submission to the person.
about_excerpt: The agent carries proof, not your private records. WebMCP blocks overreach, unlocks one consent-bound export, and leaves final submission to the person. Like Comment Story Updates Five eligibility claims cross two WebMCP sites. Birth date, exact GPA, transcript, address, student ID, and name stay in the wallet. Inspiration Browser agents can now work across websites. That creates a privacy problem: proving one fact often means copying an entire private record into the agent conversation. A fellowship may need to know that an applicant is over 18, enrolled, studying an eligible field, above a GPA threshold, and resident in an eligible region. It does not need the person's birth date, student ID, exact GPA, transcript, home address, or name. Proof Courier started with one question: can the agent carry the answer without carrying the record? What it does Proof Courier is a working two-site WebMCP workflow backed by three independent production artifacts. The fellowship verifier publishes the five claims it needs, along with the audience, purpose, expiry limit, fresh nonce, prohibited fields, and a rule that only the person may submit. The private wallet checks that request before preparing anything. Its Request Firewall blocks an unsafe audience, purpose, nonce, or request for automatic submission. If a site asks for raw records, extra claims, or a longer lifetime, the wallet releases nothing and returns a machine-readable counterproposal containing only the five derived claims and a ten-minute lifetime. Once the verifier accepts that smaller request, the wallet prepares it for visible review. The agent still cannot export anything. The person sees what will be shared, who will receive it, why it is needed, and when it expires. Only the person's approval registers wallet_export_proof . The tool works once and then disappears. The agent carries the proof to the verifier, which checks it and prepares the application. There is no agent tool for final submission. The result is simple: five eligibility claims cross between the sites. The private source values stay inside the wallet. Why WebMCP This experience depends on structured tools and live page state. The verifier gives the agent a precise request instead of making it guess from pixels. The wallet turns consent into real capability control. Before approval, export does not exist. After approval, it appears for one use. After that use, it is replaced by a read-only receipt. That 0 to 1 to 0 capability lifecycle means the person and agent see the same authority state. It also gives the agent a safe recovery path when a website asks for too much. The wallet and verifier run on separate origins. They do not share browser storage or fetch data from each other. In the tested journey, the proof returned by one WebMCP tool and passed to the other is the only bridge. How we built it Both pages register their own tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . The synthetic proof bundle uses Web Crypto. A P-256 issuer signature authenticates the credential metadata. Merkle inclusion paths reveal only the requested claims. A holder signature binds the audience, purpose, nonce, expiry, disclosure set, approval time, and one-use consent grant. The verifier rejects an untrusted issuer, wrong audience or purpose, expired proof, repeated nonce, missing or extra claim, altered disclosure, forged signature, or consent dated in the future. The wallet, verifier, and showcase deploy as independent artifacts. Each canonical origin serves only its own routes and entry chunk. The 21-check production matrix returns 200 for the owning route and chunk, and 404 for every peer role route and peer entry chunk. Release checks also keep wallet signing fixtures out of verifier and showcase artifacts, remove source maps, scan for raw synthetic record values, and verify six security headers on every role. Challenges The hardest part was separating preparation from permission. A confirmation message was not enough. The agent's actual tool inventory had to change after the visible approval and change again after the permitted export. An early version also included linkable identity metadata in otherwise safe receipts. We removed it and added checks around every agent-facing result. Privacy here is not a promise in the interface. It is a boundary tested in the data path. The Request Firewall introduced a second challenge. Refusing a bad request is easy; helping the agent continue safely is harder. The wallet now explains why the request failed and, when possible, proposes the smallest acceptable replacement. What we learned Tool schemas are part of the trust model. A useful WebMCP tool needs clear inputs, bounded output, honest annotations, and a lifecycle that matches its authority. We also learned where the human should remain in control. The agent is good at reading requirements, comparing policies, and carrying a proof. The person should approve disclosure and make the final consequential decision. How we tested it The release includes: 78 of 78 unit and contract tests 22 of 22 named adversarial privacy and authority scenarios 10 of 10 Playwright checks, including six product journeys and four wallet durability and concurrency checks 21 of 21 production route and entry-chunk isolation checks across the three role artifacts 1 of 1 complete browser journey against independently served role artifacts 5 direct tool smoke steps using GoogleChromeLabs webmcp-evals a 100/100 tool audit with zero findings in Nekuda WebMCP Workbench automated keyboard, 390px layout, and serious or critical accessibility checks An earlier deployed build also passed a native WebMCP run in the OpenAI Codex in-app browser: five synthetic claims crossed, zero private fields crossed, export disappeared after use, verification passed, and no agent submission tool appeared. That native receipt predates the IndexedDB wallet wiring and says so. The final role-isolated release was rerun through the public browser harness after production promotion. The public Evidence Room links the receipts, source revision, and limits behind these claims. Scope Every person, credential, institution, and application in the demo is synthetic. Proof Courier is an interaction and protocol prototype. Wallet export authority persists only in same-origin browser storage. Verifier challenge and replay state remain in memory and reset across reloads or application instances. It is not a production identity wallet, compliance product, W3C Verifiable Credential implementation, zero-knowledge proof, or real fellowship integration. Try it Live introduction: https://proof-courier-orcin.vercel.app Fellowship verifier: https://proof-courier-verifier.vercel.app/fellowship Private wallet: https://proof-courier-wallet.vercel.app/wallet Evidence Room: https://proof-courier-orcin.vercel.app/evidence Source: https://github.com/amanmaqsood/proof-courier Built with WebMCP, React, TypeScript, Web Crypto, Vite, Vitest, Playwright, GoogleChromeLabs webmcp-evals, Nekuda WebMCP Workbench, GitHub Actions, and Vercel Built With accessibility cryptography github-actions playwright privacy react typescript vercel vite vitest web-crypto webmcp Try it out proof-courier-orcin.vercel.app proof-courier-orcin.vercel.app github.com proof-courier-verifier.vercel.app proof-courier-wallet.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I designed and built the two-site WebMCP flow, privacy policy, cryptographic proof checks, browser tests, and judge evidence. title: Cowork Protocol
pitch: A reusable WebMCP collaboration layer for bounded attention, real human authorization, explicit presence, and scoped solo work.
about_excerpt: A reusable WebMCP collaboration layer for bounded attention, real human authorization, explicit presence, and scoped solo work. Like 1 Comment Story Updates You or me? Three in one how we work together illustration art Inspiration Web agents often receive either too much page context or too little structure to understand what a person intends. A tool catalog alone also does not answer the collaboration questions: What matters now? Who is present? Who may change what? Did a real person authorize it? Did the page actually change? Cowork Protocol explores a calmer model: collaborate when both sides are present, hand off bounded work when one side steps away, and make every transition visible. What it does Cowork Protocol is a reusable collaboration layer for WebMCP applications. It adds: Bounded attention through Follow me (pointer, click, keyboard focus, and text selection), Click focus, Text marker only, change/causality, and one-time context expansion. Token-aware escalation from a 350-character focus packet to at most 1,200 related characters, requesting more only when justified. Visible action offers that remain inert until a trusted human click authorizes the exact displayed value. Verified receipts plus latest-only causal changes and human feedback. Explicit presence modes: Cowork, Agent Solo, Human Solo, and Idle. Scoped solo leases limited by goal, target, capability, page version, expiry, and call count. Typed or spoken conversation with silence suppression, bounded turns, clickable suggestions, and optional spoken replies. Explicit capability levels , so reduced bridge guarantees are never presented as native guarantees. One Demo switch and an honest model seat: Demo on is a disclosed scripted helper; Demo off means your own model (direct OpenAI-compatible endpoint, same-origin host or Desktop Companion) — or nothing, and nothing proposes nothing. The flagship FormBuilder showcase lets a person and an agent build and review a form together. Only the attributed MIT-licensed web validation/export engine is reused from a pre-existing FormBuilder; the Cowork protocol, WebMCP layer, bridges, interaction model, tests, Browser Bridge, and showcase experience are new challenge work. Working together does not require staying in the room. A delegation grant lets a human hand off a bounded task — a goal, a call budget, a time window — while stepping away; the model drafts within that window, and returning produces a short return message naming what changed, with those specific items highlighted together. The same signal path carries a spoken or typed instruction: saying "make this required" or "make this the first question" applies immediately, without a separate click, because the grant itself already carries the human's go-ahead. After any unsupervised stretch, the interface visibly waits for a verdict — good, adjust, or different — before it is ready for the next one. And while the human is present and the model is only advising, editing a field on your own may draw one short, bounded comment from the model — never more than one at a time, and only while advising is switched on. None of this depends on the whole canvas being the only reachable point of contact: each field is now its own target, so a suggestion or a spoken instruction lands on the exact question it was meant for. Why WebMCP WebMCP supplies the structured action layer . Instead of guessing every possible action from screenshots or DOM noise, an agent receives site-declared tools with schemas. Cowork Protocol adds the missing collaboration contract around those tools: what is in focus, what may only be proposed, what requires a real human click, when delegated work expires, and how success is verified. This makes the interaction clearer: point, receive a small suggestion, click to authorize, inspect the receipt, and deliberately hand work over when stepping away. Native WebMCP implementation The live FormBuilder registers nine tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : cowork_read_focus cowork_request_context cowork_read_changes cowork_offer_action cowork_read_presence cowork_execute_solo cowork_read_feedback cowork_read_turn cowork_reply_turn The native adapter uses stable field targets and application-level verification. Proposal tools never smuggle authorization: mutations stay offer-only until the visible value is accepted by a real click. A provider-neutral conversation layer emits no turn for silence or while the agent is paused. It sends only the compact utterance, current focus, and presence. An in-page WebMCP agent can pull only the latest pending turn and must reply against its exact unique ID; stale and replayed replies fail closed. Three connector paths Native Cowork + WebMCP — stable targets, click-gated mutations, receipts, presence, and scoped solo work. Existing WebMCP bridge — a host-provided tool catalog is summarized within strict budgets; read-only-hinted tools may execute, while mutations remain offer-only. No-WebMCP Browser Bridge (the browser extension) — an optional, default-off Manifest V3 extension supplies bounded DOM/accessibility callbacks. It escalates through exact 350/1,200-character semantic tiers and finally a pointer-centered crop capped at 400×400 pixels. Visual bytes remain a one-shot extension reference, and value changes still require a trusted click. The Browser Bridge is a working bridge while WebMCP adoption grows. Its bright Dialogue Relay cockpit makes human presence, model engagement, connector route, bounded focus, offers, and handoff state visible without becoming a generic chat sidebar. Native Cowork, WebMCP, and the bounded bridge remain structured action paths; a separate labeled model pointer is reserved for a future genuine Computer Use executor and is never simulated by the current fallback. The independently movable Desktop Companion uses the same visual language, shows the configured model ID without exposing endpoint or key data, and preserves the user's selected cockpit background across reloads. It does not claim universal discovery on unrelated websites or a connected extension model client. Preferred-model host The page can discover a same-origin model host that validates the exact bounded turn while keeping endpoint, model ID, and API key in the server process. The deterministic browser gate sends 468 characters and proves that credentials never enter the page. A separate provider-backed acceptance used local Ollama 0.32.15 with qwen3:4b : a 502-character bounded turn returned the exact "Grace Hopper" offer, which changed the field only after a trusted click and produced a Verified Receipt. This is a connected local preferred-model claim, not an external or ChatGPT-agent claim. How I built it Cowork Protocol is a dependency-light JavaScript workspace using HTML, CSS, Node.js, Manifest V3, and the current WebMCP imperative API. packages/core — focus packets, causal changes, feedback, offers, authorization, receipts, presence, and leases. packages/conversation — bounded turns, latest-only inbox/reply, silence suppression, and validated offers. packages/model-transport — same-origin browser discovery and server-side OpenAI-compatible gateway. packages/native-webmcp — registration and cleanup through document.modelContext . packages/formbuilder-connector — stable field mapping and verified mutation plans. packages/bridge — bounded WebMCP-host and legacy semantic adapters. packages/reference-ui — shared human/model/relay state language across surfaces. apps/formbuilder-showcase — public FormBuilder proof. apps/browser-companion — optional Native-first Side Panel and bounded no-WebMCP fallback. apps/desktop-companion — movable loopback/tray surface with shared session authority, model identity, audio controls, and persistent appearance. Development followed strict red-green testing : each behavior began with a failing contract or browser-evidence test, then the smallest passing implementation, followed by the complete regression gate. Challenges The hardest problem was not exposing more tools; it was making human-agent handoff legible and enforceable . A model cannot be allowed to manufacture a human_confirmation argument. Offers are therefore separate from authorization, and a trusted click must still match the offer, target, arguments, page version, and expiry. Browser evidence also found real issues. A reduced-motion transition briefly moved the skip link outside the viewport at true 200% zoom. Browser-startup races could keep the extension fixture from receiving its isolated context or make a page-owned WebMCP registration appear absent before it was ready. These were closed test-first and are now reproducible acceptance gates. Evidence The released commit is e4a35ce (main, after tag v0.9.0 ). Current release evidence: 538/538 automated tests; 12/12 character and visual-budget evaluations; 10/10 deterministic juror-proof steps. Chrome 152 discovery of all nine native tools and eight native calls;
video_title: Cowork Protocol — WebMCP makes websites actionable. Cowork makes action collaborative.
video_transcript_excerpt: There's an old axiom from Watzlawick. One cannot not communicate. Work with a model and you feel it. Your pointer, your click, your silence all arrive as something. But communication isn't sending. It's a turn. I speak. You listen and work out what I meant. I wait. You answer. A word, a status, or just a change on screen. Then my turn again. Which is why silence is the hard one. Agreement? Did you step away? Did the channel die? So you do what people do. Send signals on purpose. Make your status readable and agree on the channels. WebMCP already gives your model the action layer. What's missing is how the two of you communicate and which way of working you're in. Co-worker protocol gives your model co-worker communication skills and binds them to working modes. So how does it reach you? Best case, the site ships the protocol itself. Headless. No interface required. It works with other providers and it can host our surface if a site wants one. When site doesn't, the extension brings both protocol and interface. And a desktop companion carries it out of the browser. Native is strongest. The bridge is scaffolding. One day it should be unnecessary. Look, that's Susan. She needs a survey and before she even sits down, she hands a model task. She's gone. It works alone. She arrives and one click puts them in co-work. Now she works and it watches and comments. It suggests, she chooses. And she just says it. >> Look at question three. That would be the better first question. >> Now she leads and it works. The sentence is the instruction. It moves the question and stops. >> Yes, that's better. >> Then she has to go. She doesn't vanish. She hands over. >> Draft good questions for a family leisure survey. >> A goal, a budget and a time. That's what her absence means. She's back and says so. The model reports only what's new. Question 7 to 12. >> Good ones, but go general to specific and use checkboxes instead of blank lines. >> And the work moves on. Web MCP makes websites actionable. Co-work protocol makes action collaborative. Try it with your own favorite web apps.

title: Justice Portal
pitch: The law, in words you actually use.
about_excerpt: The law, in words you actually use. Like Comment Story Updates welcome page Describe your problem page Law Library Help Page Inspiration The inspiration behind Justice Portal came from two things: my desire to learn and work with emerging technologies, and a problem I have observed in my own country, Uganda. As a developer, I wanted to challenge myself by learning something new and understanding how technologies such as WebMCP could change the way people interact with web applications and AI agents. At the same time, I kept thinking about how many people have legal rights but do not necessarily act on them when they face everyday disputes. The problem is often not that there is no law or that there is no possible action to take. Instead, people may not know what the law says, whether their situation is covered, what information they need, or what they can actually do next . Legal language can also be difficult for an ordinary person to understand. Someone may be able to describe their problem very clearly in everyday language, but struggle to translate that problem into legal terminology or determine which legal information is relevant. That led me to the idea for Justice Portal . What it does Instead of expecting people to already understand legal terminology, Justice Compass allows a person to describe their situation naturally. The system can then help them structure the problem, identify relevant information, organize the facts and evidence, and prepare possible next steps. The goal is not to replace lawyers or provide definitive legal representation. It is to help people move from: "I have a problem, but I don't know if anything can be done." to: "I understand my situation better, I know what information is relevant, and I have a clearer idea of what I can do next." Why Legal Help is a strong fit for WEBMCP Legal help is a strong fit for WebMCP because users provide real-world facts, while the website provides structured legal knowledge to interpret those facts. WebMCP connects the two by allowing an AI agent to directly use tools such as analyze_situation, search_laws, get_next_steps, draft_demand_letter, and find_help through the live website without requiring separate APIs or integrations. Since legal accuracy is important, these tools can ground the agent in curated Ugandan laws, legal sections, and forums rather than relying only on generated assumptions. WebMCP also makes Justice Portal interactive by allowing an agent to analyze situations, populate forms, navigate the site, identify relevant laws, determine missing information, create action plans and evidence checklists, draft demand letters, and connect users with appropriate legal-help organizations. Multiple tools can be combined to address issues such as eviction procedures, deposit limits, and notice requirements. In this way, Justice Portal transforms from a passive legal information website into an interactive legal assistant where people and AI agents work together to understand, organize, and respond to everyday legal problems while keeping the user involved and in control. How we built it Justice Portal is a frontend-only React 19 + TypeScript application built with Vite and Tailwind CSS. It has no backend, database, or API keys, so the legal data, case analysis, and generated documents run entirely in the user's browser, keeping sensitive information local and making the system easy to audit. The application is built around a single tool layer that powers both the user interface and AI agents. It contains a structured Ugandan legal dataset, a referral directory, and a deterministic matching engine that analyzes a user's problem, identifies relevant laws, rights, remedies, evidence, next steps, and legal-help services. Because the engine is rule-based, users can see why particular laws were matched instead of relying on a black-box model. WebMCP exposes these capabilities through 13 tools, including analyzing situations, searching laws, retrieving cases, generating action plans and demand letters, finding legal help, filling forms, and navigating the application. Both the UI and AI agents use the same tool handlers, meaning agent actions immediately update what the user sees. A built-in WebMCP Inspector allows developers to view tool schemas, test tools, inspect results and errors, measure execution time, and view the history of UI and agent calls. This makes Justice Portal both an accessible legal-information platform and a practical demonstration of how WebMCP enables AI agents to interact directly with web applications. Challenges we ran into One of our biggest challenges was understanding WebMCP and how it actually fits into the interaction between a website and an AI agent. At first, it was difficult to understand why WebMCP was necessary when an agent could already interact with a website through its normal user interface. We gradually learned that the real value is in allowing a website to expose meaningful, structured capabilities that an agent can directly use instead of relying only on visual interaction. Another challenge was ideation . We wanted to build something where WebMCP was genuinely useful rather than simply adding it to an unrelated application. We therefore had to think carefully about problems that involve multiple steps and where an AI agent could meaningfully collaborate with a human. Finally, designing the application around a frontend-only architecture with mock data required us to focus on the core experience and demonstrate the concept without spending too much time building infrastructure that was not essential to the WebMCP demonstration. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud of turning an initial idea into a working concept that demonstrates how AI agents and web applications can work together through WebMCP . One of our biggest accomplishments was understanding and implementing the idea of exposing application capabilities as WebMCP tools. Instead of treating WebMCP as another interface element, we designed tools around meaningful actions that an agent could perform within Justice Portal. Another accomplishment is keeping the human in the loop . Justice Compass is designed to assist users rather than make consequential legal decisions on their behalf. Important outputs remain reviewable and editable before the user decides what to do. Most importantly, we are proud that the project allowed us to explore a new technology while applying it to a problem that has real-world relevance. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is more than a mechanism for an AI agent to search or navigate a website. We learned how a website can expose structured tools that allow an AI agent to interact with the application's capabilities directly. This helped us understand the difference between an agent simply navigating a user interface and an agent being able to use meaningful application-level operations. We also learned how multiple WebMCP tools can be combined into a larger workflow. For example, an agent can search for relevant information, identify missing facts, create or update a case, organize evidence, and prepare a document as part of one broader task. The project also taught us the importance of designing around the actual problem being solved rather than simply choosing a technology and trying to find somewhere to use it. What's next for Justice Portal The current version of Justice Portal is a starting point. We want to expand it from a prototype into a more complete platform for helping people navigate everyday legal and public-service problems. Some of our next goals include: Expanding beyond landlord–tenant disputes into areas such as family, employment, consumer, and public-service issues. Adding more reliable and comprehensive legal information from authoritative sources. Improving the agent's ability to identify missing information and ask useful follow-up questions. Expanding the number of WebMCP tools available to agents. Improving evidence organization and document preparation. Adding stronger privacy and security protections. Exploring how Justice Portal could support different jurisdictions beyond Uganda. Continuing to improve the collaboration between humans and AI agents so that the agent handles repetitive and complex organizational tasks while the human remains in control of important decisions. Our long-term vision is for Justice Portal to become a trusted bridge between everyday people, legal information, and AI agents , helping people move from simply knowing that they have a problem to understanding their possible options and taking informed next steps. Human-governed WebMCP authority for incident response.

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 What it does 

 How we built it 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What we learned 

 What's next for RELAY — Proof Before Power 

 RELAY — Proof Before Power 

 Human-governed WebMCP authority for incident response. 

 Inspiration 

 AI agents are increasingly capable of investigating incidents and proposing production actions. 

 But sensitive execution creates a governance problem: an ordinary approval workflow can leave the underlying agent capability continuously available, with only a permission check standing between investigation and production change. 

 RELAY explores a different model: 

 What if the human decision changed what the agent was actually capable of doing on the web? 

 What it does 

 RELAY gives an agent nine persistent WebMCP capabilities for incident investigation, evidence gathering, deployment comparison, hypothesis building, recovery preparation, and verification. 

 The sensitive production execution capability does not exist. 

 The agent can investigate the incident and stage one bounded recovery proposal, but it still cannot execute production recovery. 

 Only the visible human action: 

 AUTHORIZE THIS ACTION 

 changes the live WebMCP capability surface. 

 At that moment: 

 09 → 10 

 One exact temporary capability is registered: 

 execute_authorized_recovery 

 The agent can use it once to carry out the approved recovery. 

 In the demo: 

 
 deployment #4821 becomes #4819 
 error rate falls from 31% to 0.8% 
 recovery is verified 
 execution count becomes 1 
 

 Immediately after execution, the temporary capability is removed: 

 10 → 09 

 A replay cannot execute another recovery. 

 Why WebMCP 

 RELAY is not simply an API call hidden behind an approval button. 

 The important state is the actual browser-visible WebMCP capability surface. 

 Before authorization, the production execution tool genuinely does not exist. 

 After the human decision, one exact capability appears. 

 After its single use, it disappears. 

 WebMCP makes that authority native to the interaction between the web application and the agent. 

 How it improves the user experience 

 The human does not need to manually perform the entire incident response. 

 The agent can investigate, assemble evidence, compare deployments, form a hypothesis, and prepare a bounded recovery proposal. 

 At the same time, the agent does not receive standing production authority. 

 The consequential decision remains human. 

 The resulting flow is: 

 investigation → human judgment → bounded execution 

 rather than forcing users to choose between full manual operation and persistent agent authority. 

 What humans and agents can do together 

 The agent handles the evidence-heavy investigative work. 

 The human decides whether production authority should come into existence. 

 After authorization, the agent completes the exact approved recovery without requiring the human to manually execute the production action. 

 Then the authority disappears. 

 RELAY expresses human governance as a change in agent capability, not merely as an approval flag. 

 How we built it 

 RELAY uses real document.modelContext WebMCP registration. 

 Nine persistent tools support investigation and recovery preparation. 

 The state-changing recovery execution capability is intentionally absent. 

 A human-only UI authorization dynamically registers execute_authorized_recovery for the exact approved recovery. 

 After its single execution, that capability is removed. 

 Final live QA verified the registry lifecycle directly: 

 09 → 10 → 09 

 The execution capability was absent initially, appeared only after human authorization, executed once, and was genuinely removed afterward. 

 What's next 

 RELAY is a focused demonstration of ephemeral, human-governed agent authority. 

 The same capability pattern could be explored for other consequential web actions where investigation can be delegated broadly but execution should be created narrowly, explicitly, and temporarily.

 Inspiration 

 We were inspired by a simple problem: How can we verify whether a programmer actually wrote a piece of code? 

 Traditional plagiarism and code-similarity tools mainly compare the code itself. But programmers have individual habits in the way they name variables, structure functions, use loops, format code, write comments, and manage complexity. 

 We wanted to turn these behavioral patterns into a unique Coding Fingerprint , similar to a digital identity for programming style. This idea led to StyleShield AI. 

 What it does 

 StyleShield AI analyzes a programmer's previous code samples and creates a Coding Fingerprint and Coding DNA based on their programming behavior. 

 When a new code submission is provided, StyleShield: 

 
 Extracts structural and behavioral coding features 
 Compares the new code with established coding patterns 
 Calculates a similarity score 
 Uses machine learning for prediction 
 Generates Coding DNA 
 Provides programming-style/personality insights 
 Produces an explainable verification result 
 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, we extended StyleShield with WebMCP tools such as analyze_code , get_coding_fingerprint , and explain_verification . This allows AI agents to directly access StyleShield's analysis capabilities through structured tool calls while keeping the human involved in the final verification decision. 

 How we built it 

 We built StyleShield using Python, Flask, JavaScript, SQLite, and machine-learning techniques . 

 The system extracts features such as variable naming, indentation, function structure, complexity, loops, comments, and AST-based characteristics. These features are combined to create a programmer's Coding Fingerprint and Coding DNA. 

 We then developed a Flask API that connects the frontend to the analysis modules. 

 For the WebMCP extension, we used document.modelContext.registerTool() to expose StyleShield functionality as structured WebMCP tools. These tools communicate with our Flask API and return structured JSON results that an AI agent can understand and use. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of our biggest challenges was connecting WebMCP with our existing Flask application while keeping the existing StyleShield functionality stable. 

 We faced issues with asynchronous JavaScript requests, API responses, and exposing our local Flask application through a Cloudflare Quick Tunnel. At one point, the tunnel returned an HTTP 530 error, which initially looked like an application failure. 

 After debugging, we identified the problem as tunnel connectivity rather than our StyleShield backend. We restarted the tunnel and successfully established communication between the WebMCP layer and our Flask API. 

 Another challenge was representing programming style accurately. A programmer's identity cannot be determined from one feature, so we combined multiple coding characteristics to create a more meaningful fingerprint. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that we transformed an existing programmer-code analysis concept into a WebMCP-enabled AI-assisted verification system . 

 Our key accomplishments include: 

 
 Building a working Coding Fingerprint system 
 Generating unique Coding DNA 
 Combining multiple programming-style features 
 Integrating machine-learning-based prediction 
 Building an explainable verification workflow 
 Successfully registering multiple WebMCP tools 
 Connecting WebMCP directly to our Flask analysis backend 
 Successfully receiving structured analysis results through the WebMCP-connected application 
 

 Most importantly, we learned how an existing application can be extended so that AI agents can directly use its capabilities instead of only interacting with its visual interface . 

 What we learned 

 We learned that programming style contains many subtle behavioral patterns that can be useful for identity verification. 

 Technically, we learned how to build modular AI applications with Flask, connect frontend tools to backend APIs, handle asynchronous requests, work with structured JSON responses, and integrate WebMCP into an existing web application. 

 We also learned that good human-agent interaction is not about replacing human decisions. Instead, an AI agent can gather evidence, perform analysis, and explain results while the human remains responsible for the final decision. 

 What's next for StyleShield AI 

 We plan to make StyleShield more robust and useful in real-world environments. 

 Future improvements include: 

 
 More advanced behavioral and semantic code analysis 
 Larger and more diverse training datasets 
 Cross-language programmer fingerprinting 
 Stronger confidence and explainability mechanisms 
 Continuous learning from new verified code samples 
 Integration with coding assessment and educational platforms 
 Advanced AI-agent workflows using additional WebMCP tools 
 Programmer verification history and audit trails 
 Better protection against intentional style imitation 
 

 Our long-term goal is to make StyleShield a reliable programmer identity intelligence layer that can assist organizations, educators, and developers in understanding whether code is consistent with a programmer's established coding behavior.
