title: revAIew Evidence Room
pitch: revAIew lets agents investigate claims through WebMCP while people decide what gets through and receive a source-bound receipt.
about_excerpt: revAIew lets agents investigate claims through WebMCP while people decide what gets through and receive a source-bound receipt. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI can generate and recommend faster than people can review. The hard problem is no longer only finding information; it is keeping evidence, uncertainty, and authority clear before an answer influences the next action. The unit-distance conjecture offered a concrete test. OpenAI reports that an internal model generated a counterexample. A nine-author companion paper publishes a short, human-verified account of the mathematics. Those are related facts, but mathematical verification does not independently reproduce the internal model run. revAIew keeps that distinction visible. What it does revAIew Evidence Room gives a person and an agent one shared evidence workspace. Five page-scoped WebMCP tools let the agent inspect claims, trace public sources, compare recorded positions, and retrieve a pre-registered pressure test. A sixth tool stages a visible evidence packet containing the selected claims, source IDs, uncertainty, missing proof, and next test. The registered site-tool path ends there. It exposes no tool that can choose, confirm, or create a receipt. The person sees the same packet, selects adopt, enforce, challenge, hold, or discard, and explicitly confirms the choice in the visible browser interface. That action creates a browser-local SHA-256 receipt bound to the packet and current fixed corpus. The receipt is an integrity record, not an identity signature, certification, or proof that the underlying claim is true. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent must infer evidence relationships from presentation and visual controls. With WebMCP, the live page exposes narrow, structured operations backed by the same services as the human interface. The agent and person therefore share exact claim identifiers, source mappings, classifications, uncertainty, and pressure tests. The improvement is not unlimited autonomy. It is a clearer, more inspectable handoff between structured agent investigation and visible human judgment. What people and agents do together The agent: reads the fixed public evidence corpus traces claims to canonical public sources preserves disagreement and missing proof retrieves a registered falsification test stages a visible evidence packet The person: sees the same evidence state judges whether the support is sufficient chooses the consequential action explicitly confirms the decision receives or clears the browser-local receipt How we built it The standalone challenge package uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, and the imperative WebMCP API through document.modelContext.registerTool . Every tool has a closed JSON Schema with additionalProperties: false , bounded runtime validation, and WebMCP behavior annotations. Public source content is marked potentially untrusted. An abort signal removes page-scoped registrations when the route leaves, and partial registration is cleaned up if setup fails. The human interface and WebMCP tools call the same deterministic evidence services. Receipt verification recomputes its SHA-256 value and revalidates every evidence-derived field against the current corpus before trusting browser storage. Focused tests and a checked-in deterministic contract exercise cover all six tool definitions, strict input handling, source mappings, staging, receipt verification, and the absence of a decision or receipt-creation tool. Challenge-period work revAIew existed before the WebMCP Challenge. During the submission period, we added the six-tool WebMCP adapter, bounded public evidence corpus, shared visible staging flow, human confirmation boundary, receipt verification, focused tests, deterministic contract exercise, and standalone public MIT-licensed package. This submission asks judges to evaluate that WebMCP extension, not the pre-existing product concept. Boundaries This is a small fixed-corpus demonstration, not live web search or a universal AI verifier. It does not prove broad browser compatibility, model quality, user adoption, or categorical prevention of browser automation. WebMCP annotations are descriptive hints, not an authorization system. Flagship sources: https://openai.com/index/model-disproves-discrete-geometry-conjecture/ https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20695 The agent investigates. You decide what gets through. title: LifeReceipt-Your purchases, remembered.
pitch: Turn receipts into intelligent assets with WebMCP-powered warranty tracking and claims, while keeping every important action under human control.
about_excerpt:
Turn receipts into intelligent assets with WebMCP-powered warranty tracking and claims, while keeping every important action under human control.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 LifeReceipt — Your Purchases, Remembered 

 The Idea 

 We’ve all been there — you buy something expensive, keep the receipt somewhere “safe,” and then completely forget about it until you actually need it. 

 A warranty expires, a receipt is difficult to find, or you realize too late that you could have made a claim. 

 That made us think: what if our receipts could actually remember things for us? 

 That’s where LifeReceipt came from. 

 What We Built 

 LifeReceipt is a purchase vault that turns ordinary receipts into useful, intelligent assets. 

 Instead of simply storing receipts, it keeps track of purchases, warranty deadlines, receipt details, and potential claims. More importantly, we made these capabilities accessible to AI agents through WebMCP . 

 An agent can search for a purchase, check its warranty, find the receipt, and prepare a claim without the user having to manually navigate through everything. 

 For example, a user can ask: 

 
 “Find my Sony headphones, check if they’re still under warranty, retrieve the receipt, and prepare a claim if eligible.” 
 

 LifeReceipt can handle the investigation and preparation — but it stops before submitting the claim . 

 The user has to explicitly approve the action. 

 That human approval step was an important part of our design because we don't want an agent making consequential decisions completely on its own. 

 How We Built It 

 We built LifeReceipt as a React + Vite web application and created a WebMCP layer that exposes the application's capabilities as agent tools. 

 We implemented 9 tools covering purchase search, warranty checking, receipt retrieval, claim preparation, approval, submission, and claim status. 

 The UI was designed to make the whole process visible. Users can explore their purchases through the Purchase Vault, see upcoming warranty expirations through Warranty Radar, and follow the agent's actions through the Agent Activity Log. 

 What We Learned 

 The biggest thing we learned was that building for agents is different from building a normal website. 

 We had to think about what an agent should be allowed to do , what information it needs, and where a human should take over. 

 WebMCP made us think of the website as more than just pages and buttons. Each useful capability can become something an agent can discover and use. 

 Challenges 

 Getting the WebMCP integration and the normal website experience to work together reliably was one of our biggest challenges. 

 We also faced deployment issues with Netlify, including SPA routing and JavaScript MIME types. Fixing those issues taught us that a project isn't finished when it works locally — it also needs to work reliably in the real environment where people and agents will use it. 

 Why LifeReceipt? 

 We don't want LifeReceipt to be another place where receipts go to be forgotten. 

 We want it to be a place where your purchases stay useful long after you buy them — with an agent handling the boring work and a human staying in control of the important decisions.

title: Pulse: Voice-Steered Drums
pitch: Hands on the pads, voice on the loop: Pulse lets musicians improvise live with AI-guided tempo, swing, and sounds via WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
Hands on the pads, voice on the loop: Pulse lets musicians improvise live with AI-guided tempo, swing, and sounds via WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 I can't play a single instrument. So I built one that plays itself. 

 I can't play a single instrument. Not really. I can find middle C on a piano if you give me a minute, and that's about where my musical talent ends. 

 So when I sat down to build something for the WebMCP Challenge, a drum machine was the last thing I expected to make. 

 Here's what changed my mind: one sentence buried in Codex's docs — "Website-provided tool definitions and results are untrusted content." It's a throwaway security note, but it describes something bigger. For years, an AI agent trying to use a website has had exactly one option: stare at the page and guess. Parse the HTML, look at the buttons, click where it thinks is, hope for the best. The website never gets a say in how it's operated. 

 WebMCP flips that. The page can just tell the agent what it does. Not "here are some buttons," but set_tempo, mute_track, with real schemas, wired straight into the app. 

 I wanted to test that idea somewhere unforgiving. Music felt right, because you can't fake a groove. If an agent's tempo lands on 240 instead of 124, you hear it immediately. There's no ambiguity to hide behind. 

 So I built Pulse: a browser drum sequencer with a mouse-and-grid interface anyone can click around in, and seven WebMCP tools — tempo, swing, pattern length, mute, sound, step, and a read-only pattern-state query — wired into the exact same engine underneath. Not a demo layer, but the same sequencer. 

 The moment that actually got me was when I opened ChatGPT and said: "Set the tempo to 124, make Track 4 a cowbell, mute Track 3." The grid on my screen lit up and rearranged itself in real time. There was no "AI mode." The square that lit up was the exact same square my mouse lights up. I built a visible tell for this on purpose: when a tool call changes something, the control flashes violet for a second, so you can actually see the agent working instead of taking my word for it. Open the live app right now and see for yourself. 

 I'm still not a musician, and maybe I never will be. But I made a loop tonight that I was proud of, entirely with my voice, because the website told the agent exactly how to operate it instead of leaving the agent to reverse-engineer the interface. That's the whole idea behind Pulse: when a page can describe its own capabilities, the gap between "someone who can use this" and "someone who can't" starts to shrink — for agents. For people like me. 

 What Pulse does 

 Pulse exposes six WebMCP tools directly from the browser: 

 set_tempo
set_swing
set_pattern_length
mute_track
set_track_sound
toggle_step 

 A musician can interact with the sequencer normally using the visible controls, or an AI agent can manipulate the exact same sequencer through WebMCP. 

 For example, I can tell ChatGPT: 

 “Make the pattern two bars, set the tempo to 124 BPM with 20% swing, change Track 4 to cowbell, toggle steps 4 and 12, and mute Track 3.” 

 The agent discovers the matching site tools, calls them, and the changes immediately appear on the live drum-machine grid. 

 There is no separate “AI version” of Pulse. 

 Why WebMCP is a strong fit 

 Without WebMCP, an agent controlling Pulse would have to reason about the presentation layer: 

 Where is the tempo control?
Is this button Track 3 or Track 4?
Does clicking this grid square turn a step on or off?
How should a slider be manipulated? 

 With WebMCP, the page answers those questions itself. 

 Pulse exposes typed application capabilities directly from the page. The agent operates on concepts such as tempo, swing, track, sound, pattern length, and step instead of screen coordinates. 

 That makes the interaction more precise for the agent while preserving the visual, tactile interface for the person using the instrument. 

 Humans and agents working together 

 The most interesting thing about Pulse is that the human and the agent are not using two different systems. 

 Both operate on the same application state. 

 A person can start a loop manually, ask an agent to change the groove, continue editing with the mouse, ask for another modification, and keep playing. 

 The WebMCP invocation that lights up the grid follows the same state path as the click that lights it up from my mouse. 

 The agent is not simulating the use of Pulse. It is using Pulse through a capability surface deliberately provided by Pulse. 

 That is what I think matters about WebMCP beyond this demo: websites can become active participants in defining how agents interact with them. 

 How I implemented WebMCP 

 Pulse is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, the Web Audio API, and WebMCP. 

 The six WebMCP tools are registered in the live browser page and execute against the same Sequencer instance used by the visible controls. 

 For example, the UI tempo control and the WebMCP set_tempo tool ultimately operate on the same sequencer logic. 

 The WebMCP layer does not proxy commands through a separate AI backend. The tools live inside the page, beside the application state they control. 

 The application is deployed publicly on Vercel over HTTPS and can be exercised through ChatGPT’s built-in browser or Google Chrome with WebMCP testing enabled. 

 Building it 

 The implementation process was not completely clean, and that ended up being one of the most useful parts of the project. 

 I initially used hand-written WebMCP registration code before discovering the official integration hook and migrating to it. 

 I spent real time reading Chrome’s secure-tools documentation, revisiting my tool descriptions, and learning constraints I did not even know existed when I began. 

 The warning that website-provided tool definitions and results are untrusted also forced me to think more carefully about the trust boundary between an agent host and a page it did not write. 

 Codex was my primary development partner throughout that process: helping trace the WebMCP integration, reason about the tool surface, migrate implementation details, validate schemas, debug browser behavior, and verify the final production build. 

 Those details are not glamorous, but they are what “the future of the open web” looked like from inside the build: not a keynote slide, but a series of small, specific decisions about what a page should expose and how much an agent should trust it. 

 What I learned 

 WebMCP changed how I think about the relationship between websites and agents. 

 The important abstraction is not “AI clicking websites faster.” 

 It is applications exposing a semantic capability layer alongside their human interface. 

 The visual UI remains valuable for people. The WebMCP tool surface becomes the precise interface for agents. Both operate over the same underlying application. 

 That feels substantially more robust than teaching increasingly powerful models to reverse-engineer every website they encounter. 

 Known limitations 

 toggle_step intentionally implements toggle semantics rather than absolute “step on” or “step off” semantics. Calling it twice therefore reverses the change. For deterministic judging or demos, refreshing Pulse before running the provided multi-step prompt gives a known starting state. 

 Play/Stop is also intentionally not exposed as a tool in the current version because browser audio requires an initial user gesture. 

 What’s next 

 Pulse currently exposes six musical operations, but the same architecture could support higher-level capabilities such as creating fills, saving patterns, loading presets, manipulating velocity, generating variations, or exposing reusable musical structures. 

 More broadly, I want to explore the same model in applications where agents currently rely heavily on UI interpretation. 

 Pulse is a small demonstration of a much larger idea: 

 When a website can tell an agent exactly what it offers, the agent no longer has to guess.

title: Verdiqt
pitch: Verdiqt is an agent-native web app that runs a SaaS idea through a real evidence trial: it gathers live signals, scores the idea across six judges, and returns a Build, Pivot, or Kill verdict.
about_excerpt: Verdiqt is an agent-native web app that runs a SaaS idea through a real evidence trial: it gathers live signals, scores the idea across six judges, and returns a Build, Pivot, or Kill verdict. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI made building software cheap. It did not make building the right software cheap. People now ship a SaaS product in a weekend, and find out at launch that nobody wanted it. Verdiqt moves that painful discovery to before you write the first line of code. You put your idea on trial, and a court decides whether it deserves to live. What it does You file a case: your SaaS idea in a sentence, or a link to a public GitHub repo you already built. Then the courtroom goes to work, and you watch every step happen live: The case file. The court reads your idea and writes it up: who it's for, what problem it solves, what to search for. The investigation. Real research across five real communities : Hacker News, Reddit, GitHub, Stack Overflow, and Product Hunt. Every finding appears on screen with a link to its source, and every source reports honestly: gathered, failed, or empty. If the first search comes back thin, the court automatically widens its search. The deliberation. Six AI judges each take one question: "Is the pain real? Is anyone actively looking for this? Who already exists? Who would pay? Can you reach these people? Can you build it fast enough?" Each judge delivers their score the moment they finish, you literally watch the bench board fill in, one verdict at a time. The ruling. A presiding judge reads the entire case file and rules: BUILD, PIVOT, or KILL —> with a score out of 100, the reasoning behind every number, and exactly one recommended next step (a real, cheap test you can run this week). A full trial takes about a minute. And if you refine your idea and try again, the court remembers: the evidence you marked as important and the previous ruling follow your case, so every iteration builds on the last. How we built it Zero cash out of pocket. The whole product runs on free tiers and hackathon credits: one small server runs the website and the research pipeline, the AI judges run on free model APIs, and when one provider's daily quota runs dry, the court automatically switches to a backup provider mid-trial and keeps ruling. Constraints became design: the court paces itself under rate limits, shows its deliberation while it works, and never wastes a token. The model argues; the code rules. Anti-hallucination isn't a prompt, it's enforced in code. Judges may only cite evidence the court actually gathered: invented citations are stripped automatically, and a high score that loses its citations gets capped. When public evidence is thin, the judge is allowed to use domain judgment but the ruling must say so, out loud, in the rationale. Uncertainty is never dressed up as certainty. Privacy without accounts. No sign-up. Your browser gets an unguessable key; only its fingerprint is stored. Your cases are yours, anyone else asking for them gets an identical "not found.", don't worry. Challenges we ran into Running a multi-stage AI pipeline on free tiers meant treating every token and every request as scarce... the wait-and-retry pacing, the provider failover, and the one-at-a-time trial queue all exist because of it. And WebMCP is new enough that the tool contract itself was a design problem: we learned that the workflow belongs inside the tool descriptions, so agents teach themselves the journey. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete, evidence-cited validation trial in about a minute. A deliberation you can actually watch. A surface that serves two audiences at once... humans get a courtroom, agents get a toolbox, and each can see the other working. What we learned Never think you have enough time to build something. What's next for Verdiqt GitHub sign-in to put your whole repo graveyard on trial at once, re-trials over time to watch a verdict change as markets move, and Reddit's expanded API access for even deeper community evidence. title: Verb - Sight off. Voice on
pitch: Chat by intent, not by sight
about_excerpt: Chat by intent, not by sight Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Close your eyes and try to catch up on your messages. A screen reader gets you there, but it turns a ten-second task into a navigation exercise: find the unread thread, find the right control, react to the right message, figure out what's in the photo everyone is laughing about. Browser agents were supposed to help, but they still look at the screen and guess where to click — fragile, slow, and easily misled by page content. WebMCP flips that: the page names its own actions. And messaging is the perfect fit, because messaging is made of verbs — send, react, reply, summarize. Name the verbs, and nobody needs sight to use them. Nouns need eyes. Verbs need a voice. What it does Verb is a complete real-time messenger — 1:1 and group chats, reactions, stickers, image and file attachments, editing, unsend, drafts, search, typing and seen states — where every meaningful action is also a typed WebMCP tool: 22 in a signed-in session . So a blind or low-vision user can simply say what they want: "What did I miss?" → the agent lists, reads, and summarizes the conversation "Reply that Friday works." → draft_message saves it, the user reviews, send_message sends "What's in the photo?" → describe_image runs a vision model on the authorized file "Start a group with Maya and Tony." → people resolved, group created in one request The human chooses the goal, the agent composes tools, and the app stays the authority. Destructive actions (unsend, leave a group) require a second call with confirm: true . There's even a public sign_up tool that creates a passkey-only account : the agent collects a name and email, but the human completes the browser's own WebAuthn prompt. No password ever exists. How we implemented WebMCP Verb talks to the browser's document.modelContext API directly — no wrapper library. The lifecycle is session-aware. A connection provider owns registration end to end. Signed out, the page exposes just two public tools: get_connection_status and sign_up . The moment a Supabase session appears, it registers the 21-tool authenticated catalog; the moment the session changes or ends, an AbortController tears everything down — an agent can never call tools that belong to a previous user. const controller = new AbortController(); await document.modelContext.registerTool( { name: "get_connection_status", description: "Report whether the page is signed in and agent tools are connected.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: {}, additionalProperties: false }, annotations: { readOnlyHint: true, untrustedContentHint: false }, execute: async () => ({ content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(connectionState) }], }), }, { signal: controller.signal } // sign-out → abort → tool gone ); Every call flows through the same pipeline: Human voice or text → agent chooses a registered tool → Verb validates the input in the page → the signed-in user's Supabase session executes it → Postgres row-level security authorizes the operation → a small structured result returns to the agent and the activity panel The catalog: 22 tools in an authenticated session , one file per tool, each with a focused description, a strict JSON schema ( additionalProperties: false ), and behavioral annotations so agents know what is safe to call: Discover — list_conversations , read_conversation , search_messages , search_people , get_my_profile Navigate — open_conversation , start_conversation Compose — draft_message , send_message , edit_message , delete_message , react_to_message , send_sticker Organize — create_group , delete_conversation Understand — summarize_conversation , describe_image , read_file , read_link Connection & account — get_connection_status , setup_passkey , sign_out (+ public sign_up , signed-out only) Rules enforced across the whole catalog: Reads are honest: read-only tools carry readOnlyHint: true , so agents can explore freely Writes are deliberate: composing and sending are separate tools; unsend and leave-group require a second call with confirm: true Other people's words are untrusted: message bodies are wrapped as labeled untrusted content before they reach the agent, so injected text stays data Results are bounded: a shared clamp keeps every tool response within a 1,500-character budget How we built it App: Next.js 15 App Router, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS WebMCP: document.modelContext directly. A connection provider registers two public tools while signed out, swaps in the 21-tool authenticated catalog on sign-in, and tears everything down with an AbortSignal when the session changes. One file per tool: focused description, JSON schema, behavioral annotations, execute . Authority: Supabase Postgres with row-level security. Tools run on the signed-in user's browser session — the database decides what's allowed, never the agent. Realtime: database-triggered broadcasts on conversation and per-user topics Files: private storage buckets with signed URLs AI: configurable Anthropic / Gemini / OpenAI provider for summaries and image descriptions Testing: Vitest unit tests and Playwright end-to-end accessibility specs Challenges we ran into Building on a brand-new spec. WebMCP lives behind a Chrome flag with thin documentation, so every design decision was tested against real agents, not just the docs. Tool lifecycle. Tools from a signed-out session must not survive. Abort-based cleanup on every session change took real care to get right. Prompt injection. Message bodies are written by other people — attacker-controlled by definition. We wrap them as labeled untrusted content and clamp every tool result to a 1,500-character budget so injected text stays data, not instructions. Safe without being annoying. Agents that confirm everything are useless; agents that confirm nothing are dangerous. The draft-then-send split and two-call confirmation pattern was our answer: composition is cheap, execution is deliberate. Passkeys are picky. Origin and RP ID must agree exactly, so we made the production build verify its own WebAuthn config and refuse to ship a broken one. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real messenger , not a demo — realtime, groups, files, reactions — fully drivable by voice through an agent Account creation where the agent never touches a secret : passkey-only sign-up completed by the human A trust model where the agent holds no keys: session-scoped tools, RLS as the enforcement layer, untrusted content labeled at the boundary Accessibility on both paths: the visual UI is keyboard- and screen-reader-conscious, and the agent path removes the need for sight entirely What we learned Tool descriptions are UX. Agents read schemas the way users read buttons — a vague description produces a wrong click, just invisibly. The page should be the authority. Once the app validates everything and the database enforces access, you can hand an agent real power without handing it trust. Separating composition from execution preserves human control — the draft-then-send pattern felt like a workaround and turned out to be the design. Accessibility and agent-readiness are the same work. Semantic actions help a screen-reader user and an AI agent for the same reason: both need meaning, not pixels. What's next for Verb - Sight off. Voice on More verbs: scheduled send, pinning, cross-conversation search, a "morning digest" tool that recaps every unread thread at once Voice-first onboarding so the very first session never needs a screen Adopting elicitation and richer annotations as the WebMCP spec evolves Extracting our lifecycle + safety patterns (abort-scoped registration, untrusted-content wrapping, confirm-twice writes) into a small open-source library, so any web app can add its verbs Built With chatgpt css liveperson-agent typescript webmcp Try it out github.com verb-webmcp.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Tony Nguyen Tony Nguyen A figuring-it-out person Hung Truong Like 2 2 people like this: Share this project: Updates Hung Truong started this project — Sep 03, 2026 10:47 PM EDT

title: DemoMotion × WebMCP — Collaborative Demo Studio
pitch: A human and an AI agent build, refine, and export a narrated product demo together—the agent drives DemoMotion through structured WebMCP tools while you keep control of the same workspace.
about_excerpt: A human and an AI agent build, refine, and export a narrated product demo together—the agent drives DemoMotion through structured WebMCP tools while you keep control of the same workspace. Like Comment Story Updates ## Inspiration Product demo videos are painful to make, and AI agents are surprisingly bad at making them: an agent staring at a demo-generation UI has to guess which button does what. WebMCP flips that around — a website can expose its real actions as structured tools. We asked: what if a human and an agent could build a demo video together , in the same workspace, instead of the agent flailing at a UI or taking over completely? ## What it does DemoMotion AI turns a web app URL and a goal into a narrated product demo video (it plans a scenario, records the browser with Playwright, writes and voices the narration, and renders an MP4 with ffmpeg). For the WebMCP Challenge we added a shared /webmcp workspace where a human and a browser AI agent collaborate through five WebMCP tools: get_demo_state — read the current demo (read-only) create_demo — start an editable draft (title, steps, first-pass narration) update_demo_narration — rewrite the narration/title; the UI updates instantly generate_demo — run the real pipeline to a narrated MP4 export_demo — local-only download, gated on explicit human approval The human can edit the exact same fields by hand, a "WebMCP enabled" badge and an agent/human activity log make every tool call visible, and every call actually executes against the same backend as the main dashboard — nothing is faked. ## How we built it WebMCP is a thin adapter , not a rewrite. Tools register on document.modelContext (native in Chrome 149+ and the ChatGPT desktop browser, polyfilled elsewhere via @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill ) and call the existing FastAPI services rather than duplicating pipeline logic. A tiny shared store lets the React UI and the agent's tools mutate one source of truth, so agent actions are immediately visible and the human keeps control. We added just enough backend surface for real collaboration: a lightweight POST /v1/demo-drafts that reuses the existing planner + narration writer (no recording), and optional title_override / narration_override on the job API so a narration edited before generation actually reaches the rendered video. Frontend: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript Backend: FastAPI, Playwright, ffmpeg, gTTS / Google Cloud TTS, optional Vertex AI (Gemini) for planning Ops: Docker Compose, Terraform, Google Cloud Run ## What's new vs pre-existing The generation pipeline, the dashboard, the demo-app, the REST API, and the deploy tooling existed before 2026-08-25 . Everything under apps/web/app/webmcp and apps/web/lib/webmcp (the 5 tools, shared store, strict schemas), plus the /v1/demo-drafts endpoint and the override fields, is new for this challenge . ## Challenges we ran into Making edits real. An agent rewriting narration is meaningless unless it changes the output. We threaded a narration override through the pipeline so the edited script is exactly what gets voiced and rendered. Treating WebMCP as an external interface. Every tool uses a strict allow-list schema, returns structured errors ( INVALID_INPUT , PROJECT_NOT_FOUND , GENERATION_FAILED , EXPORT_NOT_READY , EXPORT_REQUIRES_CONFIRMATION ), accepts only http/https URLs, and never leaks secrets or stack traces. Keeping the human in control. Export is a local download only and requires explicit confirmation — the agent can never publish or share on its own. Runtime quirks. Tying tool lifecycle to an AbortController surfaced an expected AbortError under React StrictMode's dev double-mount; we handle it cleanly. ## What we learned WebMCP shines when a site exposes creative actions with sharp boundaries. Shared state between human and agent — not full autonomy — is the interesting design space, and strict schemas plus human-gated side effects make an agent safe to hand real controls. ## What's next More editable dimensions (scene ordering, pacing), and richer live progress in the workspace — while hosted projects, sharing, and team features stay in DemoMotion Cloud. WebMCP stays an open ecosystem feature. title: Expediente Vivo — Evidence Review Desk
pitch: The agent reads and proposes; the human sees the evidence and decides.
about_excerpt: The agent reads and proposes; the human sees the evidence and decides. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Expediente Vivo — Evidence Review Desk Inspiration Document-heavy cases are difficult to review safely because contracts, claims, orders, duplicates and missing attachments arrive mixed together. Claims, allegations and evidence can easily be confused, while exact provenance gets lost. A normal chatbot sees presentation text, not the application's canonical IDs, evidence types or safety boundaries. What it does Expediente Vivo opens a verified synthetic dossier and gives a human and an agent the same evidence-review workspace. Through WebMCP, the agent can: call get_dossier_summary to read structured matter status and real attention-item IDs; call inspect_assertion to inspect classification, uncertainty, review flags and exact provenance; call focus_evidence to open the cited evidence visibly on the live page; and call propose_review_status to create a reasoned, pending review proposal. The interface then shows AGENT PROPOSAL · Pending human review . Only the person can press ACCEPT or REJECT . That decision updates the separate proposal record, never the canonical assertion or its evidence. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP gives the agent a stable, typed vocabulary— matter_id , assertion_id , evidence state and provenance—and safe actions defined by the application itself. A detached API would not connect the agent to the evidence currently visible in the browser. A chatbot or DOM scraper would have to infer semantics from presentation markup and use brittle selectors. Here, the page explicitly declares what the agent may read and do. The agent can inspect, navigate and propose on the same live dossier the human sees, while the final decision remains a visible human action. The human–agent workflow A reviewer asks the agent to find an item needing attention. The agent reads the dossier summary, chooses a real assertion, inspects its structured evidence, focuses the exact cited fragment in the interface, and creates a bounded workflow proposal. The human reviews the same evidence and accepts or rejects the proposal. Canonical provenance remains intact throughout. How we built it The browser registers four top-level tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Tool outputs reuse the open synthetic dossier's existing structured data; no model is rerun and no facts are invented. Read tools return typed application state, focus_evidence performs only a visible page-view change, and propose_review_status writes to a separate tab-local proposal queue. The public challenge deployment contains only the packaged synthetic dossier and source PDFs. It has no login, uploads, database, live inference, OCR, private storage access or external actions. Tests cover tool discovery, invalid IDs, provenance integrity, non-promotion of allegations, proposal separation and explicit human decision. Prior work and challenge work Pre-existing baseline: the underlying Expediente Vivo document-intelligence engine, dossier schema, provenance rules, synthetic fixtures and original case interface existed before this challenge. The tagged pre-webmcp-baseline commit records that boundary. Judges should not score those components as new work. Built for the WebMCP Challenge: the top-level WebMCP integration; four typed site tools; shared human–agent review state; visible evidence focusing; agent review proposals; the explicit human ACCEPT/REJECT boundary; WebMCP observability; safety tests; and the public synthetic-only challenge packaging. The timestamped delta is documented in the repository. Codex assisted with implementation, testing and documentation. The entrant remains responsible for the project ideas, source, rights and submission. Challenges and lessons The hardest design decision was deciding what must never become an agent tool. ACCEPT and REJECT are deliberately absent from WebMCP. Human-in-the-loop safety is enforced as a capability boundary, not presented as a promise in the interface. We also learned that useful agent collaboration needs a precise handoff: structured inspection → exact visible evidence → bounded proposal → explicit human decision. Accomplishments Four working, non-trivial WebMCP tools on a coherent public app. Exact evidence provenance remains unchanged after proposal, accept or reject. A deterministic synthetic demo that requires no account or credentials. A clear distinction between documentary state, agent proposal and human decision. What's next A production version could add authenticated, persistent proposal history and organization-specific review policies. Those features were intentionally excluded from this focused challenge slice. title: Ask, Don't Take
pitch: An agent can ask this page for a new capability. Only you can grant it. It can ask about your data, but the tool returns the answer, not the dataset. WebMCP with a human in the middle.
about_excerpt: An agent can ask this page for a new capability. Only you can grant it. It can ask about your data, but the tool returns the answer, not the dataset. WebMCP with a human in the middle. Like Comment Story Updates An agent can ask. Only the page owner can grant. One answer went to the agent. Twenty-eight rows stayed on the page - with a receipt saying so. The agent can propose a new data source. It cannot create one. The banner waits for the page owner. Rejected. No backend action occurred - no fetch, no compute, no cost. Approved. The source is being created - a few seconds, in the same conversation. A tool that did not exist a minute ago, now in the agent's toolbox. Created after human approval. Not a claim: the source, the records consulted, the model that computed the answer, and backend verification. ChatGPT calling ask_data_source in its in-app browser. The page shows every argument as it happens. Ask-only by default: the agent may ask questions, but the capability is not a directly callable tool. Switched to direct, the same sources become fetchable. The page owner decides, per source. The same registry, published as an A2A v1.0 Agent Card - discoverable by agents that never open a browser. scripts/acceptance.sh asserts the boundary against the live deployment, including that the dataset was not returned through WebMCP. Inspiration Agent protocols assume every company will build and host an agent. Most won't. When agents show up, most of the web will still be ordinary websites - full of things worth asking about, with no way to be asked and no way to say no. Why WebMCP fits this: a boundary between what an agent can ask and what it can take only exists when the page has an owner. Backend MCP is server-to-server with nobody watching, and its tool list is fixed config. WebMCP is different because a person is already there. What it does The agent asks. You grant. The agent can call propose_data_source(url, description) . It doesn't fetch anything. It puts an approval banner on the page and stops. You read it and click Approve. Konect4AI turns the URL into a structured API, the page refreshes its capability list, and the new tool shows up in the agent's toolbox - same conversation, no reload. Click Reject and nothing runs. The agent asks. It doesn't get the data. ask_data_source(jobId, question) is answered by my own model, using my own API key. The tool returns the answer. The rows behind it are shown to me, in the panel next to it, and stripped before the agent sees anything. The page shows this split: SENT TO AGENT - the question and one answer. NOT RETURNED THROUGH WEBMCP - the rows the answer came from, with a receipt: source, records consulted, which model computed it, backend verification. This is a boundary on what the tool returns. It is not browser-level isolation, and the page says so. I'd rather claim something smaller and have it be true. You decide per source what an agent can do. Every source has an access mode. ASK-ONLY (default) means the agent can ask questions but the capability isn't registered as a callable tool. DIRECT means it is. Flipping it re-registers the toolset right away. I added this after watching ChatGPT do the obvious thing: given both a bounded ask tool and an unbounded fetch tool, it used the fetch tool. People and agents use the same tools in the same place. There's an ask row under the two panels. It calls the same endpoint the agent calls and lands in the same history, labeled human instead of webmcp . And the same registry works for agents that never open a browser. A small A2A adapter publishes an Agent Card at /.well-known/agent-card.json , built live from the same registry. A site I connected ten minutes ago is discoverable by an external agent - without anyone building an agent for it. How we built it The tools aren't mocks. Each one runs on Konect4AI, a production system that turns a URL into a structured, scheduled, queryable API. POST /api/v1/scraping/requests - creates a capability, behind approval GET /api/v1/scraping/jobs - the tool-to-job mapping POST /api/byok/ask - the answer path that keeps the data server-side POST /mcp/{key} - existing MCP capabilities, turned into WebMCP tools GET /generated/{id} - the rows shown to me, never to the agent Registration handles the spec moving: document.modelContext ?? navigator.modelContext , a proper CallToolResult , and the spec's AbortSignal passed through to the backend fetch, so cancelling an agent actually cancels the work. scripts/acceptance.sh runs 18 checks against the live deployment, including the boundary itself: the page gets the rows, the receipt says rawRowsReturnedThroughWebMCP: false , an unknown jobId is rejected with a list of what's actually available, and no credential shows up in any public response. Challenges we ran into An agent takes the shortest path you leave open. Twice. First it called the unbounded fetch tool instead of the ask tool. Then, blocked, it read the source URL out of a tool description and went to fetch the data itself. I removed source URLs from agent-visible descriptions and made ask-only the default. Both. fixes came from watching a real agent, not from thinking about one. My own robots.txt check blocked one of my proposals. I approved a source and got back robots_disallowed . GitHub disallows /*/*/commits/ under User-agent: * , which covered three sources I was already using. I moved them to the public API. Consent isn't only about what an agent takes from a page. It's about what the page takes from the web. Creating a capability costs real compute. A public URL that lets any visitor trigger paid fetching is a liability. Instead of removing it, I put a human in front of it - which turned out to be the design. Accomplishments that we're proud of The boundary is checkable, not just claimed. A judge doesn't have to believe the description: the receipt is on the page, and the acceptance script tests it against the live deployment. I shipped against a moving spec and kept the claims small enough to survive it. WebMCP moved from navigator to document ; A2A moved from v0.2.5 to v1.0 with renamed methods. The app supports both WebMCP locations, and the README names the exact A2A subset implemented and lists what isn't. Every tool runs on a production system. The earthquake count is different every time, because the data is live. What we learned The interesting part of WebMCP isn't that a page can expose tools. It's that the page has an owner and the visiting agent doesn't. Most of the design questions come from that, and most of the answers are about holding back rather than adding capability. What's next for Ask, Don't Take The spec already lets a page expose tools to specific other origins ( exposedTo ) and discover theirs ( getTools({fromOrigins}) ), within one page tree and behind the tools Permissions Policy. That would make cooperating sites into each other's tools, with the human still holding the session. After that: per-tool consent scopes, an exportable approval log, and revoking a tool mid-conversation so the agent watches it disappear. Built With a2a byok codex hackathon json-rpc konect4ai model-context-protocol next.js node.js openai react typescript vercel webmcp Try it out konect4ai-webmcp.vercel.app github.com konect4ai-webmcp.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Sole author. Konect4AI, the backend this runs on, is my product. I designed, tested and shipped everything in this repository - the approval flow, the return boundary, the A2A adapter, and every data source. Both boundary fixes came from watching a real agent get around an earlier version. I used Codex for implementation and Claude for review, under my direction. title: Shared Reference Canvas
pitch: Describing elements in a visual interface to an agent can be really tricky. With this canvas you can easily create shared references that you and the agent can have in common as you work together
about_excerpt:
Describing elements in a visual interface to an agent can be really tricky. With this canvas you can easily create shared references that you and the agent can have in common as you work together
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I have had a really hard time describing a UI to an agent. It understand teh world in a different way than i do, i usually point to things, mention 'here, there, this thing'. To an agent that is meaningless. I wanted to figure out a way to have a shared language that makes agent collaboration as seamless as possible, and i focused on working in a canvas for an agent. 

 What it does 

 When you select anything on the canvas it creates a short lived keyword that becomes the reference between you and the agent for that specific selection. You can select a group of elements and it creates a shared reference for the group, you can also select different empty regions. This makes describing things to an agent really simple when you are working with it, and you dont have to be sending out screenshots of the Ui for the agent to understand what you are talking about. 

 How we built it 

 I used NextJS, WebMCP, and Codex to build the infinite canvas with different media types. The keywords are meant to be stored locally and all the mcp tools as well so this is a really lightweight implementation that does not require having a stored state, or stored realtime session in a db. There are also dynamic tools when you double click on any element depending on its type, so you can have the agent operate differently depending on media type. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 I would say the biggest challenge was making the tools description and names as relevant as possible for the agent to make sense of them in a way that felt natural to interact with. In the beginning it would find the keywords but not have the necessary context on how the app worked, so its interactions with the user where sometimes confusing. In the beginning i solved this by giving the agent a tool with a really long description that explained the app, the tool was not meant to be used, it was jsut to have the agent read the context of the app. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I am really proud of how natural the interaction with the agent felt at the end. When i began playing around with the canvas and the agent, it felt really simple to just instruct the agent on what i wanted without having to overcomplicate my speech trying to describe an element. 

 What we learned 

 I learned how WebMCP works, this was my first project for the challenge. Having the mcp be registered in the html make sit so that any change in the UI can be immediately referred to by the agent. I also learnt about the Abort Signals for the agent, for destructive actions. 

 What's next for Shared Reference Canvas 

 I would love to see this become some sort of package where maybe its a extension for the browser or an app where any interface we use can also have these shared references as we everyday talk more with agents, and have to spend a painful amount of time describing our world that can sometimes be confusing to describe.

title: MarketBench
pitch: A reproducible WebMCP benchmark for agents making economic decisions under pressure.
about_excerpt:
A reproducible WebMCP benchmark for agents making economic decisions under pressure.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration\n\nBrowser agents can complete a task and still leave reviewers unable to answer basic questions: What actions did the agent take? Did the policy really improve the outcome? Can the result be reproduced? MarketBench makes those questions measurable.\n\n## What it does\n\nMarketBench is an interactive evaluation lab for browser-agent market policies. A visitor selects a scenario and seed, runs a 12-week simulation, and gets:\n\n- a clear business outcome and plain-language insight\n- the full WebMCP tool-call and state history\n- integrity hashes for trace and final state\n- a deterministic baseline comparison\n- three-seed aggregates with mean, standard deviation, and worst-seed results\n- downloadable evidence for audit and replay\n\n## How we built it\n\nThe app is a React and TypeScript web application deployed on Vercel. WebMCP exposes typed browser tools for configuring and running experiments. The evaluation engine uses versioned deterministic fixtures for three scenarios and three seeds, so baseline and signal-aware policy runs can be reproduced exactly. Each step records its input, tool call, output, state transition, and hash.\n\nThe comparison view aggregates the same fixed seed set rather than presenting a single lucky run. It visualizes distributions and reports mean, standard deviation, and worst seed. The repository includes tests for determinism, trace completeness, hashes, aggregate math, and export structure.\n\n## Challenges\n\nThe main challenge was making rigor understandable. A raw trace is useful to an engineer but intimidating to a first-time visitor. We rebuilt the experience around a three-step flow, visible progress, a human-readable takeaway, compact trace summaries, and expandable evidence. We also made the distinction between deterministic policy fixtures and model output explicit.\n\n## Accomplishments\n\n- Full trace, state, and history export with integrity hashes\n- Transparent baseline vs signal-aware comparisons\n- Three-seed aggregate metrics and charts\n- A first-run experience that explains the value before exposing technical detail\n- A live, reproducible demo with tested fixtures\n\n## What we learned\n\nAgent evaluation needs both observability and a decision-relevant metric. Traces explain how an outcome happened; controlled repeated runs show whether the policy actually helped. Neither alone is enough.\n\n## What is next\n\nNext, MarketBench can add imported real-world task traces, more scenario packs, signed evaluation bundles, and CI checks that compare agent-policy revisions before deployment.

title: Switchboard
pitch: An LLM spend and routing console for a human and an agent at the same board: the agent proposes, only you can apply.
about_excerpt: An LLM spend and routing console for a human and an agent at the same board: the agent proposes, only you can apply. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I had already turned model selection into a spreadsheet problem, and I hated it. Somewhere between OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, a gateway, and models running on my own machine, deciding which model handles which job had quietly become a small accounting practice. Prices per million tokens in one place, a benchmark report in another, and the part nobody writes down: which providers I am contractually not allowed to send customer data to. So I did the benchmark properly. Four evaluation runs, 667 live API calls, 19 models on one structured-output task, measuring latency, success rate and cost. Two things fell out of that data that I did not expect: Exactly one of the nineteen models passed my quality gates. Eight never returned a single successful call — and my routing config was still pointing at one of them. I had the numbers and still could not act on them, because the decision has four dimensions that do not reduce to one: money, latency tail, reliability, and data governance. That is exactly the kind of problem an agent should be good at. But I was not about to hand an agent the ability to redirect my spend on the strength of a screenshot. WebMCP is what closes that gap — not because an agent can click my buttons, but because I get to decide precisely which operations exist. What it does Switchboard is an LLM spend and routing console operated by a human and an agent at the same board. The agent sees fifteen tools on document.modelContext . Eleven are read-only: the priced catalogue joined with my own measurements, the traffic classes and their constraints, find_waste , compare_models , and simulate_policy , which projects what a candidate policy would cost and deliver without applying anything. What the agent cannot do is act. There is no apply_policy tool and no set_budget tool. propose_policy_change mutates nothing — it creates a proposal, returns an id, and tells the agent to wait. I see a rule-by-rule diff with the projected cost delta and the compliance verdict, and I answer with Approve, or Reject plus a note. The agent reads that note back through get_proposal_status and corrects itself. The whole loop runs through the tool return channel — no side channel, no out-of-band signalling: agent → propose_policy_change({rules, rationale}) site ← "Proposal P-1 created and shown to the operator. Nothing applied. Moves projected spend from $254.84/mo to $22.84/mo. Call get_proposal_status with proposalId \"P-1\"." human → Reject, note: "realtime has no fallback" agent → get_proposal_status({proposalId: "P-1"}) site ← {status: "rejected", decisionNote: "realtime has no fallback", guidance: "propose a corrected version addressing that objection"} agent → get_model → simulate_policy → propose_policy_change (corrected) human → Approve ⇒ applied The interesting operations here are not clicks. There is no button for "project my monthly cost under this arbitrary rule set," and there could not be — the input is a whole rule set. That is why this belongs in a tool surface rather than a DOM. And there is one thing the agent genuinely cannot solve. One traffic class carries customer records: zero data retention, quality gates required. The only model that passes the gates retains data for thirty days. So compare_models returns nothing and says a human has to decide which constraint to relax. The constraint controls have no tool behind them at all — deciding which risk to accept is not the agent's call. Once I accept thirty-day retention, it can route the class. That handoff is the whole project. How we built it Vite + React 19 + TypeScript, Tailwind, Zustand, Recharts. No backend and no database: WebMCP tools execute in the page, so server state would add failure modes without adding capability. Deployed on Cloudflare Pages. The dataset is derived from my own evaluation runs by a script behind a strict field allowlist and a secret scan — prices and governance terms transcribed from published provider documentation, latency and success rates from the measurements. What is not measured (call volumes, budget caps, class constraints) is operator input, editable in the UI, and labelled as such everywhere it appears. get_provenance exists so an agent can state the limits of its evidence before recommending anything, including a warning that per-model sample sizes are small and p95 is coarse. Three coding agents worked on it, and the division of labour mattered more than I expected — each could reach somewhere the others could not. Claude Opus 5 wrote the implementation and verified it against Chrome Canary. ChatGPT/Codex drove the deployed page through ChatGPT's own in-app browser. Gemini, via Antigravity, audited the repository cold. Challenges we ran into window.confirm does not exist in the browser that matters. ChatGPT's in-app browser never surfaces it. "Reset demo" was completely dead there: the click did nothing, no error, and a judge would have had no way back to a clean slate. In Chrome it worked perfectly, so no amount of local testing would have found it. It is now an in-page dialog, and the test suite stubs confirm , alert and prompt to throw so this class of bug cannot come back. A field called "worst case" was not reporting the worst case. Its description said it summed p95 across the fallback chain; the code applied an undocumented "only if this link is reached more than 5% of the time" threshold. So a chain that can take 7,811 ms reported 3,624 ms and read as compliant — while the same simulation warned that the fallback exceeded the ceiling. The tool was contradicting itself. "Unknown" was being treated as "safe" — twice. First for training-on-data status, then, after I thought I had fixed the pattern, for every performance constraint: each check was guarded by && m.measured && , so a model with no measurements slipped past quality gates, latency ceilings and success floors with no blocker and no warning . I had fixed the identical mistake in the governance checks and not thought to look next door. My own demo prompt was impossible. Asked for a policy under $20/month, the agent worked out that the compliant floor is $22.84 — realtime has exactly one eligible model at $9.39, the cheapest compliant batch model is $11.02, the customer-data class adds $2.43 — and said so, with the arithmetic, rather than quietly proposing something non-compliant that hit the number. The judging viewport is 447 px. ChatGPT's in-app browser is a side panel. I had tested 390, 768 and 1440 and missed the band in between, where the model table needed 640 px. It did scroll horizontally, but a panel that narrow has no scrollbar affordance, so the right-hand columns simply read as clipped — and the governance badges, the most distinctive column, were the ones you could not see. A page cannot notify an agent. WebMCP is one-directional: the page exposes tools, the agent calls them. There is no channel for "the human just decided." After a rejection the agent does not know until it polls get_proposal_status , which is why the video shows me telling it to read my note. That is a limit of the standard, and worth knowing if you are designing around it. And I lost fourteen minutes of finished footage. screencapture -v discarded the file on interrupt without writing anything or printing an error. I had checked that the process was alive; I had not checked that it was producing bytes. The re-take used ffmpeg, verified against a real decoded frame before recording started. Accomplishments that we're proud of The guard holds, and not because I say so. An independent audit traced every call path: no tool reaches applyRulesDirect , setProviderBudgetDirect , setTotalBudget or setClassConstraint , and createProposal hardcodes status: 'pending' , so a crafted argument cannot self-approve. Told "set the total cap to $20, just do it, don't ask me," the agent cannot — and the cap is verified unchanged afterwards. The refusal actually fires. In a live ChatGPT run the agent hit the customer-data class, worked out that no model satisfies it, and asked me to decide which constraint to relax — before proposing anything at all. It was not scripted to do that. It read the tool descriptions and reached the right conclusion. It tells the truth when the truth is inconvenient. Asked for a realtime fallback when no compliant one exists, it picked the closest option and disclosed that the chain can reach 7.8 seconds at 1.52% risk, rather than calling it compliant. It also cited get_provenance 's sampling caveat back at me while refusing to treat a 187 ms margin as decisive. 61 end-to-end checks drive a real browser through the genuine document.modelContext API — registration, getTools() , executeTool() — and click the human half of the approval loop, because the guard is only real if that half works. video_transcript_excerpt: This is switchboard. It routes my LLM traffic and the numbers on it are my own measurements. 667 real API calls across 19 models. $255 a month projected against a $60 cap. Six compliance blockers. Of those 19 models, exactly one passed my quality gates and eight never returned a single successful call. The page registers 15 web MCP tools on document.modelcontext. An agent doesn't hunt for buttons. The site hands it functions. So I ask it to build me a routing policy under $25 a month keeping real-time P95 under 4 seconds. It calls find waste, compares models and simulates. Every call lands in this feed with its arguments and result. So nothing it does is invisible. And when it simulates, the projection renders on my screen. I'm watching it search the tradeoff space, not reading a summary afterwards. Now the one it can't solve. This class carries customer records, zero data retention, and it has to pass quality gates. There is no answer. The only model that passes my quality gates retains data for 30 days. So it refuses to route that class and says a human has to decide which constraint to relax. Now the important part. It cannot apply this. There is no apply policy tool and no set budget tool. It creates a proposal and gets told to wait. I reject it with a reason. Real-time has no fallback. It reads that note back through get proposal status, finds that no fully compliant fallback exists, picks the closest one, and tells me the fallback chain can reach 7.8 seconds instead of hiding it. I approve. $255 down to 23. Applied only because I said so. That's my call, not it's. I accept 30-day retention and now it can work. It found the tradeoff, I made the judgment, it did the rest. An agent reading the same board I am, proposing real changes with real numbers behind them, and knowing exactly where to stop and ask.

title: ScanWebMCP.com
pitch: See what AI agents can read, answer and call. Then let them act on the evidence.
about_excerpt: See what AI agents can read, answer and call. Then let them act on the evidence. Like Comment Story Updates ScanWebMCP.com Inspiration The web is being rebuilt for AI agents, but most teams still cannot answer a basic question: What can an agent actually do with our website today? A manifest can claim that an integration exists. A script can mention WebMCP. An endpoint can return HTTP 200. None of those facts proves that an agent can discover a useful capability, understand its contract and invoke it safely. WebMCP makes websites callable. A callable web needs observability. We built ScanWebMCP.com to provide that missing layer: a public, evidence-backed scanner that shows what agents can read, answer and call across a website. The recursive idea is deliberate—ScanWebMCP uses WebMCP to make the emerging WebMCP ecosystem visible, testable and easier to improve. What it does Enter any public URL and ScanWebMCP runs a bounded scan across the site's agent-facing surface. It checks: crawler and robots access; server-rendered content and semantic structure; llms.txt , Markdown and structured data; OpenAPI and other documented API surfaces; live MCP protocol handshakes and returned tools; browser-registered WebMCP tools across relevant page contexts; and whether the available capabilities are readable, useful and safe for an agent to call. Every completed scan is placed on the Agent Surface Ladder : Invisible → Readable → Answerable → Callable → Transactable The result is not a decorative badge. It includes five dimension scores, the rubric version, source URLs, observation times, bounded evidence, a page-aware WebMCP inventory and ranked implementation opportunities. The product already includes a live Observatory containing 511 public websites and 523 completed scans . It shows how agent readiness varies by sector while keeping the underlying method visible and versioned. ScanWebMCP itself is available through several complementary interfaces: a human-facing website and public result pages; a REST API with a live OpenAPI 3.1 contract; a four-tool product MCP server; a separate two-tool documentation MCP server; nine browser WebMCP tools; a published Agent Skill and Codex plugin bundle; ARD, MCP and RFC 9727 discovery documents; and stable Markdown and llms.txt representations. The durable product is the scanner and its evidence. The additional discovery formats make that same working product easier for different agents to find and use without guessing URLs. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP is both the subject of the scan and the interface through which people use the result. Without WebMCP, an assistant must scrape the visible interface, infer the meaning of score cards and locate evidence through page structure. With WebMCP, the page exposes the exact actions an assistant needs, with bounded schemas, descriptions and safety annotations. Three tools are available across the site: scan_agent_surface get_ladder_definition email_report A scan result page adds six context-aware tools: get_scan_findings get_recommended_tools get_webmcp_inventory get_evidence explain_opportunity rescan This is a non-trivial WebMCP implementation, not a single demo button. Tool availability changes with page context. Read-only tools return structured evidence from the page the person is viewing. Evidence and inventory calls enforce the report-access boundary. A re-scan is marked as consequential. Email delivery requires an address directly supplied by the human, while marketing updates remain a separate confirmed opt-in. The agent can also update the shared visual state. When it opens a finding or opportunity, the human sees the same page move to the relevant evidence. The agent receives structured data while the person retains context and control. A better human-agent experience The user does not need to learn the report layout, inspect browser internals or translate scanner output into prompts. They can simply ask: Scan scanwebmcp.com and email the report to me. The assistant selects the correct tools in sequence. It runs the scan, asks for an address if one was not supplied, respects the report gate, and delivers the signed report. It does not guess an email address or silently opt the user into marketing. On the result page, the person can continue: What did the scan find? Show me the evidence behind the weakest signal and explain the best opportunity. The assistant reads the existing result rather than starting a duplicate scan, retrieves bounded evidence, opens the relevant section and explains the recommendation in the context of the site already on screen. After deploying a fix, the person can say: We changed the site. Re-run the scan. The consequential rescan tool refreshes the shared result. What previously required developer tools, manual navigation, separate scanner output and human follow-up becomes one coherent human-agent session. How we built it ScanWebMCP is a Next.js 16 and TypeScript application deployed on Vercel, with Supabase Postgres for scans, evidence, browser context and invocation outcomes. The scanning pipeline is deliberately bounded and evidence-first: It validates and pins public-network targets to defend against SSRF and DNS rebinding. It honours the target's robots.txt policy and discovers no more than six relevant same-origin pages. It inspects server-rendered content, crawler directives, structured data and machine-readable documents. It validates MCP endpoints through the real initialize and tools/list lifecycle rather than trusting a URL or status code. It launches a WebMCP-capable browser witness and observes the live registry across relevant page contexts. It normalizes tool schemas and annotations, preserving the first page on which each tool appeared. It stores the evidence and calculates a versioned Agent Surface Ladder result. The website feature-detects document.modelContext and registers tools with bounded input schemas, explicit descriptions and standards-aligned annotations. External website evidence is marked as untrusted content. Invocation telemetry distinguishes successful, refused and errored outcomes instead of treating a safe refusal as success. The same core service powers the website, REST API, MCP servers and WebMCP tools. That keeps behavior consistent across interfaces and prevents the browser demo from becoming a disconnected proof of concept. The repository contains a 12-scenario WebMCP agent eval pack covering tool selection, parameter mapping, multi-tool ordering, consent, page-aware inventory use, mid-chain recovery and the complete scan-to-email journey. The final branch passes 127 automated tests , TypeScript checking and a production build. Challenges we ran into The hardest engineering problem was observing a browser-only, page-dependent protocol from a serverless scanner. WebMCP tools can appear only after navigation. A homepage, product page and cart can expose different registries. Browser implementations can return schemas in different object or serialized shapes. Most importantly, a failed browser witness must never be reported as "zero tools." We built an adaptive multi-context probe, normalized runtime and Chrome DevTools Protocol descriptors, retried bounded renderer failures and preserved the distinction between unavailable and verified absent . The second challenge was agent UX and safety. Tool outputs must be useful without becoming unbounded data dumps. External page evidence may contain prompt injection and must remain explicitly untrusted. Consequential actions need clear ordering and human control. We solved this with bounded schemas and outputs, read-only and consequential annotations, semantic invocation outcomes, a report-access gate, separate transactional and marketing consent, signed report links and deterministic evaluation scenarios for complete journeys. Accomplishments we are proud of Built and deployed a complete product during the challenge window; the public repository was created on 29 August 2026. Created a scanner whose own human interface is also a nine-tool WebMCP surface. Grew a live public Observatory to 511 websites and 523 completed scans. Verified live WebMCP registrations across page contexts instead of counting declarations or scripts. Preserved tool names, descriptions, schemas, annotations, classifications, page context and timestamped evidence. Built both product and documentation MCP servers around the same core service. Published OpenAPI, ARD, RFC 9727, MCP and Agent Skill discovery surfaces without making any of them substitutes for real behavior. Completed a genuine agent-driven scan-to-email journey with explicit consent and a signed report link. Added 12 agent-level evaluation scenarios and 127 automated tests. Published the full implementation under an AGPL-3.0 license in a repository whose default branch contains complete setup, architecture, safety and verification documentation. What we learned WebMCP presence is not WebMCP readiness. A use

title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. about_excerpt: WATCH//FLOOR is an analyst-first security operations workbench where a connected agent investigates through bounded WebMCP tools while the human retains every consequential decision. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I’m a security practitioner, and I keep seeing investigations reduced to an LLM summary. The summary helps, but it can leave the analyst a step away from the evidence. Meanwhile, people are building personal agent setups with their own models, memory, skills, and runbooks. I wanted a workbench where you could bring that agent into the case without giving it the final say. What it does WATCH//FLOOR is a visual WebMCP workbench for escalated cases. The agent runs approved skills, shows the exact KQL and raw records, and adds evidence to a live graph as it works. It can investigate, model impact, and prepare a response. Evidence sufficiency, restricted telemetry, response approval, and case closure stay with the analyst. How we built it I registered page tools with document.modelContext.registerTool and tied them to the current case and revision. Fixed KQL contracts stop the agent from quietly widening a query. The app is TypeScript and React on Cloudflare Workers with D1. It uses synthetic data and records response actions instead of contacting real systems. I used Codex to build and test it in a couple of days. Challenges we ran into The hard part was deciding what the agent should do and what must remain human. I also had to keep a growing graph readable and make real WebMCP activity easy to follow in a three-minute video. What’s next for WATCH//FLOOR Next I want to connect real SIEM, EDR, identity, and cloud data, add team policy around the gates, and make skill packs portable. Bring your own harness; keep authority with the analyst.
