title: TinyPilot WebMCP
pitch: An AI agent controls a remote physical computer through TinyPilot, without installing agent software on the controlled machine.
about_excerpt: An AI agent controls a remote physical computer through TinyPilot, without installing agent software on the controlled machine. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Remote support often becomes a conversation between someone who can see a problem and an expert explaining which keys to press. TinyPilot already brings a remote computer's display, keyboard, and mouse into a browser. We extended that shared console so an AI agent can take precise, inspectable actions while the person watches and can intervene at any time. What it does TinyPilot WebMCP exposes the dashboard's major operations as 75 browser-native tools. They cover console status and screenshots, keyboard and mouse input, display and video controls, diagnostics, networking, security, updates, power, and installed TinyPilot Pro capabilities. The tools register when the normal dashboard loads and are discovered by the WebMCP host. The demo video proves the integration against a physical TinyPilot Pro appliance and connected computer. Given a goal such as navigating Wikipedia from Common sunflower to Family Matters, the agent observes the same display as the person, sends its navigation through TinyPilot's WebMCP controls, and reaches the requested page on the attached computer. About the live demo The hosted demo uses an isolated simulated desktop so every judge can safely test the WebMCP tools without sharing access to one physical machine. In real use, the same integration runs on a TinyPilot device connected to the target computer through video and USB. The demo video shows the integration operating through physical TinyPilot hardware. Why WebMCP matters TinyPilot connects to the target's physical video output and USB input, so the target only needs to accept a monitor, keyboard, and mouse. It does not need a custom agent, browser extension, or remote-control service. This makes agentic computer use possible for operating-system installers, recovery consoles, locked-down devices, legacy systems, and remote servers where target-side software is difficult or impossible to install. The relevant context already exists in the TinyPilot page: the target computer's current display, the operator's authenticated session, and the controls the person is using. WebMCP exposes those capabilities at the moment they are useful. The person and agent share one dashboard and see the same outcome. How we built it The top-level dashboard registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a JSON schema and runtime validation. Execution reuses TinyPilot's existing authenticated frontend actions and backend interfaces, supports cancellation where applicable, and returns structured results. Sensitive values are write-only and omitted from adapter logs. Optional Pro adapters discover installed controllers at runtime without redistributing TinyPilot's licensed implementation. The repository includes the implementation, 84 JavaScript tests, the full capability map, a restricted-container demo, deployment and rollback tooling, and the upstream MIT license. The physical install was verified by exact source hashes, active service checks, native browser discovery, and a safe live status call. Challenges and what we learned The hardest part was preserving TinyPilot's existing security and interaction model while exposing a broad control surface. We mapped each dashboard capability to a typed tool, validated inputs again at execution time, made optional Pro features discoverable only when installed, and kept secrets out of results and logs. We also learned that WebMCP fits remote KVM especially well: the browser already contains the correct authenticated context and the human remains in the loop through the same live console. What is new TinyPilot Community is the open-source foundation, with its existing authorship and license retained. The challenge branch begins at upstream commit 5f34d8a66d05fb8ca3625e7458915e55cfb7fac7 and contains the WebMCP integration plus the public demo, tests, documentation, and deployment tooling. title: Tokuchu
pitch: Customize gifts for event attendees en masse using WebMCP + agents
about_excerpt: Customize gifts for event attendees en masse using WebMCP + agents Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Six years ago, I cofounded a cafe where much of our revenue has come from bulk orders for events. Event organizers often request customizations, from dietary restrictions to names printed on party favours. But the specifications for these customizations can be difficult to collect. Organizers may not yet know exactly who is attending, what each guest needs, or which details a vendor requires. That uncertainty creates a lot of manual back and forth. An intermediate source of truth gives agents somewhere to coordinate this information. I built Tokuchu to explore how WebMCP could connect an event’s attendee information with the requirements of a personalized purchase. What it does Tokuchu is a WebMCP-native application that helps your agent manage event participants and their needs. Its sister website, Customworks, is a Shopify storefront with WebMCP tools for configuring personalized merchandise and preparing a checkout. An organizer can ask ChatGPT’s browser to create an event and add attendees, then browse Customworks for a suitable gift. The store supplies the product’s customization requirements, which the agent brings back to Tokuchu. Tokuchu reconciles those requirements with attendee information and relevant shared event details. It identifies missing answers and validates the resulting values against the store’s constraints. After approval, the agent can prepare one personalized item per complete attendee, leave incomplete attendees pending, and save the checkout in Tokuchu. The organizer completes payment through Shopify. Tokuchu also supports scoped vendor access to fulfillment information, so a vendor can report an issue without receiving unrelated attendee data. How we built it I built Tokuchu with Next.js and TypeScript, with PostgreSQL persistence and deployment on Render. Its event, attendee, and vendor pages expose WebMCP tools appropriate to each page’s role. On Customworks, I added merchant tools to the Shopify storefront. get_customization returns a product’s required fields, constraints, and variants. add_customized_to_cart accepts the configured items and creates a separate personalized cart line for each included attendee. Tokuchu stores the product contract alongside the event’s records. Its validation and reconciliation logic produces a fulfillment manifest, and approvals reference a specific revision of that information. The main website entry uses ChatGPT’s browser. Tokuchu also has an interface that people and browser agents can manipulate, including an in-app chatbox that invokes its managed workflow. The final demo shows an agent entering prompts into that chatbox. A separate local Stagehand runner provides another way to exercise the cross-site WebMCP flow. Challenges we ran into It took time to configure the WebMCP tools and page instructions so ChatGPT could reliably discover and use them. Testing different scenarios also revealed edge cases that the data model did not yet account for, particularly when attendee information was incomplete or needed to be mapped to a product’s requirements. Working through those cases meant checking both what the agent understood and how Tokuchu recorded the resulting information. Accomplishments that we're proud of I’m proud of building two live websites that work together to turn attendee information into personalized orders. Setting up Customworks also gave me practical experience with agentic e-commerce, including how product customization connects to Shopify’s cart and checkout. The store is configured to support real orders once test mode is turned off. An agent can prepare much of the personalized order through the browser, with the organizer reviewing the checkout before payment. That brings the project closer to the kind of ordering workflow I would want to use at our own cafe. What we learned I learned how much the initial setup of a website matters for agents. The page metadata and instructions directed toward them need to be clear and available when they first arrive, so they can understand what the site offers and how to navigate it. Making those entry points easy to discover can be just as impactful as refining the individual tools. A useful capability becomes much easier to work with when the agent can find it and understand when to use it. What's next for Tokuchu I’d love to continue experimenting with storefronts that provide useful information for agents to process, and explore how their requirements can inform what an event organizer asks attendees. I’d also like to develop an iteration of Tokuchu that helps us process orders at our own cafe, using what I’ve learned here to reduce the back and forth around bulk orders and customizations.  Inspiration 

 I wanted Kujo SSG to generate extremely fast static sites, stay simple to work with, and fit the way software is being built now, with AI agents doing more of the work. 

 That means treating agents as first-class users. 

 The site structure, CLI, machine-readable context, and WebMCP support are all built around making it easier for agents to understand and interact with a site without scraping pages and guessing what everything does. 

 What it does 

 Kujo SSG is a static site generator built as part of the Kujo programming language ecosystem. 

 It turns structured content, templates, components, assets, and configuration into static websites that can be deployed almost anywhere. 

 It also gives those sites an agent-facing layer. 

 Kujo sites can expose functionality through WebMCP, publish llms.txt and other machine-readable context, and give AI clients a cleaner way to interact with a site than browser automation. 

 It can also be extended with things like themes, plugins, commerce, CMS functionality, and AI integrations while still producing static output. 

 How we built it 

 The Kujo SSG follows the same approach as the rest of the ecosystem: small pieces, explicit behavior, strong defaults, and composable tooling. 

 The build pipeline handles content discovery, routing, templates, rendering, assets, and final site generation. 

 Around that, I built support for reusable themes, plugins, site configuration, structured metadata, AI-readable documentation, and WebMCP. 

 WebMCP fit naturally because Kujo was already being built around structured interfaces for agents. 

 Instead of teaching an agent how to click around a website, the site can expose the actions directly. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge was adding capability without losing the simplicity of a static site generator. 

 It is easy to keep adding features until you have basically rebuilt a dynamic framework with a static export step. 

 I wanted plugins, themes, commerce, AI integrations, and WebMCP to work around the static model instead of replacing it. 

 Agent interaction was another challenge. 

 Humans can look at a page and understand what buttons, forms, and navigation are supposed to do. Agents should not have to reverse-engineer that every time, wasting time and tokens on browser use. 

 WebMCP gives us a much cleaner way to expose that functionality directly. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Kujo SSG has grown into more than a basic static site generator. 

 I've used it for real websites, documentation, content-heavy sites, commerce examples, plugin and theme systems, AI integrations, and WebMCP-enabled functionality. 

 It also works as part of the wider Kujo ecosystem instead of being a standalone tool. 

 That gives developers access to things like MCP, RAG, evaluation, observability, context management, specifications, validation, and other agent-focused tooling around the development process. 

 With WebMCP, the final website can now take part in that agent workflow too. 

 What we learned 

 A lot of value in building AI-native software comes from making software easier for agents to understand and operate. 

 Clear contracts are better than guessing, structured data is better than scraping, explicit tools are better than hoping an agent clicks the right thing and deterministic systems become more important as more of the development process becomes probabilistic. 

 Static sites work really well for that. 

 The final output is still just HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and assets, while the tooling around it can be much more capable. 

 What's next for Kujo SSG 

 I want WebMCP support to become a standard part of how Kujo sites expose functionality to agents. 

 That sits alongside llms.txt , MCP integrations, structured site metadata, and the rest of Kujo's agent tooling. 

 I'm also continuing to expand the SSG around commerce, CMS functionality, plugins, themes, reusable site kits, and AI workflows. 

 The goal is to make sites that are easy for humans to use and easy for agents to understand, modify, and interact with. 

 Static where static makes sense. 

 Agent-native where agents make sense.

about_excerpt: An agent can fill the form. You hold the pen. A benefits claim an AI agent can explain and fill through WebMCP tools, where every agent entry is reviewed by you and no tool can submit. Like Comment Story Updates The claim as it loads. Seven WebMCP tools are registered, and the header states who does what. Your own entry stays yours, in green. The agent's entries are marked in amber and wait in the review list. The recorded demonstration runs the same tools. The agent's write is refused because the person answered first. Submit is disabled and says why: six agent entries are still unreviewed. Submitted by the person, with a reference. No tool could have done this. An agent can fill the form. You hold the pen. Hold the Pen is a benefits-style claim form that an AI agent can read, explain, and fill through WebMCP tools, while every value the agent writes stays marked, reviewable, and undoable, and no tool can submit the claim. Submission is deliberately absent from the WebMCP tool contract; review and declaration happen in the page, through controls no tool can reach. Live: https://holdthepen.vercel.app · Repo: https://github.com/nischal94/holdthepen (MIT) Why WebMCP is the right fit Consequential forms (benefits, insurance, immigration) are where people most want help and least want to lose control. Hold the Pen is a benefits-style claim whose question wording models a real UK Universal Credit-style claim (income received vs earned , household definitions, carer thresholds); the programme, rules, and submission are fictional. WebMCP lets the page hand an agent typed tools against the live form the person is looking at, instead of the agent guessing at the DOM. That is what makes a hard line possible: the page decides what an agent can do, and can make "submit" something no tool does. Seven tools are registered once on the document: get_claim_state , explain , review_agent_entries , fill_field , clear_field , navigate_to_section , prepare_submission_review . There is deliberately no commit tool. How it makes the experience better Three layers, three owners. Understand (agent, read-only): explain any question, term, or the consequence of each truthful answer, without recommending one. Fill (agent): write a value that is attributed, revision-checked, and undoable. Decide (person): review every agent entry, tick the declaration, submit. Those controls live in the page; no tool can reach them. Every agent write shows a text badge, "Filled by the agent, not yet reviewed", lands in a persistent review queue with Accept / Correct / Clear, and is announced to screen-reader users by field name, never by value. The submit button stays disabled, and says why, until every agent entry is reviewed and the declaration is ticked. Any edit after the agent stages a review invalidates it. The page works with no agent at all, and a recorded demonstration shows the flow for browsers without WebMCP. What a person and an agent can now do together Before: an agent helping with a form either typed into fields with no trace of what it changed, or stopped at "you should fill this in yourself". Now: the person asks "explain the income question before I answer it" and gets the meaning; says "fill in the household section" and watches three fields fill with a visible mark and a queue count of 3; asks "get it ready for me to check" and the agent names the four missing required fields in form order and cannot go further. The page protects the person in two ways: while they are editing a field, an agent write is refused with CONFLICT_FOCUSED ; once they have answered it, the agent cannot replace it and gets CONFLICT_HUMAN_VALUE . The recorded demonstration shows the second case. The agent prepares; the person approves. Verified end to end in the ChatGPT desktop browser on the deployed site. How WebMCP was implemented Imperative API only ( document.modelContext.registerTool ), because the ChatGPT browser does not support the declarative form API or iframe tools. Registration happens exactly once per page through a manager that reports a rejected registration as a visible degraded state and never unregisters (re-registering a changed schema is a race in the draft spec). Tools read a framework-independent store at call time via getSnapshot() ; React subscribes through useSyncExternalStore . A callback closing over React state would read the state at mount forever; a regression test writes, dispatches N times, then reads through the tool. Every failure returns the same envelope ( code , problem , cause , fix , retryable ) so the agent self-corrects. Strict validation in code, loose in schema. Outputs capped at 1.5K characters. Read-only tools carry readOnlyHint ; tools that echo user text carry untrustedContentHint . AbortSignal is honoured, and both toolcancel and toolcanceled spellings are handled. 83 automated tests, including a typed fake of document.modelContext that enforces the browser contracts (duplicate names rejected, JSON-string arguments, cancellation events), axe in component tests, and eval fixtures in Chrome's expectedCall format for direct, ambiguous, and mid-chain prompts. Honest limit, stated in the README: the page cannot tell a human click from an automated one. A trustworthy human-only approval boundary is a platform primitive WebMCP does not yet have (spec issues #165 and #277); prepare_submission_review is a stand-in for elicitation, not elicitation.  ✈️ FlightClaims — Instant Statutory Flight Compensation 

 💡 Inspiration 

 When a flight is delayed, cancelled, or overbooked, most passengers don't know what to do. 

 They may not know: 

 
 Whether they can get a refund 
 Whether they can receive compensation 
 Whether the airline should provide meals or accommodation 
 How to contact the airline 
 How to write a proper complaint or claim 
 

 Passenger rights are often written in complicated regulations and spread across different websites. 

 FlightClaims makes this process simpler. 

 A passenger enters their flight details, tells us what happened, and FlightClaims helps them understand their possible options and prepare a professional request to the airline. 

 

 🛠️ What It Does 

 FlightClaims helps passengers in three simple steps : 

 1️⃣ Enter Your Flight Details 

 Enter your: 

 
 Airline 
 Flight number 
 Origin and destination 
 Flight date 
 What happened 
 

 The user can select: 

 
 ✈️ Flight delayed 
 ❌ Flight cancelled 
 🚫 Denied boarding 
 

 The app can also support uploading a boarding pass or ticket to extract flight details automatically. 

 

 2️⃣ Understand Your Possible Rights 

 FlightClaims: 

 
 Identifies the flight route 
 Calculates the route distance 
 Detects the relevant passenger-rights framework 
 Analyzes the disruption details 
 Shows possible passenger options 
 Estimates potential compensation when enough information is available 
 

 The app supports passenger-rights frameworks such as: 

 
 🇮🇳 India — DGCA 
 🇪🇺 Europe — EU261 
 🇬🇧 United Kingdom — UK261 
 

 
 Note: Results are presented as guidance or estimates and are not guaranteed compensation. 
 

 

 3️⃣ Prepare Your Airline Request 

 FlightClaims generates a professional request based on the passenger's case. 

 The passenger can: 

 
 Review the request 
 Edit the request 
 Approve the request 
 

 Then they can copy and send it through the appropriate airline channel. 

 

 🤖 How WebMCP Is Used 

 FlightClaims demonstrates how WebMCP allows AI agents to interact with a live web application . 

 Normally, an AI assistant may need to guess what information is currently available on a website. 

 With WebMCP, FlightClaims exposes structured tools that allow an AI agent to safely interact with the real application. 

 Example Tools 

 query_disruption_rights 

 Allows an AI agent to analyze the current flight case and its possible passenger options. 

 prepare_passenger_request 

 Allows an AI agent to prepare a passenger request using the flight details currently available in the application. 

 The important part: The AI works with the application's actual live state , not fake or hardcoded data. 

 

 📐 How It Works 

 FlightClaims uses airport coordinates to calculate the approximate distance between airports using the Haversine formula . 

 This helps the application analyze routes where distance is relevant to the passenger-rights framework.

title: StyleMate
pitch: Your AI personal stylist that understands your style, searches the web, compares products, and builds your outfit using WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
Your AI personal stylist that understands your style, searches the web, compares products, and builds your outfit using WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Have you ever spent 30 minutes shopping online just to find one good outfit? 

 I do. 

 Sometimes I even ask ChatGPT, "Does this shirt look good on me?" After using AI so much, it probably knows more about my style than my girlfriend does. 

 Sad, but true. 😄 

 That made me think: 

 If AI already understands me, why am I still doing all the searching myself? 

 That's how StyleMate started. 

 We wanted to build a shopping experience where you don't have to think like a search engine. You can simply tell the agent what you're looking for, and it can understand your preferences, find the right products, and help you build your outfit. 

 What it does 

 StyleMate is an AI-powered personal stylist built for fashion shopping. 

 Instead of searching through hundreds of products and manually applying filters, you can simply give StyleMate a natural-language request. 

 For example: 

 
 "I'm 5'7", I need a formal outfit for office — a shirt, trousers and shoes. My shirt size is 40, trouser waist is 32, shoe size is 9, and my budget is around ₹10,000." 
 

 StyleMate can understand the request along with the user's existing style profile. 

 It can then: 

 
 Understand the user's style preferences 
 Find personalized recommendations 
 Search the product catalog 
 Compare products 
 Check size and inventory availability 
 Build a complete outfit 
 Add selected products to the cart 
 

 The interesting part is that the AI doesn't just recommend products. 

 It can actually interact with the website through WebMCP. 

 How we built it 

 Our main idea was: 

 One brain, two front doors. 

 A user can interact with StyleMate through the normal website UI, while an AI agent can interact with the same application through WebMCP. 

 Both use the same underlying product and business logic. 

 For the agent experience, we exposed purpose-built WebMCP tools: 

 
 getUserStyleProfile — read the user's style preferences 
 getRecommendations — find suitable products 
 searchProducts — search the product catalog 
 compareProducts — compare product options 
 checkInventory — verify availability 
 addToCart — add selected products to the cart 
 

 We also use browser page controls to update the visible website, show products, display confirmation dialogs, navigate to the cart, and keep the user involved in the process. 

 The flow is simple: 

 User intent → AI reasoning → WebMCP tools → Website interaction → Human confirmation → Cart 

 We built the application using modern web technologies including Next.js, React, TypeScript, and WebMCP. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was not simply connecting an AI agent to a website. 

 We wanted the agent to interact with the actual application in a reliable and structured way. 

 We had to think carefully about: 

 
 Designing useful WebMCP tools instead of exposing generic actions 
 Keeping the agent and human UI connected to the same business logic 
 Making product search and recommendations work with natural-language requests 
 Handling size and inventory checks 
 Keeping important actions under human control 
 Making the website visually respond to agent actions 
 

 We also had to think about the difference between what an agent can do and what an agent should be allowed to do . 

 For example, searching and comparing products are safe actions, while adding something to a cart or placing an order requires more user involvement. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The biggest accomplishment is that StyleMate is not just an AI chatbot placed on top of an ecommerce website. 

 The website itself is agent-operable. 

 An agent can discover StyleMate's capabilities through WebMCP and use those capabilities to perform real shopping tasks. 

 We can start with a simple sentence like: 

 
 "Find me a formal office outfit under ₹10,000." 
 

 And turn that into a complete interaction: 

 Understand my style → Search products → Compare options → Check availability → Show me the choices → Get confirmation → Add to cart 

 We are also proud of keeping the architecture simple. 

 One brain, two front doors. 

 The human experience and the agent experience are powered by the same underlying application logic. 

 What we learned 

 We started this project thinking about AI recommendations. 

 We ended up thinking much more about agent-friendly websites . 

 Traditional ecommerce is built around the question: 

 "What product are you searching for?" 

 But people usually think in terms of intent: 

 "I have an office event tomorrow. What should I wear?" 

 That's where we see the potential of WebMCP. 

 Instead of an AI simply telling you what to click, the website can expose structured capabilities that an agent can actually use. 

 We also learned that giving an agent more control doesn't mean removing the human. 

 The best experience is: 

 AI does the searching and decision support.
Human makes the important decisions. 

 What's next for StyleMate 

 Today, StyleMate focuses on fashion discovery and shopping. 

 But the idea can go much further. 

 We want StyleMate to understand how a person's style changes over time and become a long-term personal stylist rather than a one-time shopping assistant. 

 Future possibilities include: 

 
 Smarter personal style profiles 
 Outfit planning for specific events 
 Wardrobe-aware recommendations 
 More brands and product categories 
 Better fit and size intelligence 
 Wishlist and purchase-history intelligence 
 Personalized seasonal collections 
 Agent-driven shopping across multiple stores 
 

 The bigger vision is simple: 

 Don't search. Be understood.

 Inspiration 

 Small agencies often lose money when extra client requests are completed without clear approval. We built ScopeDelta to keep scope, decisions, and delivery connected. 

 What it does 

 ScopeDelta helps teams identify work outside the agreed scope. An AI agent can organize the process, while people approve important commercial and client decisions. 

 How we built it 

 We built ScopeDelta with Next.js, React, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, and WebMCP. WebMCP lets AI agents use the product through structured tools inside the browser. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Our biggest challenge was balancing automation with human control. We also had to work around browser tool limits and protect private client information. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We created a complete workflow connecting client requests, scope changes, human approval, delivery, and client acceptance. Important actions always require confirmation. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that agents work best when their tools are simple and focused. We also learned that some decisions—especially those involving money—should always stay with people.

title: Tour Booking WebMCP Adapter
pitch: Use LLM-powered WebMCP agents to discover and prepare tours directly with local operators—cutting out marketplace middlemen while keeping payment human-controlled.
about_excerpt: Use LLM-powered WebMCP agents to discover and prepare tours directly with local operators—cutting out marketplace middlemen while keeping payment human-controlled. Like Comment Story Updates Booking Interface Codex with WebMCP Inspiration Tour bookings are often controlled by large marketplaces that sit between travelers and local operators. These intermediaries can add commissions, weaken the direct customer relationship, and make small operators dependent on centralized platforms. Our inspiration was to use WebMCP to create a more direct model. A traveler can ask an LLM what they want in natural language, and the agent can interact directly with tools published by the tour operator's own website—without scraping the page or routing the customer through a marketplace. The agent automates repetitive steps such as discovering tours, comparing departures, checking current capacity, and preparing the visible cart. The operator retains ownership of its inventory, brand, and customer relationship, while the traveler remains in control of checkout, payment, and final confirmation. What it does Tours Booking WebMCP lets an AI agent work with the same inventory and cart that the traveler sees. It exposes four WebMCP tools: search_departures searches the page's current inventory snapshot. get_departure refreshes and re-checks the capacity, price, and transfer options for a specific departure. prepare_booking validates a complete selection against refreshed capacity and atomically replaces the visible cart. get_booking_summary reports the cart contents, total price, estimated authorization amount, editability, and recommended next action. An agent can help travelers discover suitable tours, verify that enough spaces remain, and prepare a cart for review. It cannot collect contact or billing details, handle cards, authorize payment, reserve inventory, or confirm a booking. Those actions remain human-controlled in the visible booking experience. The normal interface continues to work when WebMCP is unavailable, making the integration a progressive enhancement. How we built it We built a framework-independent TypeScript adapter around WebMCP's imperative document.modelContext.registerTool() API. The host booking page supplies normalized inventory and cart-state callbacks. The adapter owns the tool descriptions, strict JSON schemas, matching runtime validation, freshness rules, response formatting, cancellation, lifecycle cleanup, and safe cart-preparation protocol. For an exact departure check or cart preparation, the adapter asks the host to refresh inventory instead of presenting cached data as current. prepare_booking validates the complete replacement cart, checks the page state before and after the asynchronous refresh, and performs exactly one atomic commit. If validation or a state check fails, the existing cart remains unchanged. Inventory-derived results are marked as untrusted content. Read-only tools are annotated accordingly, while the cart-mutating tool is explicitly identified as non-read-only. The repository also includes a backend-free Vite demo with deterministic in-memory inventory, a fake document.modelContext test harness, documentation, and agent-evaluation scenarios. Challenges we ran into One challenge was designing around an experimental browser API whose availability and behavior may change. The application still needed to remain usable in browsers without WebMCP. Freshness was another major challenge. Availability can change between an agent's search and its attempt to prepare a cart, so saved inventory cannot be presented as current. We added explicit freshness metadata, forced refreshes for exact checks, and capacity validation immediately before committing cart state. Asynchronous refreshes also introduced race conditions. Checkout could begin, another browser tab could become active, or an invocation could be cancelled while capacity was being refreshed. We addressed these cases with before-and-after state checks, serialized preparation, abort-signal propagation, and an atomic commit boundary. Finally, we wanted useful agent capabilities without quietly turning a cart tool into a payment or reservation tool. Identity, billing, cards, payments, reservations, and confirmations therefore remain completely outside the tool contracts. Accomplishments that we're proud of Built a coherent four-tool WebMCP experience rather than a single demonstration call. Connected agent actions to the same visible cart controlled by the traveler. Implemented fresh-capacity validation and all-or-nothing cart preparation. Preserved a strict human boundary around personal data, payment, reservation, and confirmation. Added 21 deterministic tests covering schemas, freshness, time zones, capacity, atomicity, concurrency, cancellation, lifecycle cleanup, and safety boundaries. Defined nine agent-evaluation scenarios covering tool selection, argument accuracy, ambiguity, unavailable data, and unsafe payment requests. Kept search responses within a compact 1,536-byte target. Created an independently runnable demo requiring no credentials, customer data, private API, or payment provider. Passed the complete formatting, testing, TypeScript build, demo build, and package-verification pipeline. What we learned We learned that designing WebMCP tools is as much a product and security exercise as it is an API exercise. Tool names, descriptions, schemas, annotations, and results collectively shape how reliably an agent behaves. We also learned that freshness must be represented explicitly. "Available" is not meaningful unless the agent and traveler know whether the information came from a current refresh or a saved snapshot. Most importantly, we learned that useful agent assistance does not require handing over the entire user journey. Agents can reduce discovery and coordination work while preserving meaningful human control over sensitive and consequential actions. What's next for Tours Booking WebMCP Next, we plan to: Deploy the demo with the browser headers and origin-trial configuration required by the active WebMCP implementation. Connect the adapter to normalized production inventory through the existing host callbacks without exposing private booking endpoints. Run the evaluation suite across additional WebMCP-capable agents and browsers. Add more inventory scenarios, accessibility testing, and localized user-facing explanations. Continue refining consent and review UX while keeping payment and confirmation human-controlled. title: LATCH — revocable authority, one object at a time
pitch: LATCH gives people revocable, object-by-object control over agent writes through WebMCP: hold one sensitive object while work continues elsewhere.
about_excerpt: LATCH gives people revocable, object-by-object control over agent writes through WebMCP: hold one sensitive object while work continues elsewhere. Like Comment Story Updates Human-held term keeps LATCH negotiations under control. WebMCP tools registered by LATCH in Chrome DevTools. LATCH pairs agent tools with human control over terms. LATCH: revocable, per-object agent authority - HOLD one deal term while the rest stay writable through WebMCP. Inspiration Every agent client I use has a switch, not a latch. The controls are set before the run: ask me before every write, or let it go. When one decision worries me mid-task, my only move is to stop everything — and lose the ten good edits the agent was about to make. That is not collaboration; it is excessive agency. A house has many doors. When one of them worries you, you do not weld the building shut. You throw a latch on that door and leave the rest of the house open. That is the whole idea of LATCH. The idea Revocable authority, one object at a time. The agent may act on every open object. The human can, at any moment, take one object out of its hands — and only that one. Everything not latched stays open, so the agent keeps working instead of waiting for approval on every small step. Three human moves cover it: HOLD protects one object, Object rejects or cuts one object, and Lock freezes the whole board once. Unlike per-step approvals, a latch does not stop the agent. Unlike after-the-fact review, it is set before the next write. A refusal tells the agent that the object is held and points it to the release path; it must ask, not override. This is not a contract feature. Six cards on a board could be six files in a repo, six keys in a config, six hunks in a PR, or six lines in a budget. The deal is only the sample data, because everyone understands: “tighten the deal, but don't touch Indemnity.” Why WebMCP A latch needs a structured channel through which the page can tell the agent: this object is off-limits, here is why, here is how to ask . WebMCP is that channel. The page registers tools; each tool's execute checks current authority before it writes and can refuse with a reason. A release asks the human, and a high-risk write requires an on-page confirmation. The pattern does not have to wait for agent clients to add a new global permission system. A page can ship it today: the human watches the same live state on which the agent acts, with no chat transcript acting as the permission boundary. What people and agents do together LATCH is a reference board with seven WebMCP tools. An agent can read the board, inspect one object, propose and apply structured changes, ask to release a held object, load a fixture, and request a final commit. The human can add a binding note, HOLD one object, Object to it or cut it, confirm high-risk writes, reject a release request, or refuse to lock. What neither side gets from a normal agent workflow: a DOM-only state is not a reliable, structured authority boundary for an agent, and a human cannot keep up with an agent that rewrites six objects at once. With a latch, one sensitive decision stays with the person while the rest of the work keeps moving. It is for anyone who lets an agent write on their behalf — the person negotiating a contract today, the developer running Codex tomorrow. Scenario A opens with six writable objects. apply_card_change rewrites one without the agent touching the UI. Hold this latches one; the other five stay writable. A write against the held object returns isError: true with a reason; its text does not change. request_release asks the human; only an on-page Confirm lifts HOLD. commit_deal is a separate final freeze; Not now keeps the board live. A / B / C are authority fixtures — all open, one held, one cut. List, Side by side, and One at a time are three attention modes over the same state, not three products. How I built it Vite, React, and TypeScript; static assets on a Cloudflare Worker. Source: github.com/MyTelexGlobal/latch (MIT). The page late-binds document.modelContext or navigator.modelContext and registers seven tools once. Reads use readOnlyHint ; agent-proposed content is marked untrusted. HOLD is a human control, not an agent tool. Tools stay registered while execute enforces current authority, so the agent's tool list never flickers and every refusal remains actionable: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "apply_card_change", description: "Replace one card. Fails if that card is on HOLD or cut.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { card_id: { type: "string" }, text: { type: "string" } }, required: ["card_id", "text"], additionalProperties: false, }, execute: async ({ card_id, text }, extra) => { const card = boardRef.current.cards.find((c) => c.id === card_id); if (card?.held) { return { content: [{ type: "text", text: "on HOLD" }], isError: true }; } // Confirm high-risk writes on the page, then replace card.text. }, }); High-risk writes, release requests, and the final commit go through an on-page confirmation. Where the client exposes requestUserInteraction , LATCH uses it to signal that a human decision is needed. Cancellation is handled without partially applying a write. Possible future LATCH is an authority layer for agentic work. A person can place a reversible HOLD on one sensitive object—code, a record, a contract clause, or a budget line—while the agent continues working on everything still open. The live deal board is the first working WebMCP expression of that pattern: one visible object, one precise human boundary, and no need to stop the rest of the agent’s work. Challenges Four things must agree at every moment: the board, the agent's tool results, the per-object HOLD control, and the confirmation dialog. Keeping tools registered — rather than unregistering them on HOLD — was the key trade-off: a stable tool list plus a refusal with a reason gives the agent a safe next step instead of making the capability disappear. Where this goes: the same latch in Codex Picture the board as a repository: HOLD auth/ while the agent refactors the rest: a guarded write path refuses auth/* with a reason and allows work to continue elsewhere. Object with a note — “keep the public API stable” — that the agent must follow for that object. request_release becomes a one-line question to the developer, not a stalled session. Lock is the merge: a separate final freeze. The developer keeps ownership of architecture, security boundaries, and product intent; the agent keeps its speed on everything that remains open. The primitives are the ones LATCH already runs over WebMCP: a refusal with a reason, a release that asks, and a confirmation that stays with the person. The board is the smallest thing that proves the interaction works; a Codex integration is a future application, not a claim about the current client. LATCH is an independent WebMCP project and is not affiliated with latch.tools. Live: https://beeeeen.github.io/blindfold/ · Source: https://github.com/Beeeeen/blindfold The four things the rules ask the description to explain Answered directly, before the narrative sections below. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Because the guarantee depends on where the code runs . A server-side MCP would have to hold the data in order to analyse it — the privacy claim would be a promise about someone's backend. In-page, the rows sit in memory the agent has no way to address, while the agent still directs the whole analysis. Take WebMCP away and this project does not degrade into a worse version of itself. It stops existing. How it creates a better user experience You can point an agent at a 99 MB spreadsheet and have an answer in seconds, without either of the two things that normally stop you: the context window and the upload. When the guard refuses, the refusal arrives with a legal alternative — "use p25, median or p75" — so the agent corrects itself on the next turn instead of dead-ending. And the page keeps a receipt: every byte that crossed to the agent, verbatim, searchable, exportable. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Three things, in increasing order of how much WebMCP is doing: Analyse a file larger than any context window, without sampling. A million rows is ~26 million tokens. The agent answers questions about all of it because it never reads any of it. Delegate authority over data you are not willing to disclose. You can now hand an agent the controls to a payroll file while it stays structurally unable to read a row. Delegation and disclosure used to be the same act. Have an agent show you something it never saw itself. render_chart takes aggregates and a shape, draws on the human's screen, and returns one sentence saying it is up and that nothing came back with it. The person gets the picture; the model gets zero bytes of data. A server-side agent cannot show you anything without first holding it. How we implemented WebMCP document.modelContext.registerTool() (with a navigator.modelContext fallback for hosts still on the pre-150 Chromium location), eight tools, no SQL. The parts that took real work: Re-registered per dataset , so tool descriptions name that file's actual columns and tiers rather than describing a generic shape. Withdrawal by AbortSignal . Chrome 152 ships no unregisterTool , so aborting the previous batch is the only way to replace a toolset without colliding with names already registered. Refusals as return values, not exceptions , each carrying a reason and a legal alternative. A write tool that returns nothing. render_chart mutates the page and discloses zero bytes. Inspiration Every real dataset hits two walls at once, and they are usually treated as separate problems. The first is size. A 99 MB spreadsheet is roughly 26 million tokens. No model reads that, so people paste a sample and get an answer about the sample. The second is disclosure. Uploading the whole file to answer one question means handing over every name and salary in it, which is why most organisations ban it outright. The realisation that started this project is that both walls have the same door. If the agent never reads the rows, the file can be any size and nothing has to be disclosed — those stop being two features and become one consequence of the same design. WebMCP is what makes it reachable: the tool executes inside the page, so the data can sit in memory the agent has no way to address while the agent still directs the work. That is not a convenience. It is a different trust model, and it only became available when tools started running in the browser. What it does Blindfold is a data workbench you drop a spreadsheet into. It reads the file into DuckDB-WASM inside your tab — no server, no upload — and exposes eight WebMCP tools to whatever agent is attached. The agent can compute almost anything: aggregates, distributions, correlations, cohort comparisons with effect sizes. It can draw charts on your screen. What it cannot do is see a row. The page revokes its own network access. A counter reading zero is the page marking its own homework, so once the engine boots Blindfold injects a CSP taking away its own ability to reach the network — connect-src 'none' , form-action 'none' , img-src data: . From then on the browser refuses fetch, XHR, WebSocket, sendBeacon and tracking pixels. There is a button that attempts all five so you can watch them fail, and you can read the policy out of document.head yourself. There is no SQL tool. Deliberately. Free-form SQL can't be proven non-disclosive without a parser and a lot of hope. The agent fills in narrow structured specs and the page compiles them to queries it controls. A leak should be impossible to express , not merely refused afterwards. Columns are graded before the agent hears about them. Direct identifiers ( full_name , email , employee_id ) are sealed : not groupable, not filterable, never returned. Personal measurements ( base_salary ) are aggregate-only. Every grade is one click to override, and changing one re-registers the entire toolset with new descriptions. k-anonymity, enforced. Any group covering fewer than five people is suppressed before it becomes a return value. compare_groups is stricter: both cohorts must independently clear k, because a "gap" computed over two people is just those two salaries with extra steps. Refusals teach. min / max on a salary is blocked — a maximum is one real person's pay — and the refusal tells the agent to use p25/median/p75 instead, so it recovers on the next turn rather than giving up. A ledger, on screen. Bytes into the page versus bytes released to the agent, values spent against a disclosure budget, calls refused, groups suppressed. A transcript, not a summary. Every call is stored with the exact text that went back, character for character. Search it for a name and there is none. Measured on a million rows — 99 MB, about 26 million tokens of text: Read and classified 3.2 s Median salary by department 0.07 s Pay gap by level, both cohorts k-checked 0.11 s Salary histogram by level 0.11 s Tenure vs pay, per department 0.04 s Bonus by level × region × department 0.09 s Sent to the agent 27 KB, about 6,800 tokens Raw rows sent to the agent 0 Pushed further on the same machine: 5,000,000 rows (502 MB) answers in 0.42s, and 10,000,000 rows — a full gigabyte, about 264 million tokens — still answers every query in under a second, releasing 7 KB. The disclosure ratio there is 1 : 37,369. One byte reached the agent for every 3,799 that did not, and on the way it found a real seeded result: a gender pay gap of about 3% at IC1–IC3 that widens to 12–14% from IC4 upward. The model never saw a salary. That 27 KB is five questions' worth. Ask fewer and it is a couple of kilobytes; ask a hundred and it climbs, which is exactly why there is a disclosure budget rather than only a per-query check. The number that does not move is the one underneath it: zero rows, at any question count. How we built it Vite, TypeScript, no framework, no backend. DuckDB-WASM is the query engine; Observable Plot draws. Tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool() , with a fallback to navigator.modelContext so the page works in ChatGPT's built-in browser and in Chrome 149+ behind the testing flag. Three WebMCP details did most of the work: Tools are registered per dataset, not once at load. Descriptions name the actual columns and their tiers, so the agent reads what it may ask for instead of discovering it by trial. Loading a second file unregisters the first file's tools. render_chart is a one-way mirror. The agent supplies aggregates and a shape; the chart appears on the human's screen; the return value is a sentence confirming it, carrying zero bytes of data. A server-side agent cannot show a person something without first holding it. This one can — that asymmetry is only available in-page. Refusals are return values, not exceptions. Each carries the reason and a legal alternative, which turns the guard into something the agent can navigate rather than something it fights. T

So watch one analyse it anyway, without ever seeing a single row. Every column is graded before the agent is told the file exists. Name, email, employee ID — sealed. It cannot group by them, filter on them, or ever receive them. The grading is a heuristic — column names and how unique the values are — so sometimes it will be wrong. One click overrules it. title: Day Canvas
pitch: Day Canvas is a visual planner where you and AI shape your day together—adding, moving, and organizing tasks live on one shared canvas.
about_excerpt:
Day Canvas is a visual planner where you and AI shape your day together—adding, moving, and organizing tasks live on one shared canvas.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Day Canvas: Building a Planner Shared with AI 

 What inspired it 

 Day Canvas began with a simple frustration: planning tools and AI assistants often live in separate places. You might describe a change in a chat, then manually reproduce it in a calendar or task list. I wanted to make that handoff disappear. 

 The idea was to create a shared workspace where a person and an AI can plan the same day together. Instead of receiving a text-only confirmation, the user can watch the canvas change as the AI adds, moves, prioritizes, or removes work. The result is a planning experience that feels collaborative, visible, and grounded in the actual schedule. 

 What I built 

 Day Canvas is a visual daily planner with a timed calendar, a task inbox, priority controls, and day/week/month/year views. Users can add blocks, drag them to reschedule, manage unscheduled tasks, and see overlapping events arranged clearly in separate lanes. 

 The defining feature is browser-native WebMCP integration. An AI agent can use tools to inspect the schedule, find open time, add or move calendar events, triage inbox tasks, and delete items. Those tool calls operate on the exact same actions as the user interface, so the canvas stays in sync and changes animate live. AI actions also have their own feedback, including activity toasts, a moving cursor for reschedules, and a deletion animation. 

 How I built it 

 I built the interface with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and a custom client-side store. The planner canvas renders a vertical time grid, while reusable components handle event cards, calendar views, inbox tasks, theme controls, and agent activity. 

 The core architectural decision was a single source of truth for task and calendar mutations. Both drag-and-drop interactions and WebMCP tool handlers call the shared functions in lib/taskActions.ts . This keeps UI actions and AI actions consistent: there is one set of validation rules, one state update path, and one way to announce changes. 

 WebMCP tools are registered in the browser after the app mounts through document.modelContext.registerTool . The AI can therefore reason about the open day using functions such as calendar summary and free-time search, then make a targeted update without a separate MCP server. 

 For scheduling, the free-time logic treats each event as an occupied interval. If an event begins at (s_i) and lasts (d_i) minutes, its occupied range is 

 [
[s_i,\; s_i + d_i).
] 

 After sorting events by start time, the app finds gaps between these ranges and returns the first gap that can fit a requested duration. That makes suggestions practical rather than merely descriptive. 

 Challenges I faced 

 The hardest challenge was ensuring that AI edits felt trustworthy. An AI must not be a separate, hidden layer that happens to modify data; its changes need to be understandable to the person looking at the plan. I addressed this by routing agent actions through the same shared action layer as user interactions and by giving those actions visible motion and feedback. 

 Calendar layout was another challenge. Events can overlap, have very short durations, recur across dates, or belong in different views. I added collision-aware lanes for simultaneous events and compact card layouts for 15- and 30-minute blocks so the calendar remains readable instead of becoming visually crowded. 

 Finally, browser-native AI integration required careful boundaries. Tool inputs are defined with schemas, calendar updates validate time formats and durations, recurring events require an end date, and free-time calculations distinguish scheduled calendar events from independent inbox tasks. These constraints help the agent make useful changes without creating impossible or ambiguous schedules. 

 What I learned 

 This project taught me that AI features are strongest when they are embedded directly in a familiar workflow. The most valuable interaction is not simply asking an AI for advice; it is seeing that advice become an understandable, reversible action in the tool already being used. 

 I also learned the value of designing state and interaction models before adding intelligence. Because Day Canvas has shared task actions and explicit scheduling rules, the UI and the AI can work together without drifting into separate versions of the truth. Good AI UX depends as much on clear product feedback and reliable state management as it does on the model itself. 

 Where it can go next 

 The current project lays the groundwork for authenticated, persistent planning with Clerk and Supabase. Next steps include resilient offline syncing, per-user timezones, production deployment, and richer scheduling assistance that respects priorities, deadlines, and personal working patterns.

title: ThermalMesh Lab
pitch: Let AI agents understand, benchmark, and optimize heterogeneous inference infrastructure through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Let AI agents understand, benchmark, and optimize heterogeneous inference infrastructure through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP-powered inference routing lab comparing Round Robin with capacity- and load-aware routing on heterogeneous workers Inspiration AI inference infrastructure is increasingly heterogeneous: workers can have very different capacities, yet simple strategies such as Round Robin still treat them as interchangeable. A slow worker can build a large queue while faster capacity remains available elsewhere. At the same time, browser agents often interact with applications indirectly by inspecting interfaces, finding controls, and deciding what to click. For infrastructure software, however, operations like comparing routing policies or inspecting a bottleneck have much richer semantics than the buttons that trigger them. ThermalMesh Lab grew from one question: What if an AI agent could understand and operate inference infrastructure through domain-level tools instead of automating a dashboard by sight? What it does ThermalMesh Lab is a browser-based simulator for heterogeneous AI inference clusters. Users can configure workers with different abstract capacities, generate deterministic workloads, and compare two routing strategies: Round Robin — equal distribution without considering capacity or load. Inference-Aware (ThermalMesh) — a simplified strategy using capacity, load, and estimated completion time. The simulator exposes TTFT, queue latency, throughput, completed and unfinished requests, worker utilization, and queue depth. The same application can also be operated by an AI agent through WebMCP Site Tools. An agent can configure the cluster and workload, run benchmarks, compare policies, inspect bottlenecks, and apply a routing strategy. Humans and agents share the same application state, so every agent action is immediately reflected in the dashboard. ThermalMesh Lab is a browser-based simulation, not a hardware benchmark. How we built it ThermalMesh Lab is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite and runs entirely in the browser. The simulation engine generates a deterministic seeded request trace and gives both routing policies the same workload, making comparisons reproducible. WebMCP is integrated through document.modelContext.registerTool() . The application exposes seven domain-level Site Tools: get_cluster_state configure_cluster configure_workload run_benchmark compare_routing_policies inspect_bottlenecks apply_routing_policy The WebMCP layer does not maintain separate agent state. Site Tools and the visible React interface call the same validated application/store operations. We also implemented a state-dependent tool lifecycle. After a valid comparison, ThermalMesh Lab dynamically exposes an eighth tool: apply_winning_configuration If the cluster or workload changes, the comparison becomes stale and that tool is removed. In the deployed application this creates a live: 7 tools → comparison → 8 tools → scenario change → 7 tools lifecycle driven entirely by application state. The application requires no backend, database, authentication, or paid API and is deployed as a static site on Cloudflare Pages. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making WebMCP a real application interface rather than a collection of tools that simply mimic button clicks. Operations such as compare_routing_policies and inspect_bottlenecks needed to represent actual infrastructure semantics while keeping the human UI and agent perfectly synchronized. Dynamic registration also introduced lifecycle problems. We had to prevent duplicate or stale registrations, ensure tools always operated on current state, and remove the winning-policy tool immediately when its comparison became invalid. The simulator itself required careful handling as well. Both policies needed identical request traces, overloaded scenarios had to remain numerically safe, and unfinished requests could not appear as misleading zero-latency samples. One of our first live agent tests produced an unexpected result: the agent realized its initial workload had completely saturated the cluster, reduced the workload, reran the comparison, and then selected a better routing policy. That showed us both the potential of semantic tools and the importance of precise tool descriptions when working with autonomous agents. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that WebMCP is not an isolated demo layer. The human interface and the AI agent genuinely operate the same application. In live testing, ChatGPT successfully discovered the Site Tools, configured the cluster and workload, compared routing strategies, analyzed the bottleneck, and applied the selected routing policy. The state-dependent lifecycle also works end to end: 7 base tools → comparison → 8 tools → invalidation → 7 tools We are also proud that the simulator does not artificially make Inference-Aware routing win. With homogeneous, lightly loaded workers, both strategies can produce effectively identical results. Under heterogeneous load, differences emerge naturally. In one live test: Round Robin completed 620 requests Inference-Aware routing completed 741 requests TTFT p95 fell from roughly 23.1 seconds to 1.7 seconds Unfinished requests fell from 123 to 2 More importantly, the agent was able to explain why: Round Robin continued sending equal traffic to a much slower worker, creating a large queue, while Inference-Aware routing shifted work toward available capacity. What we learned The biggest lesson was that WebMCP becomes much more powerful when tools represent application semantics rather than UI actions . A tool such as compare_routing_policies gives an agent far more reliable context than asking it to discover controls, run separate simulations, locate the results, and infer how the metrics relate. We also learned that agent capabilities do not need to remain static. Exposing apply_winning_configuration only when a valid comparison exists gives the agent an interface that reflects what the application can meaningfully do at that moment. The simulator taught us another important lesson: overloaded-system benchmarks can be misleading when unfinished work is ignored. A policy may appear to have better median latency simply because its slowest requests never complete inside the observation window. We therefore treat completion and unfinished work as first-class comparison signals rather than hiding them. What's next for ThermalMesh Lab The challenge version intentionally focuses on a small, reliable WebMCP experience. Next, we would like to add additional well-defined routing baselines such as Weighted Round Robin and Least Queue , along with richer workload patterns, request classes, worker failures, and longer-running experiments. ThermalMesh Lab could also evolve into a broader agent-native environment where agents design experiments, compare multiple strategies, explain tradeoffs, and iteratively search for better infrastructure configurations. The broader idea we want to explore is simple: Instead of teaching AI agents how to click through infrastructure software, make infrastructure software directly understandable to agents. title: PageCTRL
pitch: Control what agents do next. The in-page trust and security layer for WebMCP, protecting both merchants and users.
about_excerpt: Control what agents do next. The in-page trust and security layer for WebMCP, protecting both merchants and users. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP lets an AI agent call real functions inside a web page. That is a big step forward, and it creates a new problem. Those calls never leave the browser tab. No firewall sees them. No API gateway sees them. No payment network sees them. Every security tool we have sits outside the page, and the agent is now inside it. So today a shopper has two options. Give the agent everything, or give it nothing. Most people pick nothing. The numbers say the same thing. About 77% of people already use AI to help them shop. About 75% will not let it complete the payment. People want the help. They do not want to hand over the card. That gap is the whole product. We did not want to build another agent. We wanted to build the thing that makes it safe to let one finish the job. What it does PageCTRL is one script tag. It wraps every WebMCP tool on a page and puts a human back in control. It patches document.modelContext.registerTool() at load. Every registered tool then runs inside a guarded pipeline: Validate the arguments against the tool's schema. Apply the policy: allow, ask a human, or deny. Check the rate limit for that tool. Check the quantity cap across the whole cart, not one call. Check the amount cap for a single action. Reserve the spend against the session budget, atomically. Ask the human, and wait. Run the tool under a timeout. Redact personal data from the result. Scan the result for injected instructions. Append the call to a SHA-256 hash-chained journey. The policy has two tiers. The merchant sets a floor in code, and it is locked. The shopper can only make it tighter. A user setting can never loosen a merchant rule. That matters, because the shopper and the merchant do not trust each other, and neither should have to. Payment is real. The shopper saves a card once through Stripe. After that the agent can pay inside the limits, and Stripe charges the card off-session. The page never sees the card number, so no agent tool can read it. The approval itself is signed. When a human clicks Allow, a separate service on a different origin issues an Ed25519 grant bound to that exact order: the amount, the quote, the session, and the origin. The shop server refuses to charge without it. That service runs on infrastructure the merchant does not control, so a rogue script inside the merchant's own page cannot approve its own payment. Two attacks are in the live demo, because both are real: A seller's reply comes back carrying hidden instructions. PageCTRL flags it and tells the agent to treat the text as data, not as commands. A third-party widget loads late and tries to replace the checkout tool. The guard refuses, because the tool surface was sealed when the page loaded. When a block happens, the agent can ask why. It gets the real rule and the real limit back, and the same answer appears on the shopper's screen. Blocking an agent is easy. Blocking it so it can still finish the job is the hard part. How we built it The storefront is Next.js 16 with the App Router, TypeScript, and Tailwind v4, deployed on Vercel. It registers 13 tools and guards 14. The SDK is public/pagecontrol.js . It is plain JavaScript with no dependencies, about 2,000 lines. It has to be, because a merchant should be able to add it to any page with one script tag, and because a build step is one more thing that can go wrong at the trust boundary. The signing service is a small Node server on Render. It holds the Ed25519 private key, publishes the public key as a JWK, checks a bearer token and an origin allowlist, and signs one grant per approval. The domain sits on Cloudflare. We split the deployment on purpose. The shop runs on Vercel with its own Stripe key. The signing key lives somewhere else. If both ran in the same place, the merchant could mint their own approvals, and the signature would prove nothing. Payments use Stripe twice. A hosted Checkout session in setup mode saves the card. A PaymentIntent with off_session: true charges it later, which is the pattern Stripe built for a payment the customer approved and then walked away from. We used Codex for most of the implementation and Claude to plan, review, and run the adversarial passes. Challenges we ran into Serverless has no memory. The first build kept approval state in a JavaScript Map . That works on one machine. On Vercel each request can land on a different instance, so the state vanished. We moved to signed cookies and signed quotes, and stopped assuming a server remembers anything. Two clocks never agree. Grants expire in 60 seconds. Render and Vercel drift apart by a few seconds, and our 5-second tolerance rejected valid approvals. We widened it to 60 seconds, which the short lifetime still bounds. A single space cost an hour. Every checkout failed with grant_mismatch . The signature was valid. The cause was a leading space in an environment variable pasted into a dashboard, so the issuer string never matched. We fixed it by trimming every environment read, and by logging which field mismatched and both values. The log found it in seconds once it existed. Stripe has field limits. Our signed quote ID runs to about 364 characters. Stripe caps an idempotency key at 255. Every charge was rejected before it reached the card. We keyed on the quote's UUID instead. Caps have to count the cart. Our first quantity cap limited one call to five items. The agent added five, then five again. The cap now counts what is already in the cart, so a limit of five means five. The cart kept emptying itself. Loading saved receipts overwrote the basket with an empty one, and that step ran again on every remount. Hydration now carries the live basket forward. Accomplishments that we're proud of Two adversarial security reviews found 16 defects. All 16 are fixed, and each one has a regression test. The guard is real, not a mock. 45 SDK tests and 6 service tests pass, covering native WebMCP, abort signals, approval binding, and call pairing. The payment is a real Stripe charge, not a simulation. The approval is cryptographically bound to one order, and a separate origin signs it. Remove the grant and the server returns 403. We check that. And it works with a real agent. In ChatGPT's browser the badge reads Native, so these are real WebMCP calls, not a simulation of them. What we learned Guardrails are easy to write and hard to place. Every check we first put in the page had to move to the server, because anything an agent can reach, an agent can skip. An error message is part of the product. Our first blocks just said no. The agent then retried the same thing. Explaining the rule and the limit turned a dead end into a next step. Two parties do not trust each other, and a design has to say so out loud. The merchant does not trust the shopper's agent. The shopper does not trust the merchant's page. The two-tier policy and the third-party signature both exist because of that, and neither would exist if we had assumed good faith. What's next for PageCTRL Publish the SDK on npm and a CDN, with Subresource Integrity. Add a <page-control-panel> custom element, so a merchant can place the UI. Ship a hosted merchant console with real keys, usage, and dispute evidence. Support the requestUserInteraction() approval hook when it lands in the WebMCP spec, and drop our own modal in favour of the browser's. Export the hash-chained journey as signed evidence for chargebacks. Extend past shopping. Booking, support actions, and account changes have the same problem and the same shape. title: Blindspot
pitch: A five-minute bomb-defusal game where a human sees the bomb, an AI agent gets seven WebMCP tools, and neither can win alone.
about_excerpt: A five-minute bomb-defusal game where a human sees the bomb, an AI agent gets seven WebMCP tools, and neither can win alone. Like Comment Story Updates The bomb has a blind spot Blindspot is a five-minute cooperative bomb-defusal game built around a capability split. The human can see the bomb: its wire colours, keypad symbols, button markings, casing, and the coloured strip that appears during a hold. The AI agent gets the manual and seven WebMCP tools: two read tools for rules and progress, plus five narrowly scoped actions. Neither side has the complete answer in the intended tool-only run, so they must talk before the timer reaches zero. Why WebMCP is the mechanic, not a checkbox Most agent demos try to expose as much page state as possible. Blindspot asks the opposite question: what should a good tool contract deliberately withhold? get_bomb_status reports the countdown, strikes, module types, and progress, then explicitly lists the visual facts it refuses to return. The action tools can cut, press, hold, and release, but they never reveal the bomb's appearance. This makes least-privilege interface design playable. If one tool leaks a wire colour or keypad symbol, the co-op game collapses because the agent no longer needs its human partner. This is a tool-contract demonstration, not a claim that WebMCP is a browser sandbox. An agent separately granted vision or DOM access could inspect the rendered page. The mission prompt therefore asks the agent to use only Blindspot's WebMCP tools, making the seven contracts the complete interface for the run. The human-agent experience The agent calls get_bomb_status and get_manual . It asks the human for only the visual facts required by a rule. It acts through typed WebMCP calls while both participants watch every call and result appear live. On the button module, the agent holds the button, a strip lights up only in the human view, the human reports its colour, and the agent schedules the correct release digit. A successful run ends in a mission report with time left, strikes, and tool-call count. The page includes a physical bomb-console interface, responsive human and agent views, an enlarged handoff state, opt-in synthesized sound, accessible redundant colour labels, and a replayable deterministic judge seed. Implementation Blindspot is intentionally small: vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with no runtime dependencies or build step. src/tools.js declares the seven real contracts and registers each one with document.modelContext ?? navigator.modelContext , including name , description , JSON inputSchema , annotations, and execute . The same instrumented handlers update the live call feed. A fallback console is generated from those schemas only when native WebMCP is unavailable. Native sessions keep the executable controls with the connected agent. The public repo includes an MIT license, complete run instructions, a deterministic judge walkthrough, and 26 headless checks. The suite covers rules, clock throttling, all seven registration descriptors, partial registration reporting, hostile call-feed input, audio opt-in, schema-driven fallback accessibility, and bomb-appearance leak probes across fresh seeded games. GitHub Actions runs the suite and syntax checks on every push. Verified live I tested the production deployment in ChatGPT's in-app browser. It registered all seven tools from the production origin, completed the deterministic bomb through native WebMCP, and ended DEFUSED with zero strikes.
